stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner as she is due to ﬂy to Australia and has been reading in the newspapers about ‘travellers’ thrombosis’ and ‘economy class syndrome’. She is not currently on any medication, except for the combined oral contraceptive pill; she has a past medical history of ﬁbromyalgia and irritable bowel syndrome, smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks 20 units of alcohol per week. She had a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) when she was 32. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: Regular ankle and calf exercises only
explanation:
E Class 1 compression stockings There has recently been considerable interest in the risk of blood clots triggered by air ﬂights. A study from North America indicated that the risk of a fatal blood clot after a transatlantic ﬂight is < 1

in a million. Additional studies indicated that the greatest risk of a blood clot is when there are additional risk factors such as surgery in the previous few weeks. The risk is related to the duration of travel, with the lowest risk for journeys of < 6 hours. This particular patient has a moderate risk for deep vein thrombosis (DVT), as she had a DVT in the past. She is also on an oral contraceptive and smokes cigarettes, both of which increase her risk from low to moderate. A Aspirin Aspirin is not recommended as venous thromboembolism (VTE) treatment or prophylaxis. There is controversial evidence available for the use of aspirin in VTE prevention. There have been a few studies that showed it is not inferior to low-molecular-weight heparin in postoperative orthopaedic patients. In the case of this patient, however, she is at moderate risk and therefore, drug treatment is not recommended. B Class 2 graduated compression stockings Class 1 stockings are sufﬁcient for VTE prophylaxis for patients with moderate risk. Class 2 stockings are used for patients with varicose veins, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche or healed venous leg ulcers. C Class 3 graduated compression stockings If the patient’s condition (including varicose veins, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche and healed venous leg ulcers) does not respond to class 2 stockings, they are escalated to class 3 stockings. In this patient, there is no indication for class 2 or 3 stockings. D Regular ankle and calf exercises only This is recommended for patients who are low risk. This patient is at moderate risk and is recommended to do the ankle and calf exercises regularly, as well as wearing graduated compression stockings. Calf and ankle exercises should be undertaken by all people travelling on long-haul ﬂights, in addition to other recommendations by their medical doctor.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is referred from her GP complaining of menorrhagia and easy bruising. Her older sister also has menorrhagia and frequent nose bleeds.
explanation:
E Von Willebrand’s disease (vWD) Von Willebrand’s disease is a common, inherited, genetically and clinically heterogeneous haemorrhagic disorder caused by a deﬁciency or dysfunction of the protein termed von Willebrand factor (vWF). This is a large, multimeric glycoprotein which functions as the carrier protein for factor VIII, by binding to and stabilizing this factor, and it also mediates the adhesion of platelets to sites of vascular injury. The VWF gene is located near the tip of the short arm of chromosome 12. vWD is divided into three major categories: (1) partial quantitative deﬁciency (type I), (2) qualitative deﬁciency (type II), and (3) total deﬁciency (type III). Males and females are affected equally although the disease manifestations are more obvious in the female due to menstruation and the associated menorrhagia. The screening test used to diagnose the condition includes PT, aPTT (aPTT), factor VIII activity, vWF activity (ristocetin cofactor) and vWF antigen level determination. Ristocetin is an antibiotic that causes vWF to bind to and activate platelets. Platelets rapidly agglutinate in response to ristocetin, but the presence of plasma vWF is necessary for this reaction to occur. The PT is within the reference range, but the aPTT is mildly prolonged in half of these patients. The degree of platelet agglutination is proportional

to the concentration of vWF in the plasma. This is called the vWF activity or ristocetin cofactor assay, and is variably reduced in patients with vWD. A Haemophilia A In this X-linked recessive condition, PT is normal and APTT will either be severely prolonged in severe haemophilia A or normal/mildly prolonged in less severe case. It only occurs in males. B Factor V deﬁciency This is a prothrombotic condition resulting from the mutation of factor V. There is a decreased activated protein C ratio with this condition. C Christmas disease Also known as haemophilia , this is a genetic mutation of factor IX and would show normal levels of von Willebrand’s factor, normal PT and normal or slightly prolonged APTT. There would be very low or absent levels of factor IX. It also is X-linked and occurs in males. D Antiphospholipid syndrome This is a prothrombotic condition and is diagnosed by lupus anticoagulant present on two tests more than 12 weeks apart, anticardiolipin antibody presence, and the presence of anti-2-betaglycoprotein I. APTT maybe prolonged due to positive lupus anticoagulant.

stem: A 72-year-old patient is treated with warfarin for a prosthetic aortic valve. He has completed a 5-day course of oral clarithromycin for a sinus infection, and he is attending for an INR check. There is no increase in bruising or bleeding from mucus membranes. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 125 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 129 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l INR 6.8 0–1.1 Which of the following is the most appropriate management with respect to his INR?
options: Stop warfarin and review INR in 24 hours
explanation: A Stop warfarin and review INR in 24 hours This man has an artiﬁcial valve and, as such, must maintain his INR around 3.0. He is not actively bleeding and therefore the most appropriate management is to allow his INR to drift down slowly over the next few days. Given that over-reversal of anticoagulation may be associated with signiﬁcant embolic risk, dose omission in the absence of active bleeding is the safest option. C Give fresh frozen plasma (FFP) FFP or other warfarin reversal agents, such as prothrombin complex concentrate, should only be considered when there is lifethreatening haemorrhage or surgery is urgently required. B Give 10 mg IV vitamin K This risks over-reversal of the elevated INR and arterial embolism related to the prosthetic aortic valve. D Give prothrombin complex concentrate PCC is considered when patients who have been taking warfarin need to progress urgently to surgery or have life-threatening haemorrhage. E Give dextran sulphate Dextran sulphate is the reversal agent for over-heparinisation, and is not of value in treating excessive warfarinisation.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with breathlessness and chest pain, developing over a week. Examination shows a pale, jaundiced patient in some distress, pulse 110 beats per minute (bpm) and third heart sound audible with jugular venous pressure raised. Widespread crackles are audible throughout the chest. There is a 3 cm spleen palpable. An electrocardiogram shows widespread depression of ST segments. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 49 g/l 135 - 175 g/l MCV 105 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ Coombs’ test Bilirubin IgG+ 45 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l LDH 1157 u/l 140 - 280 u/l How would you best interpret these tests?
options: Raised MCV is probably due to reticulocytosis
Urine examination for haemosiderin is likely to be positive
Haemolysis cannot be conﬁdently ruled out unless the result of a haptoglobin assay is available
Raised LDH is most likely to be cardiac in origin
If haemolysis is truly present then close to 100% of bilirubin will be unconjugated
explanation:
A Raised MCV is probably due to reticulocytosis This patient has haemolytic anaemia (the IgG antibodies cause warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, i.e. the antibody is active at body temperature). Transfusion can be life-saving until immuno-

suppression can take effect. The bone marrow responds by increasing red cell production; this is in evidence in the peripheral blood by an increase in reticulocytes – immature red blood cells, which have a larger MCV. All patients with active haemolysis are at risk of acquiring folate deﬁciency due to increased metabolic demands, and all should receive replacement therapy. D Raised LDH is most likely to be cardiac in origin LDH is increased in haemolysis, although in this patient it would be prudent to exclude a cardiac cause. It is most likely to be due to haemolysis, with the ischaemic picture on ECG being related to anaemia. B Urine examination for haemosiderin is likely to be positive The haemolysis occurs extravascularly (e.g. in the liver and spleen), so measures of intravascular haemolysis (haemoglobinaemia/haemoglobinuria/ urinary haemosiderin) will be negative. C Haemolysis cannot be conﬁdently ruled out unless the result of a haptoglobin assay is available The haptoglobins are not a speciﬁc marker for haemolysis since these can be decreased or absent in other conditions as well (e.g. genetics, cirrhosis, infancy, pregnancy, burns). E If haemolysis is truly present then close to 100% of bilirubin will be unconjugated In haemolytic anaemia there is an excess of unconjugated bilirubin in the blood; because the unconjugated bilirubin is not water soluble, one will not see an increase in bilirubin in the urine. Since there is no problem with the liver or bile systems, this excess unconjugated bilirubin will go through all of the normal processing mechanisms that occur (i.e. conjugation, excretion in bile, metabolism to urobilinogen, reabsorption) and will show up as an increase in urine urobilinogen.

stem: A 67-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of weakness and lethargy with generalized bony aches and pains over the past few months. She saw the general practitioner (GP) some three months earlier because of an episode of pneumococcal pneumonia. On examination, she looks pale and tired. Her blood pressure (BP) is 135/80 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. There are no speciﬁc ﬁndings on cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 108 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 9.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelet (PLT) 162 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 182 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Albumin 23 g/l Immunoglobulin electrophoresis IgG paraprotein band 24 hour urinary protein 3.2 g Bone marrow 30% plasma cells Which of the following is the most useful test with respect to establishing prognosis?
explanation: B Beta-2 microglobulin Beta-2 microglobulin is a very useful surrogate marker for the overall myeloma disease burden. Additionally, levels of beta-2 microglobulin are elevated in chronic kidney disease and hence measurement provides a useful integrated measure of the degree of renal dysfunction and myeloma burden. In a series of 148 patients, beta-2- microglobulin > 2.5 mg/l was associated with a 5-year risk of disease progression of 64%. C CRP CRP is not a strong prognostic indicator in patients with myeloma. It is primarily a marker of systemic inﬂammation. A Haemoglobin Although haemoglobin is associated with poor prognosis in a univariate analysis, at is an Hb level < 100 g/l that drives a poor prognostic outcome. D Albumin Serum albumin < 30 g/l is a poor prognostic indicator in myeloma, because it is an indicator of signiﬁcant proteinuria and nutritional status, although it’s a less speciﬁc marker of disease burden than beta-2 microglobulin. E Platelet count Platelet count < 150 is associated with poor prognostic outcome in patients with myeloma. Hypercalcaemia, serum creatinine elevation and performance status are other markers of poor prognosis in multiple myeloma.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Department with an 18 h history of a severe headache, right-sided hemiparesis and new-onset grand mal seizures. She denied taking any medication or recreational drugs. She had a temperature of 37.6 °C, pulse 120 bpm, sinus rhythm and a blood pressure of 110/80 mmHg. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 64 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 10.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 10.0 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l International normalized ratio (INR) 1.3 < 1.1 Activated partial thromboplastin clotting time (APTT) 26 s 25 - 35 s Creatinine (Cr) 150 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urea 10.0 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Bilirubin 90 μmol/l 1 - 22 μmol/l Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 21 u/l 10 - 40 u/l Alanine aminotransferase (ALT 25 u/l 7 - 55 u/l LDH 3200 u/l 140 - 280 u/l What is the most likely unifying diagnosis?
explanation:
C Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a life-threatening multi-system disorder characterised by micro- angiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever and renal dysfunction. With the introduction of plasma exchange, the survival rate has

improved from approximately 3% prior to the 1960s to 82% now. Platelet transfusions are contraindicated. Fresh-frozen plasma, methylprednisolone and red cell support are all important additional supportive measures. A Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), also known as primary immune thrombocytopenic purpura and autoimmune thrombocytopenic purpura, is deﬁned as isolated thrombocytopenia with normal bone marrow in the absence of other causes of thrombocytopenia. B Disseminated intravascular coagulation Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a complex systemic thrombo-haemorrhagic disorder involving the generation of intravascular ﬁbrin and the consumption of procoagulants and platelets. It is seen in association with a number of well-deﬁned clinical situations, including sepsis, major trauma and abruptio placenta. It is associated with prolonged clotting times, low ﬁbrinogen, raised ﬁbrin degradation products and thrombocytopenia. D Haemolytic uraemic syndrome Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is characterised by acute kidney disease, micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia, fever and thrombocytopenia. Diarrhoea and upper respiratory infection are the most common precipitating factors. It is caused by strains of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, especially E. coli O157:H7 carrying the Shigalike toxin. E Cocaine abuse Cocaine is a complex drug that can cause lethal cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and ventricular arrhythmias. The exact mechanism of cocaine-related stroke remains unclear, and there are likely to be a number of factors involved. There does not appear to be any direct neurotoxic action, and potential mechanisms involved in cocaine induced stroke include vasospasm, cerebral vasculitis, enhanced platelet aggregation, cardio-embolism and hypertensive surges associated with altered cerebral autoregulation and cerebral blood ﬂow. Cocaine use is associated with both intracerebral haemorrhage and subarachnoid haemorrhage. As with ischaemic stroke, the exact mechanism involved is not fully understood, though mayinvolve cocaineinduced haemodynamic changes in susceptible individuals.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the Acute Medical Unit with symptomatic anaemia, requiring a blood transfusion. Ten minutes after the transfusion is started, the emergency bell is called as the nurses fear that he is having a reaction to the transfusion. On arrival, the patient complained of feeling faint and breathless. Examination shows an unwell, pale and clammy patient with a heart rate of 120 bpm, BP is 70 mmHg systolic, respiratory rate of 35 breaths per minute, temperature of 38.9 °C and GCS score 13/15. The patient’s blood group is group A rhesus-negative; the blood transfusion is group O rhesus-negative. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s deterioration?
options: Acute intravascular haemolysis due to inappropriate ABO crossmatching
Acute transfusion reaction due to donor cytokines
Bacterial contamination of the unit of blood
explanation:
D Bacterial contamination of the unit of blood Bacterial contamination is a possibility, although this is very rare with red cell transfusions and more common with platelet transfusions (which are stored at room temperature). However, if such contaminated blood is stored for a few days at room temperature (eg platelets) or for a few weeks at refrigerated temperature (eg red cells), bacteria may grow and elaborate endotoxin, which is a major adverse factor in such reactions and drives the acute presentation seen here. C Anaphylactic reaction to blood products Anaphylaxis to blood products should always be considered for patients presenting with an acute reaction, particularly if tachycardic and hypotensive, with difﬁculty in breathing. However, an anaphylactic reaction is normally an immediate process and is less likely to be seen associated with a fever. For this reason, contaminated blood products are more likely. A Acute intravascular haemolysis due to inappropriate ABO crossmatching Immunoglobulin M anti-A and anti-B antibodies cause acute haemolytic transfusion reactions, and as little as 4 ml of transfused ABO-incompatible blood can be fatal. The labelling of the blood as O rhesus-negative means that an acute transfusion reaction should not be seen. B Acute transfusion reaction due to donor cytokines When patients donate blood at the time of viral infection, increased levels of inﬂammatory cytokines may be present in the donated unit. These usually cause mild pyrexia rather than the acute symptoms seen here.

E Transfusion-related acute lung injury Transfusion-related acute lung injury is associated with acuteonset non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. It is thought to be related to donor antibodies to human leukocyte antigens, which drive neutrophil activation. The features seen here are inconsistent with non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema where inﬁltration of the lung ﬁelds would be expected.

stem: A 50-year-old white man is referred by his general practitioner (GP) with cellulitis of his right leg that has been difﬁcult to treat with oral antibiotics. The patient has been experiencing increased fatigue and breathlessness. He drinks a glass of wine at the weekends and is a non-smoker. Apart from childhood asthma, he is well and on no regular medication. On examination: Pale conjunctivae and multiple bruises over all four limbs. There is hepatosplenomegaly and cellulitis of the right leg. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 82 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 3.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 95 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 83 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Bone marrow aspirate Dry tap Bone marrow biopsy Cells with a ‘fried egg’ appearance Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase stain (TRAP) strongly positive What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Hairy cell leukaemia Hairy cell leukaemia is a β-lymphocyte disorder. The abnormal cell has hair-like cytoplasmic projections. Inﬁltration of the bone marrow leads to pancytopenia and patients have hepatosplenomegaly. The abnormal cells are strongly positive for tartrateresistant acid phosphatase stain (TRAP). Inﬁltration of the bone marrow leads to a dry tap on attempted aspiration, and a bone marrow biopsy reveals cells that are said to have the characteristic ‘fried egg’ appearance. Purine analogues and interferon have been used for treatment, and occasionally splenectomy has been required. Stains: • TRAP: tends to be positive in hairy cell leukaemia • Sudan black B stain and myeloperoxidase: tends to be positive in acute myeloblastic leukaemia • Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase stain (TDT): tends to be positive in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia • LAP: tends to be raised in polycythemia rubra vera and myeloﬁbrosis; tends to be low in chronic myeloid leukaemia. A Chronic myeloid leukaemia CML is a myeloproliferative disorder characterised by the proliferation of the precursors for white blood cells, but these precursors retain the ability to differentiate. Symptoms tend to be chronic and the blood proﬁle shows an increased (++) white cell count, with a low or normal haemoglobin and a variable platelet count. C Myelodysplasia Myelodysplasia occurs mainly in the elderly and presents with anaemia, infection or bleeding due to pancytopenia. Serial blood counts show evidence of increasing bone marrow failure and the bone marrow shows increased cellularity. Patients with <5% blasts in the bone marrow are managed conservatively, ‘gentle’ chemotherapy is used in patients with high white blood cell counts and intensive chemotherapy is usually reserved for patients under the age of 60 years. Transformation into AML occurs in around 30% of patients. Bone marrow biopsy revealing cells that are said to have the characteristic ‘fried egg’ appearance is characteristic of hairy cell leukaemia. D Myeloﬁbrosis Primary myeloﬁbrosis (PMF) is one of the chronic myeloproliferative disorders, which are collectively characterised by clonal proliferation of myeloid cells with variable morphologic maturity and haematopoietic efﬁciency. Splenomegaly is a marked feature. Bone marrow biopsy is necessary to demonstrate ﬁbrosis. Some degree of ﬁbrosis is seen in almost all patients; the ﬁbrosis is typically extensive and visualised better with a silver stain (reticulin) or a trichrome stain (mature collagen). Bone marrow sinusoids are

expanded and there is intravascular haematopoiesis. The ﬁbrosis is generally associated with atypical megakaryocytic hyperplasia, and thickening and distortion of the bony trabeculae (osteosclerosis). E Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia The most noteworthy laboratory abnormality found in CLL is lymphocytosis in the peripheral blood and bone marrow. Although the absolute blood lymphocyte threshold for diagnosing CLL has been placed at >5000/microl (5 × 109/l) B lymphocytes, a signiﬁcant proportion of patients presents with counts as high as 100,000/microl (100 × 109/l). The peripheral blood smear of patients with CLL demonstrates a lymphocytosis. The leukemic cells are typically small, mature-appearing lymphocytes with a dense nucleus, partially aggregated (clumped) chromatin and lacking discernible nucleoli. There is a narrow border of clear to slightly basophilic cytoplasm. The blood ﬁlm in this scenario is not that of CLL. Bone marrow biopsy revealing cells that are said to have the characteristic ‘fried egg’ appearance’ is characteristic of hairy cell leukaemia, and therefore CLL is an incorrect option.

stem: A 57-year-old man is referred to hospital by his General Practitioner (GP). Previously well, he gives a history of progressive weakness and breathlessness on exertion over a two week period. He is also complaining of symptoms of indigestion. On examination, he is pale and tachycardic. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. His heart sounds are normal and his chest is clear. He brings along with him results of blood tests conducted by the GP: Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 83 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.2 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l PLT 410 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l MCV 69 fl 80–100 fl Peripheral smear RBCs hypochromic and microcytic, target cells +, pencil cells +, WBC and platelet morphology normal Which one of the following would you consider the most useful test to measure?
options: Serum iron and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)
Hb electrophoresis and Hb H preparation
explanation:
B Serum ferritin This patient is most likely to have iron-deﬁciency anaemia due to gastrointestinal blood loss. Hypo-ferritinaemia conﬁrms iron deﬁciency and is the preferred screening test. Ferritin levels may

be falsely elevated in acute inﬂammatory states (ferritin is an acute-phase reactant). Stool for occult blood is a relatively insensitive test of gastrointestinal bleeding. Malabsorption, hookworm infestation and chronic haematuria may also result in iron deﬁciency. Other causes of microcytosis include haemoglobinopathy (in certain ethnic groups), anaemia of chronic disease (normal/high ferritin levels), lead poisoning (check urine and blood lead levels) and myelodysplastic syndromes with ringed sideroblasts. A Serum iron and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) In order to properly understand a value for TIBC, one also must know the serum iron, the percentage transferrin saturation and the individual clinical situation. In modern laboratory testing, serum ferritin levels are generally accepted as reliable single indicators of the presence of iron deﬁciency. C Blood lead level Acute lead poisoning can cause anaemia through haemolysis, accompanied by haemoglobinuria. There is no evidence in this scenario which would support this diagnosis. Symptoms in chronic lead poisoning usually occur with blood levels greater than 50 μg/dl. D Hb electrophoresis and Hb H preparation Haemoglobinopathy is one cause of microcytosis, but it is not the commonest and it is usually discovered earlier in life. E Liver function tests There is no evidence of liver disease from the history and clinical examination, and therefore liver function testing would not be essential for the diagnosis.

stem: A 43-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of fever and lethargy. He had ﬁnished a third cycle of chemotherapy for osteosarcoma only a few days earlier and he has an indwelling central venous catheter. On examination, he looks unwell. He has a fever of 38.9 °C and his BP is 90/60 mmHg, with a heart rate of 95 bpm and regular. There are no signs of pharyngitis and only minor erythema around the exit site for his catheter. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 104 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Neutrophils 0.2 x 109/l 2.5–7.58 x 109/l Platelets 125 x 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 122 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 174 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Alkaline phosphatase 392 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 26 g/l 35–55 g/l Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
explanation:
B Piperacillin/tazobactam This patient has febrile neutropenia, having recently completed a course of chemotherapy, and has an indwelling vascular catheter. Hence a broad-spectrum antibacterial regimen, including adequate staphylococcal and pseudomonal cover, is recommended. Therapy is not delayed while awaiting sample results, and antifungal therapy is usually considered later if non-response to therapy is seen. The rise in alkaline phosphatase levels seen here may be due to hepatic dysfunction or related to the underlying bony tumour. Guidelines

from the NICE recommend the use of monotherapy with piperacillin and tazobactam as the ﬁrst line. Additional agents can be added later, depending on culture sensitivities and local protocols. C Piperacillin/tazobactam and gentamicin The NICE guidelines recommend avoiding the use of aminoglycosides (such as gentamicin) as monotherapy or dual therapy with piperacillin/tazobactam for treatment of neutropenic sepsis, unless there are speciﬁc microbiological indications. A Gentamicin, vancomycin, ﬂucloxacillin Piperacillin/tazobactam is the cornerstone of therapy, according to the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines. Therefore, the combination of gentamicin, vancomycin and ﬂucloxacillin is inappropriate. D Piperacillin/tazobactam and gentamicin and ﬂuconazole Guidelines from the NICE recommend monotherapy with piperacillin/tazobactam for the treatment of neutropenic sepsis. Dual therapy with gentamicin is not recommended, unless microbiology dictates. In practice, antifungals are introduced in the event that a response to therapy is not seen at 48 hours, but not in the initial stages. E Piperacillin/tazobactam and vancomycin Vancomycin is not indicated in the initial management of neutropenic sepsis, unless methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is suspected. Piperacillin/tazobactam is recommended as monotherapy initially.

stem: An 18-year-old single man is referred who suffers recurrent oesophageal candidiasis. He has a background medical history of asthma treated with inhaled steroids and eczema. Labs show no B cells and reduced immunoglobulins, CD4 Tlymphocyte count is normal and platelet count is reduced. What diagnosis ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
E Primary immunodeﬁciency Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked disorder associated with eczema and thrombocytopenia, associated with reduced levels of immunoglobulins. Patients often suffer from associated autoimmune disorders and are at increased risk of lymphoreticular malignancy. A Chronic myeloid leukaemia CML has a tri- or biphasic clinical course: a chronic phase, which is present at the time of diagnosis in approximately 85% of patients; an accelerated phase, in which neutrophil differentiation becomes progressively impaired and leukocyte counts are more difﬁcult to control with treatment; and blast crisis, a condition resembling acute leukaemia in which myeloid or lymphoid blasts proliferate in an uncontrolled manner. The peripheral smear typically demonstrates a leukocytosis with a median white count of approximately 10 × 109 mmol/l. The WBC differential typically shows virtually all cells of the neutrophilic series, from myeloblasts to mature neutrophils with peaks in the percentages of myelocytes and segmented neutrophils. Blasts typically account for <2%. The presence of a greater percentage of myelocytes than the more mature metamyelocytes (‘leukemic hiatus’ or ‘myelocyte bulge’) is one of the classic ﬁndings in CML. The granulocytes of the chronic phase are morphologically normal with no evidence of dysplasia, but dysplasia can develop in more advanced disease, and particularly in the accelerated phase. The blood picture in this scenario is not consistent with CML.

B HIV infection The normal CD4 count makes AIDS less likely as the cause in this case. C Inappropriate inhaler use Inappropriate inhaler use will not provide an explanation for the blood picture here. D Infectious mononucleosis Infectious mononucleosis (IM) is characterised by a triad of fever, tonsillar pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy. The most common laboratory ﬁnding in association with infectious mononucleosis (IM) is lymphocytosis, deﬁned as an absolute count >4500/microl or, on peripheral smear, a differential count >50%. The smear may also identify signiﬁcant atypical lymphocytosis, deﬁned as >10% of total lymphocytes. The majority of reactive lymphocytes in patients with IM are CD8+ cytotoxic T cells. In one study, the severity of illness correlated with the magnitude of CD8+ lymphocytosis (as well as with blood Epstein–Barr viral (EBV) load). The blood picture in this scenario is not consistent with IM.

stem: A 78-year-old man presents with sudden deterioration of vision in his left eye, with no eye pain. There are ﬂame haemorrhages in one quadrant on retinal examination. He has a history of hypertension and is awaiting investigations for anaemia; recent haemoglobin is 105 g/l. What diagnosis ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
A Branch retinal vein occlusion Patients often complain of a sudden painless decrease of vision in the affected eye. Some patients may complain of a scotoma. The affected area of the retina has ﬂame shaped haemorrhages. Risk factors for retinal vein occlusion include systemic hypertension, hypertriglyceridaemia and hyperviscosity syndromes. Some inﬂammatory (e.g. sarcoidosis) and thrombophilic conditions (e.g. SLE) may also be involved. Management involves screening for risk factors and anticoagulation. Further management depends on which underlying condition has been identiﬁed. C Central retinal vein occlusion Patients can be either asymptomatic or present with decreased vision, photophobia and painful or red eyes. Fundoscopy shows tortuosity and dilatation of all branches of the central retinal vein, dot/blot and ﬂame- shaped hemorrhages, throughout all four quadrants and most numerous in the periphery, and optic disc and macular oedema. This tends to be more severe in ischaemic CRVO than non-ischaemic CRVO. B Branch retinal artery occlusion This is usually embolic in aetiology. Patients with branch retinal artery occlusion typically present with acute, unilateral, painless, partial visual loss. The affected area of the retina is usually more pale, with a relative absence of vasculature. Visual ﬁeld defects may be central or sectoral. Patients may also be asymptomatic. Risk factors include smoking, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes, coronary artery disease and history of stroke or tran-

sient ischemic attack. D Central retinal artery occlusion This is embolic in aetiology. The most common presenting complaint is an acute, persistent, painless loss of vision in the range of counting ﬁngers to light perception in 90% of patients. Early in the course, the fundus may appear normal. The classic ﬁndings of retinal whitening and a cherry red spot are due to opaciﬁcation of the nerve ﬁbre layer as it becomes oedematous from ischeamia. The fovea is cherry red because it has no overlying nerve ﬁbre layer. This ﬁnding may take hours to develop, and the oedema is associated with a worse visual prognosis. Over the course of about a month, the inner retina becomes atrophic as the swelling resolves E CMV retinitis Presenting symptoms vary depending on the location of retinal involvement. Posterior lesions present with diminished visual acuity. More peripheral lesions initially can be asymptomatic. Floaters often are noted if signiﬁcant vitreitis is present. The eye usually is white and quiet. In immunocompromised individuals, CMV most commonly presents as a viral necrotising retinitis with a characteristic ophthalmoscopic appearance.

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents to the Ambulatory Care Clinic with right calf swelling for the past 8 days. She has had no recent surgery, immobility or long-haul ﬂights. She has a past medical history of chronic osteoarthritic back pain but nil else of note. She smokes ten cigarettes per day and drinks ﬁve units of alcohol per week. Her body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m2 and she reports having lost around 5 kg in weight over the past few months. On examination, she has whole leg swelling of the right leg, with pitting oedema and tenderness on deep palpation. There are reduced breath sounds bilaterally at the lung bases on chest examination. Abdominal and cardiovascular examinations are unremarkable. Her heart rate is 85 bpm, blood pressure is 142/75 mmHg, respiratory rate is 19 breaths per minute and oxygen saturations 96% on room air. She is started on interim therapeutic anticoagulation and an ultrasound (US) scan of the proximal right leg venous system reveals a right leg deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the common femoral vein. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 128 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.7 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 178 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 5 µmol/l 3–17 µmol/l ALT 10 U/l 5–35 U/l ALP 120 IU/l 30–150 IU/l Albumin 33 g/l 35–50 g/l PT 14 s 10.6–14.9 s PTT 29 s 23.0–35.0 s What is the next step in management for this patient?
options: Complete cancer screening and thrombophilia testing, then switch to oral anticoagulation for three months
Complete cancer screening, including faecal immunochemical test (FIT), tumour markers and computed tomography of chest, abdomen and pelvis if positive
Complete detailed history and examination, chest Xray and electrocardiogram (ECG)
Switch to oral anticoagulation for three months and complete thrombophilia testing
Switch to oral anticoagulation for three months and discharge
explanation:
C Complete detailed history and examination, chest Xray and electrocardiogram (ECG) The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines for the management of unprovoked deep vein thrombosis (DVT) recommend investigation for cancer. This patient’s smoking history and recent weight loss point to a possible malignancy as the provoking factor for her DVT. The NICE guidelines recommend that in the ﬁrst instance, investigation for cancer should consist of: a detailed review of the patient’s history; baseline blood tests, including full blood count, renal and hepatic function, prothrombin test and aPTT; and physical examination. Further investigation for cancer should only be offered for people with unprovoked DVT if they have relevant clinical symptoms or signs. Therefore, this would be the correct next best step in management, as it will allow thorough history and examination and further detailed investigation based on current examination ﬁndings – bilateral reduced air entry at the lung bases on chest examination and possible new atrial ﬁbrillation on rhythm check of the

patient’s heart rate. A Complete cancer screening and thrombophilia testing, then switch to oral anticoagulation for three months The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines advise that general cancer screening for multiple malignancies is not recommended, and thrombophilia screening should not be completed unless the patient is due to stop anticoagulation in the case of an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis (DVT). B Complete cancer screening, including faecal immunochemical test (FIT), tumour markers and computed tomography of chest, abdomen and pelvis if positive The NICE guidelines do not recommend further investigation for cancer in people with unprovoked DVT unless they have relevant clinical symptoms and signs. Therefore, ordering a whole host of investigations for multiple cancer types is not recommended, nor is it good practice. It will cause a signiﬁcant burden to the patient and may produce false positives which may cause distress for the patient. D Switch to oral anticoagulation for three months and complete thrombophilia testing The NICE guidelines recommend that thrombophilia testing should be offered if there is a plan to stop anticoagulation treatment in patients with unprovoked DVT. It should not be offered to patients who are continuing anticoagulation treatment. Furthermore, this patient has already received interim therapeutic anticoagulation for the DVT which has caused a deranged partial thromboplastin time (likely due to the use of low-molecularweight heparin) and this will also affect thrombophilia testing. E Switch to oral anticoagulation for three months and discharge This would be the treatment course for a patient with a provoked DVT. A provoked DVT is deﬁned as a DVT associated with a transient risk factor, eg signiﬁcant immobility, surgery, trauma or pregnancy. Hormonal treatment is also considered a provoking factor and, in many circumstances, this can be removed. As this patient has none of these risk factors, this is an unprovoked DVT and therefore, management is different.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with a 20 year history of rheumatoid arthritis comes to the clinic for review. She had a recent minor trip off a curb stone, yet suffered a very severe haemoarthrosis affecting her left knee. Current medication includes Methotrexate only for her rheumatoid. On examination in the clinic her BP is 135/75 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. She has evidence of active rheumatoid disease and has a wool and crepe bandage protecting her left knee. Investigations; Hb 120 g/l WCC 8.1 x10 /l PLT 181 x10 /l Na 138 mmol/l K 4.4 mmol/l Creatinine 115 micromol/l PT 12.1 s APTT 58.2 s (fails to correct with normal plasma) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Acquired factor VIII inhibition The answer is Acquired factor VIII inhibition - Acquired factor VIII inhibition is associated with increased risk of bleeding and is closely associated with autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis and inﬂammatory bowel disease. The fact that the APTT fails to correct with normal plasma is highly suggestive of the presence of an antibody inhibitor. More aggressive treatment of her underlying rheumatoid disease is also likely to reduce the titre of any underlying factor VIII inhibitor. High dose factor VIII replacement can reduce the risk of bleeding episodes whilst treatment for her rheumatoid is escalated. C Haemophilia A Haemophilia A is incorrect, it is likely to present before the age of 54 with bleeding episodes, and prolonged APTT would correct with normal plasma. B Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome is incorrect, it is associated with prolonged APTT, but is associated with venous thrombosis rather than bleeding episodes. D Haemophilia B Haemophilia B is incorrect, it is likely to present before the age of 54, and like haemophilia A, prolonged APTT would correct with normal plasma. E Von Willebrand’s disease Von Willebrand’s disease is incorrect because similar to Haemophilia A and B, although it presents with prolonged APTT in 50% of cases, it is highly likely to present for the 1st time well before the age of 54.

stem: A 74-year-old man is admitted to the Stroke Unit, having suffered symptoms of a right-sided anterior territory ischaemic stroke. According to his wife, he has been suffering from increasing headaches and itchy skin, particularly when he was getting out of a bath or shower, during the course of the last few months. Apart from this, he has a history of hypertension, for which he takes two agents, and mild asthma treated with a salbutamol inhaler. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 188/100 mmHg, and his pulse is 90 bpm and regular. There is weakness of the right-hand side of his face and his right arm. He has signiﬁcant dysphasia. You note he has raised haemoglobin of 192g/l. Which of the following features would contribute the most towards conﬁrming a diagnosis of primary polycythaemia according to WHO criteria?
explanation:
A Erythropoeitin (EPO) below the normal range EPO level is one of the minor criteria to conﬁrm a diagnosis of primary polycythaemia. Major and minor criteria for diagnosis of primary polycythaemia are listed below: Major criteria: • Haemoglobin of > 165 g/l in men or haematocrit >49% and 160 g/l in women or haematocrit >48%, or elevated red cell mass > 25% above the mean normal predicted value • Bone marrow biopsy showing hypercellularity with prominent erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic proliferation • Presence of JAK2 617V>F mutation or other functionally similar mutations, such as the exon 12 • mutation of JAK2. Minor criteria: • Serum EPO level below the normal range WHO diagnostic criteria mandate three major criteria or the ﬁrst two major criteria and the minor criterion, are required to conﬁrm the diagnosis, because the JAK2 mutation is not always present in primary polycythaemia. D Splenomegaly Splenomegaly is a non-speciﬁc sign of haematological malignancy. It cannot therefore be used to rule in or rule out underlying primary polycythaemia. B Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) > 100 units LAP scores are relatively non-speciﬁc with respect to identifying primary polycythaemia, compared to other haematological malignancies, and are therefore no longer a part of the criteria for conﬁrming the diagnosis. C Platelet count > 400 × 109/l Platelet count may not always be above 400 in patients with primary polycythaemia, sometimes due to blood loss and platelet dys-

function. Hence, it cannot be relied upon as a diagnostic criterion. E White blood cell count > 12 × 109/l White cell count may be elevated because of infection or other haematological conditions outside primary polycythaemia. It cannot therefore be relied upon to make the diagnosis. Oxygen saturation of > 92% is another criterion which is no longer utilised in making the diagnosis.

stem: A 60-year-old man returns to the general practitioner (GP) to discuss his blood test results. He was initially investigated for peripheral neuropathy which was ultimately attributed to B12 deﬁciency and treated successfully. He has no complaints of note. His initial blood tests included a raised immunoglobulin G (IgG) level and his General Practitioner has taken the opportunity to repeat these, as below. Past medical history of note includes hypertension, which is managed with ramipril. Clinical examination reveals a blood pressure (BP) of 142/78 mmHg. Otherwise, there are no other abnormal ﬁndings. Investigation Result Normal Values Haemoglobin (Hb) 129 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 7.8 × 10 /l 4.0 – 11.0 × 10 /l PLT 192 × 10 /l 150 - 400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 µmol/l (127 μmol/l some two years earlier) 50 - 120 µmol/l Plasma Viscosity 1.78 mPa/s 1.50 - 1.72 mPa/s Immunoglobulins Immunoglobulin G (IgG) paraprotein band, total IgG elevated at 27 g Bone marrow Plasma cells < 10% Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown signiﬁcance (MGUS) The incidental ﬁnding of a paraprotein band, without evidence of end-organ damage, and < 10% plasma cell involvement of the bone marrow is typical of MGUS. Progression to myeloma is around 1% per year, and the vast majority of patients can be managed conservatively. Evidence of deteriorating renal function or impaired im-

munity may indicate that transformation to myeloma has occurred. Typically MGUS is diagnosed when patients are investigated for other conditions and immunoglobulin levels are checked. D Multiple myeloma Multiple myeloma is a dyscrasia of the plasma cells; therefore, you would expect the bone marrow biopsy to show plasma cells of > 10%. Initially, there are often no symptoms. However, in advanced multiple myeloma, there may be bone pain, bleeding, frequent infections and anaemia. A Hodgkin’s lymphoma Symptoms of Hodgkin’s lymphoma include fever, night sweats and weight loss. There may be lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, and patients feel lethargic with pruritus. Fifty per cent of cases of Hodgkin’s lymphoma are due to Epstein–Barr virus. Diagnosis is made by lymph node biopsy which shows multinucleated Reed–Sternberg cells. There is no IgG paraprotein band in Hodgkin’s lymphoma. B Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is differentiated from Hodgkin’s lymphoma by the absence of multinucleated Reed– Sternberg cells; otherwise, the symptoms are similar. Symptoms may include fever, night sweats and weight loss. There may be lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, and patients feel lethargic with pruritus. The diagnosis is made by lymph node biopsy. It may be associated with Epstein–Barr virus, human T-cell leukaemia virus and Helicobacter pylori. There is no IgG paraprotein band in Hodgkin’s lymphoma. E Waldenstrom’s macrogammaglobulinaemia Waldenstrom’s macrogammaglobulinaemia is also known as lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. It is a cancer affecting B-cells, and the main antibody in excess is immunoglobulin M, and not IgG, paraprotein. Symptoms of Waldenstrom’s macrogammaglobulinaemia are related to the hyperviscosity of excessive immunoglobulins, including visual problems – blurred vision, confusion, dizziness, headaches and loss of co-ordination.

stem: A 25-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of drenching night sweats and weight loss of 6 kg. During history taking, he denied any foreign travel, diarrhoea or cough. Clinical examination revealed a 2 cm lymph node in the right supraclavicular fossa. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 112 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.3 × 109/l (85% neutrophils, 8% eosinophils) 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 160 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Chest X-ray Mediastinal mass (5 cm) Abdominal ultrasound Normal What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Hodgkin’s lymphoma The incidence of Hodgkin's lymphoma peaks in the age grouos 15–34 and >50 years, whereas non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is much commoner in older patients. For this reason, the clinical picture ﬁts much more closely with Hodgkin's lymphoma. Hodgkin’s disease is a neoplasm of lymphoid tissue that is deﬁned histopathologically by the presence of malignant Reed–Sternberg cells with an appropriate cellular background. For an adequate sample of tissue, a formal biopsy is needed, and in this case the most accessible tissue would be from the supraclavicular fossa node. Constitutional symptoms may accompany the diagnosis of Hodgkin’s disease. Patients with fever in excess of 38°C, drenching night sweats and weight loss exceeding 10% of baseline body weight during the 6 months preceding diagnosis are designated as having ‘B’ symptoms. A typical presentation is the observation, usually by the patient, of a painless, enlarging mass, most often in the neck, but occasionally in the axilla or inguinal-femoral region. In other patients, a chest Xray demonstrates a moderate or even massive mediastinal enlargement with associated lower cervical lymphadenopathy. C Seminoma Seminomas account for one third of testicular germ cell tumours (GCTs), which are the most common malignancy in men aged 15– 35 years. The most common sign at presentation is a painless testicular mass. A Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma About 85% of all malignant lymphomas are NHLs. The median age at diagnosis is the sixth decade of life, although Burkitt lymphoma and lymphoblastic lymphoma occur in younger patients. Low-grade lymphomas do not usually present with beta symptoms, as opposed to intermediate- and high-grade lymphomas. D Thymoma Of patients with a thymoma, one third to one half are asymptomatic and one third present with local symptoms related to tumour encroachment on surrounding structures. These patients may present with cough, chest pain, superior vena cava syndrome, dysphagia and hoarseness if the recurrent laryngeal nerve is involved. One third of cases are found incidentally on radiographic examinations during a work-up for myasthenia gravis. E Aspergilloma Aspergilloma may manifest as an asymptomatic radiographic

abnormality in a patient with pre-existing cavitating lung disease due to sarcoidosis, tuberculosis or other necrotising pulmonary processes. It may also occur in cystic areas resulting from prior Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in patients with HIV infection. The clinical presentation includes haemoptysis, which may be massive and life-threatening, in 40–60% of patients and, less commonly, cough and fever.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents to the Haematology Clinic with abnormal blood results. He saw his General Practitioner earlier in the year with a 6-month history of lower back pain and fatigue. He has no signiﬁcant past medical history and is normally ﬁt and well. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 90 g/l 120–160 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 250 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 150 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Calcium (Ca2+) 3.1 mmol/l 2.2–2.6 mmol/l Peripheral blood smear Rouleaux formation Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: Induction chemotherapy and allogeneic stem cell transplant
Induction chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplant
explanation:
E Induction chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplant This patient has a likely diagnosis of multiple myeloma, given the history of fatigue, back pain and laboratory ﬁndings of anaemia, raised Cr level, hypercalcaemia and rouleaux formation. Given that this man has no signiﬁcant co-morbidities, he would be a candidate for a stem cell transplant. Treatment consists of induction chemotherapy such as bortezomib plus thalidomide plus dexamethasone (VTD) followed by autologous stem cell transplant. Overall survival for multiple myeloma post-stem cell transplant has improved signiﬁcantly in recent decades. Current data show that up to 70% of patients can still be alive at ﬁve years. C Daratumumab Daratumumab is an anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of refractory or treatment-resistant multiple myeloma. It would not be indicated as an initial management option for this patient.

A Bortezomib monotherapy Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor that can be used in the management of multiple myeloma, either as a monotherapy or in combination with other drugs. However, as this patient is potentially suitable for a stem cell transplant, this would not be the most appropriate option. Rather, induction chemotherapy should be commenced to prepare for transplantation. B Surveillance monitoring and supportive care Surveillance monitoring would be inappropriate for this patient, particularly for someone who is symptomatic and potentially a candidate for a stem cell transplant. D Induction chemotherapy and allogeneic stem cell transplant While patients with multiple myeloma and a good performance status should receive a stem cell transplant, an allogeneic transplant has a higher incidence of complications, including graftversus-host disease. Therefore, an autologous stem cell transplant is preferred.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents with fatigue and left leg pain. He has had to give up his regular jogging club due to this combination. He has noticed that he has lost around 1 stone in weight over the last two months, despite reducing his physical activity. He has no cough, is a non-smoker and was previously ﬁt and well. Investigations are undertaken. Normal Values Hb 98 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 10.2 109/l 4 - 11 x 109/l Adjusted calcium (Ca2+) 2.76 mmol/l 2.20 - 2.60 mmol/l His blood ﬁlm is shown below. What is the most appropriate initial investigation for identifying the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
E Urine electrophoresis The history of weight loss, fatigue, leg pain, anaemia, rouleaux formation and hypercalcaemia is suggestive of malignancy, speciﬁcally myeloma. Urine electrophoresis would be an appropriate ﬁrst-line investigation in this case. C Left hip X-ray The suspicion in this case is a malignant cause, given the rouleaux formation on blood ﬁlm, anaemia, weight loss and hypercalcaemia. Myeloma would be suspected. While a hip X-ray may demonstrate a lytic lesion, associated with myeloma, this would not be speciﬁc to myeloma. Therefore, this is not the best initial investigation. A Haemoglobin electrophoresis This is a case of anaemia in the context of leg pain and hypercalcaemia. The blood ﬁlm demonstrates rouleaux formation, which is the blood ﬁlm equivalent of elevated ESR. This raises suspicion of malignancy. Haemoglobin electrophoresis is useful in the diagnosis of conditions such as sickle-cell disease or thalassaemia. However, there is no suggestion of either here. B Iron studies

While iron studies are useful in identifying the cause of anaemia, the clinical presentation of leg pain and hypercalcaemia, in addition to the rouleaux formation on the blood ﬁlm, point to an alternative diagnosis. D Serum folate While reduced folate can cause anaemia, which could lead to fatigue and breathlessness, the clinical context here points away from folate deﬁciency and towards malignancy.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with the complaint of worsening back pain to his GP. The pain has been present for a couple of months and is no longer relieved with analgesia. On further questioning, the patient reports that he feels ‘tired all the time’, and has a reduced appetite with associated weight loss which he had attributed to the analgesics that he was taking. He is otherwise well at present but, 5 years previously, had been treated successfully for stage IA Hodgkin’s lymphoma. Apart from analgesics, he is on no other medication. Positive ﬁndings on clinical examination include axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy, 6 cm splenomegaly and tenderness along the length of his lumbar spine. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 81 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 3.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 1.8 × 109/l 2.5–7.8 × 109/l Promyelocytes Increased PLT 96 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Lumbar spine Xray Normal What investigation would you perform to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
options: CT scan of the thorax and abdomen
explanation: C PET CT guided Excision biopsy The suspicion here is of marrow inﬁltration secondary to a recurrence of his lymphoma. Bone marrow involvement is low at the initial presentation of patients with stages I and II of Hodgkin’s disease. Marrow inﬁltration causes anaemia, a low white cell count and thrombocytopenia. To conﬁrm the diagnosis, PET CT guided identiﬁcation of metabolic active lesion and excision biopsy of a lymph node is required. A CT scan of the thorax and abdomen CT scan of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis usually follows a lymph node biopsy, accompanied by bone marrow investigation. B Deoxyglucose-labelled PET scan PET is combined with CT for staging of Hodgkin’s, rather than being the initial investigation. D Splenectomy Splenectomy carries signiﬁcant morbidity, and given that axillary lymph nodes are signiﬁcantly more accessible, biopsy of an axillary lymph node is the preferred next step. E LDH measurement LDH is a non-speciﬁc marker of haematological malignancy and won’t help establish the underlying diagnosis.

stem: A 24-year-old man of Indian ethnic origin is referred for investigation of anaemia by his GP. He is asymptomatic and attended the surgery for new patient blood testing. He has no physical complaints. The examination is unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 125 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 340 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 65 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Haemoglobin electrophoresis reveals the following: Investigation Result Normal values HbA 91.7% 95–98% HbA2 7.1% 2.0–3.0% HbF 1.2% 1.0–2.0% Other protein bands None seen What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Beta-thalassaemia minor Loss of one beta-globin gene results in a mild reduction in normal HbA (2 × alpha- and 2 × beta-globins) production and a compensatory increase in HbA2 production (2 × alpha- and 2 × deltaglobins). These patients are asymptomatic with normal examinations and are often not diagnosed until routine bloods detect a mild anaemia and microcytosis. Haemoglobin is made up of haem (iron-containing compound that binds oxygen) and globin (protein components that bind to and wrap around haem). The majority (95–98%) of adult haemoglobin is made up of HbA (2 × alpha-globins and 2 × beta-globins). A small percentage (2–3%) of adult haemoglobin is HbA2 (2 × alpha-globins and 2 × delta-globins). Adults usually have only a small amount of fetal haemoglobin or HbF (2 × alpha-globins and 2 × gamma-globins). Thalassaemia is a haemoglobinopathy resulting from defective synthesis of globin chains that prevents normal haemoglobin production and function. There are two genes on each chromosome 16 coding for alpha-globins (four in total), and one gene on each chromosome 11 coding for beta-globins (two in total). Phenotype depends on the number of deleted or mutated genes coding for the corresponding globin. A Alpha-thalassaemia trait Alpha-thalassaemia trait is a result of mutations in two out of the four globin genes. This causes an asymptomatic microcytic anaemia as seen in this case. However, because alpha-globin is present in HbA2 in addition to HbA, you would not ﬁnd an increase of HbA2 (2 × alpha- and 2 × delta-globins) detected in haemoglobin electrophoresis as seen here. See overall explanation for an overview of thalassaemia. B Haemoglobin H disease Haemoglobin H disease is a result of mutations in three out of the four alpha-globin genes. HbH refers to a very abnormal haemoglobin consisting of four beta-globins. As this is an ineffective haemoglobin, it would cause a more signiﬁcant and symptomatic anaemia with signs of this on examination. Furthermore, haemoglobin electrophoresis would identify HbH as a separate band and the HbA2 percentage would not be raised, as this requires functioning alpha-globins. See overall explanation for an overview of thalassaemia. D Beta-thalassaemia major Beta-thalassaemia major is a result of mutations in both betaglobin genes resulting in no functioning beta- globin and therefore no HbA. Therefore this presents in childhood with severe, transfusion-dependent microcytic anaemia. Beta-thalassaemia major is not usually apparent at birth due to the predominance of fetal haemoglobin (2 × alpha- and 2 ×x gamma-globins) until at least 1 year of age.

E Sickle cell trait Sickle cell trait can also cause an asymptomatic anaemia. This is usually a normocytic anaemia, but can by microcytic. However, haemoglobin electrophoresis would pick up the abnormal HbAS. On inspection of a blood ﬁlm, characteristic sickle cells would be seen.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the General Practitioner by his mother with complaints of fever, night sweats and gum bleeding for the past seven days. He was previously well and had no similar complaints in the past. On examination, there was sternal tenderness and multiple petechiae over the lower limbs. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 64 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count 28 x 109/l 4–10 x 109/l Platelet count 32 x 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Lactate dehydrogenase 684 IU/l 100–190 IU/l Urate 0.6 mmol/l 0.1–0.4 mmol/l The patient is referred to a Haemato-oncologist for further workup and initiation of chemotherapy. During workup, which of the following would indicate a poor prognosis for this patient?
options: Achieving complete remission (CR) two weeks after initiation of chemotherapy
Cluster of differentiation 15 (CD15) negative and CDw65 negative
Normal 11q with no rearrangement of the MLL gene
Presence of t(9;22) during molecular studies
explanation: D Presence of t(9;22) during molecular studies In patients with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, the presence of Philadelphia chromosome positivity, ie t(9;22), is associated with a poor prognosis. C Normal 11q with no rearrangement of the MLL gene In patients with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, an abnormal 11q23 with rearrangement of the MLL gene indicates a poor prognosis in adults and infants aged under one year. A Achieving complete remission (CR) two weeks after initiation of chemotherapy Late achievement of CR, after three weeks, is associated with a poor prognosis. Alternative treatment regimens are started when CR is not achieved after six weeks of initial chemotherapy. B Cluster of differentiation 15 (CD15) negative and CDw65 negative CD15 and CDw65 are myeloid markers and their co-expression in this patient with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia indicates a poor prognosis. E White cell count of 28 × 109/l Rasburicase has been recommended before initiation of chemotherapy in patients with a white cell count of over 100 × 109/l and an elevated urate level, both of which are found in this patient.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with recurrent chest infections and abdominal discomfort. He was well until a year ago but has required recurrent courses of antibiotics from his general practitioner (GP) for chest infections. He has discomfort in the left upper part of his abdomen and ﬁnds that he feels full despite eating only a few mouthfuls at each meal. On examination, he has a large spleen, palpable 10 cm below the costal margin. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 87 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 23.2 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l PLT 25 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Neutrophils 0.3 × 10 /l 2.5–7.58 × 10 /l Monocytes Negative Lymphocytes 21 × 10 /l 1.5–3.5 × 10 /l Blood film Large numbers of atypical lymphocytes with abnormal villous projections (not picked up on the automated count) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Hairy cell leukaemia This gentleman has anaemia, thrombocytopenia, massive splenomegaly and monocytopenia – the last of these is classic for hairy cell leukaemia, and the diagnosis is conﬁrmed by the morphological appearances on the blood ﬁlm. The typical hairy cells are named because of their characteristic cytoplasmic projections, which appear as ﬁne (hair-like) microvilli when seen by light microscopy, phase-contrast and electron microscopy. These are abnormal B-lymphocyte cells with eccentric or centrally placed nuclei. Hairy cell leukaemia responds dramatically to the purine analogues cladribine and pentostatin, with resulting survival rates at ﬁve years of 95– 98%. B Infectious mononucleosis This is caused by Epstein–Barr Virus (EBV), and a positive monospot test is diagnostic. There is an increase in lymphocytes on full blood count. It tends to affect a younger population. A Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia

CLL can often be picked up on routine blood tests. It often presents asymptomatically, but sometimes patients have splenomegaly or enlarged lymph nodes. Smudge cells and abnormal Blymphocytes (without villous projections) are seen on a blood ﬁlm. C Splenic lymphoma with villous lymphocytes Splenic lymphoma with villous lymphocytes is a subtype of nonHodgkin lymphoma. This condition is extremely rare. Whilst the clinical presentation is extremely similar, and both can have splenomegaly with circulating lymphocytes having villous projections. This condition is however, incredibly rare with estimations being < 0.5% of all non-Hodgkin lymphomas whilst hairy cell leukaemia accounts for around 2% of all leukaemias making it statistically far more likely. Furthermore, splenic lymphoma with villous lymphocytes is actually very uncommon before age 50 with the median age of onset being around 70, versus 50 for hairy cell leukaemia. D Pro-lymphocytic leukaemia PLL is a rare subtype of CLL, which is aggressive. It has either T- or B-cell differentiation. On a blood ﬁlm, the lymphocytes do not have villous projections.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-hour history of severe pain in his lower limbs. He has a background of sickle cell disease, for which he takes regular hydroxycarbamide and phenoxymethylpenicillin. He received oral paracetamol as prehospital analgesia but still complains of severe pain. On examination, his blood pressure is 105/75 mmHg and his heart rate is 105 bpm and regular. His chest sounds are clear, and his oxygen saturations are 94% on air. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. There is severe tenderness on palpation of his lower limbs. Which of the following is the most appropriate analgesia for this patient?
explanation: D Intravenous (IV) diamorphine The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines for the management of painful sickle cell crisis recommend a strong opiate delivered by an appropriate route (ie, in this case, IV) for severe pain. A Naproxen Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are not recommended in the initial management of an acute vaso-occlusive sickle cell crisis. B Fentanyl patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) Although many patients with a painful sickle cell crisis require PCA to optimise their pain control, it is usually a diamorphine, as opposed to fentanyl, PCA. C Inhaled nitrous oxide Inhaled nitrous oxide is ineffective in maintaining pain control in an acute sickle cell crisis as it is more commonly used in surgery and dentistry. E Oral Morphine Oral morphine would not be appropriate because of the time taken to achieve adequate pain relief.

stem: A 40-year-old man presented to his GP with fatigue. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 112 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 360 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Serum Ferritin 12 μg/l 20–250 µg/l He was commenced on iron sulphate tablets for presumed iron deﬁciency anaemia. The GP has referred him to the Outpatient Clinic. The patient still feels fatigued, but also complains of numbness and tingling in the lower limbs. He recalls having an operation on his abdomen a few years ago while abroad for severe abdominal pain and upper GI haemorrhage, but cannot recall the speciﬁcs of the surgery. Otherwise, he has been ﬁt and well. Examination reveals pale conjunctivae and a lemon-yellow tinge to his skin. He has slight distal lower limb sensory loss and absence of ankle jerks with exaggerated knee reﬂexes. Abdominal examination shows a longitudinal median scar, but no organomegaly. Repeat investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 104 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.5 x 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 250 x 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 112 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Which operation is he most likely to have had?
explanation: E Partial gastrectomy The patient has combined iron deﬁciency and B12 deﬁciency. A gastrectomy can cause this scenario. Gastric acid helps iron in the ferric form to be absorbed by enhancing solubility; without it, iron absorption is therefore reduced. Vitamin B12 is best absorbed in the terminal ileum when combined with intrinsic factor, which is produced by gastric parietal cells. Partial gastrectomy is likely to have driven a signiﬁcant reduction in intrinsic factor production. C Pancreaticoduodenectomy Pancreaticoduodenectomy isn’t performed for severe upper GI haemorrhage, but is performed for resectable pancreatic or ampulla of Vater carcinomas. A Hemicolectomy Hemicolectomy should not signiﬁcantly impact on either B12 or ferritin absorption. B Terminal ileal resection Although terminal ileal resection does result in B12 deﬁciency and bile salt malabsorption, it should not lead to signiﬁcant iron deﬁciency. D Splenectomy Emergency splenectomy is performed for trauma, not for acute upper GI haemorrhage. It is also not associated with B12 or iron deﬁciency.

stem: A 77-year-old man presents to the clinic with extreme tiredness. He also complains of petechiae, bruising and has had a couple of nose bleeds over the past few months. On examination, you conﬁrm bruising and petechiae; he also looks generally pale and there is splenomegaly on abdominal examination. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 89 g/l 135–175 g/l MCV 104 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ WCC 3.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 112 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 140 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the best way to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation: C Bone marrow biopsy This man potentially has myelodysplasia or myeloﬁbrosis, and a bone marrow biopsy is therefore the most logical next step. Typical bone marrow biopsy in myeloﬁbrosis reveals non-uniform areas of reticular ﬁbrosis interspersed with some areas of increased cellularity. In myelodysplasia there is an increase in the megakaryocyte component of bone marrow, and cells may be abnormally small or large, containing cytogenetic abnormalities. A Erythropoietin levels EPO levels are most useful in differentiating primary and secondary polycythaemia (due to chronic tissue hypoxia). B B12 levels B12 levels may be reduced, although B12 deﬁciency doesn’t ﬁt with the splenomegaly seen here. D Bone marrow aspiration Trephine is preferred to demonstrate the abnormal bone marrow architecture seen in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome. E Ferritin levels Iron deﬁciency anaemia is associated with microcytic anaemia rather than the macrocytosis and splenomegaly seen here.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is being investigated for epistaxis. She has noticed increased bruising and has suffered from menorrhagia almost since her periods began.
explanation: E Desmopressin The patient has von Willebrand’s disease (vWD). Von Willebrand’s factor (vWf) is involved in stabilising factor VIII and in promoting platelet aggregation. In vWD, patients experience coagulopathy with prolonged bleeding time, prolonged aPTT (APPT) and normal PT. Their factor VIII assays can be low. Desmopressin, which is similar to antidiuretic hormone, can be used for treatment. As expected, a side-effect is hyponatraemia. For more serious bleeds or surgery, factor VIII concentrate can be used. A Platelet infusion It is not defective platelets that lead to bleeding in this case, but deﬁcient aggregation due to a lack of factor VIII. B Cryoprecipitate Cryoprecipitate has a higher infectious risk than delivery of recombinant factor VIII; hence it is not a ﬁrst-choice therapy in this situation. C Mefanamic acid Mefanamic acid is a non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drug which has a role in reducing the severity of menstrual bleeding where an underlying coagulopathy has been excluded. D Vitamin K Vitamin K is used to reverse the effect of warfarin therapy.

stem: A 33-year-old woman who is currently on a combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) requests sterilisation, as she is concerned about the risks of venous thrombosis involved with the COCP. Her 65-year-old maternal aunt developed pulmonary embolism following her knee surgery, for which she was anticoagulated. Her aunt went on to have the subsequent screening of procoagulant tendencies and heterozygous factor V Leiden was identiﬁed. The patient’s mother has suffered no problems, having had three normal pregnancies and varicose veins only. What advice could be given to the patient?
options: Check for factor V Leiden and if positive, stop COCP
Finish current pill pack and then continue with progesterone-only pill
Reassure and inform the patient that the risk is minimal in continuing COCP
Stop COCP immediately and seek a gynaecologist's opinion for sterilisation
explanation:
C Reassure and inform the patient that the risk is minimal in continuing COCP About 5% of the population in the United Kingdom carry a factor V Leiden mutation. The mutation slows the normal breakdown of factor V, leading to increased circulating thrombin levels. Heterozygotes for the mutation have a slightly increased risk of developing venous thromboembolism (VTE), although most will never

have any clinically relevant episode. Heterozygote carriers have a 4 to 8-fold increased risk of VTE, and homozygous carriers have an 80-fold increased risk. In this case, there is no evidence of a ﬁrst-degree relative having the mutation (which would have implied a need to perform screening on this patient) since the patient’s mother has not had any thromboembolic episodes. Therefore, the patient may be reassured that she may continue on the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP). D Stop COCP immediately and seek a gynaecologist's opinion for sterilisation The patient may be reassured that she may continue on the COCP and therefore, sterilisation is not necessary at this point. A Check for factor V Leiden and if positive, stop COCP From the point of view of relatives known to be affected by VTE, screening of patients for mutation is not routinely recommended, as per the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance. If a mutation is found in a patient, then immediate family members should be screened for the mutation; if found to be present, then non-hormonal contraception should be recommended unless the woman has completed her family and expresses a preference for sterilisation. In this case, the patient’s aunt has heterozygous factor V Leiden mutation. This constitutes a seconddegree relative. There is no evidence of a ﬁrst-degree relative having the mutation, since the patient’s mother has not had any thromboembolic episodes. Therefore, screening would not be recommended and the patient may be reassured that she may continue on the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP). In the event that her mother suffers a thromboembolic event and is diagnosed with factor V Leiden mutation, this advice would need to be reviewed. B Finish current pill pack and then continue with progesterone-only pill The patient may be reassured that she may continue on the COCP and therefore, switching to the progesterone-only pill is not required in this situation. E Use other methods of contraception A switch of contraception may not be required in the event that screening for factor V Leiden is required and found to be positive.

stem: A 50-year-old painter who specialises in house restoration goes to see a new GP for a routine signing-on medical. Past medical history of note includes a recent diagnosis of gout. Some blood tests are arranged, and the GP mails you to discuss the results. He reports on his e-mail that the clinical examination was unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 105 g/l 135–175 g/l MCV 60 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 190 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Ferritin 300 µgl/l 20–250 µg/l Hb electrophoresis Normal Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Lead poisoning The clue given here is in his occupation as a painter. It is still possible, even in the days of lead-free paints, that he would have had signiﬁcant lead exposure while stripping the walls in old houses. The blood picture of lead toxicity mimics that seen with iron deﬁciency anaemia; additionally, disordered handling of uric acid may lead to the development of gout. A Iron deﬁciency anaemia Although iron deﬁciency anaemia does present with microcytic anaemia, the normal ferritin level would be very unusual in this context. B Beta-thalassaemia The normal Hb electrophoresis and lack of description of an ethnic origin consistent with thalassaemia counts against this as a diagnosis. C Anaemia of chronic disease Anaemia of chronic disease is normally associated with a normochromic, normocytic blood picture. E Porphyria Cutaneous porphyrias are associated with a skin rash not seen here, and acute porphyrias are associated with paroxysms of acute psychiatric disturbance with hypertension, tachycardia and hyponatraemia.

stem: A 50-year-old man is referred to the clinic by his General Practitioner (GP). He recently suffered a fracture of his right humerus, with minimal trauma. He has been complaining of increasing tiredness over the past few weeks and months and has been unable to continue his job working in a builder’s merchants. Bloods taken at the GP practice prompted his referral: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 89 g/l 135 - 175 g/l White blood cells (WBC) 9.5 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 140 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l MCV 86 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ ESR 60 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h Sodium (Na+) 149 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.6 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 15 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 160 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.89 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Albumin 28 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Total protein 89 g/l 60 - 83 g/l An X-ray of the right humerus reported as a possible pathological fracture. What next investigation would best help to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation:
C Immunoglobulin electrophoresis The most likely diagnosis with anaemia, raised ESR, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment and raised total protein with low albumin is multiple myeloma. This is a B-cell malignancy, resulting in paraproteinaemia. The diagnosis is conﬁrmed by showing the presence of paraproteins, > 10% of plasma cells in the bone marrow and lytic bone lesions. A Chest X-ray The signiﬁcant elevation in total protein and hypercalcaemia ﬁt much better with multiple myeloma vs an underlying chest malignancy. B Radioisotope bone scan Radioisotope bone scans are insensitive, with respect to identifying lytic lesions in myeloma.
