D Prostate-speciﬁc antigen The raised total protein levels with low levels of albumin are more consistent with a diagnosis of multiple myeloma rather than of prostate cancer. Furthermore, the patient does not have any lower urinary tract symptoms and his age would be more consistent with a diagnosis of myeloma. E Serum alkaline phosphatase Alkaline phosphatase levels are signiﬁcantly lower in patients

with multiple myeloma vs patients with solid tumour bony metastases.

stem: An 18-year-old girl presents with sudden-onset dysarthria and right-sided weakness. You see her 12 h after the event and her symptoms have now resolved. She takes the oral contraceptive pill. She is in full-time education and smokes 5–10 cigarettes daily. Alcohol intake is minimal. She lives with her parents. Family history is unremarkable other than a possible deep vein thrombosis in an aunt. The examination is unremarkable, other than a lacy rash over her thighs and a grade II ejection systolic murmur. Computed tomography of the brain performed 2 h after admission is unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 123 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 3.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 135 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l PTT 45 s 23.0–35.0 s What is the most likely identity of the rash?
explanation:
C Livedo reticularis This is a case of a young woman with anti-phospholipid syndrome, also known as Hughes syndrome. This is diagnosed in patients with characteristic clinical phenomena (venous and arterial thromboembolism, recurrent ﬁrst trimester miscarriages, livedo reticularis, chorea and Libman–Sacks endocarditis) in whom positive anti- cardiolipin antibodies or a lupus anticoagulant are detected on two separate occasions, separated by at least 6 weeks. The condition is managed by lifelong anticoagulation with warfarin, at a target INR of 2–3 (higher targets were previously used, but a randomised controlled double-blind trial (Crowther et al, New England Journal of Medicine, 2003) did not support any greater therapeutic effect of high intensity anticoagulation. The paradoxical prolongation of the aPTT is due to antibodies to phospholipids, which is critical to the functioning of the assay. However, a normal APTT does not rule out the presence of a lupus anticoagulant; to rule this out you need to assess phospholipiddependent measures of clotting, such as the dilute Russell viper venom time. E Erythaema multiforme Erythema multiforme is characterised by target lesions seen in

association viral illnesses such as herpes simplex, and other infectious conditions such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae. A Erythaema ab igne Erythema ab igne is associated with reticulated erythema, hyperpigmentation, skin scaling and telangiectasia over the area which has been subject to local heat. B Erythaema chronicum migrans Erythema chronicum migrans is a rash characteristic of Lyme disease, which extends out from the original tick bite or eschar. D Erythroderma Erythroderma is associated with generalised erythema, and is most commonly seen in association with severe psoriasis.

stem: A 22-year-old man is admitted to hospital with bone pain after a recent chest infection. He has sickle cell disease and over the past few years has had increased admissions to hospital with severe bone pain episodes. The patient is interested in treatment that would decrease the frequency of admissions to hospital with these pain episodes. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
C Hydroxyurea Hydroxyurea is thought to act by increasing the production of fetal haemoglobin, which is less likely to sickle and it has been shown to decrease the frequency of admissions with pain episodes. It is also used in chronic myeloid leukaemia. Side-effects include bone marrow toxicity, gastrointestinal disturbance and skin rashes. D Penicillin Penicillin is recommended as prophylaxis for infection because of hyposplenism related to sickle cell, but will not signiﬁcantly reduce the risk of painful chest crises. A Morphine Although morphine is entirely appropriate used acutely for painful crisis, used over the longer term, chronically, it runs a high risk of driving addiction. B Pethidine Pethidine has a potentially more rapid onset of action than morphine, and therefore runs an even greater risk of addiction.

E Frequent exchange transfusions Exchange transfusion may be considered in patients with signiﬁcant chest crisis, or where there is a vaso- occlusive event such as a stroke. It is a secondary intervention for the long term in patients who fail to respond to interventions such as hydroxyurea.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents with sudden onset left-sided weakness of 24 h duration. He has sickle cell anaemia, and has required admissions in the past for management of chest crises. He is on ibuprofen for pain when necessary, penicillin V and folic acid. He smokes ten cigarettes daily and drinks 21 units of alcohol per week. His mother and father are both carriers for HbS, and he has no siblings or children. On examination, he has dense, left-sided weakness, with brisk reﬂexes and up-going plantars on the left-hand side. Computed tomography (CT) of the brain conﬁrms a right-sided hypodense lesion. His Hb is 110 g/l. What is the most appropriate short-term intervention?
explanation:
E Exchange transfusion 6–10% of sickle cell patients will suffer a stroke, usually during childhood. The risk can be predicted by transcranial Doppler measurement of the middle cerebral artery ﬂow rate, and prompt institution of a prophylactic transfusion programme to reduce the HbS percentage can prevent future strokes. Silent infarcts can lead to reduced cognition and limited educational attainment. In this case, with symptoms of acute stroke, exchange transfusion is the most appropriate next step. A Hydroxyurea There is growing evidence that in addition to its effects on painful and chest crises, hydroxyurea may impact positively on the stroke rate in patients with sickle cell disease, although in the short term exchange transfusion is more effective. B 5'-Azacytidine 5'-Azacytidine is a DNA methylating agent that can improve HbF levels where hydroxyurea has failed, but it is cytotoxic and its use remains limited, particularly given the young age of this patient. C Bone marrow transplantation Due to the high procedure-related mortality, transplant is usually only considered suitable for patients under 16 with a matched sibling donor; it is not considered superior to a transfusion therapy.

D Thrombolytic therapy 24 h after symptoms began, this patient is outside the window for thrombolysis and this is therefore not an option.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with increasing fatigue and weight loss over the past six weeks. She also complains of intermittent fevers and nosebleeds. There is no past medical history of note, and she is normally ﬁt and well with no regular medications. On examination, there is extensive bruising over her upper and lower limbs, which she says only started appearing within the last two days, despite spending most of the days in bed. There is palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Investigation Results Normal value Hb 88 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 25.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 80 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.1 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 80 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Activated partial prothrombin time 44 s 27–41 s Prothrombin time 18 s 12–15 s Fibrinogen 1.2 g/l 1.9–8 g/l Blood ﬁlm Hypergranular promyelocytes Given the likely diagnosis, what is the immediate management for this patient?
explanation:
C Fresh frozen plasma This patient has a diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), likely secondary to acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML), given the history of lethargy and constitutional symptoms associated with hyper granulated promyelocytes on blood ﬁlm. In fact, DIC is a common presentation of APML. DIC is an acquired syndrome characterised by dysregulation of the coagulation system leading to the formation of thrombi and consumption of platelets and clotting factors that, in turn, leads to bleeding. Laboratory markers of DIC include a prolonged prothrombin time, activated partial prothrombin time and decreased ﬁbrinogen and platelet count. Another laboratory marker is the presence of elevated ﬁbrin degradation products (D-dimer). Treatment of DIC includes ﬁnding and treating the underlying cause. In immediate management, fresh frozen plasma is the preferred agent for replacing coagulation factors. B Factor VIII Factor VIII is used in the management of haemophilia A, an Xlinked inherited disorder characterised by the deﬁciency of factor VIII, meaning that is almost exclusively affects males. In haemophilia A, there is a prolonged activated partial prothrombin time but normal prothrombin time. This does not match the laboratory ﬁndings of this patient. A Cryoprecipitate Cryoprecipitate is a second-line agent used in the treatment of DIC, particularly when there is a signiﬁcant reduction in ﬁbrinogen levels (below 1 g/l). Given that the ﬁbrinogen levels are above 1 g/l, fresh frozen plasma should be given initially. D Prothrombin concentrate Prothrombin concentrate is typically used in the management of

acute and signiﬁcant bleeding in patients taking warfarin and other oral anticoagulants. It contains the vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. It can be used in the treatment of DIC but is not the ﬁrst-line management. E Vitamin K Vitamin K is typically used in patients taking warfarin (ie a vitamin K antagonist) and helps upregulate vitamin- K-dependent clotting factors. It is not commonly used in patients with DIC.

stem: A 65-year-old man is admitted with dehydration following an attack of infectious gastritis. His initial blood results revealed a raised calcium and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. He has a background of hypertension, angina, chronic obstructive airways disease and diabetes. His most recent results arrive on the ward and reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 138 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.7 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l PLT 212 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 104 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 7.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca ) 2.4 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Albumin 38 g/l 35–55 g/l Immunoglobulin G (IgG) 19 g/l (monoclonal band identified) 5–16 g/l IgA 2.1 g/l 1.0–4.0 g/l IgM 1.3 g/l 0.5–2.0 g/l Urine, Bence Jones protein - CXR Heart and mediastinal contours normal, lungs clear, osteopenia of bony skeleton with no lytic lesions What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined signiﬁcance monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined signiﬁcance (MGUS), which is a monoclonal paraproteinaemia without evidence of disorders such as myeloma, Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia or amyloidosis. It is usually picked up incidentally. There is mild increase in a serum monoclonal protein without paresis of the other

monoclonal bands. The presence of anaemia, hypercalcaemia, kidney disease or lytic bone lesions points towards myeloma. The initial raised calcium is most likely to have been related to dehydration. In MGUS the urine does not contain Bence Jones protein. These patients need to be followed up as they are at increased risk of developing myeloma. A bone marrow biopsy should reveal <10% plasma cells and a skeletal survey should reveal no lytic lesions to be compatible with MGUS. B Multiple myeloma Multiple myeloma is associated with evidence of end-organ damage, where for example elevated creatinine would be expected. A greater increase in the monoclonal gammopathy may also be expected. C Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia is associated with elevated IgM and with hyperviscosity rather than the features seen here. D Inﬂammatory amyloidosis In inﬂammatory amyloidosis a polyclonal increase in immunoglobulins would be expected against a background of chronic inﬂammatory disease. E Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia CLL is associated with impaired immunity and a marked increase in peripheral blood lymphocyte count.

stem: A 69-year-old retired headteacher with rapidly deteriorating back pain comes to see you in the clinic. The pain started 6 months ago following a fall down the stairs. Lumbar spine X-ray then conﬁrmed vertebral collapse of L2 and L4. She started calcium/vitamin D3 and a bisphosphonate. The pain has now spread to her thoracic spine. The pain does not vary with time of day or exercise. Although her appetite has decreased, her weight seems steady. She smoked in her youth. She has hypertension. Current medication comprises regular opioid analgesia, a diuretic and a statin. On examination, she is pale. Her cardiovascular, chest and abdominal investigations are normal. She is non- speciﬁcally tender over her thoracic and lumbar spine. Although her neurological examination is hindered by pain, nothing of note was found. Chest Xray reveals a slightly enlarged cardiac shadow; T-spine, collapse of T5; L-spine, collapse of L2, L4. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 87 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 3.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 124 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 141 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 10.1 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Calcium (Ca2+) 2.34 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Albumin 36 g/l 35–55 g/l Bilirubin 12 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 36 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 12 IUl/l 30–130 IU/l Total Protein 84 g/l 60–80 g/l Phosphate (PO43-) 1.01 mmol/l 0.70–1.40 mmol/l ESR 42 mm/hour < 10 mm/hour CRP 6 mg/l < 10 mg/l
explanation:
C Multiple myeloma The rapidly increasing severity of back pain that does not vary with time or movement is signiﬁcant. Although her calcium is not elevated, her globulins are (by virtue of the fact her total protein is raised and albumin is relatively normal), as is her ESR. She also has renal impairment and multiple areas of vertebral collapse. Multiple myeloma is a disease in which there is accumulation of malignant plasma cells, generally derived from one clone in the bone marrow. It is characterised by the production of a monoclonal immunoglobulin that can be detected in the serum or urine. It is often associated with bone pain, kidney disease and anaemia. Diagnostic tests include bone marrow examination, the presence of more than 10% plasma cells being required for diagnosis. A skeletal survey is required for lytic lesions and serum/urine electrophoresis is needed to identify the presence of paraprotein. Urinalysis can be performed to identify Bence Jones protein. Treatment is based around melphalan chemotherapy. In patients under 65 years of age, bortezomib is often used as an induction therapy for those patients going on to high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation, which often leads to a prolonged remission compared to conventional chemotherapy. B Renal cell carcinoma Renal cell carcinomas can metastasise to the lymph nodes, bone, liver, lung and brain, so it would be one of the differentials for this patient. Renal cell cancer can present with bony involvement, anaemia and renal impairment, However, the protein level would usually be normal to low and the overall picture of this patient with raised ESR coupled with vertebral collapse and renal impairment, is more in keeping with a diagnosis of myeloma. Renal cell cancer patients often present with haematuria, unilateral ab-

dominal pain, abdominal mass, fatigue, anorexia and weight loss. A Osteoporosis Patients often present with back pain and fractures (including compression fractures) worsening slowly over time. The key points to note are the raised protein levels, renal impairment, raised ESR and proteinuria, which are not in keeping with a diagnosis of osteoporosis, meaning that this is incorrect. D Osteoporosis and over-diuresis Osteoporosis tends to have a more insidious onset. This patient’s picture is also not in keeping with a patient who has been overdiuresed. If that were the case, you would expect the patient to have a low sodium and potassium alongside a raised urea and creatinine. However, this patient has normal electrolyte levels. E Squamous cell lung carcinoma This diagnosis is a possibility in this patient. The X-ray commented on an enlarged heart border, but an X-ray is unable to exclude a central mass. The cancer could have spread to the bone but you would usually expect a raised calcium, either secondary to bony involvement or due to a paraneoplastic phenomenon of hypercalcaemia of malignancy in squamous cell lung cancer. This patient’s clinical picture does not quite ﬁt with this and, as such, means it is not the most likely diagnosis for this patient.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 24 hour history of unilateral swelling of the left leg. She has recently ﬂown back to this country from Australia. She is previously ﬁt and well, does not smoke and is on no medication. She has no family history of note. Other than the swollen leg, examination is unremarkable. Ultrasound of the deep veins of the leg conﬁrms an above-knee deep vein thrombosis, and she is commenced on enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily subcutaneously and started on 10 mg of warfarin. On the second day after starting warfarin she has developed black lesions over her buttocks. Platelet count remains stable at 205 × 109/l. What is the most likely cause of the lesions over her buttocks?
explanation:
B Protein C deﬁciency This woman has developed warfarin-induced skin necrosis (WISN); this occurs when warfarin is started and there is a defect in the protein C anticoagulant pathway. Protein C is vitamin K dependent and falls rapidly following the commencement of warfarin, leading to an initial paradoxical prothrombotic state: this

explains why heparin is started concurrently with warfarin, to cover this initial period. The condition has been reported in association with most forms of thrombophilia, but defects in the protein C pathway (classically protein C deﬁciency, but also including protein S and activated protein C resistance) are the most common pre-existing conditions. In WISN, microthrombi form in the blood vessels of the skin, particularly in adipose areas such as buttocks and breast. The condition is severe, and plastic surgery is often required. Treatment is supportive, with vitamin K and possibly fresh frozen plasma to replace protein C levels. Prostacyclin and protein C infusion have been trialled. Warfarin can be reintroduced at a lower loading dose, but recurrence may occur. E Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome This occurs either in isolation or against a background of SLE and is associated with recurrent venous thrombosis and other features such as livedo reticularis. A Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia type 2 HIT is associated with the development of necrotic skin ulcers, although the maintenance of a stable platelet count counts against this as the underlying diagnosis. C Prothrombin gene 20210 mutation The prothrombin gene 20210 mutation is a cause of thrombophilia, rather than a cause of protein C deﬁciency in association with warfarin initiation. D Antithrombin III deﬁciency Antithrombin III deﬁciency is associated with recurrent thrombosis, and is seen as an autosomal dominant congenital disorder and in patients with severe proteinuria. It is not associated with commencement of warfarin.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of fatigue, shortness of breath and abdominal discomfort. She has a past medical history of sickle-cell disease, for which she regularly takes hydroxycarbamide 500 mg twice daily. Her temperature is 36.1 °C, heart rate 100 bpm and BP 90/60 mmHg. Her respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and her oxygen saturation is 96% on air. On examination, she appears lethargic. She is cool to the touch, with a capillary reﬁll time of four seconds. Auscultation of her chest is clear, with vesicular breath sounds throughout both lungs. Her heart sounds are normal. Her abdomen is distended and tender to palpation, particularly in the left upper quadrant. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 60 g/l 120–160 g/l WCC 9.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 208 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Reticulocyte count 3% 0.5–2.5% Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for this presentation?
explanation: D Sequestration crisis The clinical presentation of sudden-onset fatigue, abdominal pain and shock in a young adult with sickle-cell disease is highly suggestive of a sequestration crisis. A sequestration crisis is characterised by the sudden pooling of blood in the spleen or liver, leading to rapid splenomegaly and hypovolaemic shock due to a sudden decrease in circulating blood volume. It most often presents in children but can also present in adults, albeit less frequently. B Aplastic crisis An aplastic crisis is characterised by decreased erythropoiesis due to infection with parvovirus B19. This results in severe anaemia and a reduction in the reticulocyte count. In this case, the reticulocyte count is raised, which suggests that the bone marrow is trying to overcome the anaemia. Additionally, the presentation of an aplastic crisis does not typically include sudden-onset abdominal pain and hypovolaemic shock, as seen in a sequestration crisis. A Acute chest syndrome Acute chest syndrome is a serious complication of sickle-cell disease, characterised by fever, chest pain and respiratory symptoms. Often, pulmonary inﬁltrates are seen on a CXR. Although abdominal pain can occur in acute chest syndrome due to splenic infarction, the presentation described here is more consistent with a sequestration crisis, given the signs of hypovolaemic shock and signiﬁcantly low Hb levels. C Haemolytic crisis A haemolytic crisis in sickle-cell disease is characterised by an increased rate of red blood cell destruction, leading to anaemia, jaundice and reticulocytosis. While abdominal pain can occur in a haemolytic crisis, the presentation described here is more suggestive of a sequestration crisis, particularly given the presence of hypovolaemic shock and rapid onset of symptoms. E Vaso-occlusive crisis A vaso-occlusive crisis is the most common type of sickle-cell crisis and is characterised by signiﬁcant pain due to microvascular occlusion by sickled red blood cells. Commonly affected areas include the upper and lower limbs. While abdominal pain can occur in vaso-occlusive crises, the sudden onset of symptoms, in combination with shock and a signiﬁcant drop in Hb level, is more suggestive of a sequestration crisis.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with indigestion of seven weeks’ duration. She has no ongoing medical problems, and is otherwise asymptomatic. She is on no medication. Examination is unremarkable. She undergoes gastro-oesophageal endoscopy, which reveals gastritis. Stomach biopsies conﬁrm the presence of a mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (maltoma/marginal zone lymphoma) of low-grade type; Helicobacter pylori is demonstrated. Computed tomography (CT) of chest, abdomen and pelvis reveals no additional disease, and a bone marrow trephine is unremarkable; the stomach wall is not clearly thickened. What treatment would you recommend?
explanation:
C H. pylori eradication therapy Maltomas, also known as marginal zone lymphomas, are low-grade lymphomas, most often diagnosed in the stomach. They are peculiar in that they are often associated with chronic inﬂammation of one of the following types: • In the stomach secondary to chronic H. pylori gastritis In the eyes secondary to Sjogren syndrome • In the thyroid secondary to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis • In the intestine secondary to Crohn’s or coeliac disease. Treatment against H. pylori is safe and will cause regression in 90% of low-grade gastric maltomas; response is less likely if cytogenetic abnormalities have been acquired (t11:18 being the most common), or if the muscularis mucosa has been invaded. This patient has early-stage disease, so triple therapy coupled with close oncological and gastroenterological follow-up is appropriate. D Partial gastrectomy Surgery is rarely employed in the treatment of gastric maltoma, because it is usually not curative and results in signiﬁcant operative morbidity. A Cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and prednisolone (CHOP)

R-CHOP (including rituximab) is a treatment option for more advanced gastric lymphoma. B Observation alone Observation alone risks signiﬁcant lymphoma progression, meaning that H. pylori eradication would then in all likelihood be ineffective. E High-dose dexamethasone High-dose dexamethasone may provide symptomatic improvement, but is ineffective in treating H. pylori, the likely trigger for maltoma seen here.

stem: A 33-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with a 1-week histo- ry of dark urine and severe fatigue. On further questioning, she admits to increasing tiredness over a matter of weeks. One day before admission, she developed severe abdominal pain and abdominal distension. On examination, she has pallor, jaundice, an enlarged tender liver and ascites. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 79 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 3.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 89 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 101 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Peripheral smear Mild polychromasia Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 144 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALT 130 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Bilirubin 54 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Urine Haemosiderin ++ Urobilinogen + Abdominal ultrasound reveals an enlarged liver, ascites and absent ﬂow in the hepatic veins. What single test would you request to conﬁrm the underlying diagnosis?
options: Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 expression
explanation:
D Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 expression This patient has paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) complicated by acute hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd–Chiari syndrome). PNH is an acquired clonal disorder of haematopoietic stem cells, characterised by a variable combination of intravascular haemolysis, thrombosis and bone marrow failure. A somatic mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan-A (PIG-A) gene on the X chromosome leads to deﬁciency of several glycosyl- phosphatidylinositol (GPI)-linked molecules. Deﬁciency of decay accelerating factor (DAF, CD55) and the membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis (MIRL, CD59) increases susceptibility to complement-mediated lysis of blood cells. Currently, diagnosis is made by ﬂow cytometric evaluation of blood, which conﬁrms the CD55 and CD59 deﬁciencies and deﬁciency of expression of other GPI-linked proteins. This test is replacing older, complement-based assays (such as Ham’s test and the sucrose lysis test) because it is less affected by blood transfusion, is more sensitive and speciﬁc and it measures the size of the PNH clone, which is useful for follow- up. A Viral hepatitis serology This patient does not have viral hepatitis. Although with similar presentation symptoms of fatigue, dark urine, abdominal pain and

jaundice, there would not be a disturbance of ﬂow across the hepatic veins or evidence of haemolysis or anaemia. B Liver biopsy A liver biopsy would not be diagnostic for PNH. It may show evidence of scarring or ﬁbrosis. There is a high risk of bleeding with liver biopsies and, with low platelets and altered liver chemistry, it may not be advisable. C Inherited thrombophilia screen PNH is an acquired condition. It is not inherited and so would not give a diagnosis of PNH on testing for inherited thrombophilias. It is likely that a thrombophilia screen would be largely negative. One study has shown an increase in anti-phospholipid antibody in some patients with PNH, although it is unsure how this affects the patient. E Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) assay Looking for G6PD deﬁciency is not appropriate in this instance. G6PD deﬁciency does produce haemolysis and jaundice but it is an X-linked inherited condition unlike PNH, which is acquired and doesn’t affect males and females differently.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-week history of easy bruising and menorrhagia. On the day of presentation, she developed ‘heaviness’ in her left arm and slurred speech. She is taking tranexamic acid, prescribed for the menorrhagia. She has no previous medical history of note. According to her husband, she was incoherent and confused for half an hour but is now alert and orientated. Examination shows a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15, normal neurological examination and normal speech. Her temperature is 37.5 °C, her heart rate 105 bpm and her blood pressure 130/70 mmHg. Her heart sounds are normal. She has several bruises on her shins and forearms. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain is normal. Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 85 g/l 135–175 g/l PLT 17 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l MCV 102 fl 80–100 fl Reticulocytes 130 x 10 /l 25–85 x 10 /l LDH 735 u/l 140–280 u/l Blood film Low counts, numerous schistocytes PT 15 s 11–14 s APTT 33 s 25–35 s Pregnancy test Negative Her tranexamic acid is stopped. She is treated with plasmapheresis and prednisolone. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term intervention following the acute episode?
explanation:
C Daily aspirin The results show anaemia with a raised reticulocyte count and lactate dehydrogenase level, implying haemolysis, and the presence of schistocytes is most compatible with a microangiopathic mechanism. Coupled with low platelets and ﬂuctuating neurological signs, this is classical for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Treatment for this is urgent plasmapheresis with fresh frozen plasma or cryosupernatant, which is thought to signiﬁcantly reduce mortality, although there is a lack of randomised controlled trials in this area. Steroids are usually given alongside plasmapheresis in the acute setting. In this patient, tranexamic acid is prothrombotic and may be worsening the condition, and hence it has been stopped. The condition is caused by an acquired autoantibody to the metalloproteinase ADAMTS13, the function of which is to control the size of von Willebrand’s factor multimers. As a result, ultra-large von Willebrand’s factor multimers, with enhanced activity, accumulate and cause increased binding of platelets to small blood vessels. The PLT count falls and red cells are damaged when they pass through the narrowed vessels, causing microangiopathy. Once the PLT count reaches around 50, patients are started on long-term aspirin to reduce the risk of platelet aggregation. A 3-monthly plasmapheresis Plasmapheresis is indicated in the acute setting of thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Ideally, it should be started within 24 hours of presentation as a delay in treatment decreases the chance of response. Around 90% of patients will respond to plasma exchange within three weeks. There are a number of complications associated with plasma exchange, including infection, venous thrombosis, hypotension due to large ﬂuid shifts and serum sickness. Furthermore, plasma exchange increases the likelihood of the development of red blood cell antibodies. Due to the high likelihood of recovery following initial treatment, and the risks associated with plasma exchange, regular plasmapheresis is not recommended. B 3- to 4-monthly platelet transfusion Platelet transfusion has previously not been recommended in patients with TTP, as it was thought to trigger the worsening of the disease. However, a retrospective review does not support this. Platelet transfusion is most likely to be considered in the acute setting if a patient is bleeding or when invasive procedures are required for plasmapheresis, alongside the administration of folic acid (as there is presumed deﬁciency from haemolysis and high demand for folate). However, long-term platelet transfusion is not recommended as the PLT count should recover with prompt plasma exchange treatment.

D Daily cyclophosphamide Cyclophosphamide and other immunosuppressants, including rituximab and ciclosporin, may be used as second-line agents after initial treatment with plasmapheresis and steroids. However, their use is often only supported by a small number of cases studies and therefore, specialists will guide these decisions. E Splenectomy Splenectomy was used before the invention of plasma exchange and there is some retrospective evidence that showed a good response to treatment. However, splenectomy puts patients at higher risk of infection with encapsulated bacteria. It is currently recommended as a last option for intervention in the acute setting due to the relative safety and transient risks of plasmapheresis. It is not recommended as a long-term treatment.

stem: A 37-year-old nurse presents to the ENT Department with a ﬂulike illness. She gives a 10-year history of tendency to have a blocked, stuffy nose and frequent recurrent coughs and colds. The Occupational Health team has also noticed that she failed to show a response to hepatitis B and tetanus vaccinations. In which immunoglobulin is she likely to be deﬁcient?
explanation:
A IgA This patient is most likely to have IgA deﬁciency, which is particularly associated with recurrent sinus infections due to encapsulated bacteria such as Haemophilus inﬂuenzae. Selective IgA deﬁciency is probably the most common of the primary immunodeﬁciency disorders, but it may also be asymptomatic. In Caucasians, IgA deﬁciency is said to occur in 1 in 600–700 individuals. There is often a deﬁcient response to polysaccharide- based vaccinations. In patients with IgA deﬁciency, 10–44% of patients may have antiIgA antibodies; this risks a severe reaction to IgA-containing products such as blood, plasma or immunoglobulin. B IgE There are few case reports in the literature regarding IgE deﬁciency. C IgD IgD immunodeﬁciency is quite rare, and individuals with this condition do not seem to be predisposed to infections.

D IgM Sometimes, in cases of IgA deﬁciency, compensatory IgM increase may occur. E IgG IgG immunodeﬁciency is also common. IgG-subclass deﬁciency and its importance have been characterised. Antibodies against pneumococcal polysaccharide antigens are predominantly IgG2 and, to a lesser degree, IgG4. Antibodies against protein antigens, such as tetanus, are predominantly IgG1 and, to a lesser degree, IgG3. Finally, antibodies against large extracellular parasites, such as Schistosoma and Filaria organisms, exclusively belong to the IgG4 subclass. The history of sinus infections in the present scenario points towards IgA immunodeﬁciency.

stem: A 37-year-old woman is admitted with confusion. She has no past medical history of note and was previously ﬁt and well. Examination reveals small petechial haemorrhages on the legs and pale conjunctivae. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no organomegaly detectable. The chest is clear and thorough systemic examination reveals no abnormalities except for a ﬂuctuant Glasgow Coma Scale. Observations: heart rate 110 bpm, BP 115/72 mmHg, temperature 38.4 °C and O2 sats 97% on room air. Investigations reveal the following: Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 93 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 13 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l PLT 34 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 5.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 168 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Plasma haptoglobin 0.19 g/l 0.3–2.0 g/l Urea 11.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l CRP 8 mg/l < 10 mg/l Bilirubin 35 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 38 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 100 IU/l 30–130 IU/l ΓGT 32 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Albumin 38 g/l 35–55 g/l Urine dipstick Blood+, protein+ Blood film Schistocytes CXR Lung fields clear, no other abnormalities detected What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome
explanation:
B Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) TTP is classically associated with the pentad of clinical signs and ﬁndings: confusion, pyrexia, kidney disease, thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. The patient in this case exhibits all of these criteria, although it should be noted that not all patients will display all ﬁve. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a condition that causes a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. The exact aetiology is unclear, but it has been found to be associated with auto-antibodies to ADAMTS13, a protein responsible for cleaving von Willebrand factor (VWF) into smaller units. Ultra-long VWF is very prothrombotic and can form a mesh in the vessels which causes fragmentation of red cells (a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia). It can be associated with pregnancy and the postpartum period, but is also seen in non-pregnant individuals. TTP is characterised by ﬁve symptoms or signs: confusion, pyrexia, kidney disease, thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia. Patients are often treated with plasma exchange. Eculizumab may be useful in patients with refractory disease. D Chest sepsis Sepsis can present very similarly to TTP, i.e. with a fever, confusion and signs of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (if deteriorated to disseminated intravascular coagulation) and is always a very important differential diagnosis to be considered in these patients. However, the history and examination suggest that there is no clear source of sepsis, the patient’s CRP is not raised and the chest X-ray is normal. A Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP) HSP classically affects children post-mild infection. This would be a differential diagnosis for petechial haemorrhages on the patient’s legs, but this patient is suffering from many other symptoms (fever and confusion) which would not be explained by HSP. Furthermore, whilst HSP can cause deranged renal function, the low platelet count, raised bilirubin and signs of haemolysis on the blood ﬁlm seen in this case are not associated with HSP. C Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome HELLP syndrome is associated with confusion, haemolysis and low platelets, as seen in this case. However, it is only seen in the setting of pregnancy, or recent delivery, usually associated with pre-eclampsia. E Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) SLE is the great mimic and can affect all organs including the kidneys, brain and blood. However, SLE is a more chronic condition than the history described here. Furthermore, if this answer referred to SLE ﬂares, these are typically in the context of a history of SLE, which this patient does not have and common-

ly presents with painful joints, rashes and fatigue. Therefore, this is not the most likely diagnosis.

stem: A 56-year-old woman has been referred to the clinic. She has had two episodes of shingles in the past 2 months and her GP had noticed persisting lymphadenopathy. The patient currently feels well and there is no past history of note. Examination reveals some petechiae on her back, cervical lymphadenopathy and mild splenomegaly. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 89 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 48 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Lymphocytes 40 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l PLT 116 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Blood ﬁlm Smudge cells What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia CLL is the most common adult leukaemia in the Western world. The diagnosis can be discovered incidentally, or patients can have symptoms of anaemia, recurrent bleeding and recurrent infections. Examination can reveal lymphadenopathy with hepatosplenomegaly. A full blood count will show a raised WBC with a lymphocytosis. The blood ﬁlm will show smudge cells, as these are more friable. Immunophenotyping will conﬁrm the diagnosis, with CD19 and CD5 white cell markers likely to be present. B Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia ALL is unlikely to be the diagnosis given that blast cells have not been found to be present on the blood ﬁlm. A Hairy cell leukaemia Hairy cell leukaemia is usually associated with a low white blood cell count rather than the mature lymphocytosis seen here. C Splenic lymphoma Primary splenic lymphoma is associated with enlargement of the spleen as is seen here, but is not associated with the marked elevation in white blood cell count. D Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is associated with peripheral lymphadenopathy and impaired immune function, although the marked

elevation in peripheral blood lymphocyte count is not seen.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is admitted for resection of a caecal carcinoma. She is not taking any medications, has no other past medical history, is a non-smoker and drinks little alcohol. Preoperative physical examination is unremarkable, with a blood pressure of 125/85 mmHg, pulse 76/min and regular. BMI is 23. Preoperative bloods reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 90 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 76 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ WCC 10.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 250 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l The operation was uneventful. with no evidence of secondary spread and the patient received 2 units of blood during the procedure. Five days later she was icteric and tired. She is apyrexial, and apart from tenderness around her scar, she tells you that her surgical pain is gradually improving. Repeat bloods reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 60 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 15.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 450 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 100 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Bilirubin 80 μmol/l 2–17 μmol/l Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 30 IU/l 10–40 IU/l ALP 100 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Blood ﬁlm Polychromasia, spherocytes Which investigation will most likely lead to a conﬁrmed diagnosis?
explanation:
E Direct antiglobulin test Delayed transfusion reactions occur 5–10 days after transfusion and are almost invariably delayed haemolytic reactions due to the development of red cell (RBC) allo-antibodies. Clinical features are usually minimal but can include unexplained pyrexia, jaundice or unexplained drop in haemoglobin. Urinalysis shows urobilinogenuria and a blood shows fragile ballooned spherocytes. Diagnosis is conﬁrmed by a direct antiglobulin (Coombs’) test that detects the presence of antibody on the RBCs. The test is performed by adding anti-human globulin (AHG) (anti-Ig G and anticomplement) to the patient’s washed RBCs. A positive test results

in red cell agglutination. D Abdominal ultrasound scan (USS) Although blood loss as a result of the procedure may result in a haemoglobin of 60 g/l, the elevated bilirubin suggests that haemolysis as the more likely cause here. A Anti-cardiolipin antibodies Anti-cardiolipin antibodies lead to prolongation of APTT and increased risk of thrombosis, rather than haemolysis. B Serum haptoglobin Haptoglobin is decreased in conditions of haemolysis, although it does not conﬁrm the underlying cause. C Reticulocyte count Reticulocytes are elevated in patients with haemolysis, although they don’t indicate the underlying cause.

stem: A 65-year-old woman is admitted with a swollen left leg which, on venous Doppler, proved to be due to deep venous thrombosis (DVT). She was started on low-molecular weight heparin. The next day, she had an episode of left-sided chest pain and coughed up blood. A ventilation–perfusion scan demonstrated an area of low perfusion. Five days later (the day after discharge), she developed central chest discomfort and a painful swollen right lower limb. Investigation Result Normal values WCC 12 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 45 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Activated partial thromboplastin clotting time (APTT) 30 s 25 - 35 s What is the likely cause of this new problem?
options: Rupture of the right calf muscle
explanation:
D Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia Heparin-induced thrombosis is the most likely diagnosis here, although it occurs much more infrequently with low-molecular weight heparin than with unfractionated heparin. It is prudent not to miss this diagnosis since the treatment is to withhold heparin. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) with a new thrombosis is a clinical diagnosis and should be identiﬁed when the above clinical features are witnessed, failing which the patient may pro-

gress to a fatal thrombosis. Type 1 HIT usually occurs in the ﬁrst 48-72 h, and the platelet count rarely falls below 100 × 109/l. The platelet count should return to normal over the next 4 days and there is no increased risk of thromboembolism. Type 2 HIT is much rarer and usually occurs 5-10 days after treatment commencement, and the platelet count usually drops below 100 × 109/l to about 50 × 109/l. This case is therefore in keeping with type 2 immune-mediated HIT. Heparin should be stopped and alternative forms of anticoagulation may be required; for advice regarding best management, a haematologist should be consulted. Possible alternative forms of anti-coagulation would include lepirudin, argatroban or danaparoid. With regard to the timing of events, it is likely the PE is related to the original DVT, and the limb thrombosis to the HIT. C Ruptured right Baker’s cyst A ruptured Baker’s cyst occurs in a patient with pre-existing knee osteoarthritis, and is associated with pain and swelling behind the knee. A Spontaneous right limb DVT Given the timing, ﬁve days after commencing low-molecular weight heparin, a new spontaneous DVT is much less likely versus one related to HIT. B Cardiac embolism Cardiac embolism is associated with a cold, pulseless lower limb, rather than the appearance consistent with a DVT seen here. E Rupture of the right calf muscle Calf muscle rupture is associated with pain over the area of muscle where the rupture has occurred, and pain on ankle ﬂexion.

stem: A 39-year-old man is currently undergoing chemotherapy for malignant melanoma which has become disseminated, with spread to his lungs and liver. He has been stable with respect to symptoms over the past few weeks and is expecting to begin the next cycle of chemotherapy in seven days’ time. He is very concerned because he suffered a minor knee sprain slipping on some steps but now has a very large left knee haematoma. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 112 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 9.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 152 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 112 U/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 187 U/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 13 µmol/l < 17 µmol/l PT 12.3 s 10.6–14.9 s APTT (APTT) 54.2 s 22–41 s Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Acquired haemophilia Acquired haemophilia occurs because of autoantibody inhibitors directed against factor VIII. This leads to quite severe soft tissue haemorrhage, as here, in the face of what may seem like a relatively minor injury. A number of conditions are recognised to cause acquired haemophilia, including autoimmune disease and malignancies such as pancreatic, colon, breast cancers and malignant melanoma. The isolated rise in APTT in the face of a normal platelet count makes platelet-related disorders and vitamin K deﬁciency much less likely. B Chemotherapy-related platelet dysfunction The normal platelet count seen here counts against an acquired platelet disorder as the cause of this patient’s symptoms. C Dysﬁbrinogenaemia Dysﬁbrinogenaemia can be associated with both bleeding and an increased risk for thrombosis. Congenital dysﬁbrinogenaemia is well described and can be associated with major bleeding, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and renal amyloidosis. D Vitamin K deﬁciency Vitamin K deﬁciency is associated with a lack of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. This leads to an increased risk for bleeding and prolongation of PT, rather than the picture seen here. E Von Willebrand’s disease Acquired von Willebrand’s disease is seen more commonly in patients with hypothyroidism, and APTT may be in the normal range. Acquired von Willebrand’s disease is seen more commonly in patients with hypothyroidism.

stem: A 35-year-old man is referred to the clinic by his general practitioner. He gives a 12-month history of intermittent night sweats, weight loss, itching and chronic cough. There is no signiﬁcant reported GI disturbance. Most recently, he has noticed increasing shortness of breath on climbing the stairs, and has been suffering from an urticarial rash. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Eosinophils 3.0 × 10 /l or greater on 3 occasions in the last year 0.04–0.4 × 10 /l Creatinine (Cr) 128 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) Negative CXR Interstitial infiltrates and small bilateral pleural effusions Echocardiogram (Echo) Suggestive of restrictive cardiomyopathy Immunoglobulin
explanation:
B Hyper-eosinophilic syndrome This is a myeloproliferative disorder of unknown cause and is rare, occurring most commonly in men in the 30– 40-year-old age group. It is associated with a persistent and markedly raised peripheral blood eosinophil count. Lung involvement may occur, as may cardiovascular involvement with ﬁbrosis and restrictive cardiomyopathy, which may lead to mural thrombus formation and considerable morbidity and mortality. There may also be associated angioedema or urticaria. Treatment is with high-dose corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone 50 mg, which leads to a response in around 50% of cases). Steroid-sparing agents such as cyclophosphamide or azathioprine may also be of some value. In those patients who carry the FIP1L1/PDGFRA mutation, imatinib is the drug of choice. A Churg-Strauss syndrome 30–40% of patients with Churg–Strauss are positive for pANCA, and they have symptoms of asthma rather than merely the chronic cough seen here. Other features include mononeuritis multiplex, GI bleeds and glomerulonephritis, which aren’t seen here. C Acute eosinophilic pneumonia Acute eosinophilic pneumonia has a much more rapid onset of symptoms, with signiﬁcant evidence of respiratory failure within 7 days to 1 month from when features ﬁrst appear. D Chronic pulmonary eosinophilia The extra-pulmonary features seen here are inconsistent versus a diagnosis of chronic pulmonary eosinophilia. Hence this is much less likely to be the underlying diagnosis.

E Chronic parasitic infection Chronic parasitic infection is a possible cause of long-term eosinophilia, although there are no pointers in the scenario to suggest exposure to an infective agent. Other features such as GI disturbance would be expected in helminth infection.

stem: A 65-year-old gentleman presented to the Emergency Department with persistent nose and gum bleeding. He had also noticed some blurred vision and frontal headaches over the past few hours. On examination, he was pale and only his gums were actively bleeding. Neurological examination revealed bilateral horizontal nystagmus on left lateral gaze. Ophthalmic examination revealed bilateral decreased visual acuity and retinal haemorrhages. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 91 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 8 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 130 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Urea 10 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 170 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.8 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Phosphate (PO43-) 1.77 mmol/l 1.1 - 1.45 mmol/l Total protein 89 g/l 60 - 83 g/l Albumin 30 g/l 3.4 - 5.4 g/l PT 16 s 11 - 14 s Activated partial thromboplastin clotting time (APTT) 55 s 25 - 35 s Peripheral blood smear Rouleaux formation What is the most likely cause for his presentation?
explanation:
D Hyperviscosity syndrome Hyperviscosity syndrome (HVS) refers to the clinical sequelae of increased blood viscosity. Increased serum viscosity usually results from increased circulating serum immunoglobulins, and can be seen in such diseases as Waldenström macroglobulinaemia and multiple myeloma. HVS can also result from increased cellular blood components (typically white or red blood cells) in hyperproliferative states such as the leukaemias, polycythaemia and the myeloproliferative disorders. The clinical presentation in HVS consists principally of the triad of mucosal bleeding, visual changes and neurologic symptoms. Plasmapheresis is the treatment of choice. This removes the circulating paraproteins and

reduces the viscosity. A Hypercalcaemia The neurological symptoms and gum bleeding do not correspond to the clinical presentation of hypercalcaemia (lack of concentration, feeling of ‘pins and needles’). B Bernard–Soulier syndrome This is caused by a deﬁciency on the surface of the platelet of the glycoprotein Ib/IX receptor that results in a failure of platelets to stick together in a clump at the site of an injury. C Glanzmann thrombasthenia This results in a deﬁciency in platelet adhesion as a consequence of a deﬁciency of the surface protein glycoprotein IIb/IIIa. E Acute kidney disease Uraemic encephalopathy would not cause the neurological symptoms described in this scenario. Acute kidney disease usually presents with anorexia, nausea, restlessness, drowsiness, diminished ability to concentrate and slowed cognitive functions.

stem: A 64-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department with a history of increasing confusion and headaches. She is noted to have multiple bruises on her shins and arms. On examination, she has a temperature of 38 °C. There is evidence of a petechial rash over her chest. She is tachycardic and has a blood pressure of 110/65 mmHg. There is evidence of bronchial breathing at the right base and 1-cm palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 55 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 18 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 20 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l PT 24 s 11–14 s APTT (APTT) 46 s 25–35 s Fibrinogen 0.6 g/l 1.5–5.0 g/l Urea 6.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Glucose 10.0 mmol/l 3.9–7.1 mmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.36 mmol/l 2.2–2.7 mmol/l Albumin 35 g/l 35–55 g/l She is admitted and started on treatment with all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) due to suspected acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) and is covered for concurrent pneumonia with intravenous (IV) co-amoxiclav and oral clarithromycin. Initially, her fever settles; however, three days into her admission, she has a fever of 38.5 °C and progressive shortness of breath that gradually worsened. On examination, she has reduced air entry at the bases bilaterally and pitting oedema in the lower limbs bilaterally up to the level of the ankles. Her respiratory rate is 19 breaths per minute, with an oxygen saturation of 96%. What is the best step in management, given the likely diagnosis?
options: Switch co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin to piperacillin and tazobactam
explanation:
B Start high-dose dexamethasone The combined presentation of a chest infection, high white cell count and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is typical of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), which is a malignancy of the bone marrow characterised by a deﬁciency of mature blood cells in the myeloid cell line and an excess of immature cells called promyelocytes. It is considered a type of acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) and is classiﬁed as the M3 variant in the internationally accepted French–American–British (FAB) classiﬁcation. Typically, APL is due to a translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17 (t(15;17). The break in chromosome 15 disrupts the promyelocytic leukaemia (PML) gene, which encodes a transcription factor. The break in chromosome 17 interrupts the retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARα) gene, which regulates myeloid differentiation. The translocation creates a PML–RARα fusion gene, which leads to increased proliferation of promyelocytes. Treatment of APL differs from that for all other forms of AML. Most APL patients are now treated with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) which activates the retinoid receptor RAR and causes promyelocytes to differentiate, which deters them from proliferating. ATRA can induce complete remission in most patients with APL by stimulating the APL-blasts to mature. However, ATRA cannot eliminate the leukaemic clone and is, therefore, used in combination with chemotherapy, including an anthracycline drug. The use of ATRA or arsenic trioxide (ATO) puts patients at risk of differentiation syndrome (DS), a cytokine release syndrome seen in APL after initiation of differentiating agents. The features of DS are respiratory distress, pulmonary inﬁltrates, fever, weight gain, pleural effusion, renal failure, pericardial effusion, cardiac failure and hypotension. Management involves high-dose systemic steroids, such as dexamethasone 10 mg intravenous (IV) twice a day, alongside ventilatory and blood pressure support. There is no need to discontinue ATRA unless the case is severe. C Start IV furosemide This patient has pleural effusions and some evidence of peripheral ﬂuid overload which could be treated with diuretics. However, the cause here is DS, meaning that treatment with high-dose steroids is most appropriate, rather than treatment with diuretics. A Start a 1-unit blood transfusion This patient’s symptoms are most in keeping with differentiation

syndrome (DS). There is no evidence of blood loss that would require a blood transfusion and administration of blood products in an individual with evidence of ﬂuid overload should be attempted with caution. D Stop ATRA This patient has developed DS, a cytokine release syndrome seen in APL after initiation of differentiating agents such as ATRA or ATO. There is no need to discontinue ATRA in DS unless the case is severe. Even in severe cases where ATRA is discontinued, steroids need to be administered as DS can be fatal if untreated. E Switch co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin to piperacillin and tazobactam Although this patient has fever and respiratory distress, her chest signs indicate bilateral pleural effusions, with little evidence of worsening chest infection that would require escalation in her antibiotic regimen.

stem: A 55-year-old gentleman complained of a 2-month history of lower back pain. He had been feeling increasingly tired over the last few months and had noted weight loss of 1 stone. He had also noted some tingling in his hands and feet. On examination, he was found to have gynaecomastia, a palpable 2 cm liver edge and peripheral oedema. There was evidence of loss of pinprick and joint position sense to the mid-shins bilaterally, and diffuse hyperpigmentation of the extremities. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 96 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 130 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l MCV 86 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ Total protein 95 g/l 60 - 83 g/l Albumin 30 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Fasting Glucose 11 mmol/l < 5.9 mmol/l Thyroidstimulating hormone (TSH) 7.5 mu/l 0.4 - 5.0 mu/l Thyroxine (T4) 50 nmol/l 58 - 178 nmol/l What diagnosis best explains the patient’s presentation?
options: Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy and skin changes syndrome (POEMS)
explanation:
D Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy and skin changes syndrome (POEMS)

POEMS syndrome is a rare multi-system disease that occurs in the setting of plasma cell dyscrasia. The pathophysiology of the disease is not known; however, elevated levels of cytokines and growth factors have been implicated. The polyneuropathy associated with POEMS syndrome is a bilateral symmetric disturbance. It involves both motor and sensory nerves, begins distally and has a progressive proximal spread. Associated cranial or autonomic nerves are not involved. Both demyelination and axonal degeneration are noted. The liver, the lymph nodes, and the spleen are the organs most frequently involved. Multiple endocrinopathies have been associated with POEMS syndrome, and most patients have more than one endocrine abnormality. POEMS syndrome is seen in the setting of a plasma cell dyscrasia. Although many plasma cell disorders have been reported in patients with POEMS syndrome, most patients are seen with osteosclerotic myeloma or monoclonal gammopathy of unknown signiﬁcance (MGUS). Classic multiple myeloma is not usually associated with the disease. C Classical multiple myeloma This usually presents with bone pain, pathological fractures, weakness, anaemia, infection (often pneumococcal), hypercalcaemia, spinal cord compression or kidney disease. It can also be accompanied by hyperviscosity syndrome (mucosal bleeding, visual changes and neurological symptoms). A Non Hodgkin’s lymphoma Most patients present with lymphadenopathy. Indermediate- or high-grade lymphomas can also be accompanied by beta symptoms (weight loss, temperature >38 °C, night sweats). B Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinaemia This is usually accompanied by hyperviscosity syndrome (mucosal bleeding, visual changes and neurological symptoms). E Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia Patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (chronic lymphoid leukaemia, CLL) present with a wide range of symptoms and signs. Onset is insidious, and it is not unusual for CLL to be discovered incidentally after a blood cell count is performed for another reason; 25–50% of patients will be asymptomatic at time of presentation. Other signs include lymphadenopathy, hepatospenomegaly, petechiae due to low platelet count, and pallor due to anaemia.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the Haematology Clinic. He had a recent diagnosis of DVT following a long- haul ﬂight, for which he has completed three months of anticoagulation. There is no signiﬁcant past medical history. Investigations show that he has a heterozygous factor V Leiden mutation. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient's condition?
options: Advise on compression stockings to be worn daily
Commence low-dose aspirin prophylaxis to prevent recurrent thrombosis
Discuss lifestyle modiﬁcations to reduce thrombotic risk factors
Initiate lifelong anticoagulation therapy with a directacting oral anticoagulant
Initiate lifelong anticoagulation therapy with warfarin
explanation:
C Discuss lifestyle modiﬁcations to reduce thrombotic risk factors Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited cause of thrombophilia. Current guidelines state that, following a DVT, patients with factor V Leiden should be managed as those without thrombophilia. Therefore, the decision to continue anticoagulation should not be based on the presence of factor V Leiden alone. To reduce the risk of further thrombotic events, lifestyle modiﬁcations, such as smoking cessation, weight management, regular exercise and avoiding prolonged immobility, are important and should be discussed with the patient. E Initiate lifelong anticoagulation therapy with warfarin For the same reasons as initiating a lifelong direct-acting oral anticoagulant, patients with factor V Leiden do not necessarily need long-term anticoagulation based on the presence of thrombophilia alone. When considering the need for ongoing anticoagulation, a full account of their past medical history and risk factors for thrombosis should be considered. As this patient had a provoked DVT, without any other known risk factors, lifestyle modiﬁcations should be the initial management. A Advise on compression stockings to be worn daily Compression stockings reduce the risk of DVT and are given as prophylaxis, particularly for patients who are at a higher risk of thrombosis. However, it is not indicated as a form of long-term management for patients with a heterozygous factor V Leiden mutation. B Commence low-dose aspirin prophylaxis to prevent recurrent thrombosis Low-dose aspirin is typically used to reduce the risk of thrombosis in patients with signiﬁcant risk factors for ischaemic heart disease or cerebrovascular disease. It is not typically recommended for primary prevention in patients with a heterozygous factor V Leiden mutation. D Initiate lifelong anticoagulation therapy with a directacting oral anticoagulant In patients with factor V Leiden, initiating long-term anticoagulation should be based on the entire clinical picture, including the risk of further thrombosis and whether the patient had a provoked

or an unprovoked DVT. In this case, the patient had a provoked DVT. Therefore, initiating long-term anticoagulation is not indicated at this stage. Rather, lifestyle modiﬁcations should be given to reduce the risk of further thrombosis.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology Clinic for a routine physical examination. He has a history of heavy alcohol use but reports no recent symptoms. He takes no regular medications. Physical examination is notable for mild pallor but is otherwise unremarkable. Blood tests reveal the following: Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 110 g/l 135–175 g/l MCV 105 ﬂ 80–96 ﬂ WCC 5.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 210 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Vitamin B12 Normal 200–900 pg/ml Folate Low 3–15 ng/ml What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s macrocytosis?
explanation:
B Folate deﬁciency Folate deﬁciency is a common cause of macrocytosis, especially in patients with alcohol use, which can impair folate absorption and metabolism. Low folate levels directly correlate with increased red cell volume and macrocytic anaemia. C Hypothyroidism Hypothyroidism can cause macrocytosis, although this is less common and usually occurs alongside other symptoms of hypothyroidism. The vignette does not suggest hypothyroid symptoms and thyroid function tests were not included, making this less likely. A Vitamin B12 deﬁciency Vitamin B12 deﬁciency often leads to macrocytic anaemia. However, the patient’s vitamin B12 levels are within the normal range, making this an unlikely cause of his macrocytosis. D Myelodysplastic syndrome Myelodysplastic syndrome can present with macrocytosis, particularly in older patients. However, there are typically abnormalities in other cell lines, such as anaemia with low WCC or PLT count, or a higher mean corpuscular Hb concentration. Given that this patient's other counts are within the normal range, folate deﬁcien-

cy remains as the most likely diagnosis here. E Chronic liver disease Chronic liver disease can cause macrocytosis due to changes in lipid composition of red cell membranes, but this patient’s LFTs are not provided and no other speciﬁc signs of liver disease are noted. Although alcohol use is a contributing factor to both liver disease and folate deﬁciency, the latter is more directly implicated here.

stem: You are called by a general practitioner who wants to discuss a case of transient thrombocytopenia with you. His patient is a 23year-old woman who presented to him with tiredness; he arranged a routine full blood count, liver function tests and urea and electrolytes. The ethylene diaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) sample revealed a platelet count of 40 × 109/l, with clumping seen on the ﬁlm. A repeat citrate sample revealed a count of 150 × 109/l. Her white blood count (WBC), haemoglobin and blood ﬁlm were all unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: D Do nothing EDTA-induced platelet clumping is thought to occur in around 0.3% of patients. It is not indicative of any underlying disease but is thought to be due to an antibody present in the sample, which promotes platelet aggregation in the presence of EDTA. The normal platelet count in the presence of a citrated sample (normally used to assess clotting) conﬁrms the diagnosis. Because the platelet count normalises in the citrate sample, there is no indication of an underlying disease. B Aspirin The normalisation of the platelet count suggests EDTA-induced platelet clumping, which requires no further treatment. A Abdominal ultrasound There is nothing in the history to suggest any signiﬁcant abnormality, and the normalisation of the platelet count suggests EDTAinduced platelet clumping, which requires no further treatment or investigation. C Bone marrow aspirate This would be an appropriate investigation if the patient had persistent thrombocytopenia, but as there is evidence of EDTA-induced platelet clumping, no further investigation is required. E Oral prednisolone Glucocorticoids would be a treatment for immune thrombocytopenia. The normalisation of the platelet count suggests EDTAinduced platelet clumping, which requires no further treatment.

stem: A 21-year-old man with a background of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presents to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of lethargy, nausea and vomiting. He was last seen in the Haematology Outpatient Clinic one week ago after completing his induction regime of chemotherapy. There is no other past medical history of note, and he has no allergies. On examination, his temperature is 37.8 °C with a heart rate of 105 bpm and a BP of 100/70 mmHg. Auscultation of his chest is clear, and his abdomen is soft with generalised tenderness. Investigation Results a week ago Results today Hb 88 g/l 80 g/l WCC 44.7 × 109/l 44.7 × 109/l PLT 71 × 109/l 21 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 142 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 5.9 mmol/l Urea 5.1 mmol/l 16.2 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 80 µmol/l 255 µmol/l Lactate dehydrogenase 300 U/l 755 U/l Adjusted calcium 2.3 mmol/l 2.0 mmol/l Phosphate 1.2 mmol/l 1.6 mmol/l Uric acid 200 µmol/l 480 µmol/l CRP 44 mg/l 50 mg/l Given the most likely diagnosis, what is the deﬁnitive treatment for this patient?
explanation:
D Rasburicase This patient has a diagnosis of tumour lysis syndrome, given the history of recent chemotherapy use and the onset of nausea, vomiting, lethargy and signiﬁcantly deranged electrolytes. The destruction of tumour cells causes the release of intracellular contents into the circulation that, in large quantities, cause acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmias and cerebral dysfunction. Tumour lysis syndrome can be classiﬁed into clinical and laboratory subtypes. Laboratory tumour lysis syndrome is deﬁned as the presence of two or more metabolic abnormalities: hyperkalaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia. Clinical tumour lysis syndrome is deﬁned as the presence of one or more clinical manifestations of the disease (eg acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmias). A closer look at this patient’s laboratory results shows evidence of clinical and laboratory tumour lysis syndrome. Tumour lysis syndrome is an oncological emergency and must be treated promptly. Treatment includes intravenous ﬂuid hydration with isotonic solution and rasburicase. Rasburicase is a recombinant form of the urate oxidase enzyme that transforms uric acid in a more soluble product that is more easily eliminated by the kidney. It is effective in both the treatment and prevention of tumour lysis syndrome. B Calcium gluconate Calcium gluconate is a reasonable management choice, given the combined hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia. However, this treatment is only effective at treating these isolated electrolyte dis-

Normal value 115–155 g/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l 135–145 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l 50–120 µmol/l < 250 U/l 2.2–2.6 mmol/l 0.8–1.5 mmol/l 200–430 µmol/l < 10 mg/l turbances. Rather, rasburicase is the most deﬁnitive management for treating established tumour lysis syndrome. A Allopurinol Allopurinol is used in the prophylaxis of tumour lysis syndrome. However, it is not used in the management of established tumour lysis syndrome which is clear here, given the onset of symptoms and deranged biochemistry results. C Hypotonic intravenous ﬂuids Intravenous ﬂuid administration is important in the prevention and management of tumour lysis syndrome. However, guidelines recommend initiating isotonic solutions, which are better at remaining within the intravascular system. However, hypotonic ﬂuids are able to pass freely into the intracellular spaces and have little impact on supporting the intravascular system and improving glomerular ﬁltration. E Urinary alkalinisation Urinary alkalinisation involves initiating sodium bicarbonate solution to prevent the ionisation of acidic substances and improve renal excretion. This method is typically used for salicylate overdose. However, urinary alkalinisation is not recommended in the management of tumour lysis syndrome.

stem: A 35-year-old patient is 1-month post-allogeneic bone marrow transplantation when her condition deteriorates. She has developed a maculopapular rash on the palms of her hands and the soles of her feet, and has become jaundiced. The patient has also been having bouts of vomiting and diarrhoea and, as a result, has lost weight. She is currently taking ciclosporin. Investigation Result Normal value Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 9.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 79 µmol/l 1–22 µmol/l ALP 310 u/l 30–150 u/l ALT 55 u/l 7–55 u/l Albumin 27 g/l 35–55 g/l Which of the following investigations should be ordered to guide treatment of the underlying condition?
options: Upper gastrointestinal (GI) tract endoscopy with biopsies
explanation:
B Cytomegalovirus (CMV) polymerase chain reaction

(PCR) The patient has acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). This presents within 100 days of an allogeneic bone marrow transplantation with a skin rash (which can progress to erythroderma), liver dysfunction (cholestatic) and involvement of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. It remains a serious cause of mortality and morbidity in bone marrow transplant recipients. Patients are staged according to the severity of involvement of the skin, liver and GI tract. Initial aggressive treatment with intravenous (IV) corticosteroids is recommended. Anti-T cell antibodies, such as OKT3, have been used in patients with resistant disease, as have rituximab and anti-thymocyte globulin. The diagnosis of GVHD is based primarily on clinical symptoms and manifestations. It is essential that infective causes of patient symptoms are ruled out due to the level of immunosuppression and the fact that identiﬁcation of infection would change patient management. Therefore, blood, urine and stool cultures and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for cytomegalovirus (CMV), human herpesvirus 6, adenovirus and parvovirus should be ordered for any patient presenting with symptoms of GVHD. Therefore, CMV PCR would be the most appropriate investigation here, as the remaining options are likely to provide more information about the degree of organ involvement of GVHD but would not signiﬁcantly change management. A Autoimmune liver panel The main hepatobiliary differentials in cases of graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) are viral hepatitis, drug- induced hepatotoxicity, veno-occlusive disease of the liver, acalculous cholecystitis and total parenteral nutrition (TPN)-associated cholestasis (if patients are receiving TPN at the time of symptoms). Autoimmune disease of the liver is an unlikely differential in the setting of a recent bone marrow transplantation, not least due to the administration of immunosuppressive medications. C Computed tomography (CT) abdomen In patients with GI tract involvement of GVHD, computed tomography (CT) abdomen may reveal diffuse colitis or feature of ileus. A CT abdomen may also reveal ascites due to abdominal serositis. However, these features are not speciﬁc to GVHD and therefore, their presence on imaging is unlikely to affect the management of the underlying condition. D Skin biopsy As the likely diagnosis in this patient is GVHD, skin biopsy is likely to show a lymphocytic inﬁltrate in the dermis. A tissue biopsy of any of the affected organs in GVHD may be ordered after appropriate laboratory and imaging studies to deﬁnitively rule in or out the diagnosis. However, it is important that basic laboratory tests are ordered ﬁrst in this patient to rule out other diagnoses which would change this patient’s management. E Upper gastrointestinal (GI) tract endoscopy with biopsies Chronic GVHD may reveal diagnostic features on upper GI endos-

copy such as oesophageal web, stricture or concentric rings. However, as this patient is suffering from acute GVHD, endoscopy will not be of value here to guide further management.

stem: A 50-year-old man with aggressive lymphoma is receiving combination chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and prednisolone. At the start of therapy he had several cervical and axillary lymph nodes, none larger than 2 cm. Several studies of investigational products are available, and he asks you about the terminology of drug development. In terms of the process of researching a new drug in the oncology setting, which of the following best applies to phase I studies?
options: The aim of a phase I study is to assess initial therapeutic activity
Phase I studies are conducted once an initial therapeutic effect in humans is demonstrated
It is common to combine phase I and II studies
Phase I studies usually recruit several hundred patients
Phase I studies are classically randomised controlled and double-blinded
explanation:
C It is common to combine phase I and II studies Phase I studies study safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, whereas phase II studies study whether there is a therapeutic response. These two phases, in practice, are often combined. D Phase I studies usually recruit several hundred patients Phase I studies study safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in an investigational agent’s ﬁrst usage in human subjects. They are not designed to assess therapeutic response, and patients should be aware of this as part of the consent process. As such, they tend to be small trials with only a few patients recruited to them. A The aim of a phase I study is to assess initial therapeutic activity Phase II studies assess whether or not there is a therapeutic response, whereas phase I studies assess safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (which may include initial hints as to the efﬁcacy of the intervention).

B Phase I studies are conducted once an initial therapeutic effect in humans is demonstrated Phase III studies are performed once initial safety and efﬁcacy evaluation is completed, and usually compare the drug with an alternative. E Phase I studies are classically randomised controlled and double-blinded Usually phase III and sometimes phase II trials are randomised controlled trials. Within the oncology trial setting, sponsors do not need to be blinded. They can be privy to all information relating to the trial, including the treatment allocated to patients and their outcomes during the trial.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with headaches, lethargy and severe intractable back pain. He also recently suffered left lower lobe pneumonia. Over the past few days, his problems have signiﬁcantly worsened and he is now unable to keep any food or ﬂuids down and is vomiting several times during the day. On examination, his BP is 162/95 mmHg and he looks pale. His pulse is 90/min and regular and there are bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 101 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 147 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 6.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 890 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Viscosity 2.78 mPa/s 1.50–1.72 mPa/s Total protein 110 g/l 60-80 g/l Albumin P-ANCA 30 g/l + 35–55 g/l Urine Protein++ USS renal tract Bilateral normal-sized kidneys, no obstruction Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
