A Multiple myeloma Whilst we are not given a serum calcium result here, the clinical history of severe backpain, headaches, lethargy and an episode of sepsis is typical of myeloma. The clinical ﬁndings of decreased serum albumin, marked elevation in total protein and proteinuria further support the diagnosis. Serum electrophoresis is likely to

reveal a paraprotein band. Slightly confusingly, p-ANCA positivity is associated with both multiple myeloma and vasculitis. A period of dehydration associated with the pneumonia may well have been enough to precipitate acute on chronic kidney disease here. B Granulomatosis with polyangiitis Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is associated with positive cANCA. P-ANCA positivity is associated with multiple myeloma. C Polyarteritis nodosa Polyarteritis nodosa may be associated with renal vasculitis, although signiﬁcant proteinuria would be unexpected in the absence of evidence of haematuria. D Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease Anti-GBM disease is associated with pulmonary haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis, rather than the picture here of acute on chronic kidney disease with proteinuria. E Waldenström’s macrogammaglobulinaemia Waldenström’s is associated with an IgM paraprotein band as well as features of hyperviscosity syndrome and cryoglobulinaemia. Although this patient has headaches which may ﬁt with Waldenstrom’s, counting against this is the back pain which suggests bony deposits of myeloma, and of course bone involvement isn’t classically described in Waldenstrom’s.

stem: A 71-year-old man is found to be anaemic on routine testing when he changes to a new general practitioner (GP). He has hypertension which is treated with lisinopril and amlodipine and has complained of back pain for the last 6 months. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 132/72 while his pulse is 85 bpm and regular. There is mild bilateral pitting oedema of the ankles. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 108 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 11.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 187 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 105 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 28 g/l 35–55 g/l Total protein 61 g/l 60–83 g/l Which of the following would ﬁt best with a diagnosis of symptomatic myeloma?
options: Femoral and lumbar spine lytic lesions on skeletal survey
8% clonal plasma cells on bone marrow sampling
explanation: B Femoral and lumbar spine lytic lesions on skeletal survey Criteria for diagnosis of symptomatic myeloma were drawn up in 2015 and are listed below: Symptomatic myeloma diagnosis criteria: • Monoclonal plasma cells in bone marrow (aspirate or trephine) ≥ 10% • Serum paraprotein ≥ 30 g/l (if IgM paraprotein exclude lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma). • Evidence of end-organ damage that can be attributed to myeloma. This is termed myeloma-related organ or tissue injury (ROTI) and commonly called the CRAB criteria: o C: hypercalcaemia (corrected Ca2+ >0.25 mmol/l above normal or > 2.75 mmol/l) o R: renal impairment (no other cause) o A: anaemia (Hb < 100 g/l or more than 20 g below normal, not due to other causes) o B: bone lesions (lytic lesions or osteoporosis). A Creatinine 105 µmol/l It is within the normal range and thus would be unusual in symptomatic myeloma. C Hb of 108 g/l It would be insufﬁcient to meet the diagnostic criteria for symptomatic myeloma. D 8% clonal plasma cells on bone marrow sampling This is more consistent with monoclonal gammopathy of unknown signiﬁcance – in myeloma, the clonal plasma cells should be >10% on bone marrow biopsy. E Urine negative for protein Proteinuria is a feature of symptomatic multiple myeloma.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with an episode of epistaxis, which settles with conservative management. Apparently, she has had a recent ﬂu-like illness. On examination, she has a number of petechiae and some bruising where she has taken knocks or bangs to her legs. She is on no signiﬁcant medication and has an unremarkable past medical history. It is understood that her aunt had a splenectomy as a young adult. She is offered treatment with steroids, but she declines because she has heard that there are potential side effects. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 110 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 16.0 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 105 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Reinforce that prednisolone 60 mg daily is the only effective treatment
explanation: C Intravenous immunoglobulin therapy This patient has idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Over recent years, a familial propensity for the development of ITP has been identiﬁed, although the particular gene for susceptibility is yet to be identiﬁed. Steroid therapy is often offered ﬁrst-line to treat ITP. A second-line option is intravenous immunoglobulin therapy, which, at the cellular level, blocks the binding sites for autoantibodies that are causing platelet destruction. D Reinforce that prednisolone 60 mg daily is the only effective treatment First-line treatment involves the use of high-dose corticosteroids. Alternative options also exist, including intravenous immunoglobulin, which would be the next most appropriate treatment for an acute presentation. Second-line treatments include rituximab and/or splenectomy. A Azathioprine 100 mg daily Azathioprine is a potential steroid-sparing agent in the treatment of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in patients who are unable to signiﬁcantly reduce their dose of prednisolone without a fall in platelet count. B Platelet transfusion Platelet transfusions may be required for uncontrolled haemorrhage, although they do not reduce the underlying autoantibody burden resulting in platelet destruction. They are not therefore the initial intervention of choice. E Splenectomy Splenectomy is required for patients who do not respond to immune intervention for treatment of thrombocytopenia.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is reviewed in the Haematology Clinic with a 4-week history of increased fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. She complains of feeling frequently tired and has been unable to attend her university lectures due to exhaustion and recurrent chest infections. There is no past medical history of note, and she takes no regular medications. On examination, she is afebrile. Her heart rate is 101 bpm and regular with a BP of 122/70mmHg. Auscultation of her chest is clear with oxygen saturation of 94% on air. There is palpable nontender cervical lymphadenopathy and a marginally palpable liver edge. Investigation Results Normal value Hb 78 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 24.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 20 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.1 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 80 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 4 mg/l < 10 mg/l Bone marrow aspirate Hypercellularity with 25% lymphoblast inﬁltration Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is an indicator of poor prognosis?
explanation:
C T(9:22) translocation This patient has a likely diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia given the acute onset of lethargy and recurrent infections, combined with the examination ﬁndings of cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatomegaly. The blood results are also suggestive of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with anaemia, thrombocytopenia and an elevated white cell count with predominant blast cells on bone marrow aspirate. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is a common childhood malignancy that generally has a good prognosis. However, there are markers of poor prognosis that include the presence of the T(9:22) translocation that codes for the Philadelphia chromosome. The Philadelphia chromosome is linked to increased resistance to standard chemotherapeutic regimes in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and, therefore, predicts a poorer outcome. A Female sex Female sex is a good prognostic indicator in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. In contrast, male sex is a poor prognostic marker. B T(12;21) translocation The t(12;21) translocation, which is responsible for the TELAML1 (ETV6-RUNX1) fusion gene, is common in childhood

ALL but rare in adults. It confers a good risk proﬁle. D WCC below 30 × 109/l A WCC of under 30 × 109/l is a good prognostic indicator for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Poor prognostic markers for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia include over 30 × 109/l or over 100 × 109/l for B- and T-cell lineages, respectively. E Young age Young age is a good prognostic indicator for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. In adults, those aged over 35 years are considered to have a higher risk of poorer outcomes.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presents with a 12 hour history of a sudden loss of power in the left arm. She is previously ﬁt and well, smokes ﬁve cigarettes daily and is on the combined oral contraceptive pill. Her grandfather had a stroke in his eighties, and she has ﬁve siblings who are well. Examination shows increased tone and brisk reﬂexes in the left arm. There is a 12 cm splenomegaly. Computed tomography of the head is normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 123 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 18.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 1035 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l
explanation:
D Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML) The history is compatible with a cerebrovascular accident, and the high platelet count is likely to be the cause. Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (a myeloproliferative disorder) usually manifests with thrombocytosis at presentation, usually with a raised white cell count that is grossly left-shifted (where promyelocytes, metamyelocytes and myelocytes are all visible on the peripheral blood). There is usually marked splenomegaly and the bone marrow is nearly always positive for the Philadelphia chromosome (the abnormally small chromosome 22 is the ‘Philadelphia’ chromo-

some). The absolute basophil count is often increased in myeloproliferative disorders. A Essential thrombocythaemia with cerebrovascular accident Essential thrombocythaemia can present with splenomegaly, but where the Philadelphia chromosome is found the disease is always classiﬁed as chronic myeloid leukaemia. There would not be a translocation of chromosomes 9 and 22 in essential thrombocythaemia. B Antiphospholipid syndrome with reactive thrombocytosis Platelet counts are characteristically low in anti-phospholipid syndrome, but are high in all the myeloproliferative disorders such as CML. Also, there would not be a translocation of chromosomes 9 and 22 in anti-phospholipid syndrome. C Cerebral lupus with reactive thrombocytosis Central lupus usually presents with low platelets and pancytopenia. It can give rise to strokes, seizures or changes to the mental state. There would not be a translocation of chromosomes 9 and 22 in lupus. E Acute myeloid leukaemia Acute myeloid leukaemia occurs when there is a maturational arrest in bone marrow cells early on in their development, leading to a variety of blood test results. These include thrombocytopenia, anaemia and low, high or normal white cell counts. Circulating blasts are seen on a blood ﬁlm and there is no translocation of chromosomes with AML.

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with fever and reduced consciousness. Her past medical history includes type II diabetes, for which she takes metformin, gliclazide and insulin therapy. She is treated with intravenous ﬂuids and antibiotics and transferred to the Medical Ward. After 48 hours into her admission, the nursing team inform the doctors that her condition has deteriorated. She has a heart rate of 130 bpm and blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg. Her temperature remains elevated at 39.1 °C. She is ﬂuid-resuscitated with 4 × 500-ml boluses of 0.9% sodium chloride. Her repeat observations show a heart rate of 120 bpm and blood pressure of 88/62 mmHg. Repeat investigations: Investigation On admission Today Normal value Haemoglobin 144 g/l 150 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count 16.1 × 109/l 15.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 406 × 109/l 555 × 109/l 150–450 × 109/l Creatinine 125 μmol/l μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l C-reactive protein 340 mg/l 310 mg/l < 10 mg/l Glucose 12.2 mmol/l 8.1 mmol/l 4–7 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Speak to Microbiology about escalating antibiotic regime
explanation: D Noradrenaline infusion Initiating noradrenaline therapy would be appropriate here. This patient is showing signs of septic shock with fever, tachycardia and hypotension. Patients who are unresponsive to 2 litres of ﬂuid resuscitation should be discussed with the Intensive Care Unit for consideration of vasopressor support to help maintain a stable blood pressure. B Haemoﬁltration Haemoﬁltration would not be appropriate, as although this patient shows signs of impaired renal function, this is likely secondary to reduced organ perfusion secondary to septic shock. Indications for haemoﬁltration include refractory hyperkalaemia and acidosis, uraemia and ﬂuid overload. These features are not seen in this patient. A Dopamine infusion In patients who remain hypotensive despite adequate ﬂuid resuscitation, appropriate antibiotic choice and noradrenaline, the addition of a second or third agent to noradrenaline may be required (eg adrenaline, dobutamine, vasopressin), with little data to support agent selection. Some studies showed improved survival with dobutamine. C Intravenous hydrocortisone Routine use of glucocorticoids should not be used in patients with sepsis. Hydrocortisone may have a role in the presence of severe sepsis not responding to adequate ﬂuid resuscitation and vasopressors. E Speak to Microbiology about escalating antibiotic regime This patient has signs of ongoing sepsis, as evidenced by her raised inﬂammatory markers and ongoing hypotension. Although it is possible that the initial antibiotic regime is inadequate in controlling her infection, this patient currently has signs of septic shock which must be addressed ﬁrst. Therefore, initiating a noradrenaline infusion takes priority over escalating antibiotics with Microbiology.

stem: An 89-year-old woman is an inpatient recovering from communityacquired pneumonia. She is on apixaban for atrial ﬁbrillation and has been put on intravenous ampicillin since admission 48 hours ago. While on the ward, she falls and hits her head. A computed tomography (CT) head shows evidence of a subdural haemorrhage which has caused a midline shift. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral vitamin K 5 mg or intravenous (IV) vitamin K 0.5–1 mg
Prothrombin complex concentrate containing factors II, VII, IX and X
Stop apixaban and repeat CT head after 24 hours to monitor for bleed expansion
explanation: D Prothrombin complex concentrate containing factors II, VII, IX and X Prothrombin complex concentrate is extremely useful for rapidly reversing over-anticoagulation. It is used if there is a lifethreatening bleed in a patient taking apixaban, eg following an acute large subdural haemorrhage. A Cryoprecipitate 10 units Cryoprecipitate contains higher levels of factor VIII and ﬁbrinogen. Its use is therefore limited mainly to the treatment of dysﬁbrinogenaemia or hypoﬁbrinogenaemia. B Fresh frozen plasma 15 ml/kg Fresh frozen plasma at a dose of 15 ml/kg is unlikely to raise coagulation factors above 20%. Higher doses, while more likely to correct adequately, can cause ﬂuid overload. Fresh frozen plasma is not virally inactivated and can cause transfusion complications such as transfusion-related acute lung injury. As such, other options for acute reversal of anticoagulation are preferred. C Oral vitamin K 5 mg or intravenous (IV) vitamin K 0.5–1 mg Vitamin K is appropriate for patients who are taking warfarin therapy and require reversal of their anticoagulation. E Stop apixaban and repeat CT head after 24 hours to monitor for bleed expansion A subdural haemorrhage in a patient taking apixaban is an indication for urgent reversal of anticoagulation.

stem: A confused 68-year-old man was brought to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of severe headaches, blurred vision and spontaneous gum bleeding. Prior to his acute presentation, he had been generally unwell for several months with malaise and weight loss. On examination, he was drowsy and had widespread lymphadenopathy and a palpable spleen. Heart sounds were normal and his chest was clear to auscultation. Ophthalmoscopy revealed several retinal haemorrhages. There were no focal neurological signs. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 100 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 3.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 130 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 170 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l MCV 96 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Urea 7.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l ESR 90 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Blood ﬁlm Rouleaux for- mation Serum immunoglobulins tests reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Immunoglobulin
explanation:
D Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinaemia This man has a hyperviscosity syndrome, which occurs when the plasma viscosity rises to a level at which the micro-circulation is impaired (typically >5). Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinaemia is the most common cause of this. Waldenstrom’s is a lymphoplasmacytoid malignancy, which tends to occur in older men. There is a recently identiﬁed genetic component with a high percentage of patients carrying the MYD88 gene. It usually presents with peripheral lymph node enlargement, enlarged spleen and symptoms of bone marrow inﬁltration, and is associated with an IgM paraprotein. The high circulating levels of IgM paraprotein form aggregates therefore increase the viscosity of the blood, leading to hyperviscosity syndrome. Criteria for diagnosis of Waldenström's macroglobulinemia (WM) include: 1. IgM monoclonal gammopathy that excludes chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and Mantle cell lymphoma 2. Evidence of anaemia, systemic symptoms, hyperviscosity, enlarged lymph nodes or hepatomegaly orand/or splenomegaly that can be attributed to an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder. Treatment is with alkylating agents or doxorubicin-containing regimes. Plasmapheresis is used for hyperviscosity due to IgM levels. Less common causes include myeloma (immunoglobulin A (IgA) or IgM paraprotein), polycythaemia or leukaemia (leucostasis). Bt Multiple myeloma Although hyperviscosity syndrome is occasionally present with multiple myeloma, most patients present with bone pain, pathological fractures, signs of hypercalcaemia, kidney disease and anaemia. IgM multiple myeloma can sometimes be difﬁcult to distinguish from WM, but the systemic symptoms usually point towards one or the other.

A Tuberculous meningitis This patient has no history of exposure to tuberculosis. TB meningitis is difﬁcult to diagnose. It usually spreads from another organ (e.g. lung) to form micro-abscesses in the meninges, and it has an insidious onset. Fevers and headaches would present early on, but later symptoms such as confusion, drowsiness and malaise arise. C Herpes simplex encephalitis Usually as a result of herpes simplex type 1 in adults, this presents with signs affecting the temporal and frontal lobes; these include confusion, personality change, drowsiness and headache. There may be seizures. This pattern of symptoms does not correlate with the patient in the question. E Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia CLL has an insidious onset and is often discovered incidentally. Those with presenting symptoms may have enlarged lymph nodes, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, fatgue, night sweats and recurrent infections. The blood ﬁlm would show smudge cells, large atypical lymphocytes and pro-lymphocytes. WCC is usually high with a high number of lymphocytes, unlike the patient in this scenario who has low WCC.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with breathlessness. He had a bone marrow transplant for acute myeloid leukaemia four months ago and needs regular blood transfusions. He thinks that he might be anaemic now and is asking for a transfusion to be arranged. Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 73 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 3.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 103 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 1.0 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Blood ﬁlm Coombs’ test Unremarkable Negative Cytomegalovirus (CMV) bone marrow donor status Negative CMV bone marrow recipient pretransplant status Negative What type of blood should be arranged?
options: Two units of ABO-matched blood from a family member
Two units of CMV-negative crossmatched blood
Two units of human leukocyte antigen-matched blood from a family member
Two units of irradiated, CMV-negative red cells
Two units of irradiated red cells
explanation:
E Two units of irradiated red cells

Irradiated blood is indicated in patients with cellular immunodeﬁciency post-stem cell transplant, those on purine analogue therapy (eg ﬂudarabine), and those with Hodgkin’s disease and congenital immunodeﬁciencies. It is to prevent engraftment by viable T lymphocytes in the donor and causing transfusion-associated graft- versus-host disease. Irradiation of blood products does not affect their quality. Patients should be informed that they need irradiated blood products and given an information card. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a transfusion- transmitted infection that can be fatal in stem cell transplant recipients. Transmission of CMV has dropped markedly with the advent of universal leukodepletion of all blood products. There is a reasonable ﬁeld of evidence that suggests, in patients who underwent haemopoietic stem cell transplantation, CMV-negative red cells do not lead to any reduction in transmission of CMV, when compared to irradiated products which are not known to be CMV-negative. C Two units of human leukocyte antigen-matched blood from a family member Non-cytomegalovirus (CMV)-screened blood runs the risk of transmission of CMV, and lack of irradiation runs the risk of the unit containing viable white blood cells which could initiate a graft-versus-host disease response. A Two units of ABO-matched blood from a family member Because of previous transfusions, the likelihood of mismatching and a subsequent transfusion reaction is very high so this would not be appropriate for this patient. B Two units of CMV-negative crossmatched blood This would not be appropriate as it runs the risk of human leukocyte antigen mismatch and the presence of T cells in the donor. D Two units of irradiated, CMV-negative red cells There are several trials that demonstrate that there is no advantage to the use of CMV-negative products vs irradiated CMV-positive products. These products are in short supply and should be saved for use elsewhere such as in elective transfusions during pregnancy.

stem: A 20-year-old woman is reviewed in the Haematology Clinic for a follow-up appointment. She has a diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and has recently completed a cycle of consolidation therapy. For the last week, she has noticed a tingling sensation in her ﬁngers and toes. On examination, there is reduced sensation in a glove-and-stocking distribution over her upper and lower limbs. Her cranial nerves are intact. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s presentation?
explanation: E Vincristine This patient has presented with tingling in her ﬁngers and toes combined with reduced sensation in a glove- and-stocking distribution. This is suggestive of peripheral neuropathy. Of the chemotherapeutic agents used to treat acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, vincristine is the most common agent causing peripheral neuropathy. Vincristine is associated with a painless peripheral neuropathy, and other side effects include constipation and jaw pain. D PEG-asparaginase PEG-asparaginase disrupts protein synthesis in tumour cells and has a number of side effects including pancytopenia, hypersensitivity reactions, hepatoxicity, cerebral toxicity and pancreatitis. However, peripheral neuropathy is not common. A Cytarabine Cytarabine interferes with pyrimidine synthesis with side effects including alopecia, pancytopenia and gastrointestinal upset. Peripheral neuropathy is not a common side-effect of this medication. B Doxorubicin Doxorubicin is an anthracycline chemotherapeutic agent associated with myocardial toxicity. There are a variety of other side effects including pancytopenia and mucositis. However, it is not a common cause of peripheral neuropathy. C Mercaptopurine Mercaptopurine is an immunosuppressant used in the maintenance phase of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and other inﬂammatory conditions such as inﬂammatory bowel disease. Common side effects include bone marrow suppression and hepatic dysfunction. However, peripheral neuropathy is not common.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with right upper quadrant pain and swelling of her abdomen over the course of the past week. She is normally completely well, and her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. She takes an occasional glass of wine and is a non-smoker and admits to drug use on two occasions as a student. On examination, her blood pressure is 135/85 mmHg and her pulse is 82 bpm and regular. She has moderate ascites and has a tender liver edge in the right upper quadrant. There is mild jaundice. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 9.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 mmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 132 U/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 178 U/l 30–130 IU/l Bilirubin 32 mmol/l 2–17 µmol/l PT 17.3 s 10.6–14.9 s APTT (APTT) 48.2 s 22–41 s Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Hepatic vein thrombosis There are a number of clues to the underlying diagnosis here – the acute nature of the hepatic decompensation, use of the oral contraceptive pill, and prolonged APTT – raising the possibility of underlying anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome. The prolonged PT is consistent with hepatic dysfunction. Ascitic tap looking for high protein content and ultrasound scanning are the investigations of choice. Local thrombolysis and venous stenting have been attempted in specialist centres. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) may be required long term for patients with persistent symptoms of hepatic decompensation. A Autoimmune hepatitis Autoimmune hepatitis is more likely to present with chronic lethargy and itching, rather than the acute presentation here. Antismooth muscle antibodies and anti-LKM1 antibodies are frequently seen in patients with autoimmune hepatitis, and high-dose prednisolone is the intervention of choice. C Hepatitis A Hepatitis A is associated with a prodromal ﬂu-like illness, often accompanied by diarrhoea. A marked elevation in transaminases, consistent with hepatocellular degeneration, is seen. D Hepatitis B Although this patient does have a history of injecting drug abuse, acute presentation with hepatic decompensation would be very unusual. The condition is diagnosed either with abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) on routine testing or when patients present with symptoms consistent with chronic cirrhosis. E Hepatitis C Like hepatitis B, hepatitis C presents with evidence of chronic liver disease or with abnormal LFTs discovered on routine testing,

rather than the acute presentation here.

stem: A 49-year-old white woman presents to a locum GP to ﬁnd out the results of some blood investigations performed by her own GP. She was found to have splenomegaly on a routine examination when she visited her GP, with feelings of excessive tiredness and fatigue. Her blood ﬁlm had shown elevated basophils and eosinophils with poikilocytes and normoblasts. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 110 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 38.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 119 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Which diagnosis would ﬁt the above data?
explanation: B Chronic myeloid leukaemia Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is one of the myeloproliferative disorders and results from an uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid cells. It is an acquired abnormality involving the haematopoietic stem cell and a reciprocal chromosomal translocation, resulting in the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome. This chromosome is present in the granulocyte, RBC and platelet precursors of >95% of patients with CML. Poikilocytes are variably shaped erythrocytes. Of the conditions listed, the only one which would cause such a marked elevation of the WCC, thrombocytopenia and mild anaemia is CML. A Sideroblastic anaemia Sideroblastic anaemia is associated with the formation of ring sideroblasts, because of defective incorporation of iron into red blood cells. C Polycythaemia rubra vera PCRV is associated with predominant elevation in haemoglobin, rather than the marked elevation in white count seen here. D Essential thrombocythaemia Essential thrombocythaemia is primarily associated with an increase in platelet count, rather than the increase in white count seen here. E Thalassaemia Thalassaemia would not account for the marked elevation in white count with immature red blood cells seen on the ﬁlm here.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents to the Haematology Clinic with progressive fatigue, weight loss and recurrent infections over the past three months. Examination reveals pallor, splenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood smear demonstrates lymphocytes with cytoplasmic projections, as shown in the image below. A bone marrow biopsy conﬁrms the presence of hairy cell leukaemia. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 90 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 2.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 70 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
explanation:
C Cladribine Cladribine, a purine analogue, is the treatment of choice for hairy cell leukaemia. It induces durable remissions in most patients by targeting hairy cells selectively. Hairy cell leukaemia is a rare Bcell lymphoproliferative disorder characterised by pancytopenia, splenomegaly and characteristic 'hairy cells' on peripheral smear. D Imatinib Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for chronic myeloid leukaemia and other cancers, but has no role in the management of hairy cell leukaemia. A Rituximab Rituximab, a monoclonal antibody against CD20, is used for hairy cell leukaemia in cases of relapse or refractory disease but is not ﬁrst-line therapy. B Splenectomy Splenectomy was historically used in the management of hairy cell leukaemia to control symptoms of splenomegaly. However,

with the advent of effective chemotherapeutic agents, it is now rarely performed. E Hydroxyurea Hydroxyurea is used to control high WCCs in conditions such as chronic myeloproliferative disorders but is not effective for hairy cell leukaemia.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is referred to the Haematology Clinic. She has suffered increasing tiredness over the past few months and ﬁnds it difﬁcult to eat because of abdominal fullness and right upper quadrant pain. She has little past medical history of note, and her only medication is amlodipine for the treatment of hypertension. On examination, her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg and pulse 85 bpm and regular. She looks pale. There is marked hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal palpation and peripheral lymphadenopathy. Investigations; Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 98 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 42.2 × 109/l (smear cells seen on the ﬁlm) 4–11 × 109/l PLT 145 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 122 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 231 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Albumin 32 g/l 35–55 g/l Bilirubin 12 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Which of the following is the most useful next investigation in conﬁrming the diagnosis?
explanation:
D Immunophenotyping The most likely diagnosis is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), and immunophenotyping to look for circulating clonal B lymphocytes expressing CD5, CD19, CD20 and CD23, and an absence of FMC-7 staining to conﬁrm the diagnosis, is an optimal next step. The differential pattern of receptor expression can also be used to differentiate from prolymphocytic leukaemia and lymphoma, as alternative differential diagnoses. A Abdominal ultrasound scan (USS) Abdominal USS will conﬁrm hepatosplenomegaly and may reveal mesenteric lymph node enlargement, but it will not conﬁrm this

patient’s underlying haematological diagnosis. B Bone marrow aspiration Bone marrow biopsy can be useful with respect to determining the prognosis in CLL because the degree of abnormality seen in bone marrow architecture is linked to poorer outcomes. As the diagnosis can usually be obtained by immunophenotyping, bone marrow biopsy is not the next diagnostic approach here. C Chromosomal analysis Chromosomal analysis may be useful with respect to determining prognosis, for instance patients carrying a deletion in chromosome 17 have a poorer outlook. E Lymph node biopsy Lymph node biopsy is more usually carried out in patients with lymphoma, rather than those with leukaemia. In CLL, if signiﬁcant enlargement of a single node or a group of nodes is seen, the node may be biopsied to rule out lymphomatous transformation.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with severe, unremitting epistaxis from both nostrils. The Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) Registrar successfully packs the nose. However, the patient complains of continuous post-nasal drip and has had several episodes of melaena. He has been suffering from prominent joint pains in the knees and hands for several months. There is no previous medical history of note, other than an uncomplicated hernia repair a year ago. Family history reveals nothing of signiﬁcance. He is on no medication. On examination, he has moderate synovitis of several proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal and large joints. His blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, heart rate 120 bpm and respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute. His skin is cool to touch. He is covered in large bruises. Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 73 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.3 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l PLT 556 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l ESR 74 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour PPT (does not correct in mixing study) 75 seconds 23.0–35.0 seconds Prothrombin Test (PT) 12 seconds 10.6–14.9 seconds Factor VIII activity Reduced What is the most appropriate therapy for this patient's bleeding?
explanation: E Recombinant activated factor VII Initially developed for use in patients with congenital haemophilia with alloantibody inhibitors, recombinant activated factor VII has been successfully used in patients with acquired haemophilia. It binds to the surface of activated platelets where it supports thrombin generation and bypasses the need for factor VIII. C Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) Given that FFP is a product derived from blood transfusion, it does contain factor VII. However, recombinant activated factor VII is much preferred, as it does not carry any risk of contamination. A Cryoprecipitate Cryoprecipitate, derived from fresh frozen plasma (FFP), contains ﬁbrinogen, von Willebrand factor, factor VIII, factor XIII and ﬁbronectin, and is not likely to be effective here compared to activated factor VII. B Desmopressin Desmopressin causes the release of von Willebrand factor from platelets, resulting in an increased level of factor VIII which is bound to it. Desmopressin may be used in patients with minor bleeding or before some elective procedures in patients with mild haemophilia A. Due to the severe nature of this bleed and the need for urgent treatment, it would not be appropriate to use desmopressin here since there would be a delay for factor VIII levels to rise in the body. D Recombinant factor VIII This patient has an acquired factor VIII deﬁciency, probably associated with rheumatoid arthritis. Acquired haemophilia is more common in the elderly or during pregnancy, often in association with concurrent autoimmune disease or malignancy. It is due to an antibody to a coagulation factor, most commonly factor VIII, often referred to as an ‘inhibitor’. Bleeding can be severe to the point that great care should be taken with cannula insertion, since compartment syndrome may ensue. Diagnosis is by performing mixing studies with patients and normal plasma – a simple factor deﬁciency will be corrected by mixing with normal plasma, but an acquired inhibitor will not correct with mixing. The inhibitor can then be measured by the Bethesda assay, which can be used to monitor response to treatment. Treatment with factor VIII is usually ineffective, as the inhibitor has rapid activity.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is admitted to the Acute Medical Ward from the Gastroenterology Clinic. She has ulcerative colitis which is usually quiescent. However, despite maximal mesalazine and prednisolone 60 mg daily, she is opening her bowels 8–10 times per day with bloody diarrhoea. On the ward, her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and her heart rate is 92 bpm. Her temperature is 37.8 °C. On examination, her abdomen is distended and tender, with sparse bowel sounds. Her right leg is also swollen. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 100 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 10.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 130 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l CRP 72 mg/l < 10 mg/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Abdominal Xray (AXR) Dilated left-sided colon with evidence of mucosal oedema Right leg venogram Above-knee deep venous thrombosis Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her deep vein thrombosis?
explanation:
E Unfractionated heparin Patients with an exacerbation of ulcerative colitis are at greatly increased risk of thromboembolic disease. This patient has an extensive right-sided deep vein thrombosis and is at signiﬁcant risk of developing a pulmonary embolus. Heparinisation is the most appropriate intervention, which can be reversed in the event that surgery is required. B Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is the usual initial drug of choice for a patient with deep vein thrombosis. Due to the state of the IBD ﬂare, surgery is a signiﬁcant possibility and LMWH would complicate this, given its half-life of 2–6 hours. Therefore, a shorter-acting drug, such as unfractionated heparin, is more appropriate. A Elastic stockings Although stockings may be considered for prophylaxis, elastic stockings are not appropriate as a treatment for above-knee deep vein thrombosis. C Rivaroxaban Rivaroxaban is a factor X inhibitor. Although it is useful as a longterm intervention for anticoagulation in atrial ﬁbrillation or venous thromboembolism, it cannot be reversed easily if surgery is required. D Thrombectomy Inﬂammatory bowel disease (IBD) ﬂares are prothrombic. Although this patient has bloody diarrhoea, anticoagulation is indicated as long as the blood loss is not itself causing anaemia or hae-

modynamic instability (which it rarely does in IBD ﬂares). Therefore, a surgical option is not necessary, as anticoagulation may be given, which is less invasive.

stem: A 45-year-old man is admitted to the Acute Medical Unit with a 4-day history of shortness of breath and intermittent chest pain. There is no known past medical history of note and he smokes 15–20 cigarettes per day. On examination, he has a temperature of 39.4 °C with a heart rate of 130 bpm and regular with a BP of 100/55 mmHg. There are coarse crackles at the right base, with a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturations of 94% on 4 litres of oxygen delivered via nasal cannula. His lower limbs are examined, and a photograph is shown below: Investigation Results Normal value Hb 98 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 22.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 90 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 10.1 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 80 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Fibrinogen 1.2 g/l 1.9–8.0 g/l D-dimer 7500 ng/ml < 500 ng/ml CRP 99 mg/l < 10 mg/l What forms part of the immediate management of this patient?
explanation: B Fresh frozen plasma This patient has a diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), given the presentation of sepsis of a likely respiratory origin. This patient has a CURB-65 score of 3 (respiratory rate over 30 breaths per minute, diastolic BP below 60 mmHg and urea over 7 mmol/l). A high CURB-65 score is associated with high mortality and an increased likelihood of complications such as DIC. DIC is an acquired syndrome characterised by dysregulation of the coagulation system leading to the formation of thrombi and consumption of platelets and clotting factors that, in turn, leads to bleeding. Laboratory markers of DIC include elevated ﬁbrin degradation products (D-dimer). Other markers include a prolonged prothrombin time, activated partial prothrombin time and decreased ﬁbrinogen and platelet count. Treatment of DIC includes ﬁnding and treating the underlying cause, which, in this case is with intravenous antibiotics. In addition to this, fresh frozen plasma is used in the immediate management of this patient. It is the preferred agent for replacing coagulation factors and is recommended as the ﬁrst-line in current guidelines. A Cryoprecipitate Cryoprecipitate is a second-line agent used in the treatment of DIC, particularly when there is a signiﬁcant reduction in ﬁbrinogen levels (below 1 g/l). Given that the ﬁbrinogen levels are above 1 g/l and fresh frozen plasma is available, cryoprecipitate is the incorrect answer. C IV immunoglobulin Intravenous immunoglobulin is used in the management of immune thrombocytopenia when there is associated bleeding or a high risk of bleeding, for example, in the preoperative setting. Although this patient has thrombocytopenia, additional signs of sepsis and signiﬁcantly raised D-dimer are more suggestive of DIC. D Low-molecular-weight heparin Low-molecular-weight heparin is used in the prophylaxis and management of venous thromboembolism (VTE). Although this patient has a raised D-dimer which is commonly used in the investigation of VTE, the history and presentation are more in keeping with pneumonia. Additionally, the combination of the purpuric rash on the lower limbs, clinical features of sepsis and a raised Ddimer are much more likely in keeping with DIC over VTE. E Prednisolone Similar to intravenous immunoglobulin, prednisolone is used in the management of immune thrombocytopenia. Prednisolone is the ﬁrst-line management of immune thrombocytopenia and is also used for managing vasculitic diseases that present with a similar rash as this patient. However, the combination of thrombocytopenia, sepsis and a signiﬁcantly raised D-dimer is more suggestive of DIC.

stem: An 18-year-old Cypriot tourist is admitted to A&E with severe abdominal pain. Over the last few days he had been coughing up green sputum and had pleuritic chest pain. He was given ciproﬂoxacin for presumed infection. This morning he awoke with sharp, very painful abdominal pain, worst in the epigastric area. No other symptoms. He drinks socially and doesn’t smoke. On examination, he is jaundiced and in pain. His temperature is 39.5 °C, pulse 120 bpm, BP 102/48 mmHg and his respirations are 20 breaths/min. His saturations on room air are 95%. Some crackles and bronchial breathing at the right base can be heard. His abdomen is generally tender on palpation but with no guarding. Chest X-ray shows shadowing at the right lung base; ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 62 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 17.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 465 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 84 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 4.5 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Glucose 5.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Albumin 38 g/l 35–55 g/l Bilirubin 71 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 62 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 124 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Amylase 45 U/l < 200 U/l MCV 97 ﬂ 80–100 ﬂ LDH 1256 IU/l 100–190 IU/l Urine Urobilinogen+ Blood ﬁlm Heinz bodies and bite cells noted What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
A G6PD deﬁciency G6PD deﬁciency is the commonest red blood cell enzyme defect. It is a condition that is X-linked recessive in inheritance and is commonly found in Mediterranean and African populations. It is often triggered by infections, certain drugs (including ciproﬂoxacin), certain foods (including broad beans) and, at times, there can be no identiﬁable trigger. When exposed to an oxidative crisis there is typically a rapid haemolysis. Patients are often noted as having anaemia, Heinz bodies on blood ﬁlm (due to haemolysis), an elevated LDH and reduced haptoglobin levels. The mainstay of treatment is supportive measures. In chronic disease, it may be ap-

propriate to consider a splenectomy. B Familial Mediterranean fever Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is an autosomal recessive disease that is more commonly found in Mediterranean populations. It is characterised by short, recurrent episodes of fever, arthritis, peritonitis and pleuritis. During an attack, patients can have raised inﬂammatory markers (WCC, ESR, CRP) and diagnosis can be made following DNA analysis looking speciﬁcally for the FMF gene. The mainstay of treatment is colchicine. Interferonα and etanercept can be used as alternatives. NSAIDs and steroids can also be used to help arthralgia and myalgia. C Atypical pneumonia Atypical pneumonia is possible in this patient, but this is only part of the picture and would not explain the patient’s blood ﬁndings such as anaemia and raised LDH. In this patient, the pneumonia ± antibiotics triggered the crisis in this G6PD-deﬁcient patient. D Acute intermittent porphyria Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is an autosomal dominant condition in which the patient has a deﬁciency of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase. It is a condition that is very difﬁcult to diagnosis, but patients often present with unexplained abdominal pain, neurological or psychiatric symptoms, dark-coloured urine and cardiac arrhythmias. E Acute pancreatitis As with this patient, most patients with pancreatitis present with severe abdominal pain which is usually epigastric. However, they tend to have a raised amylase that is greater than three times the upper limit of normal. It is not typical to develop a severe anaemia or to have the X-ray ﬁndings and symptoms of a cough. For causes, remember the mnemonic I GET SMASHED (Idiopathic, Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Malignancy, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hypercalcaemia or hypertriglycerides, ERCP & Drugs). The mainstay of treatment is supportive measures such as IV ﬂuids, keeping the patient nil by mouth, analgesia and antibiotics, if appropriate. In severe cases, patients may need admission to ICU.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is admitted with a large haematoma of the right arm after minimal trauma. She has noticed over the past few weeks increased bruising of the skin. The patient has recently completed a course of penicillin for a chest infection. She has a past history of psoriasis and hypertension. Examination reveals multiple bruises and a large painful haematoma in the right upper arm. The venepuncture site displays prolonged bleeding. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 102 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 9.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 325 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l INR 1.0 < 1.1 APTT 53 s (30–40);does not correct with the addition of normal plasma 23.0–35.0 s What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: E Acquired factor VIII deﬁciency Acquired factor VIII deﬁciency results from the development of antibodies against factor VIII, which prevent its action. This can occur in the elderly and is associated with malignancy, psoriasis, pemphigus and drugs (cephalosporins, penicillins). Patients develop bleeding tendencies and the aPTT (APTT) is prolonged (intrinsic pathway). The APTT doesn’t correct/will only correct slightly with the addition of normal plasma. The Bethesda titre can quantify the inhibitor. There is a 20% mortality rate from acquired factor VIII deﬁciency. D Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome APAS is associated with a prolonged APTT, although it results in a propensity towards thrombosis rather than increased risk of bleeding. A Von Willebrand’s disease Although Von Willebrand’s disease is associated with prolongation of APTT in 50% of patients due to low levels of factor VIII, it corrects on mixing with normal plasma. B Haemophilia A Although haemophilia A does lead to bleeding and is associated with prolongation of APTT, presentation for the ﬁrst time at this stage would be very unusual, and correction with normal plasma would be expected. C Haemophilia B Haemophilia B is associated with bleeding, although correction of clotting disorder on mixing with normal plasma would be expected.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with indigestion of seven weeks’ duration. She has no ongoing medical problems and is otherwise asymptomatic. She is on no medication. Examination is unremarkable. She undergoes gastro-oesophageal endoscopy which reveals gastritis. Stomach biopsies conﬁrm the presence of a mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALToma/marginal zone lymphoma) of low-grade type; Helicobacter pylori is not demonstrated on biopsy. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen and pelvis reveals no additional disease, and a bone marrow trephine is unremarkable; the stomach wall is not clearly thickened. What should be the next stage in this patient’s management?
explanation:
C Non-invasive testing for H. pylori Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALToma), also known as marginal zone lymphomas, are low- grade lymphomas, most often diagnosed in the stomach. They are peculiar in that they are often associated with chronic inﬂammation of one of the following types: • in the stomach secondary to chronic H. pylori gastritis in the eyes secondary to Sjögren syndrome • in the thyroid secondary to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis • in the intestine secondary to Crohn’s or coeliac disease. Treatment against H. pylori is safe and will cause regression in 90% of low-grade gastric MALTomas. Due to the importance of establishing H. pylori diagnosis, if the tumour biopsy is negative for H. pylori, it is appropriate to perform non-invasive testing such as stool antigen testing or urea breath test for H. pylori. In the event that non-invasive testing reveals a positive result, the patient should be managed with triple therapy in the ﬁrst instance. A Cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and prednisolone (CHOP) This would not be appropriate for this patient as Rcyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin and prednisolone (including rituximab) is a treatment option for more advanced gastric lymphoma. B High-dose dexamethasone High-dose dexamethasone may provide symptomatic improvement but is ineffective in treating H. pylori, the likely trigger for mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALToma) seen here. D Observation alone Observation alone risks signiﬁcant lymphoma progression, meaning that H. pylori eradication would then be, in all likelihood, ineffective. E Partial gastrectomy

Surgery is rarely employed in the treatment of gastric MALToma because it is usually not curative and results in signiﬁcant operative morbidity.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is brought into the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of worsening abdominal pain. She also complains of fatigue and nausea. There is no past medical history of note. She is 34 weeks pregnant. On examination, her blood pressure is 159/95 mmHg and her heart rate is 102 bpm and regular. Chest sounds are clear and her heart sounds are normal. She has mild pedal oedema. On abdominal examination, there is palpable right upper quadrant tenderness. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 90 g/l 135–180 g/l WCC 5.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 80 × 109/l 150–450 × 109/l Creatinine (Cr) 88 µmol/l 55–120 µmol/l Bilirubin 66 µmol/l 3–17 µmol/l ALT 210 u/l 30–40 u/l ALP 99 u/l 30–100 u/l CRP 22 mg/l < 5 mg/l Blood ﬁlm: numerous schistocytes. What would be the most appropriate deﬁnitive treatment for this patient?
explanation:
D Urgent Caesarean section This woman has evidence of pre-eclampsia. This includes a deteriorating blood picture— decreased platelet count (PLT) and abnormal liver enzymes— and hypertension. Nearly 10% of women with severe pre-eclampsia and 30–50% of women with eclampsia are affected by the syndrome of haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low PLT (HELLP). The exact relationship between HELLP syndrome and pre-eclampsia is unknown. Women with pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome develop hepatocellular necrosis and liver dysfunction. They also have an increased mortality rate, and one-third of women with preeclampsia develop disseminated intravascular coagulation. The best treatment for this woman would be for an urgent Caesarean section to deliver the baby. Mild hypertension in pregnancy has been managed with oral nifedipine or labetalol. In this case, intravenous hydralazine or labetalol may well be required for blood pressure reduction/control preoperatively. B Intravenous magnesium sulfate

Intravenous magnesium is used in the treatment of eclampsia. In contrast, this patient has symptoms of haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low PLT (HELLP) syndrome, for which magnesium is not used. A Intravenous labetalol Although this patient has evidence of hypertension and possibly the beginning of pre-eclampsia (pending urinalysis), intravenous labetalol is not a deﬁnitive treatment. Rather, urgent Caesarean section to deliver the baby and pathological placenta is the only deﬁnitive treatment. C Plasma exchange Plasma exchange is indicated for patients with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Features of TTP include haemolysis, thrombocytopenia, fever, acute kidney injury and cerebral dysfunction. Pregnancy is a predisposing factor. However, the combination of hypertension and deranged liver function tests makes HELLP syndrome most likely, for which the treatment is urgent delivery of the baby and the placenta. E Ursodeoxycholic acid Ursodeoxycholic acid is used in symptomatic relief of itching in pregnant patients with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents more commonly in the third trimester and is associated with pruritus and raised bilirubin levels. However, the presence of haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and hypertension makes HELLP syndrome more likely.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the Haematology Clinic with complaints of fatigue, easy bruising and recurrent nosebleeds over the past month. She has no signiﬁcant past medical history and takes no medications. On examination, she appears pale, with scattered petechiae on her arms and legs. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly is noted. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 75 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 1.2 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l PLT 20 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l MCV 88 fl 80–100 fl Reticulocyte cout 0.2% 0.5–2.5% Bone marrow biopsy Hypocellular marrow with decreased haematopoietic cells, no abnormal infiltrates What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Aplastic anaemia Aplastic anaemia is characterised by pancytopenia, with a hypocellular bone marrow devoid of abnormal inﬁltrates. The patient’s presentation with fatigue, easy bruising, recurrent nosebleeds and pancytopenia, with a hypocellular bone marrow, is consistent with this diagnosis. A Acute myeloid leukaemia While acute myeloid leukaemia can cause pancytopenia, it typically presents with an elevated number of abnormal myeloblasts in the blood and bone marrow. This patient's bone marrow biopsy does not show any abnormal inﬁltrates, which makes leukaemia less likely. B Myelodysplastic syndrome Myelodysplastic syndrome can present with pancytopenia and a hypocellular or hypercellular marrow, with dysplastic changes in haematopoietic cells. However, the bone marrow in aplastic anaemia is typically hypocellular without dysplasia, as seen in this patient. C Immune thrombocytopenic purpura Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) generally causes isolated thrombocytopenia without affecting Hb levels or the WCC. The presence of pancytopenia in this patient rules out ITP as a likely diagnosis. E Megaloblastic anaemia Megaloblastic anaemia, caused by deﬁciencies in vitamin B12 or folate, can result in pancytopenia but usually presents with a high MCV due to the presence of large, immature red cells. This patient's normal MCV makes this diagnosis unlikely.

stem: An 18-year-old Greek woman with beta-thalassaemia major, and who has had several blood transfusions and uses desferrioxamine for prevention of iron overload, comes to the clinic with her sister who is 25 years old and wants to start a family. They want to discuss the mutation that is the basis of the 18-year old’s underlying disease. Which of the following is the basis of beta-thalassaemia major?
options: 1 alpha- and one beta-chain gene mutation
explanation:
E 2 beta-chain mutations Beta-thalassaemia major is due to mutations in the genes coding for

each of the beta-globin chains. This results in grossly ineffective erythropoiesis and severe hypochromic microcytic anaemia with iron overload. The profound anaemia is associated with erythroid hyperplasia and extramedullary haemopoiesis. Given that her parents were unaffected by thalassaemia major but must have suffered from the thalassaemia trait, the 25- year-old sister has a 66% chance of having the thalassaemia trait, (she is symptomless, meaning that she must either be normal or carry a mutation for 1 of the 2 beta-globin genes). She should be advised to have haemoglobin electrophoresis prior to beginning a family with her new partner. D 1 alpha- and one beta-chain gene mutation Mixed alpha- and beta-thalassaemia is said to carry a milder clinical course than thalassaemia major. A 1 alpha-chain gene mutation One alpha-chain mutation leads to so-called silent alphathalassaemia, which is asymptomatic. B 1 beta-chain gene mutation This leads to beta-thalassaemia trait, which is the likely diagnosis in the 25-year-old sibling of the patient with thalassaemia major. C 2 alpha-chain gene mutations Two alpha-chain mutations lead to alpha-thalassaemia trait microcytic anaemia, which is usually asymptomatic.

stem: A 74-year-old patient presents to the GP with headache, dizziness, vertigo, vague abdominal pain and general lethargy. He has previously been ﬁt and well, with mild hypertension as his only signiﬁcant past medical history. On examination his BP is 155/95 mmHg and he has a ruddy complexion. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 179 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 19.5 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 450 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 145 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Haematocrit 0.56 You suspect primary polycythaemia. Which of the following investigations is most likely to provide a diagnosis?
explanation:
B JAK-2 mutation testing

JAK-2 mutation testing is widely available, with the V617F mutation being found in approximately 96% of patients with primary polycythaemia. The protein is a signalling protein within the JAKSTAT pathway, which drives production of red blood cells. C Arterial blood gas estimation Absence of hypoxia makes secondary polycythaemia less likely, although in conditions such as obesity hypoventilation syndrome, where hypoxia is more marked at night, hypoxia may be missed in the clinic. A LDH levels Although LDH levels are elevated in the presence of haematological malignancy, they are non-speciﬁc so could not be used to conﬁrm a diagnosis of primary polycythaemia here. D Uric acid levels Uric acid levels are raised in patients with primary polycythaemia due to increased red blood cell turnover, although elevated uric acid may also be seen due to a number of other causes. E C282Y mutation testing C282Y mutation testing is most useful as a screening test for hereditary haemochromatosis.

stem: A 30-year-old male nurse presents with prolonged bleeding after a routine dental extraction. It is two days since the procedure, and the bleeding has been continuous: he has noticed black stools on three separate occasions. Past medical history includes a postoperative haemorrhage following tonsillectomy, that required a blood transfusion. He has one brother who is well and believes a cousin may have died of bleeding during childbirth. On examination, he is pale but well perfused. Rectal examination conﬁrms melaena. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 81 g/l 135–175 g/l PT 28 s 10.6–14.9 s PTT 33 s 23.0–35.0 s Fibrinogen 230 mg/dl 125–300 mg/dl Mixing studies with 50;50 test normal plasma shows complete correction of PT What diagnosis should be considered at this stage pending further investigation?
explanation: D Inherited Factor VII deﬁciency Factor VII is the only factor unique to the PT, and deﬁciency of Factor VII therefore gives a prolonged PT and normal APTT. Deﬁciencies of II, V and X will prolong both aPTT (APTT) and PT. Deﬁciencies of XII, XI, IX and VIII will prolong APTT alone. When an abnormality is detected in the PT/APTT, the studies are repeated with a 50:50 mix of test and normal plasma: straightforward factor deﬁciencies will correct with mixing, but inhibitors (most commonly lupus anticoagulant) do not correct. B Self-dosing with warfarin Given that other family members have been affected by a clotting disorder, and PT is prolonged without prolongation of APTT, this effectively rules out warfarin self-dosing as the underlying cause. A Inherited Factor IX deﬁciency Factor IX deﬁciency results in prolongation of APTT, and would correct with normal plasma mixing. C Acquired Factor IX deﬁciency Acquired Factor IX deﬁciency would prolong the APTT and would not correct with normal plasma. E Acquired Factor VII deﬁciency Acquired Factor VII deﬁciency due to an inhibitor antibody would not correct with normal plasma.

stem: You are asked to counsel a married couple expecting a baby. They are both ﬁt and well, with no previous medical history. They both originate from South East Asia, and have no family history of birth abnormalities. There are no abnormalities on examination. Investigations reveal the following: MALE Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 117 g/l 135–175 g/l MCV 70 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Mean cell haemoglobin (MCHb) 19 pg 27–32 pg Red cell count 5.6 × 1012/l 4.7–6.9 × 1012/l Haemoglobin electrophoresis normal FEMALE Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 101 g/l 115–155 g/l MCV 68 ﬂ 76–98 ﬂ Mean cell haemoglobin (MCHb) 18 pg 27–32 pg Red cell count 6.0 × 1012/l 4.7–6.9 × 1012/l Haemoglobin electrophoresis normal What condition is the fetus at risk from developing?
explanation: C Hydrops fetalis Both patients come from an area endemic for a-thalassaemia, and appear to be carriers, with normal red blood cell counts and hypochromia/microcytosis. It’s important to remember that in athalassaemia the Hb electrophoresis is usually normal. Hydrops fetalis is associated with homozygous alpha-thalassaemia, thus driving the correct answer. B Thalassaemia intermedia The terms thalassaemia minor, intermedia and major do not pertain to a- or β-thalassaemia - rather they describe whether the patient is asymptomatic (minor), transfusion dependent (major) or in between (intermedia). Loss of a single a chain (aa/–a) is common (30% in Africa); loss of two a chains (aa/––) is less common, and co-inheritance can lead to hydrops fetalis (––/–-), where no a chains are produced, and Hb Barts is produced (a gamma-4 tetramer). Loss of three alpha chains (a–/––) leads to haemoglobin H (HbH) disease (HbH is composed of beta-4 tetramers), usually with a thalassaemia intermedia phenotype. A ß-Thalassaemia trait Patients with β-thalassaemia trait nearly always have a raised haemoglobin A2 and fetal haemoglobin on haemoglobin electrophoresis (although normal A2 variants do exist). The fact that both parents have normal haemoglobin electrophoresis means there is effectively very low/no signiﬁcant risk of the fetus developing beta- thalassaemia trait. D β -Thalassaemia major β-Thalassaemia trait in the parents has effectively been ruled out by the normal haemoglobin electrophoresis, and therefore βthalassaemia won’t occur in the fetus in this case. E Homozygous haemoglobin E Haemoglobin-E is associated with mild β-thalassaemia which presents in the ﬁrst few months of life, and isn’t usually a cause of fetal loss.

stem: You are asked to see a 20-year-old man with a temperature of 39 °C. He is an in-patient receiving an allogeneic bone marrow transplant. He was diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukaemia three months previously and was treated with imatinib mesylate, which brought about a rapid haematological and cytogenetic remission. He received myeloablative conditioning with total body irradiation and cyclophosphamide 10 days previously and received stem cells collected from his brother, with whom he is fully HLA (human leukocyte antigen) compatible. He ﬁrst became febrile ﬁve days ago and has received ceftazidime (changed to meropenem after 48 h) and vancomycin intravenously. Examination shows an unwell young man; pulse 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg, heart sounds normal; capillary reﬁll < 2 s; respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, crackles in the right mid-zone; abdomen normal. Urine output is above 30 ml/h and has been negative to date. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 93 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 0.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 12 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Blood cultures Negative at 48 hour Urine cultures Negative at 48 hour CXR Right middle lobe patchy consolidation What is the most appropriate management?
options: Add in metronidazole for anaerobic cover
Change vancomycin to linezolid to cover vancomycin resistant enterococcus
Add in acyclovir 10 mg/kg to cover systemic herpes infection
Add in liposomal amphotericin 3 mg/kg to cover invasive aspergillosis
Add in intravenous ﬂuconazole 400 mg daily to cover invasive candidiasis
explanation:
D Add in liposomal amphotericin 3 mg/kg to cover invasive aspergillosis The gravest concern is that the fevers are due to invasive aspergillosis (IA) or related fungal infection. Systemic herpes infection or candidiasis are both possible, but less likely. Diagnosing IA is difﬁcult; computed tomography of the chest is useful at identifying lesions, but is not completely sensitive or speciﬁc. Bronchoscopy with lavage suffers from the same limitations, and invasive procedures are discouraged in neutropenic patients. Various serological assays have been trialled, including using the polymerase chain reaction to detect early invasive disease. IA can only be conﬁdently diagnosed by the ﬁnding of characteristic hyphae on a biopsy specimen, but for obvious reasons this is rarely available. Vorconazole is the treatment of choice followed by posaconazole. Amphoteracin is used if neither of these agents is effective. Caspofungin, micafungin and anidulafungin can be used if ﬁrst-line agents are either ineffective or not tolerated. Any immunosuppressive drugs may be reduced, or granulocyte-stimulating colony factor can be used to rectify neutropenia whilst a patient is unwell A Add in metronidazole for anaerobic cover

The patient has been well treated for neutropenic sepsis and meropenem will provide reasonable anaerobic cover, so metronidazole is not required. B Change vancomycin to linezolid to cover vancomycin resistant enterococcus VRE would only be considered at this point if there was microbiological evidence. C Add in acyclovir 10 mg/kg to cover systemic herpes infection Although systemic herpes infection is possible, it is less likely than other infections such as fungal infections and, as such, would not be the next step in treatment. E Add in intravenous ﬂuconazole 400 mg daily to cover invasive candidiasis Invasive candidiasis should be a consideration but is less likely to be the cause of the ongoing symptoms than invasive aspergillosis and treatment of candidiasis would, therefore, not be the next step.

stem: A 69-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 5-month history of progressive lethargy and malaise. He also complains of persistent headaches, dizziness and blurred vision for the last three months. His past medical history includes hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. On examination, he appears pale and very slim. His heart sounds are normal and there is equal air entry bilaterally, with minimal expiratory wheeze. On abdominal examination, there is palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 88 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.5 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Mean cell volume (MCV) 75 ﬂ 70–90 ﬂ Platelets 350 × 109/l 150–450 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 3.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 88 mmol/l 50–120mmol/l Calcium 2.4 mmol/l 2.1–2.6 mmol/l Phosphate 1.2 mmol/l 0.8–1.4 mmol/l Serum electrophoresis shows paraproteinaemia, which is predominantly immunoglobulin M (IgM) (5 g/l). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: E Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia This patient has a diagnosis of Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia, a lymphoplasmacytoid malignancy associated with increased monoclonal production of the IgM paraprotein. Symptoms and signs include lethargy, weight loss, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Increased levels of paraproteins increase plasma viscosity, causing hyperviscosity syndrome that often presents as headache, dizziness and blurred vision. The condition is more often seen in older men, such as what is seen in this patient. D Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a malignant proliferation of lymphocytes that causes painless lymphadenopathy, in addition to systemic symptoms of weight loss, night sweats and fever. Hepatosplenomegaly is an extranodal sign. However, the presence of raised paraprotein levels is not typical of Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. A Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is a malignancy of the lymphoid lineage of cells (most commonly B cells). It is the most common malignancy in adults and is often detected incidentally. Symptoms that may be present include lethargy, lymphadenopathy, weight loss and symptoms of hyperviscosity syndrome as WCC increases. However, this patient has a raised paraprotein level with a normal WCC, making CLL unlikely. B Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown signiﬁcance (MGUS) Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown signiﬁcance (MGUS) is a benign condition that is caused by raised monoclonal paraproteinaemia without the presence of symptoms. Given that this patient has symptomatic anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly and hyperviscosity syndrome, MGUS is an unlikely diagnosis. C Multiple myeloma Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of bone marrow plasma cells that causes paraproteinaemia (typically immunoglobulin G (IgG) or immunoglobulin A (IgA)) and symptoms and signs of anaemia, renal impairment, hypercalcaemia and bone disease such as pathological fractures. Multiple myeloma presents between 60 and 70 years of age and is an important differential diagnosis to have for this clinical scenario. However, the lack of renal impairment and bone disease, along with isolated monoclonal gammopathy of IgM paraprotein, makes Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia much more likely.

stem: A 70-year-old woman who underwent right hemicolectomy opted to receive a designated blood transfusion from her daughter, who is the same blood group. Whilst on the ward undergoing the ﬁrst unit of blood she began to complain of extreme shortness of breath. Her blood pressure was markedly reduced, at 90/50 mmHg. On examination there were inspiratory crackles throughout both lung ﬁelds. Dipstick of her urine was negative for haematuria. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this transfusion reaction?
options: Granulocyte antibodies in the donor blood
Granulocyte antibodies in the recipient blood
explanation: C Granulocyte antibodies in the donor blood Transfusion-related lung injury or TRALI is thought to be related to anti-HLA or anti-granulocyte antibodies in the donor blood. Despite the fact that the donor and recipient are matched, the possibility of anti-granulocyte antibodies cannot be excluded. It is postulated that TRALI is seen more often in multiparous women who donate blood, because of the generation of antibodies to HLA antigens through multiple exposures to fetal blood. Lung symptoms are often difﬁcult to distinguish from ARDS, and management of TRALI is consistent with the management of ARDS itself. D Granulocyte antibodies in the recipient blood It is antibodies in the donor blood against neutrophils in the recipient that may have undergone priming due to an acute respiratory illness, which drive the presentation here. A ABO incompatibility ABO incompatibility is associated with an acute deterioration characterised by hypotension, tachycardia, haemolysis and symptoms similar to anaphylaxis, although the reaction isn’t mediated by IgE. It carries a mortality of up to 10%. B Rhesus incompatibility Rhesus incompatibility presents with a similar picture to ABO incompatibility, but symptoms are generally less severe. E Cytokines in the donor blood Cytokines in donor blood are associated with febrile transfusion reactions. There are normally no other sequelae apart from an increase in body temperature and mild tachycardia.

stem: A 46-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of abdominal distension, lower limb swelling and yellowish discolouration of his eyes for the past three months. The patient also complains of difﬁculty concentrating and easy fatiguability over this period and feels he has put on a lot of weight due to generalised swelling. He has had a decreased urine output for the past three weeks and there are days when he passes only about 50 ml of urine. The peripheral smear done is shown below: Which of the following has caused the red blood cell (RBC) abnormality in this patient?
explanation:
C Liver dysfunction The RBC abnormality in the given peripheral smear is macrocytosis. Liver disease is a known cause of macrocytosis. This patient’s presentation with features of volume overload and jaundice is typical of chronic liver disease. The decreased renal output in this patient may signify hepatorenal syndrome, rather than a primary renal abnormality. D Renal dysfunction Renal dysfunction has not been known to cause macrocytosis. However, chronic kidney disease may be associated with folic acid and vitamin B12 deﬁciencies, which may cause macrocytosis. In addition, patients on long-term haemodialysis may also have macrocytosis. However, in this patient, the decreased urine output is likely due to hepatorenal syndrome. A Folate deﬁciency Although folate deﬁciency can cause macrocytosis, liver dysfunction is more likely to be the cause in this patient. B Hypothyroidism Although hypothyroidism can cause macrocytosis, it is unlikely to be the cause in this patient. E Vitamin B12 deﬁciency

Although vitamin B12 deﬁciency can cause macrocytosis, liver dysfunction is more likely to be the cause in this patient.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is bought to her GP by her carer who has become concerned after noticing that the patient’s gums have progressively become more prominent over the last few months. She tried to take the patient to the dentist but no NHS dental appointments were available. The patient lives in a home since she has learning difﬁculties. Her past medical history is unremarkable except for three infections in the last 6 weeks. The carer has also noticed that recently the patient has become increasingly fatigued by even the lightest of activities and is commonly short of breath on exertion. She is not currently on any medications but has taken various courses of antibiotics recently. On examination, she is noted to be anaemic and has multiple bruises over her body. She has hypertrophic bleeding gums and, on auscultation of the heart, she is found to have a ﬂow murmur. She has mild splenomegaly on palpation of her abdomen. Routine blood tests were requested and conﬁrmed the presence of anaemia, a raised white cell count, low neutrophil count and thrombocytopenia. A blood ﬁlm shows increased numbers of blast cells and the presence of Auer rods. Given these ﬁndings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is a malignant disease of the bone marrow in which the blast cells derived from the myeloid marrow elements undergo a neoplastic proliferation. AML is distinguished by the presence of >20% blasts in the blood and/or bone marrow. It is more common in men and the prevalence increases with age, but it can affect all age groups. It is, however, becoming more common as a long-term complication of chemotherapy. Symptoms are usually related to marrow failure (anaemia, infections, bleeding) and/or organ inﬁltration with leukaemic cells (bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, gum hypertrophy, proptosis), but patients can also have constitutional symptoms (weakness, fever, lethargy). C Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) CML is a myeloproliferative disorder characterised by the proliferation of the precursors for white blood cells, but these precursors retain the ability to differentiate. Symptoms tend to be chronic and

the blood proﬁle shows an increased (++) white cell count, with a low or normal haemoglobin and a variable platelet count. B Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) AML is differentiated from ALL by the presence of Auer rods, which are eosinophilic needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions found in blast cells and that are pathognomonic of AML. D Chronic lymphoid leukaemia (CLL) The most noteworthy laboratory abnormality found in CLL is lymphocytosis in the peripheral blood and bone marrow. Although the absolute blood lymphocyte threshold for diagnosing CLL has been placed at >5000/microl (5 × 109/l) B lymphocytes, a signiﬁcant proportion of patients presents with counts as high as 100,000/microl (100 × 109/l). The peripheral blood smear of patients with CLL demonstrates a lymphocytosis. The leukemic cells are typically small, mature-appearing lymphocytes with a dense nucleus, partially aggregated (clumped) chromatin and lacking discernible nucleoli. There is a narrow border of clear to slightly basophilic cytoplasm. The blood ﬁlm in this scenario is not that of CLL. E Chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML) CMML is characterised by a progressive cytopenia in the presence of a hypercellular bone marrow and usually involves all three cell lines (myeloid/monocyte, erythroid, megakaryocyte).

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with back pain over the past several months. She has hypertension which is currently controlled on two oral agents and a long history of osteoarthritis affecting her hips and her back. On examination, she looks relatively well, has a normal blood pressure (BP) of 142/82 mmHg and there are no signiﬁcant ﬁndings on physical examination.
