Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 115 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.8 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bone marrow 8 % plasma cells MM-protein found on electrophoresis 22 g/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown signiﬁcance (MGUS) According to guidelines, this patient seems likely to have MGUS. The criteria for diagnosis of MGUS include an M-protein level of <30 g/l, <10% plasma cells on bone marrow investigation and no end organ damage associated with myeloma. There should also be no evidence of amyloidosis. E Myelodysplasia Unexplained macrocytic anaemia may predate the diagnosis of myelodysplasia by months or years, and neutropenia and low platelets are also seen. Splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy are very uncommonly seen in patients with myelodysplasia. B Multiple myeloma The fact that the percentage of plasma cells in bone marrow is less than 10% effectively rules out multiple myeloma here. C Asymptomatic myeloma Where there is no end organ damage and more than 10% of the bone marrow contains plasma cells, or M- protein is >30 g/l, then this is deemed asymptomatic myeloma. D Myeloﬁbrosis Myeloﬁbrosis is associated with anaemia, with tear-drop red cells, a leuko-erythroblastic blood picture and splenomegaly, features not seen here.

stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with a massively swollen left leg. She has most recently been laid up in bed with an episode of inﬂuenza, and puts her leg problem down to a lack of movement. Past medical history of note includes 4 miscarriages which all occurred between the 10th and the 16th week of pregnancy. She stopped taking the oral contraceptive pill in her twenties because of migraine. Examination reveals a massively swollen left leg, and USS conﬁrms an extensive deep vein thrombosis extending into the femoral vein. APTT is prolonged at 45.8 s, and does not correct on mixing with normal plasma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome

The answer is Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome, (APAS) - APAS is associated with presence of the lupus anti-coagulant, (failure of APTT to correct with normal plasma), and increased risk of both venous thrombosis and miscarriage. As such the clinical picture here ﬁts best with APAS. This patient is likely to require life long anti-coagulation. D Inherited factor VIII deﬁciency Inherited factor VIII deﬁciency, is incorrect, this is associated with increased risk of bleeding and a prolonged APTT which corrects on mixing with normal plasma. A Acquired factor VIII deﬁciency Acquired factor VIII deﬁciency, is incorrect because although it is associated with prolonged APTT that fails to correct, it is associated with increased risk of bleeding. C Factor V Leiden mutation Factor V Leiden mutation, is incorrect, it is associated with increased risk of thrombosis, although the APTT is in the normal range, ruling it out here. E Von Willebrand’s disease Von Willebrand’s disease, is incorrect, this is associated with increased risk of bleeding and a prolonged APTT and is therefore not the likely cause of this patient’s symptoms.

stem: This is the family tree of a family affected with haemophilia A (males denoted by squares, females denoted by circles). What are the chances of ‘M’ being affected?
explanation:
B 1 in 2

Haemophilia A is a sex-linked inherited disease in humans. Males are hemizygous and receive their only X chromosome from their mother. Females are heterozygous and receive one X chromosome from each parent. Consequently, if a male has an affected X chromosome, he will be affected by an X-linked disease. In the above family tree, the daughter of the affected individual will receive the diseased X chromosome from her father and a normal X chromosome from her mother, so that she is a carrier of the disease. Her son, in turn, will have a 1 in 2 chance of receiving the diseased chromosome from his carrier mother, so the chance of him being affected with haemophilia A is 1 in 2. C 1 in 3 1 in 3 is the chance of the offspring of two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder being normal (i.e. not a carrier), if they are proven not to suffer from the disease. A 1 in 1 This patient’s mother will carry the haemophilia gene on one of her X-chromosomes, but the other is normal. This means there is a 50% chance of male offspring inheriting haemophilia. D 1 in 4 1 in 4 is the chance of the offspring of two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder either being normal or suffering from the disease in question. E 1 in 6 1 in 6 doesn’t ﬁt with a pattern of Mendelian inheritance.

stem: A 40-year-old South African man presents to the Accident and Emergency Department. He is confused, but you can get a history from his wife. He is on holiday in the UK for a week. He is normally in good health and was well when he arrived in the UK. The only past history of note is an admission some 3 years earlier with acute lower abdominal pain and agitation. He is on no regular medications but took some over-the-counter antihistamines yesterday for hay fever. Since then, he has been complaining of a weak arm, vomiting and abdominal pain. When he became confused, his wife became concerned and brought him to Accident and Emergency. On examination, he is confused and hallucinating. He has bilateral wrist drop. Otherwise, examination of his peripheral nervous system and cranial nerves is normal. Pulse is 120/min and regular, and his BP is 175/100 mmHg. Examination of his chest is also normal. Examination of his abdomen reveals diffuse tenderness. Investigation Result Normal values Sodium (Na+) 120 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.0 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l He is given a bolus of IV glucose, what other measure would you take next?
explanation: A IV haem arginate This describes an attack of acute intermittent porphyria. The diagnosis requires demonstration of increased urinary excretion of the haem precursor, porphobilinogen (PBG), in the urine. Urine characteristically turns red on standing. All attacks of porphyria increase the activity of hepatic 5-aminolevulinate (ALA) synthase, which can be measured in serum. The relation between these biochemical abnormalities and the neuronal dysfunction that underlies all the features of an acute attack is uncertain. Two procedures have been shown to decrease the activity of ALA synthase in animals - carbohydrate loading and parenteral infusion of haem arginate. Consequently, these two procedures are the mainstay of the treatment along with opiate analgesia. Provoking medication, such as the antihistamines in this case, should be withdrawn. C Intravenous thiamine We aren’t given a signiﬁcant alcohol consumption history as part of the scenario, and the previous episode 3 years ago of abdominal pain ﬁts with intermittent porphyria, and thus thiamine is not likely to be effective here. B Alcohol withdrawal regime of chlordiazepoxide Chlordiazepoxide is a benzodiazepine type sedative, but it won’t manage the underlying cause of this patient’s agitation, an acute episode of porphyria. D IV cyclizine Cyclizine is an anti-emetic with some antihistamine activity; reports about its safety conﬂict with respect to use in porphyria, with some case reports suggesting it can be used and others raising the possibility that it can precipitate porphyria episodes. E Abdominal CT The symptoms of pseudo-obstruction with hypertension and hyponatraemia are most consistent with acute intermittent porphyria; the abdominal CT is therefore most likely to be normal.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner complaining of increasing bruising. She has undergone a bone marrow transplant from a human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched family member for previous acute myeloid leukaemia. On examination, she has a number of areas of bruising and looks pale. Her blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 109 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 3.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 6.0 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 121 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate form of platelets to use for transfusion?
explanation: C Gamma-irradiated Patients who have undergone bone marrow transplantation are at increased risk of transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease because of lymphocytes within the donor material. Gammairradiated blood products are generally recommended for patients undergoing human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched transfusions and those with an inherited immune system disorder, an acquired immune disorder such as Hodgkin’s disease or post-bone marrow transplantation. Irradiation minimises the chances of surviving leukocytes being found within donated platelets. B Family-donated Family-donated platelets are still associated with an increased risk of graft-versus-host disease and should therefore be avoided here. A Beta-irradiated Beta-irradiation is a technique used to sterilise pharmaceutical packaging products and medical devices. It is gamma-irradiation that is used to sterilise transfusions. D human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched Usually, HLA-matched platelets are considered for patients who have become refractory to platelet transfusions because of the presence of anti-HLA antibodies. E Washed Platelet washing is designed to remove about 99% of plasma. It does, however, result in decreased quality of platelet function, is labour- and time-intensive and can result in delays to transfusion.

stem: A 60-year-old Asian man presents to the Pre-clerking Clinic prior to his laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstones. He has a history of hypertension, for which he takes ramipril 10 mg, but no other past medical history of note. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 104 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 4.5 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 195 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 105 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l MCV 60 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ Ferritin 300 μmol/l 24 - 355 μmol/l Upper GI endoscopy Normal TIBC Normal Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to conﬁrm the underlying cause of his anaemia?
explanation: D Haemoglobin electrophoresis This man has asymptomatic microcytic anaemia and he is of Asian ethnic origin. His upper GI endoscopy is normal, as is his ferritin, which reduces the possibility of this being iron deﬁciency anaemia. The most likely cause is beta-thalassaemia trait, the diagnosis of which is best conﬁrmed with haemoglobin electrophoresis. Patients with thalassaemia trait do not usually require any intervention. Bearing in mind that his ferritin of 300 is within the normal range, his anaemia will not be responsive to iron supplementation. Chelation therapy is only required in patients with thalassaemia major. Blood loss associated with laparoscopic cholescystectomy is likely to be relatively minor, and so blood transfusion would not be required prior to surgery. A Colonoscopy This would be the appropriate investigation for iron deﬁciency anaemia after a normal gastroscopy. B Mesenteric angiography This would be the investigation of choice in cases of unexplained blood loss or unidentiﬁable source (normal gastroscopy and colonoscopy), and in persistent iron deﬁciency anaemia. C Transferrin High transferrin levels are seen in iron deﬁciency anaemia, with subsequent decrease of the transferrin saturation and increase in TIBC (total iron-binding capacity). E Bone marrow aspirate This is performed for the diagnosis of lympho- or myeloproliferative disorders.

stem: A 50-year-old man with myelodysplasia complains of breathlessness on exertion. He was diagnosed with myelodysplasia three years ago and since then has been on two units of blood every three weeks to maintain his haemoglobin above 100 g/l. He has noticed over the last three months increasing exertional breathlessness despite maintaining his haemoglobin above 10. Examination shows a slim man with greyish skin colour. His heart rate is 90 bpm, sinus rhythm. Heart sounds are normal. Jugular venous pressure is not raised. The cardiac apex is palpable at the anterior axillary line. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest and the abdominal examination is normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 113 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 1.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 23 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 0.3 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Glucose 12.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Increase the transfusion program to maintain haemoglobin above 120 g/l
Commence subcutaneous recombinant erythropoietin to raise the haemoglobin to 120 g/l
Start venesection program to reduce ferritin to less than 1000
Commence iron chelation with subcutaneous desferrioxamine
Commence hydroxyurea or similar cytotoxic to treat myelodysplasia
explanation:
D Commence iron chelation with subcutaneous desferrioxamine This patient has early signs of iron overload secondary to chronic blood transfusion – grey skin, early heart failure and diabetes. There are limited options for intervention, and given the transfusion needs of this patient with iron overload, desferrioxamine is the most appropriate choice. It needs to be given for 8-12 h per day for 5- 7 days per week and is thus a major undertaking for the patient. Side effects of therapy are common and include highfrequency deafness and retinopathy. E Commence hydroxyurea or similar cytotoxic to treat myelodysplasia Hydroxyurea won’t reduce transfusion requirements or iron overload in the short term, and thus intervention with an iron chelator is the preferred choice here. A Increase the transfusion program to maintain haemoglobin above 120 g/l This runs the risk of further worsening iron overload and won’t

improve symptoms of cardiac failure. B Commence subcutaneous recombinant erythropoietin to raise the haemoglobin to 120 g/l Commencing erythropoietin to reduce the transfusion requirement is an attractive option, but is only likely to work in patients with low transfusion requirements (<1 unit per month) and does not address the underlying problem of iron overload. C Start venesection program to reduce ferritin to less than 1000 Although this would impact on iron overload, it would worsen anaemia and defeat the object of regular transfusions.

stem: An 18-year-old woman who works at a local day nursery is admitted to the Emergency Department with a severe headache and weakness affecting the left-hand side of her face. She has been unwell for the past few days with headaches, anorexia and diarrhoea. Apparently, she has eaten the same food as a number of children at the nursery who have fallen ill with diarrhoea - two of whom are in the local hospital with kidney disease. On examination, her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg; pulse is 85/min and regular. There is evidence of a purpuric rash and petechial haemorrhages. Abdomen is soft and generally tender, and she has active bowel sounds. You conﬁrm left upper motor neurone 7th nerve palsy. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 99 g/l (schistocytes on blood ﬁlm) 135 - 175 g/l WCC 12.1 × 109/l 4.0 – 11.0 × 109/l PLT 32 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 141 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l LDH 950 u/l 140 – 280 u/l Urine Blood ++ protein ++ Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
D Plasma exchange The history and blood picture seen here is consistent with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). TTP is a rare blood disorder that features extensive microscopic clots that form in the small blood vessels throughout the body causing damage to the kidneys, heart and brain. Most cases of TTP arise from autoantibody-

mediated inhibition of the enzyme (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme) ADAMTS13 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADAMTS13), a metalloprotease (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalloprotease) responsible for cleaving large multimers of von Willebrand factor (vWF) into smaller units. The increase in circulating multimers of vWF increases platelet adhesion to areas of endothelial (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endothelium) injury, particularly at arteriole (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arteriole)–capillary (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capillary) junctions. Haemolytic uraemic syndrome has a similar pathogenic process, although it presents with predominant renal impairment rather than neurological dysfunction. Plasma exchange is the initial therapy of choice, which has been associated with a reduction in mortality rate to less than 25% since its introduction. B Intravenous immunoglobulin Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is a potential interim solution until plasma exchange is available, but there is no role for intravenous immunoglobulin therapy. A Ciproﬂoxacin Ciproﬂoxacin has no role to play in the treatment of TTP. Ciproﬂoxacin may be useful in infection; however, there is no indication of infection in this scenario. C Intravenous methylprednisolone There is no evidence that corticosteroids or antibiotics have any beneﬁt in the management of TTP. Current therapy is based on support and plasmapheresis to reduce circulating (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_circulation) antibodies against ADAMTS13 and replenish blood levels of the enzyme. Methylprednisolone will not reduce the levels of the circulating antibodies. E Platelet transfusion Platelet transfusion is contraindicated unless there is lifethreatening haemorrhage, although platelets are consumed and there is typically a thrombocytopenia in TTP. The diagnostic criteria for TTP includes fevers, change in mental status, a low platelet count, decreased renal function and anaemia due to shearing by blood clots in the small blood vessels (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia).

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with fatigue and confusion that has come on gradually over several weeks. She is a retired secondary school teacher who was still tutoring on a part-time basis until 3 months ago but has recently become reliant on family and neighbours for basic self-care. She has no previous medical history of note and is taking only antacids for occasional dyspepsia. On examination, she is obese, with a blood pressure of 175/100 mmHg. She is disorientated; tone, power and reﬂexes are all within normal limits. Plantar responses are downgoing. Fundoscopy shows prominent retinal veins, but is otherwise normal. There are bi-basal crackles at both bases. Blood tests are shown below: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 95 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.3 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 120 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Urea 10.3 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Bilirubin 21 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l Albumin 29 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Total protein 113 g/l 60 - 83 g/l ESR 95 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 2.3 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l What test is most likely to help establish the cause of confusion?
explanation:
C Serum protein electrophoresis The question asks for the test most likely to conﬁrm the cause of the confusion. Myeloma or Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia leading to clinically signiﬁcant hyperviscosity are the most likely cause here. Serum immunoglobulins do not conﬁrm the presence of a paraprotein, whereas serum protein electrophoresis will. This is because a number of inﬂammatory conditions may result in a global increase in immunoglobulins. If a paraprotein is found, a bone marrow trephine can help make a tissue diagnosis of an associated myeloma [in the case of immunoglobulin G (IgG)/immunoglobulin A (IgA) paraproteins] or lymphoplasmacytoid lymphoma [in the case of immunoglobulin M (IgM) paraprotein] and help to differentiate between Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia and myeloma, but this test will not directly help explain the patient’s confusion. Great care should be exercised before patients with hyperviscosity are transfused, as any further increase in viscosity may precipitate a cerebral event. Treatment is with chemotherapy targeted to the underlying condition and, where transfusion is urgently required, plasmapheresis ﬁrst. B Urine for Bence Jones protein Although urine for Bence Jones protein should certainly be performed in all suspected myelomas, it is extremely rare for light chain disease to cause clinically apparent hyperviscosity. This is because viscosity is directly proportional to the size of the molecule causing it; therefore, IgM, which is pentameric, is most likely to cause hyperviscosity, followed by the dimeric IgA, then IgG.

A Bone scan Bone scanning is of value in multiple myeloma, but of no utility in Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia due to only very rare reports of skeletal system involvement. D Skeletal survey The skeleton is usually not involved in Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia, meaning that a skeletal survey is not usually considered of value in the workup of the condition. E Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain MRI brain may show periventricular white matter changes, but it is not helpful in differentiating whether these are due to microvascular disease or due to an underlying hyperviscosity syndrome.

stem: A 65-year-old man is admitted to hospital with confusion. His wife says he has been complaining of abdominal pain and, in his confused state, suffered a head injury. He has a background of angina. Examination is difﬁcult, but unremarkable. Observations Observations: Blood pressure 110/60 mmHg Heart rate 120 bpm, regular Investigation Result Normal values Hb 96 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 4.9 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 360 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 135 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.6 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 12.2 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 132 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Corrected calcium (Ca2+) 3.6 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Electrocardiogram (ECG) Reduced QT interval
explanation:
D Intravenous (IV) ﬂuids This patient has hypercalcaemia, most likely due to metastatic cancer or multiple myeloma. Patients are described as presenting with bone pain, renal stones, confusion and abdominal pain (bones,

stones, psychic moans and abdominal groans). IV ﬂuids can lead to a modest, but relatively rapid, fall in serum calcium, so this would be the ﬁrst option here. C Prednisolone Steroids do lower serum calcium, more modestly where there is an underlying solid neoplasm versus a haematological malignancy, but they take a number of hours to do this. A Bendroﬂumethiazide Thiazide diuretics reduce calcium excretion and are therefore likely to further increase calcium levels in this situation. B Furosemide Loop diuretics do reduce serum calcium, but in the presence of dehydration, their use is not advised, and IV ﬂuids are the preferred initial intervention. E IV bisphosphonate IV bisphosphonates are appropriate but take 1–2 days before their use is associated with a signiﬁcant fall in serum calcium.

stem: A 53-year-old man presents with tiredness of three months’ duration. He has had abdominal pains in the past year that are ﬂeeting in nature, and he has lost one stone in weight. He is on antacids and has no signiﬁcant previous medical history. On examination, he is slim with pale conjunctivae, but otherwise, there is nothing abnormal to ﬁnd. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 55 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 523 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Ferritin 5 µg/l 20–250 µg/l Corrected Calcium (Ca2+) 2.05 mmol/l 2.1–2.7 mmol/l Colonoscopy and gastroscopy are normal (although gastroscopy was abandoned before biopsies were taken due to patient discomfort). Which investigation would be most useful in making a diagnosis?
explanation:
D Tissue transglutaminase antibodies This gentleman’s anaemia is due to iron deﬁciency, and the most

likely cause is blood loss or iron malabsorption within the gastrointestinal tract. Repeating invasive imaging is unlikely to have as high a yield as tissue transglutamase antibodies, which may reveal an underlying diagnosis of coeliac disease, particularly as this patient failed to tolerate the gastroscopy well last time. A Repeat colonoscopy and gastroscopy An adequately prepared colonoscopy and gastroscopy is likely to exclude signiﬁcant pathology from the oesophagus, stomach and colon, and thus repeating them has limited utility versus other investigations. B Isotope-labelled red cell scan Isotope-labelled red cell scans are useful to exclude signiﬁcant bleeding, not the limited chronic blood loss which is likely here. C Isotope-labelled white cell scan Isotope-labelled white cell scans are most useful in locating occult intra-abdominal abscesses. E Bone marrow aspirate and trephine Given that there is evidence of iron deﬁciency anaemia, bone marrow examination is not of value in this case.

stem: A 73-year-old woman who has long standing CLL comes to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath some 3 weeks after receiving a 3-unit blood transfusion for haemolytic anaemia. Her haemoglobin has fallen from 100g/l on discharge to 61g/l today. She has been treated with Fludarabine therapy for some months. Which of the following is the primary pathogenic mechanism in Autoimmune Haemolytic anaemia, (AIHA) associated with CLL?
explanation:
B Autoreactive T cell induction The answer is Autoreactive T cell induction - Autoreactive T cells speciﬁc for rhesus family antigens are commonly identiﬁed in patients with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. These in turn are thought to drive B cell antibody production, in tandem driving autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Most patients respond to corticosteroids, and in patients who fail to respond to corticosteroids, Rituximab can be considered for rescue therapy. C Autoreactive B cell induction

Autoreactive B cell induction is incorrect. B cells that produce antibodies to red cell components are upregulated in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia related to CLL although this is not the primary event. A Antigen presenting cell dysfunction Antigen presenting cell dysfunction is incorrect, although it is known that CLL cells may display B3, a prominent component of the red cell membrane. Thus they act as antigen presenting cells themselves. D Monocyte dysfunction Monocyte dysfunction, is incorrect because monocyte dysfunction is not a prominent feature of CLL. E Pathological B cell antibody production Pathological B cell antibody production is incorrect. B cells that produce antibodies to red cell components are upregulated in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia related to CLL although this is not the primary event.

stem: A 21-year-old African man, known to be homozygous for sickle cell disease, presents to the Emergency Department with progressive shortness of breath, right-sided pleuritic pain and dry cough over the last 12 hours. On examination, he has a fever of 38 °C. His respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute. Oxygen saturations on air are 90%. He is tachycardic and normotensive, and chest examination demonstrates a widespread expiratory wheeze. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 60 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 20 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT Chest X-ray 450 × 109/l New shadowing at right base 150–400 × 109/l He is diagnosed with acute chest syndrome, possibly related to Mycoplasma infection. What further investigation should be completed to guide prognosis and management in this case?
options: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest
explanation:
A Arterial blood gas (ABG) The appearance of a new pulmonary inﬁltrate on the chest radiograph of a patient with sickle cell disease is termed ‘acute chest syndrome’. The syndrome can develop because of infection or infarction, or a combination of the two. Infective causes include

Gram-positive or -negative bacteria, atypical bacteria and viruses. Usual organisms include Pneumococcus, Mycoplasma and Chlamydia. Acute chest syndrome is usually accompanied or preceded by pain in the chest or extremities, fever, respiratory distress and/or low oxygen saturations. The white cell count is generally high. Although the chest radiograph may be normal initially, subsequent radiographs will reveal an inﬁltrate, which may extend rapidly, involving one or more lobes as well as the pleura. Predictors of severity in acute chest syndrome include worsening hypoxia (< 10% reduction in pa(O2) from the patient’s baseline or pa(O2) < 8 kPa), increasing respiratory rate, decreased PLT count, decreasing Hb concentration, multilobar involvement on chest Xray and neurological complications. Arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling is the gold standard in determining pa(O2) and pa(CO2) in patients with acute chest syndrome. It should be performed in all adults with peripheral oxygen saturations of < 94% on air. The ABG should be performed on room air (even if the patient is receiving oxygen) unless the patient is in respiratory distress or their peripheral oxygen saturations drop to below 85% after a few seconds on room air. The results of the ABG can guide prognosis (by severity) and further management with blood transfusion and respiratory support. B Hb electrophoresis Hb electrophoresis may be used to determine a patient’s level of sickle cell haemoglobin (HbS). While this can be a helpful investigation over the long term, the level of HbS in patients with acute chest syndrome is not predictive of severity, nor will it aid in guiding further management. C High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest Although studies have shown that the extent of microvascular occlusion on HRCT correlates with the clinical severity and degree of hypoxia, it is not recommended in patients presenting with acute chest syndrome. This is because of the high dose of radiation delivered in HRCT and the fact that acute chest syndrome tends to recur and people with sickle cell disease frequently require other radiological tests. As it is not routinely recommended, it would not be appropriate for this patient. D Measurement of peak ﬂow Incentive spirometry is recommended in sickle cell patients presenting with chest or rib pain, as it has proven beneﬁcial in preventing acute chest syndrome. It should also be considered alongside chest physiotherapy in patients presenting with acute chest syndrome. However, peak ﬂow measurement is not of value in predicting the severity of acute chest syndrome or guiding management. E Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) lung scan Although pulmonary embolism is a differential diagnosis in acute chest syndrome and ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) Q scanning may be considered to rule this out while reducing the radiation dose, research shows that V/Q scanning in patients with acute chest

syndrome usually reveals widespread perfusion defects with normal ventilation, the appearances of which may be confused with pulmonary emboli when these are not actually present. It is not recommended as an initial investigation by the British Society for Haematology.

stem: A 65-year-old woman who was recently diagnosed to have Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia (WM) presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of headache and blurring of vision. She has not been started on any medications for the disease previously. The patient is willing to go through any treatment regimen as recommended by the doctor. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of the patient?
explanation:
C Plasmapheresis This patient’s presentation is consistent with hyperviscosity syndrome. Further, fundoscopy has revealed evidence of branch retinal vein occlusion with retinal haemorrhage, which establishes the diagnosis of hyperviscosity syndrome. In such patients, emergency plasmapheresis is recommended as the ﬁrst line of management. Once the symptoms have resolved, more deﬁnitive immunotherapy or chemo-immunotherapy is recommended. B Immediate treatment with ibrutinib Ibrutinib is a bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor and is the ﬁrst drug approved for use in relapsed or progressive WM. It is not beneﬁcial in hyperviscosity syndrome. A Cladribine monotherapy (× 4 cycles) Cladribine is an alkylating agent that was previously widely used in the treatment of WM. However, it is not recommended for the treatment of hyperviscosity syndrome. D Rituximab monotherapy (× 4 cycles) In treatment-naïve patients with WM, initiation of rituximab would be a reasonable option when there is a low disease burden. However, this patient has presented with features of hyperviscosity syndrome and initiation of rituximab is not the best line of action in such patients. E Rituximab, bortezomib and dexamethasone (× 4–6 cycles)

In treatment-naïve patients with WM, initiation of combination therapy with rituximab, bortezomib and dexamethasone would be a reasonable option when there is a high disease burden. However, this patient has presented with features of hyperviscosity syndrome and initiation of combination therapy with these drugs is not the best line of action in such patients.

stem: A 50-year-old man with myelodysplasia complains of breathlessness on exertion. He was diagnosed with myelodysplasia three years ago and has since been on two units of blood every three weeks to maintain his Hb level above 100 g/l. He has noticed over the last three months increasing exertional breathlessness despite maintaining his haemoglobin level > 100. Examination shows a slim man with greyish skin colour, with a heart rate of 90 bpm in sinus rhythm. Heart sounds are normal. The jugular venous pressure is not raised. The cardiac apex is palpable at the anterior axillary line. There are bilateral basal crackles on auscultation of the chest, and the abdominal examination is normal. Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 113 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 1.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 23 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Neutrophils 0.3 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l Glucose 12.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Commence iron chelation with subcutaneous desferrioxamine
Commence subcutaneous recombinant erythropoietin to raise Hb level to 120 g/l
Increase the transfusion programme to maintain Hb level above 120 g/l
Reduce the frequency of blood transfusions
explanation:
B Commence iron chelation with subcutaneous desferrioxamine This patient has early signs of iron overload secondary to chronic blood transfusion; grey skin, early heart failure and diabetes. There are limited options for intervention, and given the transfusion needs of this patient with iron overload, desferrioxamine is the most appropriate choice. It needs to be given for 8–12 hours per day for 5–7 days per week and is, therefore, a major undertaking for the patient. Side-effects of therapy are common and include high-frequency deafness and retinopathy. A Commence iron chelation with penicillamine Penicillamine is a copper-chelating compound that removes copper from the body. It is used in the treatment of Wilson’s disease where there is an excess of copper in the body. However, it does not have

a role in chelating iron. C Commence subcutaneous recombinant erythropoietin to raise Hb level to 120 g/l Commencing erythropoietin to reduce the transfusion requirement is an attractive option. However, it is only likely to work in patients with low transfusion requirements (< 1 unit per month) and does not address the underlying problem of iron overload. D Increase the transfusion programme to maintain Hb level above 120 g/l Increasing the transfusion programme runs the risk of further worsening iron overload and will not improve symptoms of cardiac failure. E Reduce the frequency of blood transfusions The problem in this patient is due to secondary haemochromatosis. While reducing the frequency of transfusions might slow the progression of the disease, the patient might become anaemic and without chelation, there will be no reduction in the excessive iron levels in the patient.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with worsening headaches, three TIAs in the past 6 months and exertional angina. He is a smoker of 30 cigarettes per day and has a history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril 10 mg daily. On examination, his BP is 165/90 mmHg and he looks plethoric. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 185 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 14.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 520 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Potassium (K+) 5.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 160 μmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Which of the following results of further investigations is most likely to differentiate between primary and secondary polycythaemia?
options: Hypoxia on arterial blood gas testing
Hypercapnia on arterial blood gas testing
explanation:
C Low erythropoietin Patients with primary polycythaemia carry a mutation that leads to hypersensitivity to erythropoietin. As such, even in the presence of low erythropoietin levels there is a drive to produce more red blood cells. The symptoms seen here are due to increased red cell mass, consequent increase in plasma volume and raised plasma viscosity.

An activating mutation in JAK2 is identiﬁed in many patients diagnosed with primary polycythaemia; this induces EPO hypersensitivity. Eventual transformation of primary polycythaemia may occur to acute myeloid leukaemia, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or chronic myeloid leukaemia. D Elevated CO levels These are elevated in carbon monoxide poisoning. Elevated CO levels of at least 3–4% in non-smokers and at least 10% in smokers are signiﬁcant. Diagnosis is conﬁrmed by demonstrating an elevated level of carboxyhaemoglobin (HbCO). A Hypoxia on arterial blood gas testing Chronic hypoxia can cause secondary polycythaemia. This can be due to various conditions such as respiratory diseases (COPD, asthma) or cardiac causes (heart failure). It is not a marker used to differentiate between primary and secondary polycythaemia. B Hypercapnia on arterial blood gas testing Hypercapnia is a marker of respiratory conditions such as COPD. Again, this will lead to secondary polycythaemia with raised erythropoietin levels. E Raised viscosity This is not a speciﬁc test and can be raised in inﬂammatory, infectious and autoimmune conditions.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents to her General Practioner complaining of lethargy. Her past history includes hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine and bendroﬂumethiazide; osteoarthritis for which she takes paracetamol; recurrent urinary tract infections for which she is currently taking a 6-week course of cephalexin; and epilepsy, for which she takes sodium valproate. On examination, she looks pale and her skin is yellow-tinged. Her heart rate is 100 bpm and regular, and her BP is 110/70 mmHg. Direct Coomb’s test is positive; serum haptoglobins are low; reticulocyte count is elevated. Urine dipstick is positive for blood. You suspect haemolysis. Which of the following agents is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
C Cephalexin The more common causes of drug-induced autoimmune haemolytic anaemia include penicillin and penicillin derivatives, cephalo-

sporins, levodopa, methyldopa, quinidine and some non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents. Discontinuing the causative agent usually leads to a rapid improvement in the condition, and a short course of oral prednisolone may accelerate recovery. A Paracetamol The main concern with respect to use of paracetamol is hepatic failure rather than haemolytic anaemia. Given that this is a widely used over-the-counter medication, it has an excellent safety proﬁle. B Sodium valproate Sodium valproate can cause anaemia, but this is related to bone marrow abnormalities rather than to haemolytic anaemia. These bone marrow abnormalities resolve on discontinuation of the medication. D Amlodipine Amlodipine in rare cases is associated with reductions in the white blood cell count and/or low platelets. E Bendroﬂumethiazide Blood dyscrasias are rarely reported in patients treated with thiazides, although these are not related to haemolytic anaemia.

stem: A 70-year-old man is brought unconscious to the Emergency Department. He had been found at his sheltered accommodation by the warden, who brought in his medications: warfarin, furosemide and amoxicillin (10-day course, ﬁve days’ doses used). Examination shows a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 5/15, a dilated left-sided pupil and right-sided upper motor neurone signs in the upper and lower limbs. A computed tomography scan of the brain shows a large left-sided subdural haematoma. Ten milligrams of intravenous (IV) vitamin K are given immediately. Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 95 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 403 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l PTT 43 seconds 23.0–35.0 seconds INR 2.0 (target INR 2.5) What additional therapy should be administered to reverse this patient’s warfarin?
options: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) up to 3000 U according to body weight
An additional dose of vitamin K 10 mg IV
explanation: A Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) up to 3000 U according to body weight Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) contains vitamin Kdependent factors and normalises clotting within minutes of administration. It is the recommended product for life-threatening bleeding due to anticoagulation with warfarin. It is plasmaderived, so there is a potential risk of transfusion-transmitted infection, and it is prothrombotic. Even though the INR is within the target range, it is still elevated, as compared to a patient not treated with warfarin, and therefore, it is reasonable to assume it has contributed towards the subdural haematoma and the patient’s clinical state. It is therefore appropriate to rapidly reverse the INR with PCC. B An additional dose of vitamin K 10 mg IV Vitamin K given intravenous (IV) will start to affect the INR for prothrombin activity within 4–8 hours. However, this patient is showing signs of temporal lobe herniation (ipsilateral ﬁxed and dilated pupil) and needs immediate cessation of bleeding if he is to survive. C Cryoprecipitate 10 U Cryoprecipitate contains predominantly ﬁbrinogen and factor VIII. It is, therefore, less effective in reversing bleeding due to warfarin, compared to PCC. D Factor VIII bypassing agent Contained in Factor VIII bypassing agents are activated factors II, VII, IX and X, and it is highly thrombogenic. Its main use is in the management of acquired inhibitors in haemophilia. E Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) 15 ml/kg stat Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) contains low levels of coagulation factors and it is estimated that even at a dose of 15 ml/kg, levels of most factors will only approach 20% of normal. In addition, the large volumes of FFP required are likely to precipitate pulmonary oedema, particularly in an elderly man on furosemide. It is only really considered if other options such as PCC are not available.

stem: An 18-year-old Caucasian with a 4-month history of nonspeciﬁc chest pain is seen in your Outpatient Clinic. She had been having intermittent twinges that initially settled with mild analgesics, but they have become more frequent and painful of late. She is most aware of them just underneath her sternum and there is no radiation. Movement does not exacerbate the pain. However, the more severe pains make her feel dizzy and she has almost passed out on three occasions. There is no history of night sweats, weight loss or fever. She is not short of breath on exertion, but admits that recently she has been too tired to play sport. She does not smoke or take illicit drugs and has recently gone off alcohol. She had asthma as a child but rarely used her salbutamol inhaler. She is on the oral contraceptive pill and has a steady boyfriend. On examination, she looks tired and slightly anxious. She is afebrile. Her pulse is 64 bpm and regular, BP 105/62 mmHg, respirations at rest 16 breaths/min and saturations 97% on room air. She has a small lymph node in the left submandibular region. Heart sounds are normal, her chest is clear and her abdomen is soft with no enlarged organs. ECG shows sinus rhythm. Chest X-ray PA reveals an enlarged mediastinum, with clear lung ﬁelds; an anterior mediastinal mass can be seen on the lateral chest X-ray. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 89 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 165 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 68 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 4.1 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Glucose 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l LDH 1652 IU/l 100–190 IU/l MCV 79.3 ﬂ 80–100 ﬂ CT of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis reveals a large anterior mediastinal mass with irregular borders, 10.1 cm × 9.3 cm × 5.6 cm, surrounding the left pulmonary artery and ligamentum arteriosum; no inﬁltration of surrounding tissues; a large group of lymph nodes in the left axilla; no abnormalities in the abdomen and pelvis. Bone marrow biopsy shows non-speciﬁc ﬁbrous tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Hodgkin’s lymphoma Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a malignant proliferation of lymphocytes. Some 25% of patients have a constitutional upset (i.e. night sweats, weight loss, fever, pruritus and lethargy). Rarely, there may be alcohol-induced pain or features due to mass effects of the affected nodes. An isolated bone marrow biopsy may not yield any signiﬁcant results as Hodgkin’s disease can cause patchy bone marrow inﬁltration, Lymph node biopsies are often more useful. Reed–Sternberg cells are evident on microscopy. Treatment depends on classiﬁcation and staging, but usually involves multiple chemotherapy agents. Prognosis is usually good. B Hairy cell leukaemia Patients with hairy cell leukaemia have inﬁltration of the bone marrow by malignant B lymphocytes (the ‘hairy cells’). This leads to failure to produce red blood cells, white bloods cells and platelets. Leukaemic cells accumulate within the spleen, leading to massive splenomegaly. Fatigue is also a key sign. Not all patients

with hairy cell leukaemia require treatment but, if they do, often single-agent treatment will sufﬁce. This patient’s presentation is not in keeping with a diagnosis of hairy cell leukaemia. C Malignant teratoma A differential for an anterior mediastinal mass includes teratoma. However, teratomas are extremely rare and are often associated with pelvic disease, which the patient in this case does not have. These are usually tumours that develop in utero but that are only picked up much later on in life. Diagnosis is usually via histology. Some teratomas contain yolk sac elements that secrete alphafetoprotein (AFP). However, AFP levels are more commonly used to monitor for disease recurrence after diagnosis rather than being diagnostic. D Thymoma This patient has an anterior mediastinal mass which could be in keeping with a thymoma. However, the mass in this patient has irregular borders and usually with a thymoma you see a smooth, encapsulated tumour. E Tuberculosis This patient has a clear lung ﬁelds on CT where you would normally expect to ﬁnd lesions. The patient also is not suffering with temperatures, productive cough or haemoptysis, all of which make a diagnosis of TB less likely.

stem: A 55-year-old man is admitted to the Gastroenterology Ward with an 8-day history of fevers, vomiting and diarrhoea. He has been unable to tolerate oral intake and reports feeling lethargic. His past medical history includes type II diabetes mellitus, for which he takes metformin and gliclazide. During his admission, he spikes a fever of 39.5 °C with a heart rate of 128 bpm and regular with a BP of 90/60mmHg. Auscultation of his chest is clear, with oxygen saturations of 94% on air. His abdomen is soft with generalised discomfort. There is signiﬁcant bruising around the BP cuff site. Investigation Results Normal value Hb 115 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 18.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 20 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 15.1 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 280 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 144 mg/l < 10 mg/l Activated partial prothrombin time 50 s 27–41 s Prothrombin time 18 s 12–15 s Fibrinogen 1.2 g/l 1.9–8.0 g/l Blood culture Gram-negative rods, awaiting full culture report What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Disseminated intravascular coagulation This patient has a diagnosis of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), likely secondary to Gram-negative septic shock. DIC is an acquired syndrome characterised by dysregulation of the coagulation system leading to the formation of thrombi and consumption of platelets and clotting factors that, in turn, leads to bleeding. Laboratory markers of DIC include a prolonged prothrombin time, activated partial prothrombin time and decreased ﬁbrinogen and platelet count. Another laboratory marker is the presence of elevated ﬁbrin degradation products (D-dimer). B Haemolytic uraemic syndrome Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is characterised by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. The syndrome presents with a history of gastrointestinal upset and is most commonly caused by Shiga-like toxinproducing Escherichia coli (0157:H7). This patient has two of these characteristics and evidence of Gram-negative rods in the bloodstream that may be suggestive of Escherichia coli. However, this patient does not have anaemia and the acute kidney injury could also be caused by eight days of dehydration secondary to diarrhoea, vomiting and reduced oral intake. A good distinguishing factor between HUS and DIC is the prothrombin time which is usually normal in patients with HUS. A prolonged prothrombin time is suggestive of DIC. C Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is a severe drug reaction to heparin that is characterised by the activation of platelets to produce a hypercoagulable state. The onset of HIT tends to follow 5– 10 days of exposure to heparin, including unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin or fondaparinux. Coagulation studies may be normal or abnormal in HIT, as HIT can also induce DIC. However, this patient is not displaying features of thrombosis; rather, he is showing signs of bleeding with signiﬁcant bruising, making HIT unlikely. D Immune thrombocytopenic purpura Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is a haematological disorder characterised by isolated thrombocytopenia. Sometimes thrombocytopenia may be idiopathic or follow a preceding viral illness. Although this patient has marked thrombocytopenia, the presence of other coagulopathic features makes DIC the much more likely diagnosis. E Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is characterised by a pentad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute renal impairment, cerebral dysfunction and fever. Causes of TTP range from being idiopathic or secondary to infection or pregnancy. Typically, patients will expect to have anaemia and thrombocytopenia, but a deranged coagulation proﬁle is not a feature of TTP.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the clinic with fever, weight loss, lethargy and a sensation of pins and needles in his feet. He is particularly concerned that he has begun to suffer increasing headaches over the past few weeks. Other past history of note is gout, which developed a few months ago. On examination, there are lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 98 g/l (normal MCV) 135–175 g/l WCC 4.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 95 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 145 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ESR 75 mm/hour < 10 mm/hour Immunoglobulin M (IgM) Paraprotein band Bone marrow Plasma cell inﬁltration Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Waldenström’s macroglobulinaemia (WM) The combination of anaemia with low white cell and platelet counts, raised ESR, plasma cell inﬁltration of bone marrow and IgM paraprotein band is highly suggestive of Waldenström’s. Death occurs either due to cardiovascular events because of increased viscosity, or due to progression of bone marrow inﬁltration leading to suppressed response to infection. Frontline chemotherapy for Waldenström’s includes the use of alkylating agents; for patients who suffer from acute manifestations of hyperviscosity syndrome, plasmapheresis is the treatment of choice. A Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) CLL is associated with splenomegaly, although the predominant abnormality seen is a rise in peripheral blood white count.

C Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) ALL is usually associated with severe anaemia and thrombocytopenia, with recurrent infections and bleeding episodes, rather than the picture seen here. D Myeloﬁbrosis Myeloﬁbrosis is not associated with symptoms of hyperviscosity (the neuropathy and headaches seen here). E Myelodysplasia Like myeloﬁbrosis, myelodysplasia is not associated with the hyperviscosity symptoms reported here.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Accident and Emergency Department with severe back pain that came on while he was iceskating. He has recently recovered from a viral upper respiratory tract infection, but is otherwise ﬁt and well. He developed back pain without any obvious trauma, and passed dark red urine: he has not passed urine since (four hours ago). He is on no medications and does not smoke or drink. There is no family history of note. On examination, he is in severe discomfort, temperature 38.3 °C, pulse 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 145/83 mmHg, peripheries are well perfused and there is no cyanosis. He is icteric. Abdominal, respiratory and cardiovascular examinations are unremarkable. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 83 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 263 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Reticulocytes 145 × 109/l 25–100 × 109/l Blood ﬁlm Direct Macrophages with ingested erythrocytes Creatinine (Cr) 195 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Coomb's test at room temperature Negative What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria This patient has developed acute intravascular haemolysis (anaemia, high reticulocyte count, jaundice, haemoglobinuria) in response to cold exposure. In PCH, an antibody that binds temporari-

ly in the cold develops in response to infection – classically syphilis, but more commonly various viral infections including Epstein– Barr virus – and on warming, dissociates and activates complement, causing rapid intravascular haemolysis, with rigors and severe bone pain. The antibody is to the P blood group, and is conﬁrmed by the ﬁnding of a Donath- Landsteiner antibody – the patient’s serum is incubated with red blood cells at 4oC and warmed, with subsequent haemolysis. P-negative blood (pp) can be used as a negative control. The Coombs test, now more appropriately called the direct agglutination test, is usually negative. Kidney disease can ensue, but patients in general have a single episode that responds to supportive care. A Cold haemagglutinin disease Cold haemagglutinin disease is not usually paroxysmal in nature, and the Coombs test is positive for C3d: the blood ﬁlm usually shows agglutination of red cells. Taking these factors together, cold haemagglutinin disease is incorrect. C Rhabdomyolysis Rhabdomyolysis is associated with signiﬁcant muscle necrosis and also with trauma, although none has been described here. D Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria PNH is associated with repeated complement-mediated haemolysis and presents with more marked urinary discoloration in the morning. E Evan’s syndrome Evans is Coombs-positive autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, a rare condition of unknown aetiology.

stem: A 71-year-old woman presents with tiredness and lethargy. Her GP had previously noted that she was anaemic and commenced iron therapy. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal Values WCC 2.1 × 109 mmol/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Neutrophils 0.9 × 109 mmol/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Lymphocytes 0.8 × 109 mmol/l 1.5 - 4.0 × 109/l Monocytes 0.1 × 109 mmol/l 0 - 0.8 × 109/l Eosinophils 0 × 109 mmol/l 0.04 - 0.4 × 109/l Basophils 0 × 109 mmol/l < 0.1 × 109/l Hb 91 g/l 135 - 175 g/l MCV 102 ﬂ 80 - 100 ﬂ PLT 90 × 109 mmol/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Bone marrow biopsy reveals increased cellularity with 10% ring sideroblast and <5% blast cells. What diagnosis ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
C Myelodysplasia Myelodysplasia occurs mainly in the elderly and presents with anaemia, infection or bleeding due to pancytopenia. Serial blood counts show evidence of increasing bone marrow failure and the bone marrow shows increased cellularity. Patients with <5% blasts in the bone marrow are managed conservatively, ‘gentle’ chemotherapy is used in patients with high WBC counts and intensive chemotherapy is usually reserved for patients under the age of 60 years. Transformation into AML occurs in around 30% of patients. A Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) Patients with AML generally present with symptoms related to complications of pancytopenia (e.g. anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia), including weakness and easy fatigability, infections of variable severity and/or haemorrhagic ﬁndings such as gingival bleeding, ecchymoses, epistaxis or menorrhagia. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy (usually unilateral) is a key component in the diagnosis of AML. The bone marrow is usually hypercellular due to a partial or almost total replacement of the normal cellular components by immature or undifferentiated cells, although AML can sometimes present with a hypocellular marrow. B Chronic myeloid leukaemia CML has a tri- or biphasic clinical course: a chronic phase, which is present at the time of diagnosis in approximately 85% of patients; an accelerated phase, in which neutrophil differentiation becomes progressively impaired and leukocyte counts are more difﬁcult to control with treatment; and blast crisis, a condition resembling acute leukaemia in which myeloid or lymphoid blasts proliferate in an uncontrolled manner. The peripheral smear typically demonstrates a leukocytosis with a median WCC of approximately 10 × 109 mmol/l. The white blood cell differential typically shows virtually all cells of the neutrophilic series, from myeloblasts to mature neutrophils with peaks in the percentages of myelocytes and segmented neutrophils . Blasts typically account for <2%. The presence of a higher percentage of myelocytes than the more mature metamyelocytes (‘leukemic hiatus’ or ‘myelocyte bulge’) is one of the classic ﬁndings in CML. The granulocytes of the chronic phase are morphologically normal with no evidence of dysplasia, but dysplasia can develop in more advanced disease, and particularly in the accelerated phase. D Myeloﬁbrosis Primary myeloﬁbrosis (PMF) is one of the chronic myeloproliferative disorders, which are collectively characterised by clonal proliferation of myeloid cells with variable morphologic maturity and haematopoietic efﬁciency. Splenomegaly is a marked feature. Bone marrow biopsy is necessary to demonstrate ﬁbrosis. Some degree of ﬁbrosis is seen in almost all patients; the ﬁbrosis is typically extensive and is better visualised with a silver stain (reticulin) or a trichrome stain (mature collagen). Bone marrow sinusoids are

expanded and there is intravascular haematopoiesis. The ﬁbrosis is generally associated with atypical megakaryocytic hyperplasia, and thickening and distortion of the bony trabeculae (osteosclerosis). E Myeloma Multiple myeloma (MM) is characterised by the neoplastic proliferation of plasma cells producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin. The plasma cells proliferate in the bone marrow, and this often results in extensive skeletal destruction with osteolytic lesions, osteopenia and/or pathological fractures. The diagnosis of MM is often suspected because of one (or more) of the following clinical presentations: bone pain with lytic lesions discovered on routine skeletal ﬁlms or other imaging modalities; an increased total serum protein concentration and/or the presence of a monoclonal protein in the urine or serum; systemic signs or symptoms suggestive of malignancy, such as unexplained anaemia, or hypercalcaemia, which is either symptomatic or discovered incidentally; acute kidney disease with a bland urinalysis; or, rarely, nephrotic syndrome due to concurrent immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis. The vast majority (97%) of patients with MM will have a monoclonal (M) protein produced and secreted by the malignant plasma cells, and this can be detected by protein electrophoresis of the serum and/or an aliquot of urine from a 24 h collection, combined with immunoﬁxation of the serum and urine.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is referred for investigation of a paraprotein found at a Well-Woman check. She is currently asymptomatic and working full-time as a teacher. She is on no medication and does not smoke. She has three sisters who are all well. On examination, the pulse is 90 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/64 mmHg, heart sounds normal, the chest is clear. There is no palpable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Neurological examination is unremarkable, with normal fundoscopy and intact sensation. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 143 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.3 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l PLT 355 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Sodium (Na ) 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Protein electrophoresis M band present Paraprotein quantification Immunoglobulin G (IgG) kappa 12 g/l Serum corrected calcium 2.24 mM Urine negative for Bence Jones protein Skeletal survey unremarkable Bone marrow aspirate shows 25% plasma cells Karyotyping no high risk features What is the most appropriate management?
options: Regular follow up with blood tests only
explanation: A Regular follow up with blood tests only This patient has probable early myeloma – bone marrow diagnostic of myeloma, but IgG paraprotein of less than 30 g/l and with no evidence of myeloma-associated organ damage (i.e. normal blood count, calcium, renal function and skeletal survey). In this case, early treatment has so far not been proven to change the course of the illness. B Melphalan and prednisolone Melphalan is reserved for the treatment of myeloma in more elderly patients with co-morbidities for whom more aggressive intervention is inappropriate. C Thalidomide and dexamethasone Thalidomide is a component of modern myeloma therapy regimens, and is thought to be effective because of anti-angiogenic properties. It is used in triple combination with dexamethasone and bortezomib. D Bortezomib Bortezomib inhibits the 26S proteasome and is therefore an indirect inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa B, leading to apoptosis. It is used as an induction chemotherapy agent in some regimens. E Vincristine, doxorubicin and dexamethasone This was previously considered the gold standard protocol for myeloma, although this has now been largely superseded by better-tolerated, more effective combination regimens.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with breathlessness on exertion of 3 months’ duration. He is usually ﬁt and relatively athletic and now needs to stop for breath on climbing a single ﬂight of stairs. His general practitioner has arranged investigations for possible renal stones, and he completed a 6-month course of warfarin for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the last year, but otherwise, he has no signiﬁcant previous medical history. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and a pulse of 100 bpm; heart sounds are normal, and the jugular venous pressure is not raised. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 63 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 2.5 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l Neutrophils 1.1 × 10 /l 2.5–7.58 × 10 /l Platelet (PLT) 75 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l MCV 80 fl 80–100 fl Reticulocytes 90 × 10 /l 25–85× 10 /l Blood film Marked anisocytosis, with polychromasia and hypochromatic cells Ferritin 10 μg/l 20–250 µg/l Urine dipstick Blood+++ Mid-stream urinalysis No cells Urine culture Negative What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) This patient has iron deﬁciency, mild pancytopenia and urine that is positive for Hb but with no red cells seen in the urine. This is most likely to be due to chronic intravascular haemolysis where free circulating Hb is ﬁltered in the kidneys (haemoglobinaemia and haemoglobinuria). A Perl’s stain of the urine will be positive due to iron absorption in uro-epithelial cells, which are then shed in the urine. The causes of chronic intravascular haemolysis are chronic micro-angiopathies, particularly chronic disseminated intravascular coagulation (often secondary to prostatic cancer) and PNH. PNH is characterised by loss of resistance to complement lysis, so that under acidic conditions, red cells are spontaneously lysed. The condition is conﬁrmed by showing loss of PIG-A anchored proteins that confer resistance to complement-mediated lysis – such as DAF (decay accelerating factor) and MIRL (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis), although in the past, the condition was conﬁrmed with either Ham’s or the sucrose lysis test. This diagnosis is also consistent with previous deep vein thrombosis. PNH is associated with a 40% prevalence of venous thrombosis in the intra-abdominal venous network and is generally prothrombotic. The mechanism for this is poorly understood. B Cold haemagglutinin disease Cold haemagglutinin disease is a rare autoimmune haemolytic disease. The cause of the disease is usually unknown in primary disease, but secondary cold agglutinin disease may be associated with certain cancers or viral, bacterial or parasitic infections. Treatment is usually supportive, with any identiﬁable causes re-

quiring treatment. This patient could potentially have cold haemagglutinin disease. However, this is less likely, given that he did not appear to have a triggering infection, and this diagnosis would not explain pancytopenia, as noted here. A Warm autoimmune haemolysis Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) is the most common haemolytic anaemia. Usually, patients present with an increased MCV and hyperbilirubinaemia. The direct Coombs test is diagnostic and also tests for antibodies attached to the surface of red blood cells. Treatment is with corticosteroids and immunoglobulins. This patient’s MCV is not in keeping with warm AIHA. Also in AIHA, you would not expect to ﬁnd Hb in the urine, meaning that AIHA is not the most likely diagnosis for this patient. C Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria is a rare AIHA, characterised by exposure to cold temperatures, leading to Hb in the urine. Triggers include viral and bacterial infections such as measles, mumps, inﬂuenza, cytomegalovirus and Epstein–Barr virus. Treatment for the disease itself is not required, as it is usually self-limiting. Antibiotics can be used to resolve bacterial infections. D Blackwater fever Blackwater fever is usually a complication of malaria whereby red blood cells haemolyse, leading to deposition of Hb within the blood vessels and urine. It is associated with pyrexia, jaundice, rapidly progressing anaemia and dark red/black urine. This patient has some features in keeping with blackwater fever, such as dark urine and anaemia, but the anaemia was insidious in onset and he has neither fevers nor any notable travel history and has pancytopenia.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a haemarthrosis of his left knee after a relatively minor traumatic incident playing football in the park. You understand from his sister that there have been a number of similar incidents over the past 10 years. The child is adopted, but you understand from previous notes that he may have a bleeding disorder which runs in the family. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 190 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Factor VIII Normal PT 13.1 s 10.6–14.9 s PTT Bleeding time 48 s Normal 23.0–35.0 s Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Haemophilia B Haemophilia B, or inherited factor IX deﬁciency, is responsible for around 20% of cases of haemophilia. Patients usually present in childhood with easy bruising, prolonged bleeding after dental work or haemarthrosis after a relatively minor incident of trauma. Both haemophilia A and B are inherited as x-linked diseases, and as such only male individuals present with the bleeding disorder. Given that his factor VIII levels are normal, factor IX deﬁciency is the likely diagnosis. Cut-offs for classiﬁcation of haemophilia range from less than 1% of normal levels of the clotting factor (severe), 1–5% (moderately severe) to 5–40% (mild). A Von Willebrand’s disease (VWD) APTT is only mildly prolonged in 50% of patients with VWD, and it is therefore less likely to be the cause of his symptoms versus haemophilia B. B Haemophilia A Haemophilia A is ruled out by the normal factor VIII levels seen here. C Acquired haemophilia Acquired haemophilia occurs later in life in patients with collagen vascular disease due to cross-reacting antibodies, and anti-clotting factor antibodies in patients treated for a number of years for haemophilia may lead to reduced effectiveness. E Glanzman thrombasthaenia Glanzmann’s is a disorder of platelet function; it is an extremely rare coagulopathy in which the platelets contain defective or low levels of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, a receptor for ﬁbrinogen.

stem: You are asked to see a 30-year-old man who is undergoing inpatient treatment for acute myeloid leukaemia. He completed combination chemotherapy 6 days ago and was well until this morning when he noticed increasing breathlessness. On examination, he is pale and clammy, with a high respiratory rate. Pulse is 130 bpm, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, and his skin is cool to touch. He is slightly drowsy and disorientated. Temperature is 35.6 °C, and he has several crops of black lesions over his arms and legs. A chest X-ray is unremarkable. Blood tests are shown below: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 73 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 0.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 13 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Neutrophils 0 × 109/l 1.5 - 7.0 × 109/l Urea 10.3 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l
options: Take blood and urine cultures and start antibiotics when results are available
Commence broad-spectrum antibiotics with antipseudomonal cover
Transfuse packed red cells to maintain Hb level above 100 g/l
explanation: D Commence broad-spectrum antibiotics with antipseudomonal cover This patient is developing septic shock. The black lesions on the skin are ecthyma gangrenosum, a cutaneous manifestation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection. Given a WCC of 0.2 and neutrophil count of 0, commencement of broad-spectrum antibiotics with antipseudomonal cover, according to local guidelines, is the intervention of choice. B Commence voriconazole In this situation, antibacterials are usually commenced ﬁrst, with antifungal cover added in patients who fail to respond after 48 h. A Biopsy the skin lesions Invasive procedures, including skin biopsy, should be avoided in patients with neutropenia; in this case, a clinical diagnosis can be made. C Take blood and urine cultures and start antibiotics when results are available This risks a signiﬁcant delay in treating any associated bacterial sepsis and a signiﬁcantly increased risk of mortality. E Transfuse packed red cells to maintain Hb level above 100 g/l Surviving sepsis guidelines suggest a target of 70 g/l for Hb is adequate.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with pleuritic chest pain of sudden onset. She has recently ﬂown back to this country from Australia. She had a previous deep vein thrombosis two years ago. She is a full-time mother of two children aged three and six. Examination shows her to be breathless, cyanosed and in distress. She is tachycardic, with a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg and a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound. There is a pleural rub. Her respiratory rate is 35 breaths per minute. Chest X-ray is clear. Investigation Result Normal Values p(O2) 7.9 kPa 11.3 - 12.6 kPa p(CO2) 3.5 kPa 4.7 - 6.0 kPa Given this patient’s presentation, what is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
B Activated protein C resistance This patient has factor V Leiden (activated protein C resistance). Of all the inherited causes of thrombophilia, factor V Leiden is the most common and is present in 3–5% of the population. It increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) by 4–5 times. Protein C is a natural anticoagulant that normally binds to, and inactivates, factors V and VIII. In factor V Leiden, protein C cannot inactivate factor V, thereby increasing its prothrombotic potential. The mutation is synergistic with the use of the oral contraceptive pill, and patients with a conﬁrmed VTE should receive three months of anticoagulant therapy. Cascade screening of adult family members is appropriate, and members who carry a factor V Leiden mutation can receive lifestyle counselling regarding contraception and long journeys. D Protein C deﬁciency Protein C deﬁciency is an inherited thrombophilia caused by a lack of the natural anticoagulant protein C. This is not to be confused with activated protein C resistance where protein C is present but cannot inactivate factor V. The overall prevalence in the population is much lower than for factor V Leiden, making it less likely. A Antiphospholipid syndrome Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired disorder that is associated with arterial and venous thromboses, thrombocytopenia and fetal loss. Recurrent venous thromboses without any other features of antiphospholipid syndrome make an alternative cause of thrombophilia more likely. C Antithrombin III deﬁciency Antithrombin III binds to, and inactivates thrombin. Thrombin acts to activate several factors in the clotting cascade, including the conversion of ﬁbrinogen to ﬁbrin. Antithrombin III deﬁciency can be inherited or acquired (eg following trauma or surgery or in chronic kidney disease) but is less common than factor V Leiden. E von Willebrand’s disease von Willebrand’s disease is the most common inherited cause of ll i th h ti

bleeding and would not be the cause of this patient’s presentation.

stem: The following panel results were seen for a transfusion recipient and the donor unit of blood. Donor sample is positive for the following antibodies; • Anti A positive • Anti B positive • Anti rhesus positive Recipient is positive for the following antibodies; • Anti-A positive • Anti-B negative • Anti rhesus negative What blood group was the recipient?
explanation: B B+ This man has antibodies to the A blood group antigen, which means he does not possess it himself. In contrast, he has no anti-B or antirhesus antibodies, and therefore he must have a B+ blood group. The donor panel suggests that the donor has antibodies to all three antigens, A, B and rhesus. As such, he or she must be blood group O–, the so-called universal donor. A AB- The presence of anti-A antibodies means this patient’s red cells cannot carry the A antigen. Blood groups B or O may be associated with anti-A antibodies. C A+ The presence of anti-A antibodies means this patient’s red cells cannot carry the A antigen. D A- Anti-A antibodies rule out the presence of the A blood group antigen. The fact that the recipient is anti-rhesus negative means that his blood cells must carry the rhesus antigen. E B- Although the fact he is anti-A positive would ﬁt with the B blood group, anti-rhesus negativity ﬁts with his red

stem: A 70-year-old woman is referred to the Haematology Clinic for review. She was referred after the discovery of some abnormal blood results by her General Practitioner during a routine workup. She feels well in herself and denies any symptoms of note. Her past medical history includes hypertension and type II diabetes, for which she takes ramipril, metformin and gliclazide. She drinks alcohol occasionally and is a non-smoker. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 132/82 mmHg and a heart rate of 75 bpm and regular. Her chest is clear and abdominal examination reveals splenomegaly. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Value Hb 125 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 50.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Lymphocytes 46.1 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l PLT 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 105 mmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with routine follow-up in three months
explanation:
A Discharge with routine follow-up in three months This patient has a likely diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), a malignancy of the lymphoid lineage that is common in the elderly population as it is often asymptomatic. Although she has marked lymphocytosis, she does not currently ﬁt the criteria for intervention with chemotherapy. Chemotherapy should only be given to patients with active, symptomatic diseases. Examples of markers of active disease include: • weight loss > 10% • extreme fatigue • fever related to leukaemia • night sweats • progressive marrow failure • autoimmune anaemia or thrombocytopenia not responding to prednisolone • massive lymphadenopathy • progressive lymphocytosis (an increase of > 50% in two months or a doubling time of less than six months). Therefore, discharge with follow-up and monitoring of full blood

count is the most appropriate choice at this stage. B Fludarabine, rituximab and cyclophosphamide Fludarabine is the purine analogue of choice for the treatment of CLL, in combination with cyclophosphamide and rituximab (FCR) for those who can tolerate the triple regimen. Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that leads to lymphocyte depletion. It is used as triple therapy for the treatment of CLL, although much poorer response rates are seen in patients with TP53 deletion. Where TP53 deletion is seen, novel agents such as ibrutinib are recommended as a ﬁrst-line intervention. C Hydroxycarbamide Hydroxycarbamide is used in the treatment of acute and chronic myeloid leukaemia, myeloproliferative disease and sickle cell anaemia. It is not used in the treatment of CLL. D Ibrutinib Ibrutinib is reserved as second-line treatment of CLL, after trialling FCR. E Imatinib Imatinib is the ﬁrst-line treatment of chronic myeloid leukaemia. The normal neutrophil count makes this patient’s elevated WCC secondary to lymphocytosis, of which CLL is the most likely.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with a 2month history of headache, dizziness and general lethargy. He has previously been ﬁt and well, with no past medical history of note. He smokes ten cigarettes per day and drinks 1–2 cans of 4% beer over the weekend. On examination, he has a blood pressure of 165/99 mmHg and a heart rate of 88 bpm. His cardiorespiratory examination is unremarkable with oxygen saturations of 94% on air. There is generalised abdominal discomfort with palpable splenomegaly and he has a ruddy complexion.
