Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value WCC 10.0 × 10 /l (Neutrophils 7, lymphocytes 1, eosinophils 0.3, basophils 0.1, metamyelocytes 0.2, myelocytes 0.1 and nucleated red cells 0.1) 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l Haematocrit 28% 0.35–0.55 Haemoglobin (Hb) 87 g/l 135–175 g/l PLT 300 x 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l MCV 98 fl 76–98 fl LDH 400 IU/l 100–190 IU/l Total bilirubin 51 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Conjugated bilirubin 0.5 μmol/l 0.0–0.4 μmol/l Peripheral blood smear Clumped cells Polyspecific sera + for complement components Which of the following is most likely to be expected on further testing?
options: Positive direct Coombs’ test (using anti-IgG antiserum) if the specimen is processed without allowing cooling
Positive indirect Coombs’ test detected with anti-IgG antibodies
Circulating antibodies against red cells bearing the I antigen
explanation:
D Circulating antibodies against red cells bearing the I antigen This patient has cold-reactive haemolysis or cold agglutinin disease. If patients develop circulating anti-IgM antibodies with speciﬁcity for polysaccharide antigens on red cell membranes, they may suffer from so-called ‘cold-reactive haemolysis’. The clinical manifestations of presence of such antibodies are haemolysis, which is generally not severe and a mild elevation of the reticulocyte count, agglutination of red cells, and an increased rate of haemolysis at temperatures below 37oC. A second clinical manifestation of cold haemolysis is the presence of acrocyanosis, characterized by marked purple discoloration of the extremities, ears and nose during cooling. IgM antibodies may be missed if the blood is allowed to cool after it is drawn because of absorption onto the patient’s own red blood cells and subsequent removal as the blood clots. Therefore, the blood should be allowed to clot at a warm temperature. Serological analysis will reveal a positive direct Coombs’ test if anti- C3 antiserum is used. The speciﬁcity of cold agglutinin antibody may be helpful in that a reaction with adult red cells compared with fetal blood is more common in benign lymphoproliferative disorders. On the other hand, antibodies

that react more strongly with fetal cells compared with adult red cells are called anti-i and are generally seen in lymphomas and in infectious mononucleosis. This patient may well have recurrence of his lymphoma, which is presenting as cold haemolytic disease because of the presence of monoclonal IgM antibody. The problem is best treated with anti-lymphoma therapy. C Circulating antibodies against Epstein–Barr virus EBV can cause autoimmune haemolysis. IgG antibodies to EBV show a previous infection, a positive IgM antibodies show a current infection. Complement components would not be positive in this case. Blood ﬁlm in EBV would show 50% lymphocytes and 10% atypical lymphocytes. A Positive direct Coombs’ test (using anti-IgG antiserum) if the specimen is processed without allowing cooling A direct Coombs’ test will be only positive with anti-C3 serum for cold reactive haemolysis, because the auto- antibody is IgGcomplement based and, in cold temperatures, IgG causes complement to irreversibly bind to red blood cells. B Positive indirect Coombs’ test detected with anti-IgG antibodies Indirect Coombs’ testing is mainly used in cross-matching for blood transfusions or prenatal testing for serum IgG antibodies that may cross the placenta and cause haemolytic disease of the newborn. E Circulating antibodies against Mycoplasma pneumoniae Gold standard testing for mycoplasma pneumoniae is having two positive IgM or IgG results 2-4 weeks apart, as a single positive may be the result of a recent previous infection and some people do not mount an immune response. Patients usually have non-speciﬁc ﬂu-like or cold-like symptoms. Many patients will have a leucocytosis and some have a raised ESR.

stem: A 30-year-old man has been admitted for elective knee arthroscopy. You are asked to review him prior to the operation. He has a past history of gallstones and had jaundice as a child, but otherwise, he is ﬁt and well. Examination reveals mild splenomegaly. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 127 g/l 135-175 g/l WCC 8.2 × 109/l 4.0-11.0 × 109/l PLT 400 × 109/l 150-400 × 109/l MCV 78 ﬂ 76-98 ﬂ MCHC 43 g/dl 32-35 g/dl Reticulocytes 3.3% 0.5-2.4% What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: E Hereditary spherocytosis Hereditary spherocytosis is inherited as an autosomal dominant condition and is one of the most common inherited haemolytic anaemias. The defect is in the membrane skeleton (usually the spectrin component), resulting in the appearance of spherocytes in the blood ﬁlm. The spleen removes these spherocytes from the blood. Symptoms are variable in severity but include anaemia, jaundice and splenomegaly. With haemolysis, patients are at increased risk of pigment gallstones. The mean cell volume is usually low and the mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration is usually high. The most sensitive test to conﬁrm the diagnosis used to be the osmotic fragility test, although this has largely been replaced by EMA binding testing now. Folic acid can be given to aid haemopoiesis, but occasionally splenectomy is required. C Iron deﬁciency anaemia Iron deﬁciency anaemia is associated with microcytic anaemia. Although increased reticulocytes are associated with haemolytic anaemia, gallstones would not be expected. A Sickle cell disease Given that this patient is 30 years old, a history of sickle cell crisis would be expected in a patient with sickle cell disease. B Sideroblastic anaemia Sideroblastic anaemia presents with more signiﬁcant symptoms of anaemia than those reported here, and also leads to iron overload, which itself can present with cardiac failure and hepatic ﬁbrosis/cirrhosis. D Thalassaemia trait Thalassaemia trait is generally associated with slightly lower MCV (in the 65–75 range) and is not associated with elevated reticulocytes.

stem: A 34-year-old woman attends the Anticoagulation Clinic for review. She currently takes warfarin for recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE), with a target INR of 3–4. In the clinic today, she reports feeling well in herself, with no symptoms to report. Her observations are within normal limits, and her examination is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result today Previous result Normal value Hb 136 g/l 132 g/l 135–180 g/l Platelets 228 × 109/l 310 × 109/l 150–450 × INR 7.9 3.4 109/l < 1.1 APTT 25 seconds 28 seconds 25–35 seconds Fibrinogen 2.1 g/l 2.5 g/l 2–4 g/l What is the next most appropriate action?
options: Hold warfarin for 24–48 hours and review
Intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex
explanation: B Hold warfarin for 24–48 hours and review The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines state that an INR < 8 in a patient with no signs of bleeding requires warfarin to be held for 24–48 hours, with review of a repeat INR. Additional agents do not need to be given unless the patient has an INR > 8 or signs of bleeding. D Intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex Intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex would not be appropriate here. Similarly to fresh frozen plasma, these agents are reserved for major bleeding in patients on warfarin therapy. A Fresh frozen plasma Fresh frozen plasma may be given to patients on warfarin therapy with major bleeding by replacing clotting factors and ﬁbrinogen. However, it is not indicated in stable patients with no signs of active bleeding. C Intravenous vitamin K Intravenous vitamin K is given in cases with an INR > 8 or any episode of major bleeding on warfarin therapy. Given the absence of bleeding and an INR < 8, it is not indicated at this stage. E Oral vitamin K Oral vitamin K is indicated for an INR > 8 with no bleeding or an INR 5–8 with minor bleeding.

stem: An 89-year-old woman is an inpatient recovering from community-acquired pneumonia. She is on warfarin for atrial ﬁbrillation, and has been put on intravenous ampicillin since admission 48 hours ago. You are contacted for advice regarding management of her high INR. She is currently well, with no symptoms or signs of bleeding. INR > 10 (target 2.5). What is the most appropriate management?
options: 5 mg of oral vitamin K or 0.5–1 mg of IV vitamin K
Prothrombin complex concentrate containing factors II, VII, IX and X
explanation: B 5 mg of oral vitamin K or 0.5–1 mg of IV vitamin K It will take several days for the INR to fall to a safe level, and patients over 70 years of age are at increased risk of haemorrhagic complications. Also at risk of haemorrhage are patients who already have minor bleeding. e.g. gum bleeding or epistaxis, or those who have bled in the past on warfarin. Both oral and IV vitamin K are potential options with an INR >8, without active bleeding at the doses described above (5 mg oral, or 0.5–1 mg IV). E Prothrombin complex concentrate containing factors II, VII, IX and X Prothrombin complex concentrate is extremely useful for rapidly reversing over-anticoagulation with warfarin, but it is a pooled plasma product and can cause disseminated intravascular coagulation: its use is therefore in life-threatening bleeding associated with over-anticoagulation. A Observation alone At an INR >10, spontaneous and potentially signiﬁcant bleeding can be seen at any time. As such, intervention with vitamin K is required. C 15 ml/kg of fresh frozen plasma A level of 15 ml/kg of fresh frozen plasma is unlikely to raise coagulation factors above 20%: higher doses, while more likely to correct adequately, can cause ﬂuid overload. Fresh frozen plasma is not virally inactivated and can cause transfusion complications such as transfusion-related acute lung injury. As such other options for acute correction of INR related to warfarin excess are preferred. D 10 units of cryoprecipitate Cryoprecipitate contains higher levels of factor VIII and ﬁbrinogen: its use is therefore limited mainly to the treatment of dysﬁbrinogenaemia or hypoﬁbrinogenaemia.

stem: A 45-year-old man is referred from his general practitioner with an abnormal white cell count found on routine testing. On examination, he has several 1–2 cm lymph nodes and 3 cm splenomegaly. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 95 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 34.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 94 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Lymphocytes 31 × 109/l 1.5–3.5 × 109/l Immunophenotype was positive for B-cell markers (CD19 and CD20) with aberrant expression of the T-cell marker CD5. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) This man has an increase in mature lymphocytes in his peripheral blood. Immunophenotyping can be used to identify leucocytes by staining them with antibodies to the ‘CD’ (cluster differentiation) system, and is standard testing in unexplained lymphocytosis. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, a condition of B lymphocytes, paradoxically expresses CD5, a T-cell marker. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) can be staged according to two systems – Binet’s and Rai’s classiﬁcations – which use a combination of clinical features and number of cytopenia. Although Binet’s stage A CLL (less than three sites of lymphadenopathy, normal platelets and haemoglobin) carries a normal life expectancy (and does not require treatment), this man has much more advanced disease with widespread lymphadenopathy and advanced marrow failure, and this is what drives the need to explain to him about limited life expectancy. Recent advances have shown that positivity to ZAP (zeta- associated protein) 70 is associated with poorer prognosis disease. A Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) Circulating blasts with markers on ﬂow cytometry consistent with immature lymphocytes are found in the peripheral blood of patients with AML. B Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) ALL blood ﬁlm examination reveals circulating blasts, and ﬂow cytometry with cytogenetics can be used to differentiate ALL from AML. AML is usually associated with blasts that are positive for CD33, whereas ALL- associated cells are not. D Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) CML is associated with an increase in mature neutrophils, with a mild increase in basophils and eosinophils, against a background of a normal lymphocyte count. E Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) NHL is associated with unexplained lymphadenopathy, night sweats and weight loss, and any elevation in white blood cell count would be much less than that seen here.

stem: A 23-year-old plumber presents to his General Practitioner with gum swelling and drowsiness. Previously ﬁt and well, he ﬁrst noticed some bleeding from his gums, coupled with easy bruising, over the last week. He takes no medications, smokes ten cigarettes daily and drinks within 21 units per week. On examination, he has markedly swollen gums, several enlarged lymph nodes in the neck and groin and 3-cm hepatosplenomegaly. Basic observations are unremarkable. Fundoscopy reveals several retinal haemorrhages and dilated retinal veins. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal values Haemoglobin (Hb) 63 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 353.7 × 10 /l 4.0–11.0 × 10 /l PLT 6.0 × 10 /l 150–400 × 10 /l Blood film Heavy infiltrate of blasts with monocytoid features Serum lysozyme 73 mg/l 4–13 mg/l APTT 45 s 25–35 s Which of the following is required to make the diagnosis in this patient?
options: Presence of 10% of myeloid blast cells in the bone marrow
Presence of 10% of myeloid blast cells in the peripheral blood ﬁlm
Presence of ghost and basket cells on the peripheral blood smear
explanation:
E Translocation t(8:21)(q22;q22) on cytogenetic analysis This patient has acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) which is most likely to be of either subtype M4 (myelomonocytic) or subtype M5 (monocytic). Typically, AML subtypes M4/5 are characterised by gum inﬁltration, organomegaly and lymphadenopathy, monocytoid blasts and raised serum lysozyme levels. Hypokalaemia and coagulopathy are common. The diagnosis of AML is pathological. It can be made either by the presence of ≥ 20% of blast cells of myeloid lineage in the bone marrow or peripheral blood ﬁlm or < 20% of blast cells if speciﬁc clonal abnormalities are present such as t(8;21)(q22;q22), inv(16)(p13;q22), t(16;16)(p13;q22) and t(15;17)(q22;q12). This option is therefore the most appropriate, as myeloid cells have already been demonstrated on this patient’s blood ﬁlm (monocytoid cells with the presence of Auer rods). Therefore, AML is conﬁrmed by the presence of this speciﬁc translocation, which is found in 5–12% of all AML cases. Chemotherapy regimens are designed to achieve induction, (attaining remission), followed by post-remission consolidation (intensiﬁcation). Regimes commonly include arabinosyl cytosine, mitoxantrone and daunorubicin. B Presence of 10% of myeloid blast cells in the peripheral blood ﬁlm

A diagnosis of AML is made by the presence of ≥ 20% of myeloid blast cells in the bone marrow and/or peripheral blood. This would be appropriate if it read ≥ 20% of myeloid blast cells in the peripheral blood or bone marrow. A Presence of 10% of myeloid blast cells in the bone marrow This is not required as 20%, rather than 10%, of myeloid blast cells, are required within the bone marrow. Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) can often be clinically indistinguishable and therefore, conﬁrmation of the origin of the leukaemic cells by immuno—or histochemistry is essential—cells can be collected from the peripheral blood or from the bone marrow for classiﬁcation. C Presence of ghost and basket cells on the peripheral blood smear The presence of basket and ghost cells indicates possible leukaemia of lymphoid origin. These cells represent large lymphoid blasts that have become damaged during the smear preparation process. This occurs as lymphoid blasts tend to be more fragile than myeloid cells. The presence of these cells on the blood ﬁlm would therefore make AML less likely. D Translocation t(5;14)(q31.1;q32.3) IL3–IGH Translocation t(5;14)(q31.1;q32.3) IL3–IGH is a cytogenetic abnormality associated with B lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma. It results in eosinophilia and would not be appropriate in this patient.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain and changes in bowel habit. She is normally well, though she was noted to have an immunoglobulin A (IgA) deﬁciency as a child. She is experiencing cramping pain and fatigue, though she denies blood in her stool. Blood tests are undertaken: Normal Values Hb 103 g/l 115 - 155 g/l Anti-endomysial antibodies negative An intestinal biopsy is undertaken, the results of which are shown below. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: A Coeliac disease This history is highly suggestive of coeliac disease, and this is essentially conﬁrmed by histology which demonstrates villous atrophy. The red herring is the negative anti-endomysial antibody; this can be absent in patients with IgA deﬁciency (which is more common in coeliac disease). Anti-tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies are more commonly used nowadays, while diagnosis can only be conﬁrmed by biopsy. C Irritable bowel syndrome Irritable bowel syndrome presents with no changes on histology; this slide shows villous atrophy, consistent with coeliac disease. B Crohn’s disease The histology in this case is not compatible with Crohn’s disease. Histology of Crohn’s disease may include ﬁbrosis, ulceration, strictures or skin lesions, all of which are absent in this case. D Lactose intolerance In lactose intolerance, small bowel biopsy is not usually necessary, given its invasive nature. Samples are usually normal without assaying for lactase activity. E Ulcerative colitis The lack of blood rectally suggests ulcerative colitis is less likely, though this does not rule it out. Histological features of ulcerative colitis include diffuse mononuclear inﬂammatory inﬁltrates, crypt abscesses and cryptitis, without skip lesions (as compared with Crohn’s disease). The histology in this question shows villous atrophy, indicative of coeliac disease.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of general malaise and bruising. On examination, she is pale with some petechiae and quite marked bruising; there are no other obvious abnormalities. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 104 g/l (normocytic) 115–155 g/l Platelet (PLT) 20 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l WCC 11.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l ESR 10 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Autoimmune proﬁle (AIP) Negative Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura In adults, ITP generally presents gradually and is associated with spontaneous bruising, petechiae and thrombocytopenia. ITP is more common in women (2.6:1) and in adults tends to present between ages 20–50. The cause is IgG anti-platelet antibodies, which are not tested as part of a standard autoimmune proﬁle, hence the negative result shown above. Management involves the use of oral corticosteroids, with splenectomy an option for patients who fail to respond to medical therapy. Chronic GI blood loss is the likely cause for the haemoglobin seen here. C Felty’s syndrome One would expect a positive rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP screen within the autoimmune proﬁle. Furthermore, whilst Felty syndrome can cause a pancytopenia, it generally follows several years of active, destructive rheumatoid disease rather than the relatively short 2-month history within the case vignette. B Systemic lupus erythematosus ITP is more likely given the negative autoimmune proﬁle, and is unlikely to cause bruising. SLE can cause an anaemia of chronic disease, haemolytic anaemia or thrombocytopenia, but the autoimmune proﬁle is likely to be positive (in particular anti-dsDNA, antinuclear, antiphospholipid or anti-Sm positive). D Rheumatoid arthritis This is less likely given the presentation of bruising and petechiae; the negative autoimmune proﬁle also points against rheumatoid arthritis.

E Infectious mononucleosis Whilst infectious mononucleosis is associated with a history of arthralgia, general malaise as well as thrombocytopenia and raised ESR, it remains an unlikely cause for this patient’s presentation. The history of bruising and the presence of anaemia and petechiae all point to an alternate diagnosis. Anaemia is rarely seen with infectious mononucleosis and in fact its presence warrants further investigation.

stem: A 32-year-old woman who has suffered a bleed post-caesarean section receives the second unit of a 3-unit blood transfusion and develops sudden onset shortness of breath, fever and cough. There is no history of ﬂank pain. The unit is immediately stopped. On examination, she looks unwell; her BP is 100/62 mmHg, with a pulse of 95/min. Her jugular venous pressure (JVP) is not elevated. Auscultation of the chest reveals bilateral crackles consistent with pulmonary oedema. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 96 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 3.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 130 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 8.1 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Transfusion Associated Lung Injury In all likelihood this is non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, as evidenced by the chest signs. The lack of an elevated JVP and the low normal blood pressure count against a diagnosis of ﬂuid overload. This ﬁts best with a diagnosis of TRALI. Two hypotheses exist as to the cause of TRALI: (1) anti-HLA antibodies are transfused into the patient, leading to neutrophil activation, release of cytokines and pulmonary oedema; and (2) neutrophils ready primed by surgery or infection react with bioactive substances in the transfused blood, leading to similar neutrophil activation. Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema can be differentiated from ﬂuid overload by measurement of BNP if there is an element of diagnostic confusion. Diuretics are not beneﬁcial in the management of the condition, and she should be managed with supportive care, including transfer to ITU for consideration of intubation and ventilation if required. The mortality of TRALI is

estimated at 5–13% depending on case series. D Circulatory overload Given that this patient is a 32-year-old woman, circulatory overload in response to a blood transfusion is extremely unlikely. The low blood pressure would also not ﬁt well with circulatory overload. A ABO incompatability ABO incompatibility leads to acute haemolysis with a severe transfusion reaction, associated with mortality of up to 10%. Symptoms are similar to anaphylaxis, although the reaction is not mediated by IgE. B Rhesus incompatability Non-ABO incompatibility reactions – for example, those associated with rhesus incompatibility, are less severe than ABO incompatibility, although signiﬁcant haemolysis is still seen. E Anaphylaxis Bacterial contamination of units of red cells is thankfully extremely rare but, where it occurs, circulatory collapse with hypotension and rigors is seen early on in the transfusion process.

stem: A 45-year-old Cypriot man attends his GP for a new patient appointment. He feels well and works long hours running a painting and decorating business. The only past history of note is mild hypertension, for which he has been recommended to lose weight and institute lifestyle improvements. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 70 g/l (MCV 68;target cells) 135–175 g/l WCC 4.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 190 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbF Slightly elevated (5%) HbA2 4% Faecal occult blood + Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Co-existent beta-thalassaemia minor and iron deﬁciency anaemia
explanation: D Co-existent beta-thalassaemia minor and iron deﬁciency anaemia We are given various clues to the diagnosis here: his nationality points us towards the possibility of thalassaemia minor, yet the anaemia seems unexpectedly severe and HbA2 levels are normal, which is out of keeping with the diagnosis. The faecal occult blood positivity, however, suggests the possibility of co-existent GI tract blood loss, and in cases of severe iron deﬁciency anaemia the HbA2 may be normal in thalassaemia minor. Hence he requires adequate investigation of his iron status, with iron studies and imaging of the GI tract to rule out occult GI blood loss. B Beta-thalassaemia minor Beta-thalassaemia minor may be associated with microcytosis, but wouldn’t ﬁt with the positive faecal occult blood reported in this patient. A Lead poisoning Lead poisoning is associated with microcytic anaemia, although it wouldn’t explain the positive faecal occult blood seen here. C Iron deﬁciency anaemia Iron deﬁciency anaemia alone wouldn’t explain the signiﬁcant reduction in MCV seen here with regard to the level of anaemia. E Hereditary spherocytosis Hereditary spherocytosis is associated with haemolysis, not with microcytic anaemia and positive faecal occult bloods as in this patient.

stem: A 72-year-old man on the Orthopaedic Ward, known to suffer from indigestion, had a 200-ml haematemesis 12 hours after receiving a treatment dose of enoxaparin after a total hip replacement. On examination, his blood pressure is 142/82 mmHg and his pulse is 85 bpm and regular. There is tenderness in the epigastrium, although his abdomen is soft. Investigations Results Normal value Hb 114 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.7 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 185 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na+) 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l PT 13.1 s 10.6–14.9 s APTT (APTT) 48.2 s 22–41 s Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: C Protamine sulfate Protamine sulfate is the direct antidote for heparin and is thought to reverse 60% or more of the anticoagulant effect of lowmolecular-weight heparin. The patient’s aPTT is mildly elevated at 48.2 s, further indicating the need for reversal with protamine sulfate. B Idarucizumab Idarucizumab is used in the reversal of dabigatran. It would not be indicated in this patient, following enoxaparin administration. A Andexanet alfa Andexanet alfa is the reversal agent for apixaban and rivaroxaban. It is not used to manage the anticoagulant effects of enoxaparin. D Prothrombin complex concentrate Prothrombin complex concentrate is used to reverse the effects of warfarin and has no role in the reversal of low-molecular-weight heparin. E Vitamin K Vitamin K is used to reverse the effects of warfarin and has no role in the reversal of low-molecular-weight heparin.

stem: You review a woman who is 34 weeks pregnant. Fetal growth has been normal so far. She presents with epigastric pain and increasing ankle oedema. Her midwife has noted her blood pressure to be 159/95 mmHg (increased from 132/81 mmHg some 2 weeks earlier). She has proteinuria. Platelet count is reduced at 7 × 109/l (down from 160 × 109/l some 4 weeks earlier). She has raised transaminases and bilirubin. What would be the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
options: Hydralazine IV and admit for bed rest
Delivery of the baby post replacement of blood products
Urgent ultrasound scan of the liver
explanation:
B Delivery of the baby post replacement of blood products This woman has evidence of pre-eclampsia, with a deteriorating blood picture (decreased platelet count and abnormal liver en-

zymes) and rapidly worsening hypertension. Nearly 10% of women with severe pre- eclampsia and 30–50% of women with eclampsia are affected by the syndrome of haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelet count (HELLP). The exact relationship between HELLP syndrome and pre-eclampsia is unknown. Women with pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome develop hepatocellular necrosis and liver dysfunction. They also have an increased mortality rate, and one third of women with preeclampsia develop disseminated intravascular coagulation. The best treatment for this woman would be to deliver the baby. Mild hypertension in pregnancy has been managed with oral nifedipine or labetalol. In this case, IV hydralazine or labetalol may well be required for blood pressure reduction/control pre-op. D Oral nifedipine and discharge Women with pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome will need more than oral nifedipine for blood pressure control. It would not be appropriate to discharge without treatment. A Hydralazine IV and admit for bed rest Women with pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome will be unlikely to settle with blood pressure control alone, so delivery of the baby is the best treatment. C Observation Women with pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome need treatment, so observation is incorrect. E Urgent ultrasound scan of the liver Although women with pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome can develop hepatocellular necrosis and liver dysfunction, an ultrasound of the liver would not be helpful in management.

stem: You are asked to review the case of a 68-year-old woman who has had a lengthy dental procedure earlier in the day. She has a background of angina. Current medications are isosorbide mononitrate and cotrimoxazole for a resistant urinary tract infection. She is complaining of a headache and breathlessness. Examination shows her to be cyanosed. Arterial blood gas on a 15 l non-rebreathe O2 mask: Investigation Result Normal Value pH 7.42 7.35–7.45 P O 39.2 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa P CO 4.1 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa O sats 70% Portable chest Xray Normal appearance What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Methaemoglobinaemia Haemoglobin carries iron in its ferrous form (Fe2+). When it is converted to the ferric form (Fe3+) methaemoglobin is created. This reduces the red cells’ ability to carry oxygen. The body has a normal reparative mechanism involving reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphatase (NADPH), which reduces Fe 3+ to Fe2+. This mechanism is not fully operational in infants, making them susceptible to methaemoglobinaemia. Drugs that provide oxidative stress, such as local anaesthetics (especially on mucosae), sulphonamides and nitrates can induce methaemoglobinaemia. Symptoms include headache, confusion, breathlessness and chest pain. Patients are cyanosed with no obvious cardiorespiratory cause, and despite increased oxygen delivery the oxygen saturations remain low. The blood is described as chocolate brown in colour and can be tested for methaemoglobin levels. Treatment is with methylene blue. If unsuccessful, exchange transfusion can be employed. B Carbon monoxide poisoning Carbon monoxide poisoning is not associated with cyanosis, but rather with a cherry red skin coloration. A Aspiration Given that the PaO2 is reported as 39.2 kPa on 15 l/min, aspiration is very unlikely. There is also no report of any vomiting or possible mechanism for aspiration during the procedure. D Pulmonary embolism There is no history of chest pain to suggest pulmonary embolism, and it would be extremely unusual to have onset of a PE in such a short period after immobility in the dentist’s chair. E Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deﬁciency We are told this patient has a history of angina and is taking a nitrate. Nitrates may precipitate haemolysis in G6PD deﬁciency, and theiruse in this patient therefore counts against G6PD and acute haemolysis as a potential cause of her symptoms.

DR. JAM

Acute Intermittent Porphyria Acute intermittent porphyria is a severe form of porphyria, resulting from a deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase.  Overview Key Facts  Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is a severe form of porphyria, resulting from a deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase.  Similar to the other porphyrias, the clinical course is as follows – clinical latency, acute episode following a precipitating event.  The main clinical features of AIP include gastrointestinal disturbance and neuropsychiatric disorders.  Management includes avoidance of precipitating factors, glucose loading and haematin infusion. During an attack, specific symptoms can be treated. Epidemiology  AIP is more common in women than in men.  AIP has a high prevalence in northern Sweden (approximately 100 per 100 000 population). Incidence in most parts of the world is 1.5 per 100 000.  AIP rarely presents before puberty. Aetiology  AIP is due to the autosomal dominant inheritance of a deficiency in porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD). PBGD is the third enzyme involved in the haem biosynthetic pathway.  The PBGD gene is located on chromosome 11. Different mutations of this gene have been identified in different AIP families, eg missense, nonsense and splicing mutations, insertions and deletions.  In most heterozygotes, AIP remains latent.  After puberty, some heterozygotes may develop a variety of non-specific symptoms. This can occur following some precipitating factors.  These factors induce delta-aminolaevulinic acid synthase (ALAS1), the rate-limiting enzyme for haem biosynthesis in the liver and cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes.  Induction of ALAS1 causes further deficiency of PBGD and accumulation of large amounts of porphyrin precursors, deltaaminolaevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG).  Factors that may precipitate AIP:  alcohol  drugs, eg barbiturates, sulphonamides, enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants like carbamazepine, phenytoin, oral contraceptive pill, rifampicin  fluctuations in female sex hormones  infections  starvation.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 Pathophysiology  Increase in ALA and PBG synthesis due to a block in haem synthesis at the PBGD reaction stage results in marked increases in urinary excretion of both porphyrin precursors and porphyrins.  Porphyrins have a reddish colour and PBG breaks down to form porphobilin – a brownish pigment (resulting in deep red urine).  Eighty per cent of those who inherit AIP are asymptomatic. Others may have a single attack or a few acute attacks during their lifetime.  Symptoms are the result of:  autonomic and peripheral neuropathies  effects on the nervous system  psychiatric manifestations  syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) – causing hyponatraemia.  Clinical Presentation  Autonomic neuropathy:  abdominal pain  constipation  vomiting  tachycardia  hypertension  postural hypotension  peripheral neuropathy.  Dark or red urine.  Respiratory failure – bulbar paresis.  Cerebellar signs.  Hypothalamic dysfunction – inappropriate ADH secretion.  Hyponatraemia – inappropriate ADH, or GI or renal sodium loss.  Psychiatric disturbances, eg features of delirium such as confusion, agitation, disorientation and hallucinations.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  delta-aminolevulinate dehydratase deficiency porphyria  hereditary coproporphyria  variegate porphyria.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Urinary porphobilinogen (PBG).  Quantitative measure of urinary porphobilinogen (PBG).  Urinary total porphyrins.  Serum porphobilinogen (PBG).  Biochemistry – hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypovolaemia may occur during acute attacks. DR. JAM

 Porphobilinogen deaminase in erythrocytes decreased by 50%.  Urine is usually normal coloured when fresh but may become brown, red or black on standing.  Increased serum cholesterol, serum iron and T4.  Abnormal glucose tolerance.  Liver function tests – sulfobromophthalein retention.  Management Non-pharmacological  Supportive care:  intravenous (IV) fluid replacement using 0.9% saline or 5% dextrose with normal saline  identify precipitating factors and remove whenever possible. Pharmacological:  Mild acute attack:  haemin – IV haemin; clinical improvement can be seen within 1–2 days; this is also used as first-line in a severe acute attack  alternative can be glucose in the form of at least 300 g dextrose (10% glucose) IV (IV glucose in large volumes increases the risk of hyponatraemia).  Recurrent non-cyclic attacks:  preventative haemin – haem arginate 3mg/kg IV once or twice weekly  monitor serum ferritin levels in these patients, as there is a risk of iron overload.  Frequent recurrent cyclic attacks in women:  preventative GnRH analogue. Surgical  Liver transplant.  Prognosis  Eighty per cent of heterozygotes remain asymptomatic and never become unwell. It is advised for these carriers that they should have precautions to avoid harmful factors.  Acute attacks have a low mortality and most patients will have a complete recovery.  Over months or several years, advanced motor neuropathy may recover completely. However, there may be neuropathic pain or residual weakness.  Most symptomatic patients will have only a single attack or a few attacks during their life.  In a few patients, neuropathic pain may become chronic, especially after frequent acute exacerbations:  narcotic analgesics may be required for long-term pain management in these patients  these patients are at increased risk of depression and suicide.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Other  The following should be monitored in patients with AIP, at least yearly:  urinary porphobilinogen (PBG)  control hypertension; monitor renal and hepatic function  mild increases in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) are common  after age 50 years, liver imaging is recommended at least yearly in patients with a history of symptoms and test for elevated urinary PBG levels for early hepatocellular carcinoma detection.  Complications of AIP include hypertension, chronic renal failure, hepatocellular carcinoma. Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is a malignant disease of the progenitor lymphoid cells.  Overview Key Facts  Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is a malignant disease of the progenitor lymphoid cells.  It is the most common paediatric cancer but also occurs in the adult population.  ALL represents 12% of leukaemias, although 80% of cases occur in children.  Persistent fatigue, bone pains, recurrent infections and early satiety are all features of ALL.  Signs include lymph node enlargement, extensive bruising and hepatosplenomegaly.  Presence of 20% or more lymphoblasts in the bone marrow (bone marrow examination) is the definite diagnosis.  Treatment includes chemotherapy and stem cell transplantation.  Current chemotherapy regimens achieve remission in 80–90% of patients, although rates of only around 75% are achieved in higher-risk individuals.  Long-term side-effects of treatment include heart failure, sterility, secondary malignancies, and neurotoxicity.  Disease-free survival is approximately 63% at ten years for children, it is 25–35% in adults.  For children under one year of age, the prognosis is also poor with a cure rate of only around 30%. Epidemiology  The global incidence is approximately 3 : 100 000 annually. DR. JAM

 Predominantly affects children, and peaks of incidence are seen between two and four years and over 50 years.  ALL represents 12% of leukaemia, although 80% of cases occur in children. Aetiology  Genetic factors, (patients with trisomy 21 have a 10–20 times incidence of ALL versus the general population).  Environmental factors: radiation and smoking. Pathophysiology  Genetic mutation through somatic changes of lymphoid progenitor cells results in uncontrollable proliferation and clonal expansion.  The leukaemic blast cells infiltrate the bone marrow (and other organs).  Normal function of the bone marrow is disrupted resulting in pancytopenia.  Clinical Presentation  Pallor.  Unexplained bruising/petechiae.  Persistent fatigue.  Unexplained fever.  Persistent headache (central nervous system (CNS) involvement).  Hepatosplenomegaly.  Increased susceptibility to infection.  Persistent bone pain.  Abnormal blood result: anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, low white cell count.  Lymphadenopathy.  Differential Diagnosis  Acute myeloid leukaemia.  Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.  Chronic myeloid leukaemia.  Myelodysplastic syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Urgent full blood count: pancytopenia.  If leukaemia suspected, urgent 2-week referral for specialist investigation:  peripheral blood smear (peripheral blasts cell)  bone marrow examination: for definite diagnosis – presence of 20% or more lymphoblasts in the bone marrow  cytogenetics: Philadelphia chromosome positive t (9;22)/BCR–ABL1 (relatively high incidence in adults and associated with poor prognosis)

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  immunophenotyping studies  imaging: computed tomography (CT) scan to examine spread to other organs.  Management  Combination therapy is required. Non-pharmacological  May require CNS radiotherapy for CNS involvement.  Supportive treatment to manage specific symptoms and sideeffects of chemotherapy. Pharmacological:  Multi-agent systemic chemotherapy in phases: is used for remission induction, consolidation, and maintenance therapy.  Corticosteroids.  CNS intrathecal therapy with methotrexate, steroids and cytarabine.  Immunotherapy. Surgical  Stem cell transplantation  is not suitable for all patients  is associated with significant risks  can be curative.  Prognosis  Current chemotherapy regimens achieve remission in 80–90% of patients, although rates of only around 75% are achieved in higher risk individuals.  Long-term side-effects of treatment include heart failure, sterility, secondary malignancies, and neurotoxicity.  Disease free survival is approximately 63% at ten years for children, it is 25–35% in adults.  For children under one year of age the prognosis is also poor, with a cure rate of only around 30%. Acute Myeloid Leukaemia Acute myeloid leukaemia is a haematological cancer, ultimately resulting in bone marrow failure and subsequent thrombocytopenia.  Overview Key Facts  Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is a haematological cancer ultimately resulting in bone marrow failure and subsequent thrombocytopenia. DR. JAM

 AML results from the accumulation/rapid proliferation of poorly differentiated myeloblasts in the blood which can infiltrate the liver and spleen.  Patients can present with fatigue, dizziness, chest pain, pyrexia, recurrent respiratory tract infections, bleeding gums, gingivitis, abdominal fullness.  Investigations include full blood count, coagulation screen where the most common abnormality is disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Blood film will show at least 20% myeloblasts. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is most often raised alongside uric acid levels. Immunophenotyping helps distinguish between acute lymphocytic leukaemia (ALL) and AML. Cytogenetic analysis of the bone marrow helps to provide important prognostic information.  Histological findings determine AML classification.  Treatment modalities are determined by patient factors such as functional status and age, alongside prognostic recommendations. Treatment options include chemotherapy, biological agents and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in select patients. All patients should be evaluated for involvement in clinical trials.  Acute promyelocytic leukaemia warrants immediate treatment as it is life-threatening.  High incidences of relapse lead to a 5-year survival rate of 25%. Epidemiology  More common in older adults with over half of cases diagnosed in those aged 65 and over. The median age of diagnosis is 68.  No significant difference in incidence between men and women.  Other risk factors include previous chemotherapy, previous haematological dyspoiesis, congenital disorders, radiation exposure, benzene exposure and karyotype abnormalities and in rare cases, there is a genetic component. Aetiology  The most common associated factor is an antecedent haematological disorder, eg myelodysplastic syndrome, aplastic anaemia.  Congenital disorders, eg Down syndrome, Fanconi anaemia, neurofibromatosis. Usually, these patients present with AML in childhood.  Enzymatic polymorphisms.  Familial syndromes, eg germline mutations in genes such as AML1.  Environmental exposure, eg radiation, tobacco, benzene.  Previous exposure to chemotherapy. Pathophysiology  The inability of rapidly proliferating myeloblasts to mature/differentiate into mature blood cells, eg neutrophils, platelets or red blood cells leads to their accumulation in the blood.  This developmental arrest leads to two pathological processes:  the first is that it leads to a marked reduction in the number of mature blood cells being produced, resulting in neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and anaemia

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  the second results from the inability of the abnormal myeloblasts to undergo programmed cell death (apoptosis) which results in their accumulation in the bone marrow and blood.  Bone marrow failure, leading to neutropenia that can lead to severe life-threatening infections with organisms such as Candida spp. and Aspergillus spp. A diagram to show the cells in which AML can develop from:  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentation:  pallor  ecchymoses or petechiae (due to thrombocytopenia)  fatigue  dizziness  palpitations  dyspnoea  infections  fever  lymphadenopathy  hepatosplenomegaly  mucosal bleeding. Bone marrow failure (anaemia, neutropenia) Organ infiltration Fatigue Exertional dyspnoea Dizziness Chest pain/myocardial infarction (if history of coronary disease) Pyrexia Upper respiratory tract infections Bleeding gums (thrombocytopenia/DIC) Left upper quadrant fullness (splenomegaly) Early satiety (splenomegaly) Gingivitis Respiratory distress and altered Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) (leukostasis) DR. JAM

 Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  acute lymphocytic leukaemia  biphenotypic leukaemia  myelodysplastic syndrome  chronic myelogenous leukaemia blast crisis  myelofibrosis  aplastic anaemia  drug-induced bone marrow failure  leukemoid reaction  vitamin B12 deficiency.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Full blood count – anaemia, macrocytosis, leukocytosis, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia.  Peripheral blood smear – blasts and Auer rods on blood film.  Coagulation bloods – normal.  Electrolytes – normal or may be increased calcium, potassium, phosphorus, uric acid and lactic acid with decreased calcium.  Renal function – normal or elevated urea.  Liver function tests – normal or elevated.  Lactic dehydrogenase – elevated.  Bone marrow biopsy/aspiration – hypercellular bone marrow and blast infiltration with > 20% blasts, Auer rods.  Immunophenotyping and molecular studies – useful for subclassification.  Cytogenetics for prognostic information.  Lumbar puncture – normal or malignant cells.  HLA antigen typing.  Chest X-ray – consolidation, cardiomegaly or pulmonary infiltrates.  Echo – cardiac function before chemotherapy.  Bone marrow aspirate highlighting Auer rods (red arrows):

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Management  Chemotherapy – chemotherapeutic agent depends on genetic differentiation of myeloid cells but the most common initiating agents are cytarabine, idarubicin, daunorubicin; gemtuzumab ozogamicin (CD33 positive), midostaurin (FLT3 mutationpositive).  Supportive care – hydroxycarbamide + allopurinol + rasburicase.  Stem cell transplant.  Prognosis  The 5-year survival is approximately 20–25%.  Poorer prognosis in older patients, those with poor cytogenetics, multidrug resistance and co-existing medical conditions.  Other  Complications:  tumour lysis syndrome  leukostasis  neutropenia  pancytopenia  infections  disseminated intravascular coagulation  central nervous system leukaemia  all-trans retinoic acid differentiation syndrome  delayed therapy-related complications, eg cardiomyopathy, hypothyroidism. DR. JAM

Anaemia Anaemia is defined as a reduced concentration of haemoglobin in the circulation.  Overview Key Facts  Anaemia is defined as a reduced concentration of haemoglobin (Hb) in the circulation.  for men this is typically < 130 g/l  for women this is typically < 120 g/l.  Classified by average size of red blood cells, ie mean cell volume (MCV).  small red cells: microcytic < 80 fl  normal-sized red cells: normocytic 80-100 fl  large red cells: macrocytic > 100 fl.  Risk factors - extremes of age, chronic illness, inflammatory conditions, female sex, breastfeeding and pregnancy (may be dilutional).  Management is dependent on underlying cause.  Anaemia generally has a good prognosis and is curable in most instances; however, the overall prognosis and associated complications of anaemia varies by cause, type and severity. Epidemiology  Normal Hb varies with age and sex.  Infants and women typically have lower normal levels of Hb.  Neonates typically have higher normal levels of Hb than adults – average neonatal Hb is 170, it should be noted neonates have fetal haemoglobin (fHb) which has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin.  Incidence and demographics factors vary by cause of anaemia.  The most common cause worldwide is iron deficiency, with global prevalence of approximately 30% of non-pregnant women and 38% in pregnant women, with prevalence of 14% in non-pregnant women and 23% in pregnant women in the United Kingdom.  Vitamin B12 deficiency prevalence is around 20% in those over 60 (6% in under 60). Condition Serum iron Transferrin Iron deficiency ⇣ ⇡ Chronic disease ⇣ ⇣ Haemochromatosis ⇡ ⇣ Thalassaemia major ⇡ Normal Thalassaemia minor Normal Normal Pregnancy/OCP Normal ⇡

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 Aetiology  Microcytosis (low MCV) – iron deficiency, typically a lack of dietary iron (most common), thalassaemia trait, sideroblastic anaemia and anaemia of chronic disease (often normocytic).  Normocytosis (normal MCV) – acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, bone marrow/renal failure, haemolysis (can be cause by drugs, eg cephalosporines, levofloxacin, methyldopa etc).  Macrocytosis – B12/folate deficiency, alcohol excess, reticulocytosis, cytotoxics and hypothyroidism. Pathophysiology  Decrease in quantity of Hb, or impaired oxygen-carrying capacity of Hb, except for physiological dilution of pregnancy which is the bodies inability to increase red blood cell (RBC) production in line with increases in plasma volume.  Caused by decreased production of blood, blood loss, or increased blood breakdown; occasionally combination of all three. Causes of folic acid deficiency Lack of intake: poverty, crank diets Lack of absorption: inflammatory bowel disease or surgical resection Increased requirement: pregnancy, haemolytic anaemias  Clinical Presentation  Many patients may be asymptomatic, especially with gradual onset.  Pallor and signs of active bleeding.  Signs of decreased oxygen-carrying: exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, chest pain and dizziness.  Increased cardiac output – palpitations, ejection systolic murmurs and cardiac failure (especially in elderly).  Clinical signs: koilonychia, angular stomatitis, glossitis, jaundice and hepato/splenomegaly.  Differential Diagnosis n Ferritin Marrow iron Features ⇣ - Responsive to iron therapy ⇡ ++ Unresponsive to iron therapy ⇡ +/- Normal ++++ Reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin Normal ++ Normal Normal DR. JAM

Other differentials – myelodysplasia, haemolysis, drug toxicity, chronic kidney/liver disease and generalised malnutrition.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Mostly biochemical diagnosis based on Hb values on full blood count (FBC).  for men this is typically < 130  for women this is typically < 120.  Clinical – assess for nutritional deficiencies, ongoing bleeding (eg GI bleeding, recent surgery), jaundice, malignancy and chronic inflammation.  FBC – low Hb defines anaemia; MCV to stratify cause; confirm normal haematocrit.  microcytic – perform iron studies (serum iron, transferrin, ferritin)  normocytic – check reticulocyte count to determine whether hypo/hyperproliferative  macrocytic – perform peripheral smear and examine for megaloblasts (caused by vitamin B12/folate deficiency and drugs, eg methotrexate).  Urea and Electrolytes – if impaired kidney function suspected:  urea may be elevated following haemolysis, eg due to upper GI bleed and enteral reabsorption at a point distal to the bleeding point  Hb may be falsely low due to dilutional anaemia, eg if fluids are given or blood is taken from a vein with an infusion running through it, this can be identified by the haematocrit falling.  Prothrombin time/activated partial prothrombin time – especially relevant if taking anticoagulants.  If bleeding suspected:

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  endoscopy – if GI loss suspected (eg colonoscopy, gastroscopy)  abdominal ultrasound – rapidly identify bleeding following abdominal trauma/ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm  joint X-ray – long bones may be a source of blood-loss  group & save ± cross-matching – if patient is likely to need transfusion. Definitions that may be noted on blood film:  Anisocytosis – variation in sizes of red cells (eg iron deficiency).  Nucleated blood cells/Blasts – nucleated precursors to all blood cells; seen in myeloproliferative disorders/severe iron deficiency anaemia  Cytopenia – low component of one or more blood cell type.  Hypochromia – decreased density in haemoglobin staining (eg thalassaemia).  Leukaemoid reaction – profound leucocytosis (increased white cells) in severe illness; also seen in leukaemia.  Poikilocytosis – variation in shapes of red cells (eg iron deficiency).  Polychromasia – red cells in different ages (staining differently; young = bluer).  Reticulocytes – large, immature red cells, showing active erythropoiesis; increased in haemolysis.  Spherocytes – spherical cells (eg hereditary spherocytosis).  Schistocytes – fragmented red cells in intravascular haemolysis (eg microangiopathic anaemia).  Target cells – red cells with central staining in liver disease/hyposplenism (eg thalassaemia). DR. JAM

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Management Management involves investigating and treating the underlying cause of the anaemia.  Conservative  Correct nutritional deficiencies – eg iron/B12/folate supplementation.  Optimise medication – eg retitrating warfarin and monitoring international normalised ratio (INR) or consideration for novel oral anticoagulants (NOACs).  Medical  Managing sources of bleeding – eg H. pylori eradication treatment for peptic ulcer disease.  Replacing red blood cells – prescribing packed red cells after G&S/X-matching – 1 unit of red blood cells is around 350 ml of blood and should raise the Hb by 10, this can be variable however. DR. JAM

Surgical  Operating on site of chronic bleed – eg removal of bleeding colorectal tumour.  Managing site of acute bleed – eg reducing long bone fracture.  Prognosis  Although anaemia generally has a good prognosis and is curable in most instances; the overall prognosis and associated complications of anaemia varies by cause, type and severity.  Patients with severe anaemia, especially those of advancing age, are at risk of heart failure and other cardiac or pulmonary complications.  Complications of:  vitamin B12 deficiency – neurological sequelae, cognitive deficit, optic atrophy and neural tube defects  folate deficiency – prematurity in pregnant mothers, cardiovascular disease and neural tube defects  iron deficiency – cognitive and behavioural impairment (especially children), reduced exercise endurance, reduced immunity, pregnancy related complications such as preterm delivery and postpartum fatigue/depression.  Aplastic Anaemia Aplastic anaemia is defined as pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow in the absence of an abnormal infiltrate or marrow fibrosis.  Overview Key Facts  Aplastic anaemia is defined as pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow in the absence of an abnormal infiltrate or marrow fibrosis.  It is most often an idiopathic pancytopenia with hypocellular marrow and no abnormalities, eg dysplasia, blasts, fibrosis.  Clinical presentation includes:  neutropenia – frequent/recurrent infections  anaemia – fatigue, pallor, dyspnoea, tachycardia  thrombocytopenia – bleeding, bruising.  Blood tests may show leukopenia, neutropenia, anaemia and thrombocytopenia and bone marrow biopsy shows hypocellular bone marrow.  Treatment includes immunosuppressants and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Epidemiology  Affects approximately two people in every one million each year.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Biphasic age distribution between 10 and 25 years and >60 years.  No difference in gender prevalence.  More common in East Asia, likely due to exposure to toxins, viruses and drugs, as well as increased genetic risk due to polymorphisms of TNF-α, interferon gamma and drugdetoxifying enzymes.  Most common congenital cause is Fanconi anaemia. Aetiology Congenital causes Fanconi anaemia Dyskeratosis congenita Shwachman–Diamond syndrome Amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia Reticular dysgenesis Acquired causes Cytotoxic drugs and radiation ⇢ cancer Rx Drugs: anti-seizure ⇢ carbamazepine, phenytoin antibiotics ⇢ sulfonamides, chloramphenicol NSAIDs ⇢ phenylbutazone, indomethacin anti-thyroid medications ⇢ methimazole, propylthiouracil gold, arsenicals Toxic chemicals ⇢ benzene, solvents, glue vapours Virus ⇢ parvovirus B-19, EBV, HIV, seronegative (non-A to -G) hepatitis virus Immune disorders ⇢ SLE, GVHD, eosinophilic fasciitis Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) Thymoma Pregnancy Anorexia nervosa Inherited marrow failure syndromes  Fanconi anaemia:  most common  autosomal recessive or X-linked  mutations in genes that code for nuclear complex involved in DNA damage response.  Dyskeratosis congenita:  X-linked  triad of abnormalities with nails, reticulated skin rashes and leukoplakia  mutations cause decreased telomerase function which usually maintains the stability of chromosomes and maintains bone marrow cell proliferation  Schwachman–Diamond syndrome:  autosomal recessive DR. JAM

 produces exocrine pancreatic dysfunction, neutropenia, aplastic anaemia, myelodysplastic syndrome and skeletal abnormalities.  GATA2 deficiency:  mutations in GATA2 result in dysfunction in zinc finger transcription factors involved in haematopoiesis  causes cytopenia, myelodysplastic syndrome, acute leukaemia, infection, immunodeficiency and lymphoedema. Pathophysiology  Deficiency of hematopoietic CD34+ stem cells is the basic mechanism of all aplastic anaemias.  Acquired forms:  CD4 T-cell mediated autoimmune attack against haematopoietic system  deficiency and dysfunction of T-regulatory cells and increased CD4 T-helper cells which reduce suppression of cytotoxic CD8 T cells  pro-inflammatory environments created which cause apoptosis of haematopoietic stem cells.  Congenital:  defects in DNA damage repair mechanisms, abnormalities of telomerase maintenance or ribosome function.  Clinical Presentation  Recurrent infection.  Fatigue.  Pallor.  Bleeding/easy bruising.  Tachycardia.  Dyspnoea.  Persistent warts.  Symptoms/signs related to underlying disorders:  Fanconi anaemia – hearing loss, pigmentation abnormalities, urogenital abnormalities  dyskeratosis congenita – nail malformations, oral leukoplakia, reticular rash.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  radiation injury  chemotherapy  infection – human immunodeficiency virus, tuberculosis, overwhelming sepsis  megaloblastic anaemia – deficiency of vitamin B12 or folate  infiltrative disorders:  fibrosis – myeloproliferative neoplasms such as primary myelofibrosis

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  malignancies – myelodysplastic syndromes, acute myeloid leukaemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, carcinoma  infectious agents – tuberculosis, fungi.  hypersplenism  endocrine – hypothyroidism.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Full blood count – two or more cytopenias including Hb < 100 g/l, platelet < 50 × 109/l, absolute neutrophil count < 1.5 × 109/l.  Reticulocyte count – corrected reticulocyte percentage < 1% or absolute reticulocyte count < 20 × 109/l.  Bone marrow biopsy and cytogenetic analyses – hypocellular marrow with no abnormal cell population:  bone marrow biopsy is required to make a diagnosis of aplastic anaemia.  Genetic tests:  Fanconi anaemia – chromosomal breakage testing  dyskeratosis congenita – sequencing for TERC, TERT, TINF2 and DKC1 genes  Schwachman–Diamond syndrome – SBDS gene  GATA2 disorders – GATA2 gene.  Management  Aplastic anaemia is divided into non-severe, severe and very severe: Non-severe Bone marrow cellularity < 25% Peripheral blood cytopenias not fulfilling criteria for SAA or vSAA Severe (SAA) ≥ 2 or more of: absolute neutrophil count (ANC) < 500/μl platelets < 20 000/μl reticulocyte count < 20 000/μl Very severe (vSAA) Criteria for SAA and ANC < 200/μl Acquired disease Non-severe  Monitoring and/or immunosuppressants:  immunosuppression – lymphocyte immunoglobulin, antithymocyte globulin, methylprednisolone and ciclosporin  blood product transfusion  antibiotics and antifungals. Severe  < 50 years:  first-line – matched related donor allogeneic stem cell transplant DR. JAM

 second-line – immunosuppressive therapy – lymphocyte immunoglobulin, anti-thymocyte globulin, methylprednisolone and ciclosporin  third-line – matched unrelated donor allogeneic stem cell transplant  fourth-line – eltrombopag (oral thrombopoietin receptor agonist)  plus – blood product transfusions, antibiotics, antifungals.  > 50 years:  first-line – immunosuppressive therapy – lymphocyte immunoglobulin, anti-thymocyte globulin, methylprednisolone and ciclosporin  second-line – matched related donor allogeneic stem cell transplant  third-line - matched unrelated donor allogeneic stem cell transplant  fourth-line – eltrombopag (oral thrombopoietin receptor agonist)  plus – blood product transfusions, antibiotics, antifungals. Congenital disease  first-line – matched related donor allogeneic stem cell transplant.  second-line – matched unrelated donor allogeneic stem cell transplant.  third-line – androgen therapy – danazol, oxymetholone (binds to the oestrogenic element of TERT gene causing increased telomerase expression).  Plus – blood product transfusions, antibiotics, antifungals.  Prognosis  Prognosis improved in those with less severe disease (in younger patients), with over 90% survival rates in those without severe disease.  5-year survival is 61% but this decreases to 38% in patients over 60 years of age.  Long-term survival of > 80% for younger patients with a matched relative donor.  Higher rate of survival in younger patients treated with immunosuppressants (90%) vs those aged over 60 (52%).  Other  Complications:  post stem cell transplant:  graft failure  graft vs host disease  myelodysplastic syndrome  acute myelogenous leukaemia  solid tumours

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  complications following treatment with androgen therapy – hepatotoxicity, virilisation. Autoimmune Haemolytic Anaemia Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is the destruction of red blood cells.  Overview Key Facts  Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is the destruction of red blood cells.  Three subtypes – warm agglutinin autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA), cold agglutinin AIHA, paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria.  The most common form of AIHA is warm agglutinin haemolytic anaemia which accounts for 80–90% of cases.  Presents with symptoms including fatigue, dyspnoea, jaundice, pallor and splenomegaly.  Haemolysis recognised by anaemia, reticulocytosis, high lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), high indirect bilirubin and low haptoglobin.  Important investigations include Coombs test to differentiate immune from non-immune causes, blood counts and peripheral blood smear.  Differential diagnoses include paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, blood transfusion reactions, G6PD deficiency and cryoglobinuria.  In severe anaemia, blood transfusion should be initiated early.  Glucocorticoids are first-line for warm agglutinin AIHA.  Avoidance of cold is first-line in cold agglutinin AIHA and paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria.  Prognosis depends on the underlying inciting cause as most of the cases are secondary. Epidemiology  A most common form of AIHA is warm agglutinin haemolytic anaemia which accounts for 80–90% of cases.  Affects more women than men.  Can arise spontaneously or in patients who are already affected by systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), lymphoma or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.  Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria is a rare subtype that is only seen in children < 5 years of age. Aetiology Warm agglutinin AIHA Cold agglutinin AIHA Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria DR. JAM

Primary/idiopathic infection Malignancy ⇢ leukaemia, lymphoma Drugs ⇢ penicillin, α-methyldopa Autoimmune or inflammatory disorders ⇢ SLE Evans syndrome Immunodeficiency ⇢ HIV, Wiskott– Aldrich syndrome Pregnancy Infections: mycoplasma pneumonia CMV, EBV ⇢ infectious mononucleosis Pathophysiology  Warm AIHA (80–90%):  autoantibodies are generated against the Rh complex or against glycophorin antigens on red blood cells  these autoantibodies bind the red blood cells and are recognised by the macrophages of the spleen and liver resulting in extravascular haemolysis.  Cold AIHA:  IgM autoantibodies (called cold agglutinins) bind to red blood cells at temperatures < 37°C and cause haemolysis  the target antigen on red blood cells is ‘I’ or ‘i’ on the red blood cell surface membrane.  Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria (PCH):  in PCH, antibodies are generated against the red blood cell P antigen  in cold temperatures these antibodies bind red blood cells and fix complement, resulting in intravascular haemolysis.  Clinical Presentation Signs and symptoms common to all types are listed below.  Symptoms due to anaemia:  fatigue  dyspnoea on exertion  palpitations  bounding pulse.  Signs and symptoms due to haemolysis:  jaundice  pallor  dark urine.  Warm AIHA:  splenomegaly

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Evans syndrome – AIHA plus immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)  thromboembolism – stroke, deep venous thrombosis (DVT), myocardial ischaemia or infarction.  Cold AIHA:  acrocyanosis, livedo reticularis  skin ulceration  Raynaud’s phenomenon  haemoglobinuria  pain or discomfort on swallowing cold food or liquids.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  anaemia secondary to blood loss  blood transfusion reaction  underproduction anaemia  cryoglobulinemia  paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Laboratory changes in all haemolytic anaemia:  low haemoglobin, low hematocrit  raised RC ⇢ underestimation of HbA1c  raised LDH, raised indirect bilirubin  low haptoglobin  haemoglobinaemia, haemoglobinuria. Therefore, order D-dimer levels in all patients and keep a low threshold for further investigations.  Positive direct Coombs test showing the presence of spherocytes as in warm AIHA: DR. JAM

 Management  Warm AIHA:  Haemoglobin ≤ 70 g/l or haemodynamic compromise, dyspnoea or symptoms suggestive of central nervous system or cardiac ischaemia ⇢ immediate blood transfusion  screen for deep vein thrombosis and replace folic acid  glucocorticoids and/or rituximab ⇢ first-line therapy:  if recovery occurs in 2–3 weeks ⇢ taper corticosteroids.  persistent disease:  second-line medications such as cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, danazol, ciclosporin or sirolimus  or splenectomy. Management Corticosteroids ⇢ first-line Rituximab Splenectomy for refractory disease Rituximab ± fludarabine Glucocorticoids Complications Lymphoproliferative disorders Venous thromboembolism Ischaemia and peripheral gangrene Blood Products And Transfusion Reactions Iron supplements – treating iron deficiency after investigating other causes of anaemia.  Overview Key Facts Products Supplement products  Iron supplements – treating iron deficiency (eg iron deficiency anaemia (IDA)) after investigating other causes of anaemia, inflammatory states (AE - diarrhoea/constipation and black stools).  Therapeutic B12 – B12 deficiency, cyanide poisoning (displaces cyanide ion), hereditary deficiency of transcobalamin II.  Folate supplements – prevention of neural tube defects, unexplained infertility, folate deficiency (eg Crohn’s/coeliac, phenytoin and alcohol).  Erythropoietin (EPO), naturally produced by the kidney and, to a small extent, the liver, it drives the formation of new red blood cells (RBCs) from the bone marrow. Synthetic EPO can be given to stimulate the body’s natural production of RBCs; as such is has been sued as a performance-enhancing drug by some athletes for these benefits.  Intravenous (IV) iron (eg CosmoFer or Ferinject) can be used when oral iron is poorly tolerated, has an insufficient clinical effect or a large volume of iron is required to supplement low stores.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 37°C ⇢ negative anti- IgG, positive anti-C3 Avoidance of cold temperatures ⇢ first-line  Transfusion products  Packed red cells (PRCs):  indications – bleeding; chronic anaemia (haemoglobin (Hb) = 70 g/l, = 100 g/l in cardiovascular disease (CVD), symptomatic anaemia  duration – 2–4 hours; must be completed within 4 hours  in an emergency can be given state however  target – Hb 70–90 g/l after transfusion; each unit of blood increases Hb ~10 g/l  caution – may develop autoantibodies to donor antigens, so need new G&S if transfusing after three days; avoid overloading in patients with cardiovascular problems  it is this reaction to donor agents (often cytokines) driven) which can cause pyrexia when receiving a transfusion.  Platelets:  indications – haemorrhagic shock (trauma), thrombocytopenia, bleeding, pre-op low platelet  duration – 30 minutes  target – one dose increases platelets ~20–40 × 109/l.  Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) – contains proteins for normal clotting:  indications – Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), haemorrhage 2º to liver disease, massive haemorrhage (after the second unit of PRC)  duration – 30 minutes.  Cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen, vWF, factor VIII, fibronectin) – FFP with added fibrinogen (if deficient):  indications – DIC with low fibrinogen, von Willebrand's disease, massive haemorrhage  duration – stat.  Cell Salvage (not strictly a blood product):  used in theatre when large volumes of blood loss is expected  patient blood is collected through suction and filtered in theatre in an ongoing process  can then be given back to the patient after and even during the procedure as a transfusion would be DR. JAM

 the patient received their own blood back, hence reduces the risk of transfusion-related problems  can be used in patients who decline blood products yet are at risk of bleeding.  Types of donation  Donated blood transfusion – provided by the blood bank.  Autologous blood transfusion – patient will deposit prior to elective surgery.  Apheresis donation – desired component selectively withdrawn while remaining blood is transfused, eg only plasma and platelets taken from a donor.  Complications General complications  Clotting abnormalities – dilution effect (no platelets in PRC); should administer FFP after four units of PRC.  Electrolyte – ⇣ Ca2+ (chelation by calcium-binding preservative), ⇡ potassium (K+) (haemolysis of RBCs).  Hypothermia – PRCs are thawed from frozen, so may be cooler than body temperature – can be transfused through a ‘warmer’ which bring the blood up to body temperature.  Immunosuppression – poorer survival in cancer patients who are transfused.  Acute complications  Acute haemolytic reaction (ABO incompatibility) – wrong blood prescribed/administered:  presentation – haemoglobinuria, ‘sense of dread’, urticaria, fever and flank pain  management – stop transfusion, fluid resuscitation, high flow oxygen and inform the blood bank  can be life-threatening; this is why observations are done before when starting and during a blood transfusion in order to recognise this condition promptly.  Transfusion-associated circulatory overload:  presentation – dyspnoea and circulatory overload signs (especially in cardiac failure)  management – chest X-ray (CXR); furosemide (to at-risk patients after the second unit) and oxygen.  Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) – a form of ARDS:  presentation – pulmonary oedema features, dyspnoea, can be acute  management – regular observations, CXR, ABG and oxygen.  Mild allergy – eg pruritus; treatment – antihistamine (chlorpheniramine), continue transfusion but observe.  Anaphylaxis – hypotension, anaphylactic symptoms; treatment – stop transfusion, ABC approach.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Non-haemolytic febrile reaction – unpleasant but nonthreatening; treatment – antipyretics/histamines, observe.  Infective shock – hypotension, no anaphylaxis; treatment – stop transfusion, basic resus, blood cultures, IV abx, lactate, fluid resuscitation.  Delayed complications  Infection – hepatitis B/C, HIV, vCJD risk; low risk due to high screening.  Graft versus host disease – HLA-mismatch; if non-irradiated blood given to immunocompromised; presents with fever, diarrhoea/vomiting and skin rash:  iron overload – repeated transfusions (eg thalassaemia)  liver – deranged liver function tests, cirrhosis  pancreas – diabetes mellitus  chorionic villus sampling (CVS) – cardiomegaly, conduction disturbances  joints – arthralgia  skin – hyperpigmentation  endocrine (pituitary iron deposition) – hypogonadism (delayed puberty, infertility), hypoparathyroidism (calcium metabolism), hypothyroidism  treating iron overload:  subcutaneous infusions (desferrioxamine) – 3–5 times a week overnight from the age of two  oral (deferasirox) – once a day solution, but check for liver/renal toxicity.  Checking blood type  Blood groups:  Rhesus D status (RhD) – 85% are RhD positive:  the issue is if a RhD negative woman is pregnant with an RhD positive child, the mother will develop anti-D antibodies – anti-D is given if an RhD negative woman reports any PV bleeding after 12 weeks gestation  if a second child is also Rh-positive, anti-D antibodies will attack the fetus resulting in haemolytic disease of the newborn.  Routine antenatal anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis should be given to all rhesus-negative (RhD-negative) women who have not already been sensitised (i.e. no anti-D antibodies present at 28 weeks).  It can be given as two doses of at least 500 IU at 28 and 34 weeks or as a large single dose of 1500 IU at 28 weeks gestation.  ABO group (presence of A/B antigens on red blood cells) – O negative is the universal donor; AB positive is the universal acceptor. ABO blood type: DR. JAM

 Group and save (G&S) – determine the patient’s blood group and screens for atypical antibodies:  process – ~40 minutes; no blood issued  indications – blood loss is not anticipated but may be required at a later stage.  Crossmatch (X-match) – physically mixes patient blood with donor blood to detect immune reactions:  process – only done after G&S; ~40 minutes; blood issued for transfusion  indications – if blood loss is anticipated.  Requesting blood products  Taking blood for G&S/X-match – check three points of ID (name, date of birth, patient ID number), gain consent, label bottle, and request form at the bedside.  Often two samples are needed, if not an emergency, 15 minutes apart, preferably by a different practitioner.  Infection status of blood – cytomegalovirus (congenital infection ⇢ sensorineural deafness, cerebral palsy) negative blood indicated during pregnancy, intrauterine transfusions, neonates (= 28 d).  Irradiated products – to decrease the risk of GvHD if: receiving from family members, Hodgkin's lymphoma, recent allo-HSCT, alemtuzumab/chemotherapy (purine analogues eg fludarabine), intrauterine transfusion.  Prescribing – each unit of blood must be prescribed individually and the duration of transfusion specified.  A full set of observations – before transfusion, at 20 min, at 1 hour and after transfusion – this is to recognise potential transfusion-related reactions.  Delivery – via green/grey cannula (risk of haemolysis if cannula too narrow); use blood giving set (since it contains filter).

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is a slow progressive haematological cancer that occurs in older adults.  Overview Key Facts  Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) is a slow progressive haematological cancer that occurs in older adults.  Presents with asymptomatic lymphadenopathy or lymphocytosis on routine full blood count (FBC).  Diagnosed by FBC, a blood smear shows smudge cells and flow cytometry tests.  Treatment options are conservative watchful waiting, chemoimmunotherapy, targeted therapies or stem cell transplant.  Complete remission achieved in 25–50% of patients with firstline treatment. Epidemiology  Most common leukaemia in the West.  A disease that affects middle-aged to older people with a median age of diagnosis at 70 years.  Risk factors include age > 60 years, male, White ethnicity and positive family history. Aetiology  May develop as a result of multiple genetic events that affect tumour suppressor and oncogenes, which causes increased cell survival and reduced apoptosis of cells. Pathophysiology  CLL cells are CD5-, CD19- and CD23-expressing monoclonal B lymphocytes.  These cells can infiltrate the lymphatic system and organs such as the liver, spleen and bone marrow which contribute to the clinical presentation of the disease.  Gene abnormalities associated with poor prognosis include mutations in TP53, NOTCH1, SF3B1, ATM and BIRC3.  Clinical Presentation  Most patients present asymptomatically following an FBC, performed for another indication.  Patients can present with:  shortness of breath  fatigue  lymphadenopathy  splenomegaly  hepatomegaly (uncommon)  recurrent infections DR. JAM

 autoimmune reactions, eg autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, immune thrombocytopenic purpura.  Differential Diagnosis  The leukaemic phase of lymphoma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  White cell count – elevated with lymphocytosis > 5 × 109/l.  Blood film – smudge/smear cells.  Haemoglobin – Hb < 110 g/l.  Platelets – platelets < 100 × 109/l.  Flow cytometry – positive for C5, CD19, CD20 and CD23.  Peripheral blood smear showing CLL cells (lymphocytes with dark staining and scant cytoplasm):  Management  Observation – for those with asymptomatic early-stage disease.  Chemotherapy – for patients with active, symptomatic disease - fludarabine + cyclophosphamide + rituximab is now recommended as first line therapy by NICE.  Other options include  Alkylating agents - Chlorambucil/cyclophosphamide/bendamustine  Purine analogues - Fludarabine (not used as monotherapy)  Ibrutinib or venetoclax or idelalisib.  Allogeneic stem cell transplant – patients with TP53 mutations have a poor prognosis and should be considered for stem cell transplant if they achieved remission following medical treatment.  Prognosis  Complete remission achieved in 25–50% of patients with firstline treatment.  Relapse rates high, with many patients needing further treatment after 2–3 years.  Gene abnormalities associated with poor prognosis include mutations in TP53, NOTCH1, SF3B1, ATM and BIRC3.  Other factors associated with poor prognosis include:  beta-2-microglobulin (B2M) levels > 3.5 mg/l
