Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia Chronic myeloid leukaemia is a malignant disorder resulting from the presence of the BCR-ABL fusion oncogene that occurs from translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22.  Overview Key Facts  Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is a malignant disorder resulting from the presence of the BCR-ABL fusion oncogene that occurs from translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22.  Characterised by myeloid hyperplasia of bone marrow and subsequent dysregulation of haematopoiesis.  Separated into three main stages – chronic phase (asymptomatic), accelerated phase (disease progression) and blast crisis (rapid progression, similar to acute leukaemia).  Symptoms/signs include malaise, fever, weight loss, night sweating and abdominal pains.  However, many patients present asymptomatically in the chronic phase following a full blood count (raised white cell count, anaemia).  Initial treatment is with tyrosine kinase inhibitors; bone marrow transplantation may be required.  Prognosis depends on the stage, with the best prognosis for patients in the chronic phase. Epidemiology  People of all ages can be affected, however, it most commonly occurs between 65 and 74 years of age. DR. JAM

 Risk factors include male sex and exposure to ionising radiation. Aetiology  Ionising radiation is the only known exposure risk. Pathophysiology  Translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (Philadelphia chromosome).  BCR gene on chromosome 22 is fused to the ABL gene on chromosome 9 to create a BCR-ABL fusion oncogene.  BCR-ABL is an active tyrosine kinase that phosphorylates and changes the activity of downstream signal transduction proteins which enable the transformation of haematopoietic stem cells into malignant cells. Diagram showing which cells CML originates from:  Clinical Presentation  Many patients will be asymptomatic and present incidentally in the chronic phase with:  splenomegaly  weight loss  sweating  left upper quadrant discomfort  epistaxis  arthralgia  sternal tenderness.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:  leukaemoid reaction  benign neutrophilic leukocytosis  atypical CML  chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia  essential thrombocythaemia  Ph+ acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Diagnosis/Investigation  Many patients will present asymptomatically following a full blood count (FBC).  FBC – elevated white cell count (WCC), anaemia; can have normal platelet count, thrombocytosis or thrombocytopenia.  Complete metabolic profile – may have elevated potassium/LDH/uric acid due to increased cell turnover.  Peripheral blood smear – mature myeloid cells, elevated basophils and eosinophils.  Bone marrow biopsy (required to confirm phase of the disease) – granulocytic hyperplasia.  Cytogenetics – Philadelphia chromosome positive t(9,22).  Quantitative reverse transcription PCR – detection of BCRABL fusion.  Fluorescent in situ hybridisation – t(9,22) positive. Coagulation Cascade Haemostasis is the physiological process of stopping bleeding by formation of a thrombus.  Overview Key Facts  Haemostasis is the physiological process of stopping bleeding by formation of a thrombus.  Primary haemostasis is achieved by mechanisms such as vasoconstriction following endothelial injury and platelet aggregation.  Secondary haemostasis is achieved by the activation of the coagulation cascade, ultimately resulting in a fibrin clot (also known as a thrombus).  The coagulation cascade is a sequence of events that is triggered by the activation of the intrinsic or the extrinsic coagulation pathway.  These two pathways share a final common pathway, resulting in the formation of a fibrin clot.  The system can be divided into three areas, with each area representing one of the three basic screening tests of coagulation:  prothrombin time (PT):  measures the extrinsic system and the final common pathway  the international normalised (prothrombin) ratio (INR) is derived from the PT and measures the same thing.  activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT):  measures the intrinsic system and the final common pathway  prolonged APTT should prompt assay of factors XII, XI, IX and VIII.  thrombin time (TT):  measures the final part of the common pathway  it is prolonged by lack of fibrinogen to convert to fibrin and by inhibitors of this conversion (including heparin and high levels of fibrin degradation products).  Disorders of the coagulation cascade can lead to either bleeding disorders or thrombotic disorders:  bleeding disorders:

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  haemophilia A and B  factor V, X, VII and XIII deficiency  prothrombin deficiency  disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)  vitamin K deficiency  microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia  liver disease.  thrombotic disorders:  protein C and protein S deficiency  factor V Leiden  antiphospholipid syndrome. Representation of the coagulation cascade: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation Disseminated intravascular coagulation is a syndrome that is characterised by an inappropriate systemic activation of the coagulation cascade, leading to small and medium vessel thrombosis and subsequent organ dysfunction.  Overview Key Facts  Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a syndrome that is characterised by an inappropriate systemic activation of the coagulation cascade, leading to small and medium vessel thrombosis and subsequent organ dysfunction.  Rapidly developing disseminated intravascular coagulation is a medical emergency. DR. JAM

 The condition can also lead to massive haemorrhage due to exhaustion of clotting factors.  DIC is a complication of other underlying pathology rather than being a primary event itself.  Sepsis is a common cause of DIC, with DIC estimated to occur in 30–50% of patients with severe sepsis.  Bleeding from puncture and/or injection sites, external orifices and extensive bruising are commonly seen.  Management involves treating and/or reversing the cause and supportive therapy.  DIC can lead to massive haemorrhage, end-organ failure, and is often a fatal condition. Epidemiology  DIC occurs in response to other pathology. There are no predisposing factors in terms of age, sex or race. Aetiology  Common causes:  infection: septicaemia (commonly gram negative)  malignancy  incompatible blood transfusion  obstetric emergencies  liver failure  widespread tissue damage from severe burns/trauma. Pathophysiology  Inappropriate activation of the coagulation cascade and fibrinolytic pathway leading to excessive consumption of platelets and/or coagulation factors and intravascular deposition of fibrin. Fibrinolytic pathway:  Clinical Presentation  Acute presentation:  bleeding from at least three places:

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  venepuncture/cannulation sites  gastrointestinal tract  the ears, nose and throat.  confusion  fever  skin may show signs of petechiae, purpura, thrombosis and necrosis  extensive bruising at puncture sites and site of trauma  acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).  Subacute:  DIC develops over weeks/months, usually secondary to malignancy and some of coagulation tests are normal  some signs may be thromboembolic manifestations.  Differential Diagnosis  Severe liver failure.  Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.  Idiopathic purpura fulminans.  Vitamin K deficiency.  Haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes (proteins) and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  There is no single laboratory test that can establish or rule out the diagnosis of DIC and the diagnosis should include both clinical and laboratory information.  Bloods:  coagulation: prolonged APTT, prothrombin time/INR, thrombin time  low fibrinogen  high fibrin degradation products  low platelets  D-dimer: raised.  Management  Identify and treat the cause of DIC – in many cases, the DIC will resolve when the underlying disorder is properly managed.  Supportive therapy. Non-pharmacological  ICU admission: monitor and maintain normal physiological parameters (blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature). Pharmacological:  Transfusion: fresh frozen plasma, platelet, cryoprecipitate, factor concentrates.  In patients with thrombosis predominant DIC, heparinisation may be required. DR. JAM

 Prognosis  Complication: DIC can lead to massive haemorrhage, end-organ failure, and is often a fatal condition.  Mortality is estimated to double in sepsis of DIC develops.  With appropriate and early diagnosis and intervention, DIC can have a good outcome.  Prognosis often depends of the underlying condition. G6PD Deficiency Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is an Xlinked recessive condition, more common in people of Mediterranean, Asian and African descent.  Overview Key Facts  Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is an X-linked recessive condition, more common in people of Mediterranean, Asian and African descent.  Severe deficiency tends to occur most commonly in people of Mediterranean descent.  People are usually asymptomatic until a trigger precipitates haemolysis.  Triggers for haemolysis include infections, certain medications (predominantly antimalarials and certain antibiotics) and fava beans.  G6PD deficiency results in haemolysis when red blood cells are placed under oxidative stress.  Most people are asymptomatic and not aware that they have the condition unless they become exposed to a trigger or undergo testing.  Some people (usually with < 10% of normal G6PD enzyme activity) may suffer from chronic haemolysis and require regular blood transfusions.  Babies may present with neonatal jaundice, appearing within 24 hours of birth and often necessitating exchange transfusion.  Haemolysis is self-limiting after stopping the precipitant.  Symptoms of severe haemolysis may include tachycardia, jaundice and dark urine.  Diagnosis can be made by measuring G6PD enzyme activity; this may be measured using a rapid fluorescent spot test or quantitative spectrophotometric analysis.  During an attack, blood tests will usually show raised reticulocytes, increased unconjugated bilirubin, increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and low haptoglobin. A blood film during an attack may show Heinz bodies, bite cells or blister cells.  The mainstay of treatment is the avoidance of the triggers of haemolysis.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  In rare cases of severe anaemia, a blood transfusion may be necessary.  Prognosis is generally good; most people will have a normal life expectancy and can live a normal life with avoidance of triggers. Epidemiology  It affects > 400 million people worldwide.  It is more common in people of Mediterranean, Asian and African descent.  As an X-linked recessive condition, it predominantly affects men.  G6PD variants have been classified by the World Health Organization (WHO) into classes I–V according to the degree of enzyme deficiency, with class I being the most severe and classes IV and V largely clinically insignificant:  severe deficiency tends to occur most commonly in people of Mediterranean descent  African populations tend to have higher enzyme levels and milder haemolysis. Aetiology  Genetics:  inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern  therefore, predominantly affects men, but can affect female homozygotes in high-prevalence areas or in rare cases of X-inactivation (lyonisation)  most mutations arise from amino acid substitutions  > 200 mutations have been identified.  Triggers for haemolysis in people with G6PD deficiency:  fava beans  ingestion of naphthalene (found in mothballs)  infections leading to severe haemolysis:  hepatitis A and B  cytomegalovirus (CMV)  pneumonia  typhoid fever.  other infections may also cause haemolysis of varying severity.  medications*: Medications with a risk in most patients with G6PD deficiency Medications with a risk in some patients with G6PD deficiency Fluoroquinolones Dapsone (and other sulfones) Nitrofurantoin Methylthioninium chloride Aspirin (up to 1 g daily is usually OK) Chloroquine (acceptable for treatment or prophylaxis of malaria) Menadione Quinine DR. JAM

Primaquine Quinolones Rasburicase Sulphonamides (including co-trimoxazole) Sulfonylureas Pathophysiology  Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is an enzyme that catalyses the first step of the pentose phosphate pathway.  It catalyses the reduction of NADP to NADPH.  NADPH is involved in the production of reduced glutathione which protects cells from oxidative damage.  In G6PD deficiency, red cells are vulnerable to oxidative stress caused by certain triggers (medication, foods infections) which leads to haemolysis.  The severity of symptoms usually has a direct correlation with the degree of enzyme dysfunction.  There is never a complete deficiency of G6PD, as this would be incompatible with survival.  Clinical Presentation  Most people are asymptomatic and not aware that they have the condition unless they become exposed to a trigger or undergo testing.  Some people (usually with < 10% of normal G6PD enzyme activity) may suffer from chronic haemolysis and require regular blood transfusions.  May present with neonatal jaundice, appearing within 24 hours of birth and often necessitating exchange transfusion:  in rare cases, if untreated, may lead to bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus).  Haemolysis may be triggered by infections, medications, fava beans or diabetic ketoacidosis, usually occurring > 24 hours after exposure to the trigger.  Haemolysis is self-limiting after stopping the precipitant.  Symptoms of severe haemolysis may include:  tachycardia  jaundice  dark urine.  Gallstones are more common in G6PD deficiency.  Splenomegaly may be present.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses may include:  sickle cell anaemia  thalassaemia  haemolytic disease of the newborn  methaemoglobinaemia  hereditary spherocytosis.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Diagnosis/Investigation  G6PD enzyme activity:  rapid fluorescent spot test – detects the generation of NADPH; if the blood spot fails to fluoresce under UV light, the test is positive  quantitative spectrophotometric analysis  testing can be inaccurate in acute haemolysis because older erythrocytes with lower levels of G6PD enzyme activity will have been haemolysed and young erythrocytes and reticulocytes may have a much higher level of G6PD enzyme activity.  Blood film (during an attack):  Heinz bodies (denatured haemoglobin seen inside erythrocytes)  bite cells (cells with Heinz bodies that have passed through the spleen and been incompletely destroyed by splenic macrophages)  blister cells.  Blood count is normal between attacks.  During an attack:  raised reticulocytes  increased unconjugated bilirubin  increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)  decreased haptoglobin  urinary haemosiderin.  Management  The mainstay of treatment is avoidance of the triggers of haemolysis.  Folic acid supplementation may be beneficial.  If neonatal jaundice, phototherapy or exchange transfusion may be required.  In rare cases of severe anaemia, a blood transfusion may be necessary.  Splenectomy can be considered for patients with chronic haemolytic anaemia.  Prognosis  Prognosis is generally good; most people will have a normal life expectancy and can live a normal life with avoidance of triggers.  Kernicterus is a severe complication and rapid diagnosis and treatment of neonatal jaundice is essential. DR. JAM

Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is a condition characterised by the destruction of red blood cells, kidney failure, and low platelet count, often caused by certain strains of E. coli bacteria.  Overview Key Facts  Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is a triad of:  microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia  thrombocytopenia  acute kidney injury.  It is the most frequent cause of acute kidney damage in children.  Typical HUS is associated with bloody diarrhoea and is caused by E. coli O157:H7 strain.  Atypical HUS may be associated with systemic conditions (such as altered state of consciousness, hypertension, malaise).  It is caused by genetic mutations in the complement system. Epidemiology  Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is a rare disorder and it is more common in children.  Children under 16 years of age have a strong association for developing HUS but those who are less than 5 years old are most commonly affected.  90% of cases of HUS in children are secondary to infection of E. coli O157:H7.  10% of cases of HUS are atypical and are not caused by bacteria. Aetiology  Typical HUS is caused by the following pathogens:  E. coli  Streptococcus pneumonia  Shigella dysenteriae type 1  viruses such as human immunodeficiency virus and coxsackievirus.  The enterohaemorrhagic strain of E. coli (EHEC) having serotype O157:H7 is the main and the commonest strain responsible for HUS.  E. coli O157:H7 strain produces Shiga-like toxin or verotoxin.  It is transmitted by contaminated food or drinks, such as beef or unpasteurised milk from an infected cow.  Atypical HUS is caused by:  exposure to medicines such as tacrolimus and ciclosporin  mutations in the complement pathway  systemic conditions such as pregnancy and lupus.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 Pathophysiology  In E. coli O157:H7, ‘157’ refers to the O antigen present in the lipopolysaccharide cell wall and ‘7’ refers to the H antigen located on the flagella of the bacteria.  E. coli secretes Shiga-like toxin or verotoxin when it attaches to the intestinal wall after entering into the digestive tract.  Shiga-like toxin gets absorbed into intestinal vessels and is transferred to immune cells such as neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.  This toxin is then carried by the immune cells to the blood capillaries of the renal, gastrointestinal and central nervous systems  it attaches to globotriaosylceramide or Gb3-receptor of endothelial cells of blood capillaries, which has a strong affinity for Shiga-like toxin.  After entry into the endothelial cells, the toxin stops protein synthesis in the cell by inhibiting the activity of aminoacyltRNA and cell suicide pathways are activated due to fragmentation of DNA by the toxin.  The lining of blood capillaries gets disrupted and this disruption is then repaired by primary hemostasis, which is the formation of platelet plugs in the kidney vessels or intestinal vessels to prevent bleeding.  Thrombin and fibrin are deposited in the microvasculature of the organs.  Platelets are sequestered at the site of primary haemostasis and erythrocytes are damaged as they pass through the partially occluded microvasculature and thus haemolysis occurs.  Clinical Presentation  Classical findings in the patient with HUS are profuse diarrhoea and dark brown urine (haematuria).  Profuse diarrhoea turns bloody 1–3 days after onset.  Diarrhoea is often associated with fever, abdominal pain and vomiting.  Symptoms of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia include:  lethargy  fatigue  palpitations  weakness  jaundice.  Easy bruising, purpura and sometimes severe bleeding are indicative of thrombocytopenia.  Symptoms of acute renal failure include:  oedema  weight gain  oliguria.  Patients having HUS associated with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura may have neurological findings which include:  visual disturbances  altered mental status DR. JAM

 seizures  stroke.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses of abdominal pain, diarrhoea and other symptoms of HUS include:  disseminated intravascular coagulation with sepsis  thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura  HELLP syndrome  inflammatory bowel disease  inherited diseases of the complement system.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Physical assessment should always include temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure, weight and assessment of hydration.  A complete blood count shows anaemia and thrombocytopenia.  High white blood cell count with low platelet count is an early indicator of HUS.  A blood smear shows schistocytes or helmet cells and low platelet count.  Renal function test shows high blood urea and creatinine levels.  Serum electrolyte test shows hypernatraemia.  Lactate dehydrogenase if high is an early indicator of HUS.  Liver function tests show raised unconjugated bilirubin.  C-reactive protein is high in active HUS.  The clotting screen shows decreased levels in the early stages of HUS.  Stool culture is done for culture and phage typing of E. coli.  PCR is done for the confirmation of genes of virulence factors.  Urinalysis shows haematuria or proteinuria.  A urine culture may also be performed in some cases.  When atypical HUS is suspected, other specialist tests must be done, including:  mutational analysis of specific complement genes  ADAMTS13 assay.  Management  General management usually includes:  hospital admission  fluid and electrolyte therapy  antihypertensive therapy and dialysis when required.  Supportive treatment includes:  heparin  urokinase  dipyridamole  fresh frozen plasma transfusion

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Shiga-toxin binding protein  steroids.  Treatment for atypical HUS includes:  plasmapheresis  specific targeted treatments, eg factor H concentrate  kidney or liver transplant.  Prognosis  Typical HUS has a good prognosis.  Fatality is more common in infants, small children and elderly patients.  Atypical HUS has the worst prognosis and it may lead to endstage kidney disease.  Other  The toxin of E. coli O157:H7 is a Shiga-like toxin due to its structural similarity with the Shiga toxin produced by Shigella dysenteriae.  The incubation period for E. coli O157:H7 is 1–7 days and HUS usually occurs within 14 days after the onset of bloody diarrhoea.  HUS is more common in rural populations, children of six months to five years of age and older people with altered immune responses.  Conjugate vaccines against E. coli O157:H7 are in development for the prevention of HUS. Haemophilia Haemophilias are bleeding disorders which vary in severity according to the relative deficiency of the clotting factor concerned  Overview Key Facts  Haemophilias are bleeding disorders which vary in severity according to the relative deficiency of the clotting factor concerned  Haemophilia A is due to reduced synthesis of Factor VIII  Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) is due to a deficiency in factor IX.  Inherited as an X-genetic recessive disorders, generally affecting male boys born to mother carriers.  Some women who carry the haemophilia gene may have prolongation of APTT  Presentations vary from mild cases leading to prolonged bleeding after venepuncture to severe non-triggered lifethreatening bleeding. DR. JAM

 Acquired haemophilia can be seen in systemic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis because of anti-Factor VIII antibodies. Epidemiology  Haemophilia A: 1 : 5 000 of live affected men.  Haemophilia B: 1 : 30 000 of live affected men.  The most severe forms nearly exclusively occurs in men.  Presentation occurs by one year of age in 90% of severe cases. Aetiology  Mostly X-linked recessive genetic disorder, but may also result from acquired (autoimmune) disorders.  30% not familial (sporadic/new mutations). Pathophysiology  Genetic defects such as deletion, mutation or insertion of the X chromosome.  Sporadic cases occur with acquired autoimmune disorders.  Leads to clotting factor deficiencies which subsequently affects the coagulation cascade at specific points. Representation of the coagulation cascade:  Clinical Presentation  Severe haemophilia (< 1 IU/dl):  frequent spontaneous deep muscular haematomas and haemarthroses, usually resulting in joint deformity  usually presents at < one year olds.  Moderate haemophilia (1–5 IU/dl):  occasional spontaneous bleeds and severe bleeding from injuries

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  presentation in the first two years of life.  Mild haemophilia:  increased/delayed bleeding only after an injury or surgery  presentation usually when older than two years old.  Differential Diagnosis  Disseminated intravascular coagulation.  Vitamin K deficiency.  Disorders of fibrinogen or fibrinolytic production.  Platelet disorders.  von Willebrand’s disease.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Clinical features including:  presence of risk factors  history of recurrent bleeding.  Plasma factor VIII and IX assay.  Blood test:  full blood count  liver function tests.  Laboratory coagulation profile showing:  prolonged APTT  normal prothrombin time (PT) and von Willebrand factor (VWF).  For carriers, antenatal testing – amniocentesis/chorionic villus sampling (CVS) for mutation analysis during pregnancy.  DNA-based analysis for specific genetic mutations.  Imaging may be required to rule out acute haemorrhage, for example, in patients presenting with acute neurological impairment such as an intracranial bleed.  Management  Management is complex based on severity and presentation of life-threatening/non-life-threatening situations. Non-pharmacological  Physiotherapy.  Hydrotherapy.  Patient education on treatment and prevention of bleeding.  Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and intramuscular (IM)/joint injections. Pharmacological:  Factor VIII/IX concentrate intravenous infusion.  Acquired factor VII deficiency can be treated in mild cases with desmopressin or factor VIII but in severe bleeding an agent that DR. JAM

bypasses FVIII, either an activated prothrombin complex concentrate or recombinant factor VIIa is required.  Synthetic vasopressin (intravenous (IV)/subcutaneous (SC)/intranasal):  effective for mild haemophilia limited benefit for patient with severe haemophilia  not effective in haemophilia B.  Fibrinolytic inhibitors:  tranexamic acid is usually effective for mild haemophilia  it should be avoided in heamarthrosis or deep muscular haematomas.  Analgesia in acute bleeding episodes.  Vaccination against Hepatitis B.  Prognosis  Prognosis is dependent on severity.  Up to 60% of patients with haemophilia A have severe forms.  Prognosis is improved with proper treatment and prevention of injuries.  Genetic therapies are currently under development which may further improve prognosis.  Complication of disease:  degenerative joint disorders (arthritis)  life-threatening haemorrhage.  Complication of treatment:  viral infections such as hepatitis and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) from transfusion if concentrate not virally inactivated  development of antibodies against the administered coagulation factors  opiate addiction. Heparin Anticoagulants are usually initiated in secondary care, a dedicated clinic in a hospital, or an outreach clinic in primary care.  Overview Key Facts  Anticoagulants are usually initiated in secondary care, a dedicated clinic in a hospital, or an outreach clinic in primary care.  Heparin is a fast-acting anti-clotting agent which can be used in prophylaxis and treatment of thromboembolic disease.  Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) works by binding to antithrombin and enhancing its ability to inhibit two clotting factors: factors Xa and IIa.  UFH is licensed for use in:

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  prophylaxis of:  venous thromboembolism (VTE) in medical/surgical patients  VTE in pregnancy  clotting in extracorporeal circuits  clotting in catheters, cannulas or indwelling intravenous infusion devices.  treatment of:  mild, moderate and severe pulmonary embolism (PE)  deep-vein thrombosis  unstable angina  acute peripheral arterial occlusion  haemodialysis.  Dosing  Treatment of mild-moderate PE, unstable angina or acute peripheral arterial occlusion = 5 000 units (loading dose) intravenously (IV) followed by 18 units/kg/hour.  Treatment of severe PE = 10 000 units (loading dose) (IV) followed by 18 units/kg/hour.  Treatment of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) = 5 000 units (loading dose) (IV) followed by 18 units/kg/hour or 15 000 units subcutaneously (SC)/12 hours.  Thromboprophylaxis in medical patients = 5 000 units (SC) every 8–12 hours.  Thromboprophylaxis in surgical patients = 5 000 units (SC) for one dose, taken two hours before surgery and then 5 000 units every 12 hours.  Thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy = 5 000–10 000 units (SC) every 12 hours.  Haemodialysis = 1 000–5 000 units initially (IV) followed by 250–1 000 units/hour.  Monitoring  Laboratory monitoring is essential, preferably on a daily basis (adjust dose accordingly).  Platelet count should be measured before treatment with heparin + regular monitoring if taken for > four days.  Plasma K+ should be measured in patients at risk of hyperkalaemia before starting heparin and regularly thereafter.  Cautions  Elderly.  Severe hypertension.  Contraindications  Acute bacterial endocarditis. Aetiology  Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited defect in the structural proteins of red blood cell membranes (usually dominant inheritance).  Abnormalities result in changes in red cell shape due to defects in skeletal proteins – alpha spectrin, beta spectrin, ankyrin, band 3 protein, protein 4.2. Pathophysiology  Normal red blood cells are biconcave flexible discs that are able to pass through small and large blood vessels.  Spherical red blood cell shape is caused by defects in structural membrane proteins.  Flexibility of red blood cells decreases and they are removed by the spleen due to fragility.  Increased red cell destruction causes hyperbilirubinaemia, elevated reticulocyte count and splenomegaly.  Clinical Presentation  Presentation:  pallor  jaundice  splenomegaly  fatigue.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  non-haemolytic anaemia, eg iron deficiency  other causes of haemolytic anaemia, eg G6PD deficiency  other causes of jaundice, eg hepatitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Full blood count – haemoglobin (Hb) may be reduced or normal, mean corpuscular Hb concentration may be elevated, mean corpuscular volume may be normal or reduced.  Reticulocyte count – elevated.  Blood smear – spherocytes present.  Serum bilirubin – elevated unconjugated bilirubin.  Serum aminotransferases – normal.  Direct anti-globulin test – negative.  Peripheral blood smear in hereditary spherocytosis:

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Management  Supportive care.  Red blood cell transfusions.  Folic acid supplementation.  Splenectomy with pre-op vaccination regimen and/or cholecystectomy or cholecystotomy (due to increased incidence of gallstones).  Post-splenectomy antibiotic pneumococcal prophylaxis – phenoxymethylpenicillin or amoxicillin.  Prognosis  Most people are asymptomatic after splenectomy and symptoms and signs improve.  Long-term risk of infection and thrombosis after splenectomy, but deaths from sepsis are rare.  Patients must receive genetic counselling if they want to have children.  Other  Complications include:  aplastic crisis  gallstones  bone marrow expansion  extramedullary haematopoiesis  post-splenectomy sepsis  post-splenectomy vascular complications. Hodgkin’s Lymphoma Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a haematological B-cell malignancy. DR. JAM

 Overview Key Facts  Hodgkin’s lymphoma (HL) is a haematological B-cell malignancy.  It is one of the most common cancers of young people.  The condition is differentiated from non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma due to the presence of Reed–Sternberg cells at biopsy.  Aetiology is not clearly understood; however, there is significant association with Epstein–Barr virus.  The most common symptom of Hodgkin’s lymphoma is lymphadenopathy.  Other symptoms may include night sweats, fever, weight loss and pruritus.  There are four stages of the disease, classified based on the Ann Arbor clinical staging of lymphomas.  Patients with signs or symptoms suggestive of Hodgkin’s lymphoma should be referred under the 2-week wait rule (adults) or consider assessment within 48 hours in children and young people.  Diagnosis is confirmed by the presence Reed–Sternberg cells (biopsied sample).  Treatment: chemotherapy +/- radiotherapy. Epidemiology  Approximate incidence 2 000/year in the United Kingdom.  Diagnosis peaks at ages 15–34 and then again in those greater than 60 years of age.  Higher risk in men than women. Aetiology  Specific causal factors unknown, more likely to be multifactorial.  Epstein–Barr virus infection is found in significant proportion of the cases.  Genetic susceptibility. Pathophysiology  Clonal transformation of B-cells.  Reed–Sternberg cells are characteristic feature of the disease. These are giant abnormal lymphocytes, usually binucleated. Reed–Sternberg cells: hallmark cells of Hodgkin's lymphoma:

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Clinical Presentation  Painless cervical and/or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.  B symptoms: fevers, night sweats, weight loss.  Alcohol induced pain is seen in fewer than 10% of patients.  Differential Diagnosis  Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL).  Infectious mononucleosis.  Reactive lymph nodes.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Bloods:  full blood count: neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, normocytic anaemia, eosinophilia  erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) elevated  lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) elevated: this is a useful guide to volume of disease in high grade lymphomas  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) testing, (patients with HIV are at increased risk of Hodgkin’s lymphoma).  Biopsy: for definite diagnosis; characterised by the presence of Hodgkin's cells and Reed–Sternberg cells.  Imaging studies: computed tomography (CT)/positron emission tomography (PET) scan.  Ann Arbor clinical staging of lymphomas:  stage I: one involved lymph node group  stage II: two nodal areas on one side of the diaphragm  stage III: lymph nodes on both sides of the diaphragm  stage IV: involvement of extra nodal tissues such as liver or bone marrow.  Management  Patients and their families/carers should be provided information regarding the condition and management, as well as being provided information regarding support services.  The mainstay of treatment is chemotherapy for all stages. Two combinations are commonly used:  doxorubicin hydrochloride (Adriamycin), bleomycin sulfate, vinblastine sulfate, and dacarbazine (ABVD). DR. JAM

 bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin hydrochloride (Adriamycin), cyclophosphamide, vincristine, procarbazine and prednisolone (BEACOPP).  Autologous transplantation may be considered in a physiological stable patient.  Radiotherapy may be used as an adjunct for stage I and II disease.  Prognosis  Dependent on clinical stage of disease, bulk of tumour, and histopathological type.  5-year survival is 85%.  Complications of treatment, eg secondary, malignancy, cardiac diseases.  The risk of breast cancer is greatest in women treated with supradiaphragmatic radiotherapy (SRT) during adolescence and young adulthood.  Increased risk is, however, seen in most studies with SRT up to the age of 30–40 years, in total risk is thought to persist for at least 20–25 years after treatment. Immunodeficiency Immunodeficiency can be classified as either primary or secondary, by the faulty component, or according to individual clinical syndromes. It results in partial or full impairment of the immune system leading to a suboptimal response to infection.  Overview Key Facts  Immunodeficiency can be classified as either primary or secondary, by the faulty component, or according to individual clinical syndromes.  it results in partial or full impairment of the immune system leading to a suboptimal response to infection.  Primary immunodeficiency is inherited and arises from genetic defects in B and T cells, these patients usually present at birth or early childhood.  Secondary immunodeficiency is acquired and a result of disease or environmental factors and includes HIV/AIDS, malnutrition or medical treatment (eg chemotherapy).  There are over 300 types of immunodeficiency.  Both forms of immunodeficiency result in recurrent infections.  Investigations in primary care include full blood count and antibody levels and become more specialised in secondary care.  Management includes prophylactic antibiotics, immunoglobin replacement or bone marrow transplant in primary immunodeficiency whereas treatment for secondary immunodeficiency focuses on the underlying disorder causing immune suppression, eg HAART (Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy) for HIV/AIDS.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 Primary immunodeficiency (PID):  Rare and usually the diagnostic remit of paediatricians.  Mostly inherited single gene disorders that present in infancy or early childhood, however common variable immunodeficiency is the exception and usually presents in adulthood.  B-cell defects account for 50% of primary immunodeficiency, T-cell defects account for 30%, phagocytic deficiencies 18%, and complement deficiencies 2%. Secondary immunodeficiency (SID):  Due to disease or medication is common and is encountered by adult physicians on a daily basis in routine practice.  Common in people hospitalised for:  malignancy  HIV  malnutrition  metabolic disorders  renal disease requiring dialysis  protein loss (eg nephrotic syndrome). Epidemiology Primary:  six million people live with PID worldwide but 70-79% undiagnosed with 5000 of these individuals in the United Kingdom (UK)  there are 39,000 PID related hospital admissions in 2014-2015 in the UK. Secondary:  it is more common than primary immunodeficiency disorders which are relatively rare  more common in developing world where people are more likely to suffer from malnutrition and/or HIV/AIDS  there are 100,000 patients with HIV in the UK and 600 HIVrelated deaths in the UK in 2015  15000 HIV related hospital admissions in 2014–2015 in the UK. Pathophysiology Patterns of immunodeficiency  Neutrophil defects:  result in recurrent bacterial or fungal skin infections (cellulitis/abscesses)  eg primary: chronic granulomatous disease; secondary: diabetes mellitus.  Complement deficiency:  can be uncovered incidentally as it is not always symptomatic – many are undiagnosed DR. JAM

 most important clinical associations with complement deficiency include hereditary angioedema and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  when infections occur it usually implies a final common pathway defect manifesting with recurrent and/or invasive Neisseria spp. infections  eg primary: inherited final common pathway deficiencies, secondary: eculizumab (C5 inhibitor used for paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria).  B cell/antibody deficiency:  results in sinopulmonary infections/bronchiectasis  eg primary: common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency, Bruton’s hypogammaglobulinaemia; secondary: chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, rituximab, gold, and phenytoin.  T cell deficiency:  infections are opportunistic eg Pneumocystis jirovecii, invasive viral infections (cytomegalovirus), intracellular bacterial infections (eg salmonellae and mycobacterial infections)  eg primary: DiGeorge syndrome, severe combined immune deficiency (SCID), ataxia telangiectasia, secondary: HIV infection, ciclosporin and anti-CD3 therapy.  Clinical Presentation  Immunodeficiency disorders characterised by:  recurrent, persistent and complicated infections (often bacterial) affecting:  respiratory tract (eg pneumonia, bronchitis and sinusitis)  mouth (eg thrush and gingivitis)  ears (eg otitis)  skin (eg pyoderma and warts).  general symptoms:  fevers/chills  loss of appetite/weight loss  abdominal pain – due to hepatomegaly/splenomegaly  chronic diarrhoea – causing failure to thrive in infants/children  poor growth and weight loss.  Diagnosis/Investigation Primary and secondary immunodeficiency:  Initial tests in primary care:  full blood count (FBC), IgG, IgM and IgA  microbiological swabs  chest X-ray.  Specialist tests:

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  lymphocyte response assays  antibody response to immunisation of diphtheria, tetanus and pneumococcal polysaccharides  phagocytosis assay  flow cytometry.  Management Primary and secondary immunodeficiency: Non-pharmacological  Healthy lifestyle and protection from infection (eg regular dental checks).  Chest infections – physiotherapy and lung exercises. Pharmacological:  Prophylactic antibiotics (eg for those who have undergone splenectomy).  Antivirals (eg amantadine).  Intravenous (IV) or subcutaneous (SC) immunoglobulin replacement. Surgical  Bone marrow transplant – definitive treatment for T-cell deficiency conditions and those with bone marrow destruction following chemotherapy treatment. Primary immunodeficiency specifically:  Other experimental treatment:  cytokines  thymic transplants  gene therapy  stem cell transplantation.  Prognosis  Primary immunodeficiency is most commonly genetic and has lifelong implications.  Better prognosis if the condition is diagnosed early and infections treated regularly.  Worse outlook for patients with severe combined immunodeficiency where patients tend to have chronic illness and require intensive treatment.  Secondary – tend to resolve when underlying pathology is treated. DR. JAM

Lead Poisoning Lead poisoning occurs when lead accumulates in the body, leading to various health issues such as developmental delays and neurological symptoms.  Overview Key Facts  Occupational or home exposure to lead.  No normal level so interventions should be started when there are signs of increased exposure.  Causes neurodevelopmental dysfunction in children and multisystem dysfunction in adults including cardiovascular, renal, neurological and haematological issues.  Chelation therapy is the mainstay of treatment.  Complicated by acute lead encephalopathy.  Acute symptoms may resolve with interventions, but neurological and cardiovascular toxicities are often irreversible.  Long-term monitoring required as lead can be present in bone for many years after exposure. Epidemiology  Major risk to children (especially those aged 18–24 months) in developed countries is from inhalation of lead-based paints and soil and dust that has been contaminated with lead-based paints.  In adults, the exposure largely is occupation from battery manufacturing, radiator repairs or exposure to old lead paint.  Increased risk in patients who live in old housing with poorly maintained paint surfaces. Aetiology  Inhalation or ingestion of lead particles leads to toxicity.  Sources of exposure include:  deteriorating paint surfaces

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  occupational exposure, eg heavy construction, battery production  bullet firing ranges  folk medications, eg azarcon, greta  lead-contaminated water  toys  fetal exposure. Pathophysiology  Smaller lead particles are better absorbed.  Lead particles compete with minerals such as zinc and calcium to cause problems with mitochondrial function, neurotoxicity and haem-dependent processes.  Lead mainly binds to red blood cells but can be found in plasma if levels are very high (> 60 μg/dl).  > 90% of lead is stored in the bone which provides a long-term storm of lead to target tissues even after exposure had ended.  Toxicity is targeted at multiple systems:  renal – potent toxic to proximal renal tubules causing Fanconi syndrome  cardiovascular – hypertension, coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease  neurodevelopmental – notably in children.  Clinical Presentation  Children – cognitive impairment, behavioural changes, headache, agitation, loss of appetite, constipation, somnolence.  Altered mental state.  Cerebellar signs.  Seizures.  Coma.  Colicky abdominal pain.  Hypertension. DR. JAM

 Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  iron-deficiency anaemia  non-lead peripheral neuropathy  arsenic poisoning  encephalitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Whole blood lead level – blood lead > 0.4 μmol/l in children, or > 1.2 μmol/l in adults.  Full blood count – can show microcytic hypochromic anaemia.  Serum ferritin – can be reduced.  Management  Removal from the source of exposure.  Chelation therapy – dimercaprol, succimer or sodium calcium edetate.  Intensive Care Unit admission and supportive care – for acute lead encephalopathy.  Prognosis  Much of the poisoning is not reversible as lead remains in bone stores for many decades after exposure has ended.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Requires long-term follow-up.  Acute lead encephalopathy – survival is good in children with intensive care but children often have remaining neurological damage.  Cardiovascular and neurological toxicity is often not reversed by chelation treatment.  Other  Complications:  anaemia  neurodevelopmental delay  hypertension  coronary artery disease  ischaemic stroke  peripheral vascular disease  cognitive dysfunction  cancer  hearing loss  Fanconi syndrome  chronic renal failure. DR. JAM

Methaemoglobinaemia Methaemoglobinaemia occurs when red blood cells have excessive methaemoglobin (MetHb >1%). MetHb cannot bind oxygen and is unable to deliver oxygen to tissues.  Overview Key Facts  Methaemoglobinaemia occurs when red blood cells have excessive methaemoglobin (MetHb >1%). MetHb cannot bind oxygen and is unable to deliver oxygen to tissues.  It is an important but uncommon cause of hypoxia and is reversible.  Patients commonly present with cyanosis not matching their level of clinical presentation, symptoms related to low oxygen levels (fainting, lightheadedness), chocolate-coloured blood and hypoxia that does not improve with supplemental oxygen.  Methaemoglobinaemia can be congenital or acquired:  the most commonly acquired cause is from toxins and drugs  the most common congenital cause is cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency.  The gold standard investigation is checking MetHb levels in the blood.  The mainstay of treatment is supportive oxygen and methylene blue which reduces ferric iron to ferrous iron:  if this is contraindicated then ascorbic acid is used, or other supportive treatment such as hyperbaric oxygen therapy or exchange transfusion.  The prognosis is usually determined by the amount of end-organ damage that is caused by hypoxia. If MetHb levels reach 70%, mortality rates are very high. Epidemiology  The epidemiology is not well known.  It is more common in infants < 4 months as they are more susceptible, with fetal haemoglobin more likely to be oxidised and lower levels of NADH reductase.  Congenital methaemoglobinaemia (cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency) is more common in Navajo, Puerto Ricans, Athabaskan people from Alaska and Yakutsk people of Siberia.  Acquired methaemoglobinaemia in people with glucose-6phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is more common in Mediterranean and African people. Aetiology Congenital  Cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency.  Pyruvate kinase deficiency:  reduced NADH production  NADH is a cofactor for cytochrome b5 reductase.  Haemoglobinopathy (haemoglobin M disease):

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  alters the structure of globin units:  tyrosine replaces histidine which allows oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+  limits the ability of reducing enzymes. Acquired  Toxins are the most common cause:  toxins can oxidise or produce oxygen to convert Fe2+ to Fe3+  local anaesthetics  aniline dyes  benzene derivatives  chloroquine  nitrites  metoclopramide  antibiotics (dapsone)  sulphonamide  smoke.  Diet.  Stress:  sepsis.  Fetal haemoglobin oxidises more easily:  more common in premature infants  level of NADH reductase increases with age; there are low amounts when young. Pathophysiology  Red blood cells (RBCs) are made up of haemoglobin which transports oxygen around the body:  tetramer of four globins, each containing a haem group  haem:  iron held in porphyrin ring  iron binds oxygen  each haemoglobin unit can carry four oxygen molecules  ferrous and ferric iron states  majority of iron is Fe2+ or ferrous ion:  Fe2+ is functional and can bind oxygen.  ferrous ion (Fe2+) can be oxidised to its ferric state (Fe3+)  Fe3+ is not functional and unable to bind oxygen  results in a left shift of the oxygen-dissociation curve  increased oxygen affinity of haemoglobin  less oxygen available to tissues.  haemoglobin with Fe3+ is methaemoglobin (MetHb).  Having more MetHb in the body results in:  haemoglobin carries less oxygen DR. JAM

 oxygen release at tissues is impaired causing more hypoxia.  RBCs are exposed to oxidative stresses which normally cause ferrous ions to be converted to ferric ions:  this is usually maintained at < 1% by protective pathways that reverse the oxidation  protective pathways:  cytochrome b5 reductase pathway:  removes 95–99% of MetHb produced in normal circumstances.  NADPH MetHb reductase:  the minor role is to remove MetHb  uses glutathione and G6PD to reduce MetHb to haemoglobin.  Clinical Presentation  Patients commonly present with the following symptoms:  MetHb <10% of total Hb:  unlikely to have symptoms.  MetHb 10–20% of total Hb:  cyanosis.  MetHb 20–30% of total Hb:  presyncope  headache  tachycardia  anxiety.  MetHb 30–50% of total Hb:  confusion  dizziness  tachycardia  tachypnoea  tiredness.  MetHb 50–70% of total Hb:  seizures  arrhythmias  respiratory depression  coma.  MetHb > 70% of total Hb:  death.  One should be suspicious of methaemoglobinaemia if the patient appears clinically well but is cyanotic or if the SpO2 is low and does not improve with oxygen.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  heart failure  sulfhaemoglobinaemia  argyria.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Methaemoglobinaemia is usually diagnosed clinically. Clinical presentation  A patient would likely present with cyanosis or, if more severe, with worse symptoms.  The history is extremely important to identify any reversible cause for methaemoglobinaemia. Investigations  Blood sample which appears brown and does not oxidise when exposed to air.  Urine samples may be discoloured.  Arterial blood gas (ABG) sample:  may include MetHb or need to be requested  normal PaO2 (or raised if on oxygen) but reduced SaO2.  Co-oximetry.  Pulse oximetry (less accurate than co-oximetry).  MetHb = gold standard investigation.  Full blood count:  Hb levels.  ECG:  rule out differentials or arrhythmias.  Potassium cyanide:  can distinguish MetHb from sulfhaemoglobin.  Chocolate-coloured blood:  Management  Patients who are at low risk may not need active treatment, but supportive treatment only. DR. JAM

 Patients require active treatment if:  MetHb > 30%  MetHb < 30% and symptomatic.  Other considerations include:  evidence of tissue hypoxia (eg end-organ damage)  co-morbidities  haemoglobin levels  chronic or acute methaemoglobinaemia. Non-pharmacological  Supportive treatment:  ABCDE approach  remove any reversible causes/toxins  oxygen  observe and monitor MetHb levels.  Active treatment:  if pharmacological treatment fails:  consider exchange transfusion  consider hyperbaric oxygen. Pharmacological:  Supportive treatment:  intravenous (IV) dextrose.  Active treatment:  methylene blue:  reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+  1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes  if the first administration fails, discuss with National Poisons Information Service and consider further dose.  ascorbic acid:  if methylene blue is contraindicated, eg G6PD deficiency.  Prognosis  Patients with methaemoglobinaemia usually have a good outcome if it is detected and treated promptly. Acquired methaemoglobinaemia is usually mild and if treated promptly is rarely fatal.  The prognosis is usually determined by the amount of end-organ damage there is due to hypoxia. If MetHb levels reach 70%, mortality rates are very high.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 Monoclonal Gammopathy Of Undetermined Significance Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance is a condition involving abnormal proteins in the blood that may progress to certain blood cancers.  Overview Key Facts  Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is more common in older age, in men and people of Black ethnicity.  It is a pre-malignant disorder that is asymptomatic but associated with low risk of progression to multiple myeloma and other plasma cell malignancies.  Diagnostic criteria – the presence of monoclonal M protein in serum or urine, <10% plasma cells in bone marrow, absence of lytic bone lesions, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal insufficiency or amyloidosis.  Differential diagnosis commonly includes multiple myeloma or Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia.  No specific treatment unless required, but follow-up is encouraged.  Increased risk of fracture due to osteoporosis.  Patients progress to more advanced disease at a rate of 1% per year. Epidemiology  The mean age at diagnosis is 70 years.  More common in older age, men and Black ethnicity.  Less than 2% of patients are diagnosed before the age of 40.  The rate of progression to multiple myeloma is the same for Black and White ethnicities. Aetiology  Risk increased in:  family history – 2–3 times more common in patients with first-degree family members with history of MGUS or multiple myeloma  Black ethnicity – 2–3 times more common in Black compared with White people  personal history of autoimmunity or immunodeficiency  radiation exposure  occupational exposure to pesticides  genetic – translocations of immunoglobulin heavy chain locus on chromosome 14q32. Pathophysiology  Patients with IgG or IgA MGUS can progress to multiple myeloma or other plasma cell malignancies. DR. JAM

 Patients with IgM MGUS have an increased risk of progression to Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and other types of non-Hodgkin lymphomas.  Clinical Presentation  Clinically asymptomatic, usually an incidental finding.  Positive family history.  History of radiation or pesticide exposure.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  multiple myeloma or smouldering myeloma  amyloidosis  Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia  chronic lymphocytic leukaemia  non-Hodgkin lymphoma  chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Disease Diagnostic criteria Multiple myeloma (MM) Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥ 10% or biopsy-proven bony or extramedullary plasmacytoma* and any one or more of the following myeloma-defining events: end-organ damage due to MM: raised Ca2+ ⇢ > 11 mg/dl or > 1 mg/dl above normal renal insufficiency ⇢ Cr > 2 mg/dl or CCl < 40 ml/min anaemia ⇢ Hb < 10 mg/dl or > 2 mg/dl below normal bone lesions ⇢ ≥ 1 osteolytic lesion on skeletal radiography, computed tomography (CT) or PET-CT ≥ 1 biomarkers of malignancy: clonal bone marrow plasma cell* ⇢ ≥ 60% involved : uninvolved serum free light chain ratio ⇢ ≥ 100 > 1 focal lesion on magnetic resonance imagining (MRI) Smoldering MM Both criteria must be met: serum monoclonal protein (IgG or IgA) ≥ 30 mg/dl, or urinary monoclonal protein ≥ 500 mg/24h and/or clonal bone marrow plasma cells 10–60% absence of myeloma-defining events or amyloidosis

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) All three criteria must be met: serum monoclonal protein < 30 mg/dl bone marrow plasma cells < 10% absence of myeloma-defining events or amyloidosis (or Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia in the case of IgM MGUS) *Clonality should be established by showing kappa/lambda light chain restriction on flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry or immunofluorescence.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Electrophoresis with immunofixation and measurement of serum immunoglobulins – positive for monoclonal M protein but < 30 g/l.  Ful blood count with differential – normal.  Serum calcium – normal.  Serum creatinine – normal.  Urinalysis and 24-hour urine collection with electrophoresis and immunofixation – identifies the isotype of monoclonal protein.  Serum-free light-chain assay – normal.  Metastatic bone survey – negative.  Management  Counselling – patients should be counselled that this a premalignant condition with low risk of progression to malignancy.  Monitoring – patients should be followed up regularly (usually annually) to detect progression with routine blood tests and serum and urine monoclonal M protein.  There is an increased risk of fracture; therefore, evaluation for osteoporosis with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan along with vitamin D and calcium levels must be done.  Prognosis  Life expectancy is thought to be shortened in patients with MGUS due to an increased risk of haematological malignancies.  Patients progress to more advanced disease at a rate of 1% per year. Clinical type Progression Non-IgM MGUS (IgG, IgA or IgD MGUS) Smouldering multiple myeloma Multiple myeloma DR. JAM

AL amyloidosis Light chain deposition disease Other lymphoproliferative disorder IgM MGUS Smoldering Waldenström macroglobulinaemia Waldenström macroglobulinaemia Non-Hodgkin lymphoma IgM multiple myeloma Light chain MGUS (LC-MGUS) Idiopathic Bence Jones proteinuria Light chain multiple myeloma AL amyloidosis Light chain deposition disease Multiple Myeloma Multiple myeloma is the malignancy of plasma cells and accumulation in the bone marrow.  Overview Key Facts  Multiple myeloma is the malignancy of plasma cells and accumulation in the bone marrow.  Characterised by the secretion of monoclonal immunoglobulins (Ig) in the blood or urine and associated tissue/end organ damage.  Presentation is a spectrum from asymptomatic and incidental findings to presentation with renal failure.  The condition is usually diagnosed by series of blood tests, serum electrophoresis and imaging.  The condition is incurable, but can be managed with pharmacological and surgical options.  Survival varies greatly and can range from a few weeks from diagnosis to more than 20 years. Epidemiology  Multiple myeloma accounts for 1% of all malignancies; 10% of haematological malignancies.  Incidence: 4 per 100 000 per year.  IgG and IgA myeloma are most common; IgM/IgE myeloma is rare.  Usually presents in patients over 65 years of age.  Multiple myeloma is more common in men of Afro–Caribbean origin.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 Aetiology  Aetiology is unknown.  Incidence associated with exposure to radiation, and genetics.  The male sex is a risk factor, as well as black ethnicity.  There may be genetic link (increased risk if a first-degree relative has had multiple myeloma). Pathophysiology  Multiple myeloma is the clonal proliferation and accumulation of plasma cells in the bone marrow.  Myeloma plasma cell is a post-germinal centre plasma B-cell that have exhibited immunoglobulin class and antigen selection.  Myeloma plasma cells secrete monoclonal Ig or Ig light chains (paraprotein or M-protein (‘M-band’) in the serum and/or urine.  The M-protein most commonly produced by malignant plasma cells is IgG, followed by IgA.  Bence Jones proteins (free monoclonal kappa (κ) or lambda (λ) light chains) may also be secreted in the urine by myeloma plasma cells.  There is impairment of normal Ig production resulting in immuneparesis / hypogammaglobulinaemia predisposing individuals to infections.  Bone disease: occur as a result of cytokines released by plasma cells that activate osteoclasts and suppress osteoblasts/or the growth of the abnormal plasma cells in the bones. Therefore, osteolytic lesions occur and hence, pathological fractures.  Kidney disease: deposition of the Bence Jones proteins in the distal tubules in the kidney and hypercalcaemia (secondary to bone destruction).  Clinical Presentation  The ‘CRAB’ acronym may be used to remember the main signs and symptoms: (hyper)-calcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, and bone pains.  Patients may be asymptomatic detected on routine testing.  Symptomatic patients may present with:  bone pain (common and usually back pain), pathological fracture  anaemia  fatigue  recurrent infections  hypercalcaemia  renal impairment.  Differential Diagnosis  Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS): non-malignant plasma cells and absence of tissue/end organ damage.  Solitary plasmacytoma.  Amyloidosis.  Heavy chain disease. Pharmacological:  Analgesia: avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) (due to renal impairment).  Conventional therapy agents (chemotherapy/nonchemotherapy), eg thalidomide, bortezomib.  Corticosteroid.  Bisphosphonates.  Thromboprophylaxis.  Vaccination for seasonal influenza and pneumococcus.  Other Treatments  Blood transfusion may be required.  Local radiotherapy.  Stem cell transplantation (usually younger patients < 65 years with good functional status at diagnosis).  Prognosis  Multiple myeloma is an incurable disease and relapse usually occurs 2–5 years after treatment, although with modern interventions some patients survive for eight years or more.  Better prognosis in < 65 years old and fitter people, (median survival of around seven years).  Complications include:  anaemia  renal failure  amyloidosis (10%)  pathological fractures/bone pain  renal failure and infections – major causes of death. Myelodysplasias/Myelodysplastic Syndrome Myelodysplastic syndrome is a group of malignant haematopoietic disorders characterised by dysplastic changes in one or more cell lineages.  Overview Key Facts  Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is a term for a group of malignant haematopoietic disorders characterised by dysplastic changes in one or more cell lineages.  The bone marrow functions ineffectively and does not produce sufficient numbers of mature cells causing cytopenias.  There is a predisposition to developing acute myeloid leukaemia (AML).  Most cases of MDS have no known cause (primary), however, 10% is secondary which is usually caused by radiation or chemotherapy.  Clinical presentation is variable and often patients present with symptoms relating to their cytopenia – lethargy, bleeding, recurrent infections.  Cytopenias are the most common sign and MDS should be suspected in any unexplained cytopenia or macrocytosis.  The mainstay of investigation is a bone marrow aspirate and trephine which will show hypercellular marrow due to poor haematopoiesis.  Cytogenetics can be helpful – 64% of patients have chromosomal abnormalities in 5, 7 and 8.  Diagnosis is generally of exclusion of other non-MDS causes of cytopenia.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Treatment can be supportive in low-risk or older patients with comorbidities or can be more aggressive with chemotherapy in well patients, but only an allogeneic stem cell transplant will be curative.  Supportive treatment includes blood transfusion and iron chelation therapy with desferrioxamine. Lenalidomide can be used for transfusion dependence.  Some newer drugs such as azacitidine, decitabine and lonafarnib, tipifarnib and lenalidomide have shown some efficacy in slowing transformation to AML. Epidemiology  MDS generally affects the elderly with an incidence of 30 in 100 000 a year in those over 70 years – 80% of cases are diagnosed in those over 60 years old.  Under 70 the incidence is around 4 in 100 000 population/year.  Prevalence of MDS is rising – this is thought to be secondary to an ageing population and improving diagnostics.  Men and smokers are at higher risk of developing MDS. Aetiology  90% of MDS is primary, of no known cause.  10% of MDS is secondary, usually due to radiotherapy or chemotherapy.  This tends to develop around five years post-treatment.  Very rarely, occupational exposure to radiation, organic solvents or benzene has been associated with MDS.  Secondary MDS has a much poorer prognosis. Pathophysiology  The bone marrow is either hypo- or hypercellular with chaotic growth and abnormal cells proliferate and mature.  This causes peripheral cytopenias due to insufficient manufacture of healthy marrow cells, which can affect platelets, leukocytes or erythrocytes.  Both degree of affected cells and aggression of disease are very variable, from indolent to a rapid progression to AML.  Clinical Presentation  Many patients may present asymptomatically and the condition is identified on blood tests requested for another reason.  Anaemia – can range from mild to severe, generally mixed microcytic and macrocytic. Patients often present with gradually worsening symptomatic anaemia.  Neutropenia – very variable. Patients can present with recurrent or atypical infections.  Thrombocytopenia – platelets are both decreased and have abnormal function meaning patients may complain of petechiae, nosebleeds, bleeding from gums, haemoptysis, haematuria or rectal bleeding.  Constitutional symptoms – anorexia, weight loss, fever may be present and are usually a sign of more progressive disease.  Signs – are generally non-specific. Patients may have signs of bleeding and pallor and signs of anaemia such as tachycardia, DR. JAM

hypotension. Splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy are not usually features of MDS.  Risk factors – prior exposure to chemo/radiotherapy.  Differential Diagnosis  The differential is wide as MDS presents non specifically.  Differentials of anaemia include haematinic deficiency, CKD, haemolysis, bleeding.  Differentials of neutropenia include viral infection, drugs including chemotherapy and immunosuppressants.  Other causes of thrombocytopenia include drugs, haemolysis, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).  Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML).  Aplastic anaemia.  Reactive bone marrow dysplasia, eg alcohol excess, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), chemotherapy and severe systemic illness.  Myeloproliferative disorders.  Diagnosis/Investigation  MDS is a diagnosis of exclusion and all other non-MDS causes of cytopenia must be excluded first.  Full blood count – mixed anaemia, normocytic and macrocytic and other cytopenias; however you can also get neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, monocytosis.  Blood film – shows dimorphic red cells (two populations), RBCs with anisocytosis (variable sizes) and poikilocytosis (abnormal shape). Pappenheimer bodies and basophilic stippling can also be present.  Bone marrow aspirate and trephine – shows hypercellular marrow due to ineffectual haematopoiesis and the presence of blast cells.  Cytogenetics – chromosomal abnormalities in 48–64% of cases – these are most commonly found in chromosomes 5, 7 and 8.  Other investigations – a full screen is done to exclude other causes of anaemia and assess if patients are fit for treatment; this includes ferritin, B12, folate, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, chest X-ray, electrocardiogram.  Management Low-risk disease  Patients with stable, low-risk disease may not require any treatment but regular monitoring at a haematology clinic.  The risk of progression to AML in this subset is low.  Treatment is mainly supportive and focused on the correction of cytopenias (usually anaemia) if causing symptoms.  Iron overload is a common side-effect of regular transfusions and iron chelation therapy with desferrioxamine is recommended if ferritin levels exceed the recommended limit.  Erythropoietin and GCF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) can improve cytopenias and overall quality of life and are very safe. They do not, however, improve mortality.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Lenalidomide has been recommended by the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) for low-risk MDS as an option for treating transfusion-dependent anaemia where other options have not been successful. High-risk disease  The only curative treatment is allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation for large group population, although chemotherapy has been successful in small case studies.  A high number of varying forms of chemotherapy have been trialled for MDS yet their results have been poor.  If the patient is well, an aggressive approach with fludarabine phosphate, cytarabine and G-CSF (FLAG) can be used.  More commonly, the patients are older with comorbidities, so a gentler approach is preferred.  Some newer drugs such as azacitidine, decitabine and lonafarnib, tipifarnib and lenalidomide have shown some efficacy in slowing transformation to AML.  NICE recommends azacitidine for adults who cannot undertake stem cell transplantation and who have intermediate/high-risk MDS.  Prognosis  MDS is a variable disease, with the mean survival at about 1–3 years.  The risk of transformation to AML is 25–35% at 5 years.  The most common cause of death is bone marrow failure, including infection and bleeding, which usually occurs before progression to AML has happened.  Other  MDS has overlap with other haematological conditions including myeloproliferative diseases (particularly chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia), severe aplastic anaemia and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Myeloproliferative Disorders Myeloproliferative disorders are a group of disorders characterised by malignant clonal proliferation of bone marrow stem cells.  Overview Key Facts  Myeloproliferative disorders are a group of disorders characterised by malignant clonal proliferation of bone marrow stem cells.
