Epidemiology  Most commonly present in patients greater than 65 years old. Aetiology  Genetic mutations (eg JAK2 gene), Philadelphia chromosome. Pathophysiology  Clonal proliferation of a pluripotent stem cell, causing varying degrees of abnormal proliferation of RBC, WBC, and platelet progenitors in the bone marrow.  Differential Diagnosis  The presentations may overlap between the different myeloproliferative disorders.  Other causes of thrombocytosis include:  other malignancy  bleeding  infection.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Polycythaemia vera: (high haemoglobin, haematocrit, red cell count, white cell count) + extramedullary haematopoiesis.  Essential thrombocythaemia: high platelet count.  Myelofibrosis: anaemia, leukoerythroblastic film, teardrop poikilocytes + extramedullary hematopoiesis.  Chronic myeloid leukaemia: granulocytosis and thrombocytosis.  Management Non-pharmacological  Lifestyle modification: smoking cessation and weight loss if obese to reduce the risk of thromboembolic events. Pharmacological:  Cytoreductive agents (hydroxycarbamide, hydroxyurea).  Antiplatelet.  Anticoagulation.  BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor.  Tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Surgical  Haematopoietic stem cell transplant.  Prognosis  A number of factors are associated with a poor prognosis in myeloproliferative disorders, including:  age > 65 years  marked anaemia, (Hb < 100 g/l)

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  white count > 25 × 109/l  circulating blasts > 1%.  Philadelphia chromosome negative myeloproliferative disorders can spontaneously transform to acute leukaemia. Myelofibrosis:  Stem cell transplant may be curative but the procedure carries a high mortality rate.  Complications of myelofibrosis include:  bone marrow failure leading to:  haemorrhage  anaemia  infection  acute leukaemia  portal or pulmonary hypertension  heart failure  cachexia  organ failure  death.  Median survival is around five years. Neutropenia Neutrophils are produced in the bone marrow and make up an essential part of our immune system.  Overview Key Facts  Neutrophils are produced in the bone marrow and make up an essential part of our immune system.  Abnormalities of function or amount can result in lifethreatening susceptibility to infection.  The most common causes of neutropenia are infections and drug-induced.  Culprit infections include human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis, brucellosis, typhoid, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).  Culprit drugs are varied but include antithyroid, anticonvulsants, cytotoxic agents and clozapine.  Patients should have a thorough evaluation to look for potential causative infections.  Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency and should be treated promptly with intravenous (IV) antibiotics.  G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) can boost neutrophil counts and can be used prophylactically during chemotherapy to prevent infections.  Febrile neutropenia has significant mortality. The highest rates of mortality (18%) are associated with Gram-negative bacteria. DR. JAM

Epidemiology  Neutropenia is commonly thought of as being caused by chemotherapy regimes as an expected side-effect.  However, sometimes neutropenia is an unexpected finding, and thoughtful consideration must be applied to ascertain the cause.  The incidence is dependent on the cause – infection being the most common, followed by drug-induced (including chemotherapy), with an incidence of 1.6–9.2 cases per million. Aetiology  The most common causes of neutropenia in order are infections and drug-induced; however, it is important to consider all aetiologies.  In children under two years, the most common cause is primary autoimmune neutropenia. Congenital  Rare disorders which interfere with neutrophil production include Kostmann syndrome, X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, Shwachman–Diamond syndrome.  Ethnic variation, which is more common in patients of African descent, is benign, but useful to identify.  Cyclical neutropenia occurs rarely in children, whereby they get fever, lethargy, anorexia and mucosal ulceration. Acquired  Decreased/ineffective neutrophil production:  malignant bone marrow infiltration  aplastic anaemia  vitamin B12/folate deficiency  chemotherapy, radiotherapy  drugs including phenytoin, alcohol, chloramphenicol  infections, eg EBV, hepatitis B and C, HIV, CMV, typhoid fever.  High neutrophil turnover:  Felty syndrome  hypersplenism  acute bacterial infections  malaria.  Other mixed/unknown cause:  measles  viral infection  drug-induced – NSAIDS, antibiotics, anticonvulsants, diuretics, diabetic medication and antidepressants  autoimmune neutropenia – most common in children < 2 years. Classification  Mild 1–1.5 × 109/l.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Moderate 0.5–0.99 × 109/l.  Severe 0.2–0.5 × 109/l.  Very severe < 0.2 × 109/l. Pathophysiology  Neutrophils are produced in the bone marrow and make up an essential part of our immune system.  Abnormalities of function or amount can result in lifethreatening susceptibility to infection.  With low functioning levels, defined as < 1.0 × 109/l, endogenous bacterial infection, as well as fungal infection, is more common.  Clinical Presentation  Neutropenia can be an incidental finding in a well patient.  However, it is most commonly diagnosed in patients who present with recurrent bacterial infections.  Symptoms include fever, malaise, infection or mouth ulcers.  Febrile neutropenia, defined as two temperatures > 38.5 °C and neutrophils > 0.5 × 109/l, can present in well patients to those in septic shock.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  sepsis  typhoid fever  brucellosis  viral infections – HIV, hepatitis, EBV, influenza  drug-induced – clozapine, antithyroid drugs, sulfasalazine  chemotherapy/radiotherapy  haematological malignancies – leukaemia, lymphoma, aplastic anaemia  B12/folate deficiency  alcohol excess  inflammatory disorders – SLE, RA.  Diagnosis/Investigation  It is useful to ascertain if the patient belongs to a high-risk group – active cancer, recent cytotoxic medications, on immunosuppressants or have any other immunosuppressive disease such as HIV.  Given infection is a common cause for neutropenia itself, patients should have a thorough evaluation to look for potential causative infections.  Blood cultures are crucial if the patient is septic.  Other investigations may include chest X-ray, lumbar puncture, CT thorax/abdomen/pelvis, antibody serology for brucellosis, viral screen to include hepatitis, HIV, CMV, EBV.  Other diagnostic tests – blood film and a bone marrow aspirate/biopsy if bone marrow infiltration is considered. DR. JAM

Sometimes, lymph node biopsy or flow cytometry can be required.  Cessation of possible culprit drugs and monitoring can identify the cause – usually, this will return to normal within 1–3 weeks.  Nutritional screens including B12, folate, copper can be considered.  Anti-neutrophil antibodies (ANAs) can be tested if an autoimmune cause is likely.  Management  Febrile neutropenia should be treated as a medical emergency and treated immediately with broad-spectrum antibiotics while awaiting speciality advice if required.  Severe neutropenia (< 0.2 × 109/l) requires urgent inpatient management.  Withdraw potential drug causes. Neutropenia should resolve within a few weeks.  Antibiotic prophylaxis is generally recommended until neutrophil count recovered.  Addition of G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) can be used to increase neutrophil counts, although it does not have a proven mortality benefit.  Treatment of potential causative infections is crucial.  Malignancies can be managed with chemotherapy and bone marrow transplant in some cases.  Prognosis  Febrile neutropenia has a significant mortality. Prompt use of IV antibiotics has reduced the need for ICU to only 5% of cases in the UK.  Mortality can be up to 11% in haematological malignancies.  The highest rates of mortality (18%) are associated with Gramnegative bacteria. Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a haematological malignancy that may arise from the B cells (85%), T cells or natural killer cells.  Overview Key Facts  Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) is a haematological malignancy that may arise from the B cells (85%), T cells or natural killer cells.  The condition is differentiated from Hodgkin’s lymphoma due to the absence of Reed–Sternberg cells at biopsy.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is five times more common than Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  Incidence increases with age; the median age at presentation is above 50.  Aetiology is not clearly understood; however, there are numerous associations including genetics, certain infections such as Epstein–Barr virus, immunodeficiency and chemical exposure.  The most common symptom of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is asymmetric painless lymphadenopathy.  Other systemic symptoms may include night sweats, fever and weight loss.  Patients may also present with symptoms of anaemia, organomegaly, oropharyngeal, central nervous system (CNS) skin involvement, or infection due to cytopenia.  There are four stages of the disease, classified based on the Ann Arbor clinical staging of lymphomas.  Patients with signs or symptoms suggestive of NHL should be referred under the 2-week wait rule (adults) or consider assessment within 48 hours in children and young people.  Diagnosis is confirmed by lymph node biopsy (excisional/core needle biopsy) – Reed–Sternberg cells are absent.  Treatment is chemotherapy +/- radiotherapy. Epidemiology  There are 13 000 new diagnoses of NHL annually in the United Kingdom.  NHL is five times more common than Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  Can affect all age groups but incidence increases with age – median age at presentation is above 50.  Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common type of lymphoma. Aetiology  The exact cause is unknown.  Genetic factors may play a role, hence family history is relevant.  Increased risk is associated with:  viral and bacterial infection, eg Epstein–Barr virus, H. pylori  autoimmune disorders  chronic inflammation  primary or secondary immunodeficiency  exposure to chemicals. Pathophysiology  Genetic mutations occurring at any stage of lymphoid cell development resulting in heterogenous clonal lymphoid tumours.  85% arise from the B lymphocytes, the remainder arise from T lymphocytes and natural killer cells.  Characterised by an irregular pattern of spread.  Extra nodal disease is common. DR. JAM

 Clinical Presentation  There is a spectrum of presentation, and may vary depending on severity and type of lymphoma.  Superficial lymphadenopathy: the most common symptom is asymmetric enlarged painless peripheral lymph nodes.  Associated systemic symptoms (B-symptoms):  persistent fever  unexplained splenomegaly  night sweats  shortness of breath  weight loss.  Oropharyngeal involvement affecting the oropharyngeal lymphoid structures present as sore throat or noisy/abnormal/obstructed breathing.  Cytopenia secondary to the involvement of the bone marrow may present with anaemia related symptoms or infections.  Abdominal organs involvement in advanced disease: hepato/splenomegaly and related symptoms or with acute abdomen symptoms. This is the second most common extra-nodal site affected after the bone marrow.  CNS involvement.  Skin involvement presenting as dry patches/scaly with associated pruritus.  Lymphocytosis +/- physical symptoms (asymptomatic).  Differential Diagnosis  Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  Acute lymphocytic leukaemia.  Other leukaemias.  Infectious mononucleosis.  Hepatitis – especially Hepatitis C.  Cytomegalovirus.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Detailed history and examination.  Diagnosis can be made by lymph node biopsy (excisional/core needle biopsy).  Bone marrow analysis – required for confirmation.  Staging tests: Imaging ultrasound/positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) scan/chest X-ray.  Blood tests: full blood count, white cell count, liver function tests, urea and electrolytes, lactate dehydrogenase.  Lumbar puncture may be required in high-grade cases.  Tests to identify possible underlying triggers may include: testing for:  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)  Hepatitis B  Hepatitis C

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1)  H. pylori serology.  Classification The World Health Organisation (WHO) Classification of NHL includes:  B-cell neoplasms:  high-grade:  diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (most common NHL)  mediastinal large B cell  primary central nervous system lymphoma  primary effusion lymphoma  Burkitt's lymphoma  mantle cell lymphoma.  low-grade:  follicular lymphoma (around 25% of all cases)  mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma  Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia.  T-cell neoplasms:  high-grade:  enteropathy-type T-cell lymphoma  peripheral T-cell lymphoma  subcutaneous paniculitis-like  systemic anaplastic  angio-immunoblastic.  low-grade:  mycosis fungoides  cutaneous T cell lymphoma Ann Arbor Clinical Staging of Lymphomas  Stage I: One involved lymph node group.  Stage II: Two nodal areas on one side of the diaphragm.  Stage III: Lymph nodes on both sides of the diaphragm.  Stage IV: Involvement of extra nodal tissues such as liver or bone marrow.  Management  Treatment is based on the histological subtype and severity of symptoms at presentation.  Prevention and monitoring for neutropenic sepsis also forms an important part of treatment – ie antibody prophylaxis in patients with severe neutropenia. Non-pharmacological  In low-grade NHL in patients who are asymptomatic, a watchand-wait approach may be used. DR. JAM

 To reduce risk of overwhelming bacterial infection, patients with NHL should be vaccinated against Meningococcus group C and Haemophilus influenzae group B. Pharmacological:  Chemotherapy used on its own or in combination with radiotherapy or with biological agents is the mainstay of treatment for most forms of symptomatic NHL.  Chemotherapy regimes may include rituximab with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone (RCHOP) or fudarabine with cyclophosphamide and rituximab (FCR).  For primary CNS lymphoma, high-dose methotrexate plus dexamethasone.  Stem cell transplantation may be used in some forms of NHL alongside chemotherapy as first-line treatment. Low > 94% 1–2 Low–Intermediate 79% 3–5 Intermediate–High 53% Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is a rare type of acquired haemolysis caused by an intrinsic red cell abnormality.  Overview Key Facts  Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is a rare type of acquired haemolysis caused by an intrinsic red cell abnormality.  There is a lack of complement regulatory glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchored proteins (CD55 and CD59) due to a haematopoietic stem cell fault of the PIGA gene, on the X chromosome.  It is a rare disease that can arise at any age and can be lifethreatening.  Haemolysis releases haemoglobin, which is filtered into urine producing haemoglobinuria, a classic sign of PNH.  The clinical triad of PNH is haemolytic anaemia, pancytopenia and large vessel thromboses.  Aplastic anaemia is a risk factor for developing PNH, especially in young patients.  The gold standard for diagnosis is flow cytometry or fluorescent aerolysin.  The first-line treatment is eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody directed against complement protein C5, which is usually required lifelong.  Thrombosis should be anticoagulated.  Stem cell transplant is curative and should be considered in young patients with severe disease, but it comes with high risks such as infection, graft versus host and death.  Prognosis is not well known, but most studies state a median of 10–15 years survival post diagnosis; however, some patients can live for decades with minor symptoms. Epidemiology  PNH is rare, with an incidence of 1–1.5 per million of the population.  PNH can arise at any age but is more common in young adults with a median age of diagnosis 35–40 years.  Generally, it is more severe in children and teenagers, often presenting with aplastic anaemia.  It is closely related to aplastic anaemia, with 30% of PNH arising from aplastic anaemia.  The severity is dependent on the proportion of red cells which are derived from the faulty stem cell. Aetiology  PNH is caused by a spontaneous genetic mutation of the PIGA gene.  The stem cell mutation of the PIGA gene on the X chromosome means stem cells pass this gene on to all of their mature cells.  This means there is a lack of complement regulatory proteins CD55 and CD59 (GPI-anchored proteins) on these abnormal stem cells.  These proteins protect the cell from destruction, are involved in clotting and others are involved in fighting infection.  The majority of the symptoms of PNH (abnormal clotting, haemolysis, infection) result from this protein deficiency in stem cells. Pathophysiology  Erythrocytes are destroyed by our own complement system, due to an absence of GPI-anchored proteins on the surface membrane. GPI proteins are also involved in clotting and fighting infection on leukocytes.  Haemoglobin (Hb) is usually contained within erythrocytes, except in haemolysis when it is released into the circulation. Hb is then filtered by the glomeruli into the urine and produces the classic symptom of haemoglobinuria.  The pathophysiology of thrombosis remains less clear.  Clinical Presentation  These three features are pathognomonic of ‘classic’ PNH:  an acquired haemolytic anaemia due to the haemolytic action of complement  multiorgan large vessel thromboses – usually venous  a mild-to-severe pancytopenia.  Common presentations:

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  haemoglobinuria (presenting feature in 20%) and occurs in 50% of patients, generally more noticeable in the morning  Budd–Chiari syndrome – hepatic venous thrombosis – occurs in 10%  thrombosis – usually venous, eg DVT, cerebral sinus or occasionally arterial  aplastic anaemia – occurs in approximately 20%  fatigue  shortness of breath  recurrent infections  bleeding easily which can be difficult to stop  anaemia (> 90% at presentation) with signs of haemolysis  abdominal pain due to smooth muscle dystonia  erectile dysfunction  dysphasia  dyspnoea.  Uncommon symptoms and signs:  bleeding and neurological signs.  Risk factors:  aplastic anaemia – 70% of patients who have had aplastic anaemia have a copy of PNH cells, generally small and indolent; growth of these, enough to cause symptoms, occurs in 15–30% of aplastic anaemia patients  marrow hypoplasia is a feature of PNH and some may proceed to bone marrow failure  myelodysplasia.  Differential Diagnosis  Paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria – haemoglobinuria caused by cold exposure, generally in children.  Autoimmune warm haemolytic anaemia – Coombs test is positive.  Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia – blood films shows schistocytes.  Myoglobinuria – a sign of rhabdomyolysis.  Abdominal thrombosis – due to other causes, eg infection, ischaemia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Urine dip – shows blood but microscopy will not show red cells – haemoglobinuria.  Urine microscopy stained for iron (haemosiderinuria) caused by haemolysis.  Full blood count (FBC) may show anaemia and pancytopenia with features of haemolysis (raised LDH, raised reticulocytes, raised bilirubin, low haptoglobin).  D-dimer is likely to be high indicating thrombosis.  Bone marrow will show hyperplastic marrow during haemolysis or hypoplastic during aplastic phase.  Direct Coombs will be negative.  Imaging can be helpful in demonstrating thrombosis, eg MRI for sagittal vein thrombosis or liver ultrasound scan (USS).  Specific tests include flow cytometry to detect CD59 and CD55 (DAF) – absence is diagnostic – as well as fluorescent aerolysin which is the most sensitive and accurate test. These are the gold standard for diagnosis of PNH.  Management  Treatment of PNH is aimed at the three major diagnostic criteria. It depends what is the most prominent aspect at the time of diagnosis. Treatment also depends on the severity of the symptoms:  haemolysis  thrombophilia  marrow hypofunction. Haemolytic anaemia  First-line treatment is eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody directed against complement protein C5. This inhibits haemolysis and prevents nitric oxide deprivation, leading to a rise in Hb and generally helping with other symptoms such as fatigue.  This is a treatment that is usually required lifelong.  The treatment is expensive, so there are strict criteria for its use – haemolysis, severe anaemia, renal impairments and thrombosis should all be present.  Steroids can sometimes be used for an acute attack but longterm steroids are not recommended.  Endogenous erythropoietin (EPO) has been found to be of benefit in some patients, usually in patients with concurrent aplastic anaemia.  Supportive treatments such as transfusions are recommended if Hb falls below 80 g/l.  Iron supplementation is often required as PNH patients lose up to 20 times more iron per day than a healthy person. Thrombosis  Low molecular weight heparin, warfarin or newer agents can be used for anticoagulation in PNH as long as the platelet count is above 50 for proven thrombus – it is still recommended that this is continued lifelong.  If there is cerebral thrombosis, dexamethasone or mannitol can be used to lower intracranial pressure.  Medications that increase the risk of thrombosis, eg contraceptive pill, should be avoided. Marrow hypofunction  This is treated with ciclosporin and antithymocyte globulin first line.  Allogenic bone marrow transplantation (BMT) is the only cure and may be appropriate for those patients who do not respond to first-line treatment or those with severe disease. It is usually reserved for young patients with severe marrow failure prominent disease.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  BMT comes with a high risk of infection, graft versus host disease, chronic morbidity and death.  Prognosis  PNH is a rare disease and therefore the prognosis is not entirely known.  Most studies demonstrate a median post-diagnosis survival of 10–15 years.  Some patients, however, can live for decades with minor symptoms.  Thromboembolism is the most common cause of death in PNH patients.  Some patients have subclinical PNH, which does not typically progressive to clinical PNH. These patients do not need specific treatment. Polycythaemia Vera Polycythaemia vera is characterised by erythrocytosis, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis and splenomegaly.  Overview Key Facts  Polycythaemia vera (PV) is characterised by erythrocytosis, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis and splenomegaly.  Median age of diagnosis is 61 years.  Associated with JAK2 mutation in the majority of cases.  JAK2 V617F mutation activates biochemical pathways that are usually involved in the signalling of erythropoietin (EPO) receptors leading to unregulated red blood cell production.  Associated with increased risk of thrombosis, haemorrhage, transformation to acute leukaemia or myelofibrosis.  Diagnosis requires increased haemoglobin or haematocrit along with the presence of JAK2 mutation and bone marrow biopsy.  Treatment targeted at phlebotomy, low-dose aspirin and cytoreductive therapy.  Survival is shorter with the leading cause of death attributed to complications of cardiovascular disease. Epidemiology  More common in older patients, with the median age of diagnosis estimated to be 61 years of age.  Very rare in patients under the age of 40 years, with an estimated 10% of cases thought to be below this age.  Gender distribution approximately equal but venous thrombotic events more common in women and arterial thrombotic events more common in men.  Estimated to affect 30–35 people per 100 000. DR. JAM

Aetiology  JAK2 V617F mutation implicated in almost all cases of PV which leads to clonal haematopoiesis.  Risk factors for PV include age > 40 years, Budd–Chiari syndrome and family history.  Several other less common mutations have also been identified including TET2 and ASXL1.  Familial cases of PV can occur but are sporadic and are likely acquired rather congenital in nature. Pathophysiology  JAK2 V617F mutation activates biochemical pathways that are usually involved in the signalling of EPO receptors.  This causes expansion of red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets which are thought to contribute to the increased viscosity of blood as well as producing prothrombotic factors that contribute to thrombosis.  Clinical Presentation  Increase blood viscosity:  hypertension, headache  erythromelalgia ⇢ burning cyanosis in hands/feet  transient visual disturbances.  Features of thrombosis – stroke, MI, PE, DVT.  Bleeding.  ⇡ RBC turnover ⇢ gouty arthritis.  Aquagenic pruritus ⇢ itching worse with water (warm).  Facial plethora ⇢ ruddy cyanosis.  Splenomegaly. MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  secondary polycythaemia (due to hypoxia, testosterone excess or elevated erythropoietin level)  essential thrombocythaemia  chronic myelogenous leukaemia  congenital polycythaemia.  Diagnosis/Investigation WHO diagnostic criteria  Men:  Hb > 165 g/l  Hct > 49%.  Women:  Hb > 160 g/l  Hct > 48%.  Bone marrow biopsy ⇢ hypercellularity for age with trilineage growth.  JAK2 mutation or decrease EPO levels.  White blood cells – elevated.  Platelets – elevated.  Mean corpuscular volume – low.  Liver function tests – may be elevated if co-existing Budd– Chiari syndrome.  Management  Low-dose aspirin in all patients.  PV and platelet count > 1 million ⇢ evaluate for acquired von Willebrand syndrome (aVWS) ⇢ avoid aspirin.  Maintenance of hematocrit <45%.  Phlebotomy ⇢ absolute iron deficiency ⇢ do not give iron supplementation.  Management of cardiovascular risk factors.  Low-risk PV ⇢ ≤ 60 years and no history of thrombosis ⇢ phlebotomy:  indications of cytoreductive therapy in low-risk patients:  uncontrolled PV-associated symptoms  progressive raised leukocyte or platelet counts  symptomatic or progressive splenomegaly  poor tolerance of phlebotomy.  High-risk PV ⇢ all others that are not low-risk ⇢ phlebotomy + cytoreductive therapy  hydroxyurea first-line  alternative ⇢ INF, busulfan.  < 40 years or pregnant ⇢ INF.  Ruxolitinib is a JAK1/2 inhibitor ⇢ used if severe pruritus, symptomatic splenomegaly, or symptoms of post-PV myelofibrosis that failed to respond adequately to first-line therapies.  Prognosis  Most common causes of death in patients include cardiovascular complications and transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia.  Median survival in untreated symptomatic patients is 18 months from the time of diagnosis.  Median survival in patients undergoing regular treatment is 14– 18 years from the time of diagnosis.  Other  Rapid review: polycythaemia vera Genetics Normally EPO activates JAK2 tyrosine kinase ⇢ differentiates late myeloid cells into erythrocytes JAK2 mutation ⇢ constitutively active JAK2 gene Clinical features ⇡ Blood viscosity: hypertension erythromelalgia ⇢ burning cyanosis in hands/feet

DR. JAM

 Stem cell transplantation is the definitive cure, this is reserved for people aged under 17 with severe disease unresponsive to medical therapy.  Prognosis is dependent on disease severity, the condition is associated with numerous acute and chronic medical conditions.  Life expectancy for patients with the condition has improved over the last decades due to improvements in management of complications in childhood, but is significantly reduced compared to the general population. Epidemiology  Sickle cell disease is common and occurs in 1 in 2 000 births in England.  Screening is offered to all newborns and pregnancy women in the UK.  The highest incidence is in Black African and Black Caribbean people, and also people who live in or have migrated from areas where malaria is prevalent (as the carrier state is protective against malaria). Aetiology  Sickle cell crises in affected individuals can be triggered by:  infection  stress  trauma  pregnancy  surgery  cold weather  hypoxia  dehydration  alcohol  acidosis. Pathophysiology  Polymorphism resulting in glutamic acid replacing valine at ßglobin chain position 6.  The condition causes the production of abnormal production of the ß-globin chain of Hb – there are 2 a chains and 2 ß chains:  HbS polymerises when deoxygenated, causing erythrocytes/ red blood cells (RBCs) to deform.  Deformed RBCs are sickle shaped in appearance and termed ‘sickle cells’.  Sickle cells are fragile, and haemolyse easily, their morphology means they can block small vessels.  Sickled HbS (ααSS) polymerise if deoxygenated ⇢ vasoocclusion ⇢ haemolysis ⇢ ⇡ bilirubin.  Inheritance is autosomal recessive:  homozygous (HbSS, sickle cell disease) – both ß chains abnormal ⇢ produce only HbS (ααSS)  heterozygous (HbAS, sickle cell trait) – one ß chain abnormal ⇢ produce HbA (ααßß) + HbS (ααSS).  Organisms commonly associated with the condition include:

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  strep pneumonia, haemophilus, meningococcus ⇢ meningitis, UTI, osteomyelitis.  Clinical Presentation  Sickle cell trait is usually asymptomatic, but patients may be at risk of vaso-occlusive episodes if oxygen deprived. Patients may also present with haematuria.  Presentations of sickle cell disease can be varied including:  chromic haemolysis may also be asymptomatic and well tolerated (may not need treatment) except during a crisis  acute presentation of vaso-occlusive crisis due to red blood cell (RBC) morphology leading to small vessel occlusion, typically in bone marrow causing hypoxia to those tissues which results in pain, asplenia (due to encapsulated infections), aplastic crisis (due to parvovirus B19) causing sudden reduction in marrow production  sequestration crisis occurs commonly in children who have not yet undergone splenic atrophy – blood pools within the spleen leading to hepatosplenomegaly  sickle crisis temperature change, infection, stress, pregnancy → small vessels occluded by sickled cells → painful due to hypoxia of affected tissues, typically bone marrow, associated swelling of hands and feet in children  acute sickle chest syndrome – cough, chest and/or rib pain, desaturation, fever, increased respiratory rate, lung infiltrates can have small emboli and infarctions.  Differential Diagnosis  Blood films – polychromasia and macrocytosis (due to reticulocytes); may point to diagnosis:  sickle-cell anaemia – sickle cells  thalassaemia – hypochromic microcytic anaemia  microangiopathic haemolysis – schistocytes  malignancy – abnormal cells  hereditary spherocytosis/autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – spherocytes  hereditary elliptocytosis – elliptocytes  glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency – Heinz bodies, blister cells.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Patients may present with symtoms, or cases may be detected by national screening programmes (pregnant women and newborns in the UK).  Tests to aid diagnosis include:  full blood count (FBC)  reticulocyte count  blood film  specialised tests such as sickle solubility test/Hb electrophoresis – confirms diagnosis, distinguishes homozygous/heterozygous states.  Management  All patients with features of moderate to severe sickle cell crisis (eg temperature above 38 °C, no temperature but with moderate pain in children and chest symptoms) need urgent admission to hospital and managed with:  analgesia  intravenous fluid rehydration  if signs of infection: chest X-ray, midstream urine sample (MSU), antibiotics  blood transfusion if sharp fall in Hb or reticulocytes.  Patients who have mild symptoms and/or no fever may be managed at home with advice on increased fluid intake, avoiding trigger factors (eg cold/activity) and analgesia.  General measures on diagnosis Management of chronic complications needs multidisciplinary input and regular follow up.  All patients should be referred for haematologist review.  Genetic counselling; prenatal testing; parental education.  Preventative – prophylactic pneumococcal vaccine influenza vaccination annually, hepatitis B vaccine.  Prophylactic antibiotics (penicillin) lifelong.  Management of anaemia – ie folic acid supplementation.  Hydroxycarbamide may be used to prevent acute painful crises and acute chest syndrome.  Surgery  Surgery may include splenectomy for acute splenic sequestration.  Cholecystectomy for symptomatic biliary disease.  Hip replacement surgery is often required in late disease.  Stem cell transplantation is the only definitive cure and can be considered in children and young people who have had severe disease-related complications unresponsive to hydroxycarbamide.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Prognosis  Prognosis is dependent on disease severity.  The condition is associated with numerous acute as well as chronic complications:  Acute:  acute painful crisis  acute abdomen  anaemia  acute chest syndrome  infections  osteomyelitis  priapism (persistent painful erection)  renal impairment  neurological sequalae.  Chronic:  chronic pain  anaemia  epilepsy  eye damage  gallstones  pulmonary hypertension  impaired growth and cognitive impairment in children  renal disease.  Life expectancy for patients with the condition has improved over the last decades due to improvements in management of complications in childhood; up to 90% are thought to survive beyond 20 years of age and significant numbers are alive at aged 50. Subdural Haematoma Intracranial haemorrhage is a collective term for numerous conditions that occur when a blood vessel within the skull ruptures or leaks leading to accumulation of blood within intracranial spaces.  Overview Key Facts  Intracranial haemorrhage is a collective term for numerous conditions that occur when a blood vessel within the skull ruptures or leaks leading to accumulation of blood within intracranial spaces.  Intracranial haemorrhage can be classed by location (intra-axial or extra-axial haemorrhage) or underlying cause (trauma, vascular malformation, tumour-related haemorrhage, hypertension or cerebral venous thrombosis).  Intra-axial haemorrhage (intracerebral haemorrhage): DR. JAM

 basal ganglia haemorrhage  lobar haemorrhage  pontine haemorrhage  cerebellar haemorrhage.  Extra-axial haemorrhage:  extradural haemorrhage (EDH)  intralaminar dural haemorrhage  subdural haemorrhage (SDH)  subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH)  intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH)  subpial haemorrhage.  A subdural haematoma is a form of intracranial haemorrhage that leads to the formation of a clot over the surface of the brain in the subdural space.  The collection of blood lies between the dura and the arachnoid mater.  It usually occurs due to rupture of the bridging veins from shearing forces or laceration of the brain.  Both acute and chronic subdural haematomas present most commonly after mild-to-moderate head injury.  Spontaneous subdural haematoma is rare but can be caused by conditions such as clotting disorders, arteriovenous malformations and aneurysms.  Subdural haematomas are more likely to occur in older patients or patients with a significant alcohol history, as they are more likely to experience cerebral atrophy – there is a larger distance for bridging veins to cover, so they are at greater risk of being damaged.  The condition is also associated with a higher incidence in babies and very young children, adults with a history of alcoholism and patients on anticoagulation therapy.  Acute subdural haematoma:  arises in approximately one-third of patients with a severe head injury  patients may initially have a lucid period with subsequent deterioration as the haematoma continues to form.  Chronic subdural haematoma:  often due to traumatic brain injury that may be so mild that the patient may not recall the incident  patients present around 2–3 weeks after this incident  mild headache, confusion and coma are the symptoms of chronic subdural haematoma, with progressively worsening symptoms  less often, there may be a gradual onset of focal neurological signs  patients are often older and may also have a history of alcoholism or be on anticoagulation  these patients may present acutely if there is a large rebleed into a pre-existing subdural haematoma.  Treatment depends on the size of the haematoma, the chronicity and clinical signs/focal neurology.

 Subdural haematomas are more likely to occur in older patients or patients with a significant alcohol history, as they are more likely to experience cerebral atrophy – there is a larger distance for bridging veins to cover, so they are at greater risk of being damaged.  The condition is also associated with a higher incidence in babies and very young children, adults with a history of alcoholism and patients on anticoagulation therapy. Pathophysiology  The meninges are connective tissue membranes that line the skull and vertebral canal, covering the brain and spinal cord; they consist of three layers:  dura mater – outer layer  arachnoid mater – middle layer  pia mater – inner layer.  Epidural space describes the potential space between the vertebral column and the dura mater.  Subdural space describes the space between the dura and the arachnoid mater.  Subarachnoid space describes the space between the arachnoid and the pia mater.  A subdural haematoma describes the collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid mater.  It usually occurs due to rupture of the bridging veins from shearing forces or laceration of the brain.  This is often caused by trauma.  Spontaneous subdural haematoma is rarer but can be caused by conditions such as clotting disorders, arteriovenous malformations and aneurysms. Types of brain haemorrhage:  Clinical Presentation  Acute subdural haematoma:  presents most commonly after mild-to-moderate head injury

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  more likely to occur in older patients or patients with a significant alcohol history, as they are more likely to experience cerebral atrophy  subdural haematoma arises in approximately one-third of patients with a severe head injury  the condition is also more commonly found in babies, adults with a history of alcoholism and patients on anticoagulation therapy  patients may initially have a lucid period with subsequent deterioration as the haematoma continues to form  focal neurology may be present, depending on the area of the brain compressed.  Chronic subdural haematoma:  often due to traumatic brain injury that may be so mild that the patient may not recall the incident  patients present around 2–3 weeks after the incident  mild headache, confusion and coma are the symptoms of chronic subdural haematoma, with progressively worsening symptoms  less often, there may be a gradual onset of focal neurological signs  patients are often older and may also have a history of alcoholism or be on anticoagulation  these patients may present acutely if there is a large rebleed into a pre-existing subdural haematoma.  Patients with subdural haematoma may also present with signs of raised intracranial pressure.  Raised intracranial pressure (ICP)  Normal ICP = 10 mmHg; abnormally raised ICP > 20 mmHg.  A haematoma within the constant volume of the skull will cause extrusion of an equal volume of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and venous blood initially (compensation) – ICP is maintained.  When the compensatory mechanisms reach their limit, the ICP will increase exponentially as the haematoma increases in volume.  Causes of raised ICP include:  haematoma  focal oedema – secondary to contusion or haematoma  diffuse cerebral oedema – secondary to ischaemia  obstruction to CSF flow (rarely seen in acute trauma)  obstruction to venous outflow (can occur as a result of a tight cervical collar).  The effects of raised ICP include:  temporal uncal herniation – cranial nerve III compression and pupil dilation  motor weakness (corticospinal tract compression)  compression of cardiorespiratory control centres if the brainstem herniates through the foramen magnum (coning)  Cushing’s response – respiratory rate (RR) decreases, heart rate (HR) decreases, systolic BP increases, pulse pressure increases. DR. JAM

 Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses for intracranial haemorrhage are as follows:  stroke  dementia  prion disease  subdural empyema  epilepsy of the temporal lobe  frontal lobe syndrome  encephalopathy  hydrocephalus  other forms of traumatic brain injury.  Diagnosis/Investigation  A clinician with safeguarding training should be involved in the initial assessment of patients with head injuries and should follow local guidelines as appropriate.  ABCDE approach should be undertaken as soon as possible.  Basic observations (O2 saturations, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and temperature) will help to assess the stability of the patient and the likelihood of injuries.  Establishing a patient's Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is crucial in identifying the likelihood and severity of head injuries – GCS > 12 is associated with earlier recovery and minimal complications long term. MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Patients may have other associated injuries – important to assess all systems.  ECG if there are suspected cardiac events that may have led to the development of head injury.  Arterial and venous blood gas (ABG/VBG) will help in assessing the patient – look for acidosis (inadequate ventilation), electrolyte imbalances, etc.  Baseline blood tests: full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&Es), liver function tests (LFTs), clotting, group + save/cross-match, troponin (if suspecting cardiac events leading to fall or head injury), etc.  C-spine investigation – X-ray or computed tomography (CT) of cervical spine within < 1 hour if C-spine thought to be at risk or patient has GCS < 13. CT head criteria  Adults who have sustained a head injury should receive a CT head scan within < 1 hour if they have any of the following risk factors:  GCS < 13 on initial assessment in Emergency Department (ED)  GCS < 15 at 2 hours after initial assessment in ED  suspected open or depressed skull fracture  any sign of basal skull fracture:  haemotympanum – bleeding in the middle ear cavity with an intact tympanic membrane  ‘panda eyes’ sign – bruising around both eyes  CSF leak from ear or nose  Battle's sign – bruising over the mastoid process posterior to the ear.  focal neurological deficit  post-traumatic seizure  > 1 episode of vomiting.  For children who have sustained a head injury – a CT head scan should be done within 1 hour if more than one of these risk factors are present:  loss of consciousness lasting > 5 minutes  abnormal drowsiness  three or more episodes of vomiting  dangerous mechanism of injury (high-speed road traffic accident, fall from a height of >3 metres, other high-speed injuries)  amnesia (antegrade or retrograde) for > 5 minutes  children < 1 year with bruising, swelling, lacerations > 5 cm on the head.  If 0–1 of these risk factors are present, children should be observed for a minimum of four hours.  Adults and children without sufficient risk factors and who are having anticoagulant treatment – perform CT within 8 hours. Imaging For Subdural Haematoma  CT scan of the head is good for detecting acute subdural haematoma (SDH).  Subacute SDH may be more difficult to detect with plain CT, therefore MRI or CT with contrast is preferred.  Chronic SDH is usually detectable on non-contrast CT. CT scan showing the characteristic halfmoon/slither shape of a subdural haematoma:  Management  Management depends on:  the size of the haematoma  presence of focal neurology  clinical signs  chronicity of the haematoma.  Patients with small haematomas with no associated symptomatology may be treated conservatively – observation and serial CT monitoring.  Any clotting defects should be corrected.  Generally, most haematomas > 5 cm require surgical excavation. Surgical treatment  Burr hole drainage.  Craniotomy.  Repeat surgery is required in 25% of cases.  General management of head injuries  Ensure patients airway, breathing and circulation are stable and being monitored.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Establish GCS early on – patients with GCS ≤ 8 require early involvement from the anaesthetics and critical care teams (may require intubation).  Establish the need for C-spine imaging and CT head with regards to the risk factors outlined above.  Adequate analgesia and pain management should be carried out (eg splinting fractured limbs and catheterising a full bladder) – pain can raise ICP.  Discuss patients with neurosurgery if there are:  new or abnormal changes seen on imaging  persisting coma (GCS ≤ 8) after initial resuscitation  unexplained confusion lasting > 4 hours  deterioration in GCS after admission  progressive focal neurological signs  seizure without full recovery  penetrating injuries  CSF leak.  Neurological observations should be carried out for GCS, pupil size or reactivity or limb movements. Major head injuries  The aim of management is to prevent secondary cerebral damage.  Adequate ventilation needs to be maintained with PaO2 >13 kPa and PaCO2 4–5 kPa:  intubation may be required in patients with absent gag reflex, PaO2 <9 or PaCO2 >5.3  rule out potential pneumothoraces before considering ventilation.  Maintain adequate mean arterial pressure (MAP).  Mannitol: 0.5–1g/kg over 10–30 minutes to help reduce ICP.  Metabolic: correct any imbalances which may contribute to impaired consciousness, eg hypoglycaemia.  Prognosis  The prognosis of subarachnoid haematoma is variable and depends on the extent of the bleed as well as the development of complications.  Complications of subdural haematoma include:  raised intracranial pressure  cerebral oedema  seizures  permanent neurological or cognitive deficit including coma and persistent vegetative state  recurrence  death due to cerebellar herniation.  Mortality rates for acute subdural haematoma can be up to 50% if complicated by parenchymal brain injury.  Even uncomplicated cases are associated with mortality rates of up to 20%. Thalassaemias The thalassaemias are a group of genetic diseases of decreased haemoglobin synthesis due to decreased or absent synthesis of the alpha or alpha/beta globin chain which is normally found in haemoglobin molecules.  Overview Key Facts  The thalassaemias are a group of genetic diseases of decreased haemoglobin (Hb) synthesis due to decreased or absent synthesis of the alpha or alpha/beta globin chain which is normally found in haemoglobin molecules.  This may subsequently cause a haemolytic anaemia.  Thalassaemia may be classified by the polypeptide chain affected, ie α-thalassaemia or β-thalassaemia.  The condition affects 4 in 100 000 births annually and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.  Over 300 mutations giving rise to the condition have been identified.  Phenotypes vary from asymptomatic individuals (carriers – known as thalassaemia trait) to severe anaemia or even death in utero.  Symptom of severe haemolytic anaemia including pallor and splenomegaly may be present at birth in severe cases.  Treatment depends on severity and may include transfusion, iron chelation or splenectomy.  Stem cell transplantation is curative but is usually only effective in younger patients. Epidemiology  The condition is more common in Mediterranean, Middle East and Far East areas.  Alpha thalassaemia is prevalent in India, Southeast Asia and Africa.  Beta thalassaemia is prevalent in China, Southeast Asia, the Middle east and the Mediterranean.  There is an equal sex distribution as the condition is not related to sex chromosomes. Aetiology  Under production of one of the globin chains causes the remaining chains to precipitate, damaging the red blood cell (RBC) membranes, cellular osmotic imbalance -> haemolysis while still within the marrow.  Alpha thalassaemia – caused by gene deletions on chromosome 16:

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  pathophysiology – autosomal recessive gene deletion ⇢ ineffective haematopoiesis ⇢ unstable RBCs ⇢ haemolysis ⇢ anaemia  α+ haplotype (αα/-α, -α/-α) - low risk; ⇣ mean cell volume (MCV)/mean cell haemoglobin (MCH); Africa/India  α0 haplotype (αα/--) - high risk; ⇣ MCV/MCH; South East Asian/east Med  HbH disease (-α/--) - thalassaemia intermedia (periodic haemolysis, but not intensive)  Hb Barts hydrops (--/--) - stillbirth.  Beta thalassaemia – caused by point mutations in beta-globin genes (chromosome 11):  pathophysiology – autosomal recessive gene mutations ⇢ RBC maturation interfered ⇢ ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis ⇢ anaemia  ß-thalassaemia trait (ß/ß0, ß/ß+) - microcytic anaemia; only one ß globin mutated  ß-thalassaemia intermedia (ß0/ß+, ß+/ß+) - occasional transfusions eg stress, pregnancy  ß-thalassaemia major (ß0/ß0) - severe microcytic, hypochromic → splenomegaly. Pathophysiology  Under-production of one of the globin chains causes the remaining chains to precipitate, damaging the red blood cell (RBC) membranes, leading to cellular osmotic imbalance and haemolysis while still within the bone marrow.  Alpha thalassaemia:  Autosomal recessive gene deletion causing ineffective haematopoiesis and unstable RBCs leading to haemolysis and eventually anaemia  α+ haplotype (αα/-α, -α/-α) – low risk; ↓ mean cell volume (MCV)/mean cell haemoglobin (MCH); Africa/India  α0 haplotype (αα/--) – high risk; ↓ MCV/MCH; South East Asian/east Med  HbH disease (-α/--) – thalassaemia intermedia (periodic haemolysis, but not intensive)  Hb Barts hydrops (--/--) – severe homozygous alpha thalassaemia, is associated with stillbirth.  Beta thalassaemia:  autosomal recessive gene mutations interferes with RBC maturation causing ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis and eventually anaemia  β-thalassaemia trait (β/β0, β/β+) - microcytic anaemia; only one β globin mutated  β-thalassaemia intermedia (β0/β+, β+/β+) – occasional transfusions eg stress, pregnancy  β-thalassaemia major (β0/β0) - severe microcytic, hypochromic → splenomegaly. DR. JAM

 Clinical Presentation Clinical presentation is varied; the presentation and stage of presentation depends on condition severity in severe forms anaemia and splenomegaly may be present at birth.  Thalassaemia trait is often associated with being clinically asymptomatic or mild anaemia.  Alpha thalassaemia in its most severe homozygous form causes stillbirth. Signs and symptoms associated with the condition may include:  pallor Condition Serum iron Transferrin Iron deficiency ⇣ ⇡ Chronic disease ⇣ ⇣ Haemochromatosis ⇡ ⇣ Thalassaemia major ⇡ Normal Thalassaemia minor Normal Normal Pregnancy/OCP Normal ⇡  Blood films – polychromasia and macrocytosis (due to reticulocytes); may point to diagnosis:  thalassaemia – hypochromic microcytic anaemia  alpha thalassaemia – Mexican hat cells  sickle-cell anaemia – sickle cells  microangiopathic haemolysis – schistocytes  malignancy – abnormal cells  hereditary spherocytosis/autoimmune haemolytic anaemia – spherocytes  hereditary elliptocytosis – elliptocytes  glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency – Heinz bodies, blister cells. MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  jaundice  haemolytic anaemia (often progressive)  hepatosplenomegaly  frontal bossing of the skull (due to extramedullary haematopoiesis)  dysrhythmias  cardiac failure (myocardial siderosis)  endocrine presentations include:  diabetes  hypoadrenal crisis  hypocalcaemia.  Differential Diagnosis Ferritin Marrow iron Features ⇣ - Responsive to iron therapy ⇡ ++ Unresponsive to iron therapy ⇡ +/- Normal ++++ Reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin Normal ++ Normal Normal  Diagnosis/Investigation Bloods:  full blood count (microcytic anaemia, may be associated raised WCC and reduced platelets)  blood film (microcytic hypochromic picture, Mexican hat cells may be seen in alpha thalassaemia)  iron panel (serum iron and ferritin is elevated)  Hb electrophoresis for diagnosis – HbA2 greater than 3.5% is diagnostic. Imaging:  skeletal survey to check for bone deformities  chest X-ray may shos signs of cardiac failure MRI to monitor myocardial siderosis (can be caused by iron overload and subsequent accumulation within the myocardium, reduced plasticity leading to reduced LV ejection fraction).  Other tests include ECG; bone marrow examination may be required to exclude other diagnoses.  Management Management depends on the type of thalassaemia and subsequent severity of symptoms. Non-pharmacological  Patients with thalassaemia minor may not require any medical treatment.  All families should be offered genetic counselling.  Patients and their families should be given education around the condition and provided with information regarding available support avenues.  Lifestyle advice includes:  promoting fitness  healthy diet (avoiding high iron content foods); folate supplements may help even if not deficient.  Medical management may include regular (three weekly) lifelong blood transfusions in severe cases (maintain Hb > 95 g/L) – to suppress extramedullary haematopoiesis. Pharmacological:  Iron-chelation (deferiprone + ascorbic acid) – binds to iron, preventing its deposition within tissues.  Hydroxyurea – may be beneficial.  Ascorbic acid for increased iron excretion in urine.  Gene therapy is an area of interest and is being investigated as an avenue of future treatment. Surgical  Splenectomy (avoid until at least five years old to avoid infection risk).  Curative treatment is bone marrow transplant, which offers a better prognosis when carried out at a young age.  Prognosis  Prognosis is related to severity of the condition and varies greatly amongst individuls.  The prognosis for both alpha and beta thalassaemia trait is excellent.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  For severe alpha and beta thalassaemia, morbidity and mortality is generally increased although prognosis is improving. Many complications are associated with transfusion treatment and subsequent iron overload although this is now being counteracted with the use of chelation therapy.  Overall prognosis following stem cell transplant is excellent, with almost 80% being disease-free following transplant.  Complications of blood transfusions include: transfusion reactions, infection, iron overload. Iron overload may also lead to:  endocrine - increased anterior pituitary iron deposits causing hypogonadism, decreased PTH/thyroid hormones; risk of diabetes mellitus  bones - osteoporosis, bony overgrowth, short stature  heart - iron overload causing cardiac failure, and dysrhythmia  liver - chronic iron overload may lead to cirrhosis; transfusion-acquired hep B/C; hepatocellular cancer. Thrombocytopenia Thrombocytopenia is a condition characterised by a low platelet count in the blood, which can lead to an increased risk of bleeding.  Overview Key Facts  Low circulating platelet count (< 150 000/μl).  Results from a reduced production of platelets, increased clearance of platelets or sequestration of platelets in the spleen.  Common causes include drugs, haematological diseases, viral infections and pseudothrombocytopenia.  Clinical features include bleeding, petechiae, purpura and ecchymoses.  Diagnosis is made with a full blood count (FBC).  Further investigations are ordered based on the history and physical examination.  Differential diagnosis includes clotting factor deficiencies or other bleeding disorders.  Management is based on the aetiology of thrombocytopenia. Epidemiology  Varies according to the cause of thrombocytopenia.  Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) mainly affects young women. DR. JAM

Thrombophilia Thrombophilia describes a group of disorders that cause abnormality of blood coagulation, leading to an increased risk of thrombosis.  Overview Key Facts  Thrombophilia describes a group of disorders that cause abnormality of blood coagulation, leading to an increased risk of thrombosis.  Thrombophilia can be caused by inherited and acquired factors.  Patients usually present with venous thromboembolism manifestations.  Investigations such as blood tests and genetic analysis maybe required to identify the underlying cause.  Life-long anticoagulant therapy may be required for management. Epidemiology  Congenital thrombophilia affects up to 10% of the population.  Inheritable causes account for up to 50% of venous thromboembolism (VTE).

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia in Caucasians. Aetiology  Inherited: genetic mutations resulting in deficiency or qualitative defect of natural anticoagulants (Group 1) and increased procoagulant effects (Group 2):  factor V Leiden  prothrombin (factor II) gene mutation  protein C, protein S, anti-thrombin III deficiency.  Acquired:  polycythaemia  essential thrombocythaemia  hormonal therapy  lupus anticoagulant/antiphospholipid antibodies  malignancy/pregnancy/nephrotic syndrome. Coagulation cascade Pathophysiology  Deficiency of the natural anticoagulants or excess of procoagulants results in an imbalance and hypercoagulable state.  Antithrombin is the most common inherited natural anticoagulant deﬁciency.  Others include protein C (vitamin K-dependent natural anticoagulant) and protein S. Could also cause thrombocytopenia.  Clinical Presentation  The patient may be asymptomatic: commonly seen in congenital cases.  Venous thromboembolism: recurrent/untriggered or at a young age:  deep vein-thrombosis (DVT)  pulmonary embolism (PE)  hepatic portal vein thrombosis.  The patient may have a positive family history.  Recurrent miscarriage.  Unusual site of thrombosis ie porta vein/sagitall sinus thrombosis.  Thrombosis at multiple sites.  Warfarin-induced skin necrosis (protein C deficiency).  Differential Diagnosis Thrombophilia may be due to:  factor V Leiden mutation  factor C deficiency  factor S deficiency  antiphospholipid antibody syndrome  liver disease  nephrotic syndrome  malignancy  inflammatory bowel disease  heart failure.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Diagnosis/Investigation  full blood count (FBC)  peripheral blood smear  clotting studies: PT, Thrombin time, APTT, fibrinogen  APC resistance test  lupus anticoagulant  anticardiolipin antibodies  assays for Antithrombin and Proteins C and S deficiency  DNA analysis for the factor v Leiden mutation. Note: investigations should be carried out when the patient is not pregnant/on anticoagulant therapy.  Management Non-pharmacological  Minimising VTE risk – promote hydration and mobility.  Avoidance of oestrogen containing contraceptives/hormone replacement therapy.  Pre-pregnancy counselling. Pharmacological:  Anticoagulation in acute thrombosis.  Consider thromboprophylaxis – may be short term, or indefinite for example in patients with greater than 2 spontaneous VTE episodes. Surgical  Inferior vena cava filter insertion may be required in patients with recurrent thromboembolic events despite anti-coagulation.  Prognosis Prognosis is dependent on numerous factors including:  the specific thrombophilia  family history  previous history of VTE  age  immobility  obesity  pregnancy/postpartum  hormone use. Complications of thrombophilia include:  those related to VTE  those related to anticoagulation  antiphospholipid syndrome is related to miscarriage  warfarin induced-skin necrosis – rare and related to protein C deficiency. DR. JAM

Tumour Lysis Syndrome Tumour lysis syndrome is a metabolic disorder and a life-threatening complication of malignant diseases such as haematological malignancies and solid tumours.  Overview Key Facts  Tumour lysis syndrome is a metabolic disorder and a lifethreatening complication of malignant diseases such as haematological malignancies and solid tumours.  A triad of metabolic disturbances is responsible for tumour lysis syndrome, including:  hyperuricaemia  hyperkalaemia  hyperphosphataemia.  Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery or ablation procedures can also cause tumour lysis syndrome.  It is an oncological emergency and is common in adults, as well as in paediatric age groups, and it may lead to acute kidney injury, fatal arrhythmias and even death.  A massive release of intracellular ions results in electrolyte disturbances.  A complete metabolic and biochemical profile must be performed for the diagnosis of patients. Epidemiology  The incidence of tumour lysis syndrome is about 42% in patients with high-grade non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.  Its prevalence is not related to race or sex.  Malignancies associated with tumour lysis syndrome include (with their respective incidence shown):  non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (30%)  solid tumours (20%)  acute lymphocytic leukaemia (13%)  acute myeloid leukaemia (19%).  Tumour lysis syndrome has a mortality rate of 21%.  Certain factors increase the incidence of tumour lysis syndrome such as:  tumour burden  tumour with a high rate of proliferation  high sensitivity to chemotherapy  renal impairment.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 Aetiology  Tumour lysis syndrome is a result of the release of cellular contents when tumour cells break down, usually in response to chemotherapy and, very rarely, spontaneously. Some of the malignancies associated with tumour lysis syndrome are:  haematological malignancies such as acute leukaemia with high white blood cell count  lymphomas  other solid malignancies such as hepatoblastoma and neuroblastoma.  Apart from haematological malignancies, chemotherapy, radiotherapy surgery and ablation procedures may also lead to tumour lysis syndrome.  Tumour lysis syndrome is also associated with steroid administration, monoclonal antibodies and biologics:  bortezomib  thalidomide  paclitaxel  etoposide  zoledronic acid  hydroxyurea.  Rare causes include:  general anaesthesia in patients undergoing surgery  fever  pregnancy. Pathophysiology  A massive release of intracellular ions, such as phosphate and potassium, and products of proteins and nucleic acids into the bloodstream is responsible for the development of tumour lysis syndrome. This may result in:  hyperkalaemia  hyperuricaemia  hyperphosphataemia  hypocalcaemia (secondary to precipitation with phosphate)  raised urea and creatinine levels due to acute renal failure.  Hyperuricaemia causes crystallisation of uric acid in renal tubules that may result in obstructive uropathy.  Kidney ischaemia results because of vasoconstriction which is caused by scavenging of nitric oxide by uric acid (nitric oxide is a vasodilator as it relaxes the inner smooth muscles of blood vessels).  Uric acid also acts as an inflammatory agent and leads to the release of other pro-inflammatory cytokines such as protein I and tumour necrosis factor-alpha.  These cytokines are chemoattractants for white blood cells and cause renal injury.  Lysis of tumour cells causes a massive release of intracellular potassium ions.  Obstructive uropathy by uric acid deposition in renal tubules limits the excretion of potassium and results in hyperkalaemia. DR. JAM

This deposition occurs in the tubular epithelium and lamina, and also may involve the renal pelvis and calyces and the ureter, causing long-standing inflammation.  Increased breakdown of tumour cells also causes a massive release of phosphate ions in the bloodstream.  Obstructive uropathy limits the excretion of body solutes, such as phosphate, and results in hyperphosphataemia.  High serum levels of phosphate cause chelation of calcium ions, resulting in hypocalcaemia.  Hypocalcaemia causes arrhythmias, tetany and seizures.  Long-term urinary obstruction, due to deposition of urate crystals in the kidneys and ureter, also causes hydroureter, hydronephrosis and kidney failure. Pathophysiology of tumour lysis syndrome:  Clinical Presentation  History of weight loss.  Dyspnoea, orthopnoea and tachypnoea.  Dysuria, flank pain and haematuria.  Nausea, vomiting, seizure attacks, tetanic spasms and change in mental status.  Facial oedema.  Abdominal distension.  Palpitations.  Lethargy.  Metallic taste in the mouth.  Joint pain.  Pruritus.  Gangrene.  Differential Diagnosis  The differential diagnosis depends on the complications of tumour lysis syndrome.  Conditions that may result in hyperkalaemia include:  hypocalcaemia  congenital adrenal hyperplasia  digitalis toxicity

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  thermal burns.  Conditions that cause hyperphosphataemia include:  multiple myeloma  monoclonal antibody  vitamin D intoxication  pseudohypoparathyroidism  rhabdomyolysis.  Conditions that may result in hyperuricaemia include:  gout  pseudogout  hyperparathyroidism  hypothyroidism  alcoholic ketoacidosis  type 1 glycogen storage disease  haemolytic anaemia  uric acid nephropathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis will depend on a complete patient history and physical examination.  On physical examination, signs of hypercalcaemia include:  carpal spasm  pedal spasm  tetanus  Chvostek’s sign  Trousseau sign.  Other signs include:  muffled heart sounds  rales and rhonchi due to volume overload.  Certain investigations will also be done to determine the cause of tumour lysis syndrome, including:  full blood count – shows leukocytosis with anaemia and thrombocytopenia  serum uric acid – shows hyperuricaemia  serum electrolytes – shows hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia  renal function tests – shows increased creatinine levels  X-ray and computed tomography to locate an abdominal mass  electrocardiography – shows signs of hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia  blood urea nitrogen and lactate dehydrogenase – will be raised  urinalysis.  Management  Rapid expansion of intravascular volume: DR. JAM

 it is recommended to use crystalloids.  Intravascular fluid should be started 48 hours before initiation of chemotherapy.  Allopurinol:  this can decrease the production of uric acid; however, it is not helpful in the treatment of hyperuricaemia.  Recombinant urate oxidase:  this will treat hyperuricaemia associated with leukaemia and lymphoma.  Sodium bicarbonate for urine alkalinisation:  to increase the solubility of uric acid in the urine, 40–50 mEq/litre of sodium bicarbonate is administered.  Calcium:  calcium chloride, calcium resonium and calcium gluconate are administered to treat hypocalcaemia.  Haemodialysis:  this should be done for the treatment of life-threatening complications such as hyperkalaemia and hyperphosphataemia associated with acute kidney injury.  Febuxostat:  this is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, decreasing the production of uric acid. It provides better control of tumour lysis syndrome than allopurinol since it does not cause the hypersensitivity reaction linked to allopurinol.  Prognosis  Recombinant urate oxidase decreases the severity of tumour lysis syndrome.  The prognosis of tumour lysis syndrome depends on the underlying malignancy.  The mortality rate is 15% in patients with tumour lysis syndrome associated with haematological malignancies.  Solid tumours associated with tumour lysis syndrome also have a poor prognosis.  Other  Avoid gentamicin in patients with tumour lysis syndrome.  Avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and iodinated contrast.  To prevent tumour lysis syndrome, the following measures should be adopted:  adequate hydration at least three times/day before the start of chemotherapy is recommended  start xanthine oxidase inhibitors prophylactically  prophylactic administration of recombinant urate oxidase.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2 Venous Thrombosis Venous thrombosis is the thrombosis (formation of a blood clot) in the venous system, usually the deep venous system of the lower limb, and rarely the pelvis and the upper limb.  Overview Key Facts  Venous thrombosis is the thrombosis (formation of a blood clot) in the venous system, usually the deep venous system of the lower limb, and rarely the pelvis and the upper limb.  Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) may be classified as unprovoked or provoked by the presence of risk factors.  Diagnosis is usually clinical, based on history, clinical examination and confirmed by urgent venous ultrasound scan.  Immediate management with anticoagulant is required to prevent the incidence of venous thromboembolism (VTE) complications, such as pulmonary embolism (PE). Epidemiology  Incidence of clinically symptomatic VTE is approximately 1 to 2 per 1 000 population.  Approximately two-thirds are DVT and one third are pulmonary embolisms.  The incidence of VTE rises greatly in those who are critically ill, to nearer 40%. Aetiology  There is an increased risk of DVT associated with the following:  malignancy  smoking  age > 60 years  heart failure  severe infection  vasculitic disorders  obesity  thrombophilia  previous DVT.  Other factors which may temporarily increase the risk of DVT include:  immobility (eg surgery)  traumatic injury  hormone therapy especially oestrogen-contained therapy  pregnancy  post-partum period  dehydration. DR. JAM

Pathophysiology The risk factors are summarised by Virchow’s triad, these factors result in the formation of a clot within the deep venous system.  Blood flow stasis: ie immobility  Endothelial injury: ie surgical trauma  Hypercoagulability conditions: ie malignancy, thrombophilia, smoking. Virchow's triangle:  Clinical Presentation  Usually, patients present with:  unilateral leg swelling and pain  associated tenderness  skin colour changes  vein distention  occasionally mild pyrexia.  Presentation is rarely bilateral.  Many patients may be asymptomatic and DVT may only be discovered incidentally during clinical examination of patients with risk factors.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses for venous thrombosis are as follows:  cellulitis  complications of trauma to the limb  thrombophlebitis  acute limb ischaemia  heart failure  vasculitis

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  ruptured baker cyst  compartment syndrome  nephrotic syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Physical examination.  DVT Well’s score (to estimate the probability of the presence of a DVT).  D-dimer test.  Lower limb venous ultrasound.  Offer further investigation if a DVT seems unprovoked eg thrombophilia testing, investigation for intra-abdominal or pelvic cancer.
