 Management Pharmacological: (NICE)  Usually, treatment is continued for three months in provoked DVT cases and six months for unprovoked cases.  Initial treatment (continued for at least five days and until the INR is ≥ 2 for at least 24 hours)  treatment dose low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) or Fondaparinux  if severe renal impairment, then use unfractionated heparin: IV loading dose, followed by IN infusion and monitoring of clotting.  Oral anticoagulant started at the same time, once levels of this are therapeutic, ie INR 2–3 can stop low molecular weight heparin.  If there is recurrence, target INR should be increased to 3.5. Surgical  Thrombolysis or surgical thrombectomy is reserved for severe thrombosis with associated venous gangrene.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Prophylaxis  DVT prophylaxis is more effective than treatment in identified high-risk groups and should be considered in all patients who are hospitalised or admitted for surgery.  Types of thromboprophylaxis include:  mechanical (early mobilisation of inpatients)  TED stocking, pneumatic compression boots  pharmacological (heparin).  Prognosis  The major complication of DVT is death secondary to pulmonary embolism.  Other complications include:  post-thrombotic syndrome: chronic venous hypertension  limb pain  swelling  hyperpigmentation  dermatitis DR. JAM

 ulcers  venous gangrene  lipodermatosclerosis  bleeding secondary to the treatment of DVT. Von Willebrand Disease Von Willebrand disease is a genetic bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor, a protein that plays a crucial role in blood clotting, leading to prolonged bleeding and easy bruising.  Overview Key Facts  Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most common inherited coagulation disorder.  vWD occurs due to a deficiency of von Willebrand factor (vWF).  Most patients have type I vWD where there is decreased concentration of VWF. It is often inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder.  It usually presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (eg nosebleeds) or excessive bleeding from minor wounds, although many patients may be asymptomatic.  Management depends on the severity and type of vWD.  It is usually a mild condition with an excellent prognosis. Epidemiology  Incidence – up to 1% in the general population.  Inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder.  Equally as common in men and women but due to the prominent symptom of menorrhagia, more women are likely to be diagnosed.  A clear family history is not always evident as there may be incomplete penetrance and variable expression.  Type I is the most common form; accounting for 75% of cases.  The severe type III accounts for just 5%, the remainder being type II. Aetiology  Due to a mutation in the von Willebrand factor (vWF) gene.  Genetic and environmental factors that can affect vWF levels include age, blood type, thyroid status, inflammation and stress.  Rarely, patients can develop acquired von Willebrand syndrome (avWS) – most frequently associated with lymphoproliferative disorders. Pathophysiology  vWD is caused by a quantitative or qualitative defect of vWF.

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  vWF is a protein made in endothelial cells and megakaryocytes.  It mediates platelet aggregation and adhesion to exposed subendothelium at sites of vascular injury.  It also binds and stabilises coagulation factor VIII.  Patient with vWD will have symptoms characteristic of platelet dysfunction (mostly mucosal bleeding).  Clinical Presentation  Typically presents with bruising and/or mild-to-moderate mucocutaneous bleeding:  nosebleeds  menorrhagia (women with vWD are five times more likely to suffer from this than women without the condition)  prolonged bleeding after surgical incisions or dental procedures.  Severity of bleeding symptoms correlates with a reduction in the function of VWF.  In type III, factor VIII is also severely decreased; these patients may experience more severe bleeding:  joint bleeding  recurrent gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding.  There are many patients with vWD who will have very mild disease and never need to seek medical attention.  In those with mild disease, the concurrent use of aspirin or NSAIDs can precipitate bleeding that might not have occurred otherwise.  Differential Diagnosis  The differential diagnoses include a number of inherited or acquired bleeding disorders, for example:  haemophilia A – inherited deficiency of coagulation factor VIII; usually, bleeding is severe and it presents early in life  platelet function disorders:  Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia – rare but severe platelet disorder  Bernard–Soulier syndrome (BSS) – rare disorder, with thrombocytopenia and giant platelet cells  in the laboratory, platelet aggregation would be abnormal in these conditions.  Diagnosis/Investigation  vWD should be considered in the following patients:  increased bleeding – especially mucocutaneous  positive family history of vWD  mild thrombocytopenia  mild prolongation of activated partial thromboplastin time (aPPT) (not explained otherwise).  These patients should be investigated: DR. JAM

 full blood count (FBC) – usually normal, with normal platelets (those with type II may have mild thrombocytopenia)  activated partial thromboplastin time (aPPT) – usually normal, or mildly prolonged  vWD screening tests:  vWF antigen (quantitative measurement of protein level – diagnostic if < 0.3 IU)  vWF activity (functional assays)  factor VIII activity.  Diagnosis is based on both clinical (symptoms and family history) and laboratory findings.  There is no definitive genetic testing to identify type I vWD.  Management Pharmacological:  The treatment approach varies according to the type of vWD.  If patients are asymptomatic, treatment is usually not required.  Patients with active severe haemorrhage should be resuscitated appropriately, and also receive vWD-specific treatments.  Patients should be cared for in collaboration with a haematologist.  Type I vWD:  all patients should be trialled on desmopressin (DDAVP) unless contraindicated  desmopressin results in the release of vWF and factor VIII from endothelial stores  in those undergoing surgery, a vWF-containing concentrate should be used  antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid) can be used in addition – both prophylactically or therapeutically.  Type II vWD:  desmopressin is usually ineffective but should still be trialled  most surgical procedures and bleeding refractory to antifibrinolytics will require vWF-containing concentrate.  Type III vWD:  patients will require treatment with vWF-containing concentrates  most vWF-containing concentrates contain both vWF and factor VIII  for elective surgery, treatment with vWF concentrate should start at least 8 hours before the procedure.  First-line treatment for those with menorrhagia is oral hormonal agents:  the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) and progesterone-only pill (POP) usually decrease menstrual blood flow

MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  benefits of hormonal treatment should be weighed against potential risks  tranexamic acid can also be used  desmopressin nasal spray is an alternative to the above  intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) – evidence for use in vWD is sparse but it is known to reduce menstrual bleeding.  Those with vWD should avoid the use of medicines that interfere with platelet function.  In those with chronic blood loss, iron stores should be assessed regularly and iron deficiency treated with iron replacement.  Prognosis  Most patients will require intermittent acute treatment for bleeding throughout their life.  Patients usually respond well to treatment. Warfarin Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist used for anticoagulation as prophylaxis or treatment.  Overview Key Facts  Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist used for anticoagulation as prophylaxis or treatment.  Anticoagulants are usually initiated in secondary care, a dedicated clinic in a hospital, or an outreach clinic in primary care.  Warfarin acts by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) as well as the anticoagulant proteins C and S.  Clinical Uses/Dosing  Warfarin is licensed for:  prophylaxis of systemic embolism in people with rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation  prophylaxis after insertion of prosthetic heart valves  prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism  transient attacks of cerebral ischaemia (TIA).  Dosing:  initially 5–10 mg taken on day one  subsequent doses dependent on international normalised ratio (INR)  lower induction dose can be given over 3–4 weeks for patients not requiring rapid anticoagulation (eg in atrial fibrillation) DR. JAM

 a lower induction dose (5 mg) can be given to: elderly patients, people with low body weight, liver disease, cardiac failure or high bleed risk (maintenance 3–9 mg).  doses should be taken at the same time each day. Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) and Pulmonary Embolism (PE):  Duration of treatment will vary for each patient but warfarin should usually be continued for at least:  six weeks in distal DVT  three months in proximal DVT or PE with known temporary risk factors and low risk of recurrence  six months in proximal DVT of unknown cause  long-term treatment in recurrent DVTs/PE. Atrial Fibrillation or Prosthetic Heart Valves:  Warfarin treatment is usually long term.  Monitoring  Base-line prothrombin time should be determined.  In early treatment, patients should have INR monitoring daily/on alternate days.  Once INR is stable and within range (usually 2.0–3.0), monitoring intervals can be increased twice weekly for 1–2 weeks.  INR should be measured at least every 12 weeks once stable.  Cautions  Women of child-bearing age should be warned about the danger of teratogenicity.  Patients with recent haemorrhage/high bleeding risk. MIL ALRAJHI Hematology part 2  Contraindications  Haemorrhagic stroke.  Clinically significant bleeding.  < 72 hours of major surgery with severe bleed risk.  < 48 hours post-partum.  Pregnancy – teratogenic.  Bleeding disorders (eg thrombocytopenia, haemophilia, liver failure or renal failure).  Potential bleeding lesions (recent trauma, ulcers, biopsy etc).  Interactions  The effect of warfarin can be reduced or abolished by vitamin K, including that found in health foods, food supplements, enteral feeds, or large amounts of some green vegetables or green tea.  Major changes in diet (especially involving salads and vegetables) and in alcohol consumption can affect anticoagulant control.  Pomegranate juice increases the INR in response to warfarin.  Side-effects  Common/very common:  haemorrhage – 2–4% annual risk of heavy bleed requiring transfusion.  Rare/very rare:  alopecia  nausea  vomiting.  Management ght Novel Oral Anticoagulant (NOAC) Rivaroxaban Edoxaban Apixaban Dabigatran III bits Inhibit activated factor Xa Direct thrombin inhibitor rgan May be asymptomatic Signs/symptoms: haemorrhage into any organ bruising May be asymptomatic Signs/symptoms: haemorrhage into any organ DR. stem: A 63-year-old man is admitted to Accident and Emergency with a 5-day history of vomiting, diarrhoea and bloody stools. The diarrhoea and vomiting stopped 2 days ago, but he noticed his abdomen was distended and had constant colicky pain. He also complains of dyspnoea on minimal exertion and increasing urinary frequency, with small volumes of urine. Apart from attending a wedding reception a week ago, he has only eaten home- made food. He has hypertension and gout and takes an ACE inhibitor, calcium-channel blocker, allopurinol and a statin. He is a nonsmoker but enjoys a bottle of red wine at weekends. On examination, he is pale and slightly agitated. His temperature is 37.1 °C, pulse 96 regular, BP 142/92 mmHg. His respirations are 24 breaths/min at rest and his saturations are 96% on room air. His heart sounds are normal but basal crackles can be heard on chest examination. His abdomen is distended and tympanic, mildly tender and bowel sounds are reduced. Rectal examination reveals a brown stool. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 98 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 28.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 x 109/l PLT 65 × 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Sodium (Na+) 130 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K+) 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 284 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 40.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Albumin 12 g/l 35–55 g/l Bilirubin 100 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 60 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ALP 61 IU/l 30–130 IU/l MCV 91 ﬂ 80–100 ﬂ LDH 1240 U/l 100–190 IU/l CRP 354 mg/l < 10 mg/l The blood ﬁlm shows schistocytes and burr cells. Chest X-ray reveals alveolar shadowing at both bases, with small bilateral pleural effusions. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
C Haemolytic–uraemic syndrome HUS is characterised by the triad of micro-angiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney disease. Typically, HUS occurs after a prodrome of diarrhoea. In adults, HUS is usually caused by the enterohaemorrhagic serotypes of Escherichia coli, especially E. coli O157:H7. The source of the infection is usually contaminated beef, poultry or cider, although faecal-tohand transmission can occur. HUS is associated with: malignant hypertension; infection (e.g. E. coli, Shigella spp, HIV); vasculitis; radiation nephritis; collagen vascular diseases (e.g. scleroderma); cryoglobulinaemia; malignancy, mainly adenocarcinoma; drugs (e.g. oral contraceptive therapy, chemotherapy, ciclosporin); bone marrow transplantation; eclampsia; and postpartum acute kidney disease. Uraemia cannot explain all the haematological ﬁndings in this case, particularly the presence of schistocytes and burr cells on the blood ﬁlm. These indications of micro-angiopathic anaemia suggest red cell trauma due to ﬁbrin deposition in the microvasculature. When thrombotic micro-angiopathy involves the kidneys, thrombosis of glomerular capillaries and renal arterioles can lead to kidney disease. In the severe form of the disease, bilateral cortical necrosis and irreversible kidney disease may occur. Plasmapheresis with fresh-frozen plasma as the replacement ﬂuid is the current treatment of choice. Renal replacement therapy might also be required. Some patients can have atypical HUS. This is an extremely rare, progressive and potentially life-threatening condition seen in both children and adults and which often (70%) has a genetic component. It can also be referred to as diarrhoea-negative HUS. It is commonly caused by mutations in the complement regulatory proteins causing a chronic, uncontrolled activation of the complement system leading to systemic thrombotic micro-angiopathy which ultimately causes sudden or progressive damage to vital organs. Historically, approximately 40% of patients died or developed chronic kidney disease following their ﬁrst episode of atypical HUS. Subsequent episodes led to 65% of patients dying, requiring dialysis or suffering long-term renal damage in spite of plasma exchange. More recently, eculizumab has been used in patients with atypical HUS. Eculizumab is a human monoclonal antibody, produced from murine myeloma cells, that binds to complement C5 and blocks pro-thrombotic and pro-inﬂammatory processes. It has been found to improve renal function, reduce thrombotic microangiopathic activity and improve patient quality of life, although there is a lack of randomised controlled trials. A Crohn’s colitis Crohn’s usually presents in 15–25-year-olds, although there is a second peak at around 55–70 years. As in this patient’s case, the presentation is one of severe diarrhoea and abdominal tenderness with distension. Patients often also suffer with perianal ﬁstulae and mouth ulcers. This patient is unlikely to have Crohn’s disease as the diarrhoea lasted only 48 h and also, after this point, the patient noted increased urinary frequency. If the patient had Crohn’s colitis, you would expect ongoing diarrhoea (possibly bloods) with

acute kidney disease as a result of ﬂuid depletion secondary to diarrhoea. B Gastroenteritis You may have considered gastroenteritis as a possible diagnosis given the history of a recent meal out with subsequent diarrhoea lasting 24–48 h. However, gastroenteritis would not explain the subsequent increase in urinary frequency. D Polyarteritis nodosa PAN is a necrotising arteritis of small and/or medium vessels without glomerulonephritis. Patients often present with skin lesions, mononeuritis multiplex and involvement of the GI tract, heart, central nervous system and kidneys, as well as myalgia. Bloods show a hypergammaglobulinaemia, leucocytosis and raised neutrophil count. The mainstay of treatment is with corticosteroids. This patient is unlikely to have PAN as you would expect a raised protein level, and although GI and renal symptoms can be present, these are less common compared to the incidence in other diseases. E Legionella pneumonia If the patient had a Legionella pneumonia you would expect them to have a cough and fevers in addition to the hyponatraemia, auscultation ﬁndings and dyspnoea. This also doesn’t fully explain his abdominal ﬁndings or bloody diarrhoea. Legionella pneumonia could be on your differentials but is not a unifying diagnosis for this patient’s ﬁndings.

stem: A man aged 62 years is referred to the Haematology Clinic for review. He received a routine blood screen from his general practitioner (GP) that revealed a raised ESR (85 mm/h) and a raised immunoglobulin G (IgG) paraprotein band (1.9 g/l). No urinary light chain excretion was detected. Three years later, he remains well; however, he still has an increased ESR and IgG paraprotein band, though there is still no urinary light chain excretion. Which of the following diagnoses ﬁt best with this clinical picture?
explanation: B Monoclonal gammopathy of unknown signiﬁcance (MGUS) MGUS occurs in older people and is characterised by the presence of a paraprotein band (immunoglobulin G [IgG] <20 g/l). Patients may be asymptomatic and the condition discovered by chance. Blood count is usually normal, and there is no renal dysfunction. No speciﬁc treatment is required. Around 1% of patients with MGUS may progress to myeloma annually. In many patients with disease progression, immunoglobulin (Ig) gene rearrangement can be detected in B lymphocytes before the appearance of myeloma. This suggests that MGUS is a clonal, pre-malignant condition. C Myeloma There is no light chain excretion in the urine that would conﬁrm the diagnosis of myeloma, and no organ involvement (e.g. bone, liver, spleen). A Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinaemia This is one of the malignant monoclonal gammopathies and is a chronic, indolent, lymphoproliferative disorder. It is characterised by the presence of a high level of a macroglobulin (immunoglobulin M [IgM]), elevated serum viscosity and the presence of a lymphoplasmacytic inﬁltrate in the bone marrow. D B-cell lymphoma Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a collective term for a heterogeneous group of lymphoproliferative malignancies with differing patterns of behaviour and responses to treatment. Most NHLs (80–85%) are of B-cell origin. There is no distinct paraprotein in the serum electrophoresis, but there may be a diffuse increase in the IgG region. E Chronic myeloid leukaemia Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML), also known as chronic myeloid leukaemia, is a myeloproliferative disorder characterised by increased proliferation of the granulocytic cell line without the loss of their capacity to differentiate. It accounts for 20% of all leukaemias affecting adults. Again, there is no distinct paraprotein band on the serum protein electrophoresis and the natural history is not indolent.
